This page features a decorative **marbled paper** <term>marbled paper: a technique used in bookbinding to create patterns that resemble marble or other stone by floating pigments on a liquid surface and transferring them to paper.</term> pattern, which serves as the **endpaper** <note>The paper at the beginning or end of a book that is partially pasted to the inside of the cover to hide the binding construction.</note> of the volume. 

The design is composed of organic, "stone" or "shell" shaped spots in shades of olive green, reddish-brown, and cream. These colorful shapes are set against a dark, near-black background and are interconnected by thin, energetic veins of yellow and white. 

Along the right edge, a small portion of the book's leather binding is visible. It is adorned with a fine **gold-tooled** <term>gold-tooling: the process of decorating a book's leather cover by pressing heated metal tools into the surface through a thin layer of gold leaf.</term> border, featuring a delicate, lace-like pattern.

# The Heart of Philosophy
### Translated from Latin into French at the request of Philip the Fair <note>King Philip IV (1268–1314), whose reign was marked by the translation of many scholarly works from Latin into the common tongue to make knowledge accessible to the court.</note>, King of France. Newly printed in Paris.

<image-desc>A large woodcut printer's mark featuring two lions <term>rampant</term> <note>A heraldic term meaning the animals are shown standing on one hind leg with their forepaws raised.</note> supporting a shield. The shield contains a fleur-de-lis <note>The stylized lily that served as the royal emblem of France.</note> and the initials "I P" <note>Standing for the printer, Jehan Petit.</note>. Above the shield is an intricate knot design entwined with foliage. Below the lions, a banner reads "JEHAN PETIT".</image-desc>

### These are sold in Paris on Great Saint-Jacques Street at the sign of the Golden Fleur-de-lis. <note>Rue Saint-Jacques was the heart of the Parisian book trade during the Renaissance; "signs" were used to identify shops before the use of street numbers.</note>

# The Prologue
aa ii

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a scholar or scribe in a medieval study. The man is seated at a high-backed wooden chair, writing in a large book resting on a slanted desk. The room features a tiled floor, a window with leaded glass panes, and various scholarly tools including a revolving bookstand holding an open volume, inkwells, and shelves containing books and scrolls. A cupboard or doorway is visible in the background to the right.</image-desc>

Those who in times past applied themselves to the task of making and composing various books, in both prose and rhyme, won the favor of kings, dukes, counts, and princes. And they were accustomed to record and give an account at the head of their books the names of those for whom they produced them, in order to better please their said lords and masters: 

Just as was the <term>romance</term> <note>original: "romant"; a long narrative about knightly adventures, typically written in the common language rather than Latin.</note> of Perceval the Welshman, which bears the title of his name, and named him the "Welshman" who was a knight of <term>Troy</term> <note>original: "Troye"; while this may refer to the ancient city of Troy, it likely refers to the city of Troyes in France, which was a major center for chivalric literature and the home of Chrétien de Troyes.</note> and of Flanders. Likewise, there was made the Romance of the great King Alexander, of his deeds and <term>valiant acts</term> <note>original: "vaillantises"</note> and feats of prowess, and of his master Aristotle, who instructed him so well and taught him several sciences, which later served him well and brought him renown throughout the whole world: 

Wherefore, by comparison to the Romance made of his deeds, there is no value in being ashamed or hesitant to put into writing the deeds of virtuous men who have performed...

<summary>This prologue introduces the work by appealing to the literary tradition of "Romances," citing the importance of recording the lives of great figures like Perceval and Alexander the Great. It highlights the role of scholarly instruction and the custom of dedicating books to noble patrons to preserve the memory of virtuous deeds.</summary>
<keywords>prologue, chivalry, Alexander the Great, Aristotle, Perceval the Welshman, patronage, biography, medieval literature</keywords>

# The Prologue

...to put into writing their good and sumptuous doctrines; not because those who made them and took marvelous pains to wake night and day did so for vain glory, or to receive favor, or for the hope of acquiring any earthly goods: but only to keep a memory of their good and profitable doctrines, prowess, and honorable sciences that they performed and taught—as Tymeo <note>Tymeo refers to Timaeus, a character from Plato's dialogues, often portrayed in the Middle Ages as a master of natural philosophy.</note> did for Placides, about whom this present book is made and constituted—almost as an amateur and zealot of all science and all philosophy, and of every good deed; not being ungrateful for his knowledge, but wanting to liberally show and teach it to all those who desire to acquire and know science to first serve God, and to honor and govern themselves in this world according to justice and perfect wisdom, to acquire everlasting grace for body and soul. **¶ And for this, my sovereign lord Philip the Fair, King of France, after your command, I have translated this present book to your honor and for the profit and utility of all creatures: For in the said book one may learn and know several teachings: That is to say, you will find in this book named the "Heart of Philosophy" several inquiries and questions from Placides to the philosopher Tymeo, and the answers contained therein.** Likewise, there is the treatise of the <term>sphere of the world</term> <note>original: "espere du monde"; the medieval model of the universe consisting of concentric celestial spheres.</note>, of the <term>computus</term> <note>original: "compost"; a technical manual used to calculate the dates of the religious calendar, such as Easter.</note> and Calendar, all illustrated. In order to instruct and teach several people to know how they should govern themselves throughout the year according to the commandment of our mother Holy Church, concerning the course of the sun and the moon, fixed and movable feasts, and other celebrations. Of the <term>leap of the moon</term> <note>original: "sault de la lune"; a calculation used to reconcile the lunar and solar calendars.</note> and the <term>leap year</term> <note>original: "bissexte".</note>. And I have also made and translated this book not to have or acquire glory or praise, for I have had no care for vain praise or glory during my life—

**¶ But I have clearly proven it when I translated from Latin into French the material sphere and the calculation of the <term>computus</term> <note>original: "compost"</note> by meters and by verses, by tables and by the <term>hand-reckoning</term> <note>original: "les mains"; referring to the "computus manualis," a mnemonic system using the joints of the hand to calculate dates.</note> that I have placed and illustrated herein; and I did not do it for glory, nor for wealth, nor for any earthly gift: For never in my life did I take account of flattery, nor of envy, nor of earthly honor: For all is but a vain and broken thing, and we see that each day in a single movement man passes from this world to the other and loses the flower and glory of the world: for all this is like the flower of the hay which is green today and dry tomorrow; and considering this, while fleeing idleness in my simple youth, I took very great pleasure in putting this book here from Latin into French: and because the old age of man is always of good counsel and we follow their good deeds, I have wished, for the honor of you, my said lord, to put this present book from Latin into French. I will first put the table of the questions asked by Placides to Tymeo in order, and the answers of the same, and on which leaf they are located. Afterward, I will put the table of the illustrated sphere of the heaven and the world, and of the order of the world, and then the table of the <term>computus</term> <note>original: "compost"</note> and Calendar, and the practice of it so that everyone may know and understand it.**

<summary>The translator concludes his dedication to King Philip the Fair, explaining that he translated the work from Latin into French to provide a useful guide to philosophy, astronomy, and the church calendar. He emphasizes that the work was undertaken for the public good and the service of God rather than for personal glory or earthly reward.</summary>
<keywords>Philip the Fair, Tymeo, Placides, Cœur de Philosophie, Computus, Sphere of the World, astronomy, church calendar, Latin to French translation</keywords>

### ¶ Here begins the table of this present book.

I, the translator, have placed at the beginning of this book what philosophy is, and how it is defined in Greek and in Latin. Folio 1.

Then I have followed with how kings and great lords should entrust their children to the study of wise clerks. f. 1.

How Placides was entrusted to the philosopher Tymeo to be taught, and concerning the question that Placides asked Tymeo: why he had received him sooner than he had the Emperor’s son. Folio 1.

How, afterward, Placides asked his master what <term>natural folly</term> <note>In a medieval context, this usually refers to an innate lack of reason or a natural intellectual disability.</note> is. And of the response that his master gave him. Folio 2.

Following this, it speaks of the triumph of kings, and what is meant by the royal scepter. f. 2.

How Alexander the Great embraced his master Aristotle. Folio 3.

How Tymeo reproves Placides for being so bold as to ask questions. f. 3.

# The Figure of the Armillary Sphere

->**A representation of the celestial machine and the movements of the heavens.**<-

<note>This woodcut illustration serves as a visual aid for the text. It depicts an armillary sphere—a physical model used by scholars to visualize the Great Circles of the heavens and the position of the Earth in the cosmos.</note>

### The Components of the Sphere

The sphere consists of several interlocking rings that represent the primary astronomical markers:

*   **The Zodiac (Ecliptic):** The wide diagonal band crossing the center. It is marked with the twelve signs through which the sun appears to travel throughout the year:
    *   **The Twins** (Gemini ♊︎)
    *   **The Bull** (Taurus ♉︎)
    *   **The Ram** (Aries ♈︎)
    *   **The Fishes** (Pisces ♓︎)
    *   **The Water-Bearer** (Aquarius ♒︎)
    *   **The Sea-Goat** (Capricorn ♑︎)
    *   **The Archer** (Sagittarius ♐︎)
    *   **The Scorpion** (Scorpio ♏︎)
    *   **The Scales** (Libra ♎︎)
    *   **The Virgin** (Virgo ♍︎)
    <note>The remaining signs, Leo and Cancer, are likely on the side of the sphere hidden from the viewer's perspective.</note>
*   **The Celestial Equator:** The central horizontal ring dividing the sphere into northern and southern halves.
*   **The Tropics:** The rings positioned above and below the equator, representing the limits of the sun's path.
*   **The Meridian:** The large vertical ring that encompasses the entire framework.
*   **The Earth:** Represented by the small dark orb at the very center of the rings, following the geocentric model where the universe revolves around us.

->*A hand emerges from the clouds to hold the handle of the universe, signifying divine order.*<-

# The Heart of the Secrets of Philosophy.

Here we must know that philosophy is the love of wisdom: for "philosophy" is a Greek word and is composed of two Greek names; one is *philos* <note>original: "philos"</note> which means as much as "love," the other is *sophos* <note>original: "sophos"</note> which means as much as "wisdom" in Latin. Therefore, a philosopher is a lover of wisdom. These are and were the masters who valued nothing on earth except knowledge. And these were such men as we shall tell you in the text without further preamble.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'J' featuring floral and foliate motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Once there was a time when those who were first wise held the power, the prize, and the lordship over all things: for there was never a time when force was worth as much as <term>sense</term> <note>In this context, "sense" (sens) implies wisdom, intellect, and moral direction.</note> on earth—that is to say, among the creatures under God. For God’s sense is force—that is, a righteous force—and God’s force is sense; I shall not speak of that force at all, nor of God's secrets, for no one but Him should meddle in them. And for this reason, **Cato of Rome** <note>Referring to Dionysius Cato, the purported author of the *Distichs of Cato*, a collection of moral advice very popular in the Middle Ages.</note> says: "Leave off inquiring into what the secrets of God are; and since you are mortal, occupy yourself with inquiring into and taking care of those things which are mortal." And although sometimes [force] might be valued as wisdom by the judgment of men, it was never worth as much: for the strong and foolish must always perish, while the weak and wise must thrive. And therefore, success is better than destruction. It is true, then, that wisdom is worth more than force; this is as clear as day, to be understood simply as we shall show more clearly hereafter. 

But whoever could find wisdom and force together would so embellish and improve the one by the other that nothing should prevail against those two things. And for this reason, the ancients thought to have both. The high-born men of the ancient life gave their children to be raised by philosophers to learn wisdom and sense; and the philosophers were themselves armed, feared, prized, and honored, even though they did not wish to uncover or reveal the **secrets of nature** to the laity for many good reasons that we shall state hereafter. And this is because most of the secrets of the philosophers concern nature. If one told everyone their own nature, there are some who would be the worse for it, and some would become prideful: the foolish and those of a bad <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval science, "complexion" referred to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, choler, and melancholy) which determined a person's physical health and character.</note> would be the worse for it, and those of a good complexion would grow proud. 

Because of this, it happened that an Empress wished to give one of her sons to be taught by a philosopher, which philosopher was named **Timaeus**; and this Timaeus did not wish to receive him because he was foolish by nature, by virtue of his complexion. And a King gave to this same Timaeus his son, who was a beautiful youth, noble, wise, and of good complexion; and the philosopher received him willingly and loved him dearly, and took great pains to teach him, as we shall tell you hereafter. Many people wondered why the philosopher had sooner received the son of a minor king than the son of a great emperor: but Timaeus did not tell everyone. But it so happened that the young king's son, who was named **Placides**, questioned his master and said to him:

# The Heart of the Secrets of Philosophy. Folio 1.

->A i<-

Here we must know that philosophy is the love of wisdom: for "philosophy" is a Greek word composed of two Greek names; one is *philos*, which means as much as "love," and the other is *sophos*, which means as much as "wisdom" in Latin <note>original: "sapience en latin"</note>. Therefore, a philosopher is a lover of wisdom. These are and were the masters who held nothing on earth dear except for knowledge. And these were such as we shall describe to you in the text without a rubric <note>rubric: a heading or introductory instruction, often written in red ink to stand out from the black text</note>.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'J' featuring floral and foliate motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

**J**adis—Long ago—there was a time when those who were first wise held the power, the prize, and the lordship over everything: for there was never any time that force was worth as much as wisdom <term>sens: wisdom, good sense, or mental faculty</term> on earth; that is to say, among the creatures under God. For God's wisdom is force—it is a righteous force—and God's force is wisdom. I shall not speak of that force at all, nor of the secrets of God; no one but He should involve themselves in such things. And for this reason, Cato of Rome <note>referring to the *Distichs of Cato*, a popular medieval collection of moral advice</note> says: "Cease to inquire what the secrets of God are; and since you are mortal, concern yourself with inquiring into and taking care of things that are mortal." And although force was sometimes prized by the judgment of men as if it were wisdom, it was never worth as much: for the strong and foolish must always perish, while the weak and wise must succeed <term>cheuir: to manage, survive, or achieve a successful end</term>. Therefore, success is better than destruction. It is true, then, that wisdom is worth more than force; this is as clear as day, as we shall show more clearly hereafter. But if one could find wisdom and force together, the one would so embellish and improve the other that nothing should prevail against those two things. 

And for this reason, the ancients thought to have both. The great men of the ancient life gave their children to be raised by philosophers to learn wisdom and sense; and so the philosophers were armed, feared, prized, and honored, even though they did not wish to reveal the <insert>secrets of nature</insert> to the laity <note>laicz: laypeople, or those outside the scholarly and clerical world</note> for many good reasons that we will state hereafter. And this is because most of the secrets of the philosophers concern nature. If one were to tell everyone about their own nature, there are some who would be the worse for it, and some would become proud: the fool and those of bad <term>complexion: in medieval medicine, the balance of humors—blood, phlegm, choler, and melancholy—that determined a person's physical and mental character</term> would be worse off, and those of good complexion would grow proud. 

Because of this, it happened that an empress wanted to give one of her sons to a philosopher to be taught; this philosopher was named **Tymeo** <note>Timaeus</note>. And this Tymeo did not want to receive him because the boy was a fool by nature, by the force of his complexion. But a king gave his son to this same Tymeo, and the boy was a handsome youth, noble, wise, and of good complexion; the philosopher received him willingly and loved him dearly, and took great pains to teach him, as we will tell you hereafter. Many people wondered why the philosopher had sooner received the son of a petty king than the son of a great emperor, but Tymeo did not tell everyone his reason. Eventually, it happened that the king’s young son, who was named **Placides** <note>Placidus</note>, questioned his master and said to him:

# The Heart of the Secrets of Philosophy. Leaf 1.

->A i<-

Here we must know that **philosophy** is the love of wisdom: for "philosophy" is a Greek word and is composed of two Greek names/ the one is *philos* which is the same as saying **love**/ the other is *sophos* which is the same as saying **wisdom** <note>The original text notes "sapience en latin," referring to the Latin *sapientia* as the equivalent of the Greek *sophos*</note>. Therefore, a philosopher is a lover of wisdom. These are and were the masters who value nothing on earth except knowledge. And these men were such as we shall describe to you in the text without further preamble.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'J' featuring floral and foliate motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

**J**ust as there was once a time when those who were first wise held the power, the prize, and the lordship over all: for there was never a time when force was worth as much as **wisdom** <note>original: *sens*—referring to good sense, intelligence, or wisdom</note> on earth/ that is to say, among the creatures under God: for the wisdom of God is force/ it is a righteous force/ and the force of God is wisdom/ and of that force I shall not speak/ nor of the secrets of God/ for no one but Him should interfere with them/ and for this reason **Cato of Rome** <note>Referring to the *Distichs of Cato*, a popular medieval schoolbook of proverbs</note> says: "Leave off inquiring what the secrets of God are/ and since you are mortal, occupy yourself with inquiring and caring for things that are mortal." And although sometimes wisdom was valued by the judgment of men, it never was worth as much as it should be: for one must always cherish the strong man who is foolish only a little, and the weak man who is wise. And thus resourcefulness is better than destruction. It is true then that wisdom is worth more than force/ this is as clear as day/ to be understood simply as we shall show more clearly hereafter: but he who could find wisdom and force together would so embellish and improve the one with the other that against these two things nothing would be of any value.

And for this reason, the ancients thought to have both. And the high-ranking men of the ancient life gave their children to be raised by philosophers to learn wisdom and sense/ and so the philosophers were loved, feared, prized, and honored/ even though they did not wish to disclose or reveal the secrets of nature to the **laity** <note>original: *laicz*—the uneducated or those outside the clerical/scholarly class</note> for many good reasons that we shall state hereafter. And for this very reason, most of the secrets of the philosophers concern nature. And if one told everyone their nature, there are some who would be the worse for it/ and some would grow proud: the foolish man and the one of **bad temperament** <term>complexion: The medieval medical theory that a person's physical and mental character was determined by the balance of the four humors</term> would be the worse for it, and the one of good temperament would become proud.

Because of this, it happened that an Empress wished to give one of her sons to be taught by a philosopher/ which philosopher was named **Tymeo** <note>Likely referring to Timaeus, a character from Plato's dialogues often treated as a historical figure in the Middle Ages</note>/ and this Tymeo did not wish to receive him because he was a fool by nature, by force of his temperament. And a King gave to this same Tymeo his son, who was a handsome youth and noble and wise and of good temperament/ and the philosopher received him willingly and loved him greatly/ and took great pains to teach him as we shall tell you hereafter. Many people wondered why the philosopher had sooner received the son of a minor king than the son of a great emperor: but Tymeo did not tell this to everyone: but it so happened that the young son of the king, who was named **Placides**, questioned his master and said to him:

The Heart of Secrets

### This is the illustration of the king’s son as he speaks to his master about the emperor’s son.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting three figures. In the center, a seated master or scholar in robes and a hood gestures with his hand. To the left, a standing man in a long tunic addresses him. To the right, another standing man, possibly a traveler or servant holding a staff, looks on. "Master," said Placides to Tymeo, "tell me, for I wonder greatly why, in your mercy, you found me more receptive <term>solutif</term> <note>original: *solutif* — in this context, it means amenable or ready to absorb instruction</note> to your teaching than the emperor’s son." "Because," said the philosopher, "one should not give precious stones to swine, for they would prefer filth. And he who speaks and teaches wisdom <term>sapience</term> to fools gives precious stones to swine. For the fool is like the rooster who finds a sapphire; he feels it is hard and cannot bite it or make use of it, so he would rather have found a rotten pea or a grain of wheat than a fine sapphire, no matter how great a fortune it is worth."

Likewise, the fool would prefer a piece of cheese; or a fool would sooner speak some mockery than something good or of sound sense. And the emperor’s son is a fool, so I did not wish to admit him to my teaching. "Oh, master," said Placides, "it seems to me that the more foolish he is, the greater his need for instruction."

Tymeo replied: "Placides, you know well that it is true that if someone sows wheat or any good seed, when some of the grains fall upon a hard rock or a paved path, the birds eat them or they rot and die without bearing fruit or multiplying. But when it falls on good soil, it multiplies and bears fruit. And therefore, no one should sow in a place where the seed would be lost, but rather in a place where it can multiply. 

And I tell you that teaching is the seed of wisdom in the heart of a wise man. But the fool has a heart like a hard stone, upon which no seed can take root or be nourished; for in the heart of a fool who is a fool by nature, the seed of wisdom cannot take hold. And when someone possesses a clear natural intellect <term>cler sens naturel</term>, he is like good wheat-bearing soil that needs nothing but good seed. And he who puts good seed there, grain grows and multiplies. For this reason, one must sow in such places where the seed is well-used—that is to say, to teach those who are naturally wise and not those who are natural fools <term>folz naturelz</term> <note>The "natural fool" was a common medieval classification for someone born without the capacity for reason, distinguishing them from those who simply act unwisely.</note>. And the emperor’s son is a natural fool, and you are wise; therefore, I would rather teach you than him. For in him, wisdom could not bear fruit, as I have told you. Thus I could gain neither sense nor honor through him, but in you, I could. And for this reason, I did so."

<summary>In this dialogue, Tymeo explains to his student Placides that wisdom should only be taught to those capable of receiving it, using the biblical parable of the sower and the metaphor of the rooster and the jewel to justify excluding the "naturally foolish" emperor's son.</summary>

# On Philosophy. Leaf ii.

**A ii**

**M**aster," said Placides to Tymeo, "by your grace, you are my master and so you ought to guide and teach me. / You speak to me of what is natural <term>soi naturel</term> <note>original: *soi naturel* — referring to the natural self or the essence of nature</note>, yet I do not know what nature is; / I pray you, therefore, that you teach it to me." "Placides," said Tymeo, "you ask of me a very great thing, and a very great reward awaits him who learns such things; / for this reason, Alexander of Macedon gave a great treasure to Socrates, his master, from which it happened that Socrates, who was a fine philosopher, thought so much upon his great treasure that when any of his disciples asked him a question, he was so deep in thought / that he did not know how to respond; / until it happened that one of his disciples, who knew well that this Socrates was melancholy by nature <term>melencolieux par nature</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "melancholy" was one of the four humors. It was associated with deep thought but also with obsessive brooding or a "clouded" mind.</note> /—and no one can cast off their own nature—/ said to Socrates: "You are changed in your wits: for when we ask you anything, you do not respond in a way that would have you held for a philosopher; / look to what is causing this: for it would be good for us to amend it, otherwise your memory will perish / and the fame of your wisdom <term>sapience</term> will be extinguished, which would be a great pity." Socrates thought long upon this / but could not immediately know, because of his melancholy, from where this distraction came to him. Yet he perceived that what his disciples had told and taught him was the truth / and said he believed it was because of the great honors shown to him at the court of Alexander: for Alexander loved him, as did all those of the court for the sake of his love. So Socrates fled by night without leave and without Alexander's knowledge; / for he feared that Alexander would keep him by force if he had known he wished to go, because of the great love he had for him. In this manner he departed / and took with him that disciple who had told him his wits were diminished / and carried away his great treasure and was a very great while at sea, for a long time. And after they had been there a long time, Socrates asked his disciple if his wits, which had long been troubled, had returned and cleared. And his disciple answered him that they had not grown worse. Then Socrates realized that he did not know what could be causing this if it were not the profound thoughts he had regarding his treasure. And then he saw and knew it to be true—as it was and ever shall be—that earthly riches <term>richesses terriennes</term> are acquired with great pain, / pursued with great fear, and abandoned with great anguish. So he cursed his treasure and conceived such a great hatred for it that he could not even wait until he reached land, nor would he give it to anyone to whom it might do good; instead, such was his melancholy that he cast it into the sea / and kept only so much as would allow him to live strictly, and then he came to Thebes. / There his mind cleared, and he was as fine a philosopher as he had ever been; / and he stayed there so long that Alexander—who was very sorrowful to have lost him / and had sent people to seek and search for him in many places, though he could not be found—Alexander had already begun to reign over all the world. Afterward, Alexander fought a great battle with his people near Thebes and conquered it by force. ¶ In those times, it was the custom that when anyone conquered a land, a people, or a region, they were shown a great manner of honor.

### ¶ Here is the illustration of how King Alexander embraces his master the philosopher.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting two figures in medieval academic or clerical robes. On the left, a man wearing a cap and long gown stands facing right. There Alexander showed a great example to all that one must in all places honor one’s master. ¶ "Master," said Placides, "I have dared to ask you for two reasons. One is because I have a great desire to serve you with all my power—and no one can ask for more than one’s power allows—and that is the first reason. The other is that you say one must sow in good earth; and you tell me that 'good earth' is the heart of a man who willingly retains wisdom <term>sapience</term> <note>From the Latin *sapientia*, meaning deep wisdom or spiritual knowledge</note> and who is well-disposed <term>complexionne</term> <note>Referring to the medieval concept of 'complexion,' the physical and mental disposition of a person based on their bodily humors</note> for it. And you have told me that you took me into your teaching <term>doctrine</term> for this very reason, because I am well-disposed for it; and I tell you that I have a good talent for retaining what I learn. Therefore, I must dare to ask you: for he who has need of fire must seek it out with his finger.

¶ Master," said Placides, "sometimes you have told me that there are two things in this world that are worth nothing when they are hidden <term>mucees</term> and not brought into the light. One is wealth <term>auoir</term> which is in the earth beneath the ground: for as long as it stays there, it is a thing of no value. The other is knowledge <term>sens</term> <note>The word *sens* here implies both 'understanding' and 'practical wisdom'</note> that is hidden, which is worth nothing if it is not shown. And you have told me many times that knowledge is of such a nature that he who shows more of it, has more of it, and he who sows more of it, more returns to him. Therefore, you should always teach knowledge and wisdom, especially in a place where it can bear fruit. For this reason, I dare to ask you such a high question; master, tell it to me, I pray you, and may God allow me to repay you for it."

--- Page 38 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue between the master Tymeo and his student Placides, following their discussion on the "good soil" of a receptive heart. Here, Tymeo begins to explain the fundamental structure of the universe and the nature of God using Scholastic philosophical concepts.</meta>

<header>The Heart of Secrets</header>

Placides, said Tymeo. I will tell you, and I pray that you take pains to understand me: for it is a very lofty and subtle thing. Placides, I tell you that there are two kinds of nature. The first is called *Natura Naturans* <note>original: "nature naturant"; literally "nature naturing," referring to the creative power of God as the source of all things</note> / and the other is *Natura Naturata* <note>original: "nature naturee"; literally "nature natured," referring to the created world and all things within it</note>. *Natura Naturans* is the kind of nature by which all natures are made and by which all other natures are sustained. And *Natura Naturata* refers to all the things that are beneath nature / and in many ways it was once named—and still is—*Natura Naturans*. This is despite the fact that the First Cause, which we call God, cannot truly be named. The Greeks call him **Theos** <note>original: "Theos"; the Greek word for God</note> which means as much as "God" / and truly, this is God. Others called him the "First Cause" because he is the thing from which all things will take, have taken, and do take their beginning / and without him, nothing can exist, nor ever was, nor ever shall be. Others call him the "Creator" because he is the cause by which everything was created / just as I have told you. Others call him the "Mirror of Eternity" <note>original: "mirouer de pardurablete"</note> / and they say that in this mirror all things always shine / and he shines in all things, and without his favor nothing can exist. He was called the "Mirror of Eternity" / because he will never have an end, nor did he ever have a beginning. These are the two natures that exist, and there are no others: but these natures are divided in many ways: for these are all the things that are beneath God, which were all together before "generation" <note>the process of bringing things into being</note> was made, and God—who is generation itself—divided them in many ways beneath him.

And just as there are two natures / so there are two generations. The "generation that engenders" <note>the act of creating or giving birth</note> and the "generation that is engendered" <note>that which is created or born</note>: but understand well that God, who is the first thing, neither engenders nor is engendered: but he contains both the generation that engenders and that which is engendered.

Of the "engendered generations," I say there are two kinds. One is "engendered and engendering" <note>something that was created, but then goes on to create other things</note>. The other is "only engendered and not engendering" <note>something created that does not produce further physical things</note>. Those that are "engendered and engendering" are the four elements <term>four elements|the classical elements of earth, water, air, and fire, which medieval science believed were the building blocks of all physical matter</term> and the bodies within them which produce one another. And all these things are corruptible <note>original: "corruptibles"; in this context, it means things that can decay, change, or cease to exist</note> / I say "corruptible" because they can certainly be corrupted. That is to say, they come to an end and become things other than what they are now. Just as we will tell you more clearly hereafter, everything in its proper order, one after the other. 

Those things that are "engendered"—that is to say, created, which means as much as being "commanded to be"—and do not engender others are things such as the power of heaven, the angels, and souls. And among these, there are some that will never end, as you will hear hereafter if you wish to listen well. I tell you that these "engendered generations" that do not engender are all beneath the "engendering generation"—and they do not produce by changing, but by "crying out" <note>original: "cryant"; likely a reference to the "Music of the Spheres" or the angelic voices praising God, though it may also be a variant of "créant" (creating)</note> / so they were all together in the beginning when God was the First Cause. The King created all those above; there was high lordship / and it is his role to sustain and govern that high lordship. It is a bold thing even to think of knowing this. And in this, God showed a great sign of love when he willed that man should have the sense to know this, and when he granted him this dominion.

<summary>Tymeo explains the medieval cosmological view of "Nature," distinguishing between God as the creative force (Natura Naturans) and the world as the created result (Natura Naturata). He further categorizes existence into things that are created and create (the elements) and things that are created but eternal (angels and souls).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Tymeo and Placides. On the previous page, Tymeo introduced God as the "Mirror of Eternity" and "Natura Naturans" (Nature Naturing). Here, he explains why humans are physically built to look toward the heavens and addresses the student's question about God's physical form.</meta>

# On philosophy. Folio .iiii.

A iiii

God gave man this manner of carrying his face high so that he sees the sky/ and because he loves and loved him more than any other creature he ever made. And to this same point, Ovid agrees with the other philosophers/ and says: "He gave to man a face held high and commanded him to see the sky and to raise his countenance upright toward the heavens." <note>original: "Os homini sublime dedit celumqz videre. Jussit et recte ad celos tollere vultus." A famous quote from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* describing the creation of man.</note> This is to say that God made man with a high face to see the sky: for in the sky are the secrets of God and the high virtues and the throne and the seats for the high spiritual creatures, to speak in broad terms: for to speak rightly, spirit occupies no place/ as we will describe to you more fully hereafter.

Master, said Placides/ you would pass over this lightly/ but I do not believe that any man can retain words well unless they question and ask about anything they doubt. And for this reason I wish to ask you: for I do not want to forget or bypass anything. So I pray you, master, tell me if that *Natura Naturans* <term>Nature Naturing: a philosophical term for God as the creative force that gives birth to all natural things</term> of which you spoke, which is God, has any form or figure. And his master responds to him: "Yes, a good one."

Placides, said Tymeo. I will tell you my thoughts on this. No man or any other thing can know this: for just as a child in its mother's womb can see nothing, so no mortal creature can see its Creator—though I do not say this of spiritual beings: for we must believe that the good spirit is like the child who, in its hour, sees its father. Likewise, the good spirit which is pure and clean and without sin sees its Creator. And the evil spirit, which is darkened by sin, descends into shadows and sees neither the light nor the virtue of its Creator/ and know that everything which is bright is of him & without him cannot exist/ and the Creator contains all things within himself by likeness. We all, therefore, cannot see him. And since no mortal creature ever saw him, it would be difficult to describe his form.

Ah master, said Placides, you told me that this Mirror of Eternity <note>original: "mirouer de pardurablete"</note> shines in all things, and all things in him; therefore he sees us and we see him. Is it your opinion, said Tymeo, that because he is the Mirror of Eternity and shines in everything & everything in him/ that you understand it thus? You understand it poorly. He shines in everything: for he knows and sees and recognizes everything/ and everything shines in him. For it is necessary for us to feel his power, and without his grace <note>original: "faveur"; here meaning divine grace or favor</note> we can do nothing/ rather it is necessary for us to feel his grace in that he makes us move and speak. We are like an earthly mirror of glass: for in a mirror one can recognize nothing without daylight or brightness. And by the grace and the illumination <note>original: "enluminement"</note> of the day or the brightness, we can see our figures there/ and the mirror does not see nor give off light unless its power is given to it by another light. Likewise, as long as it is seen that God enlightens us and wills to put into us his brightness and his high virtue, which is true illumination <note>original: "enluminance"</note>. So long can we move & speak and feel, and without him we cannot. But he has not given us the power to see him in this life. And for this reason we do not know how to say what form God has.

<summary>Tymeo explains that humans are designed to look upward at the heavens and clarifies that while God (the Mirror of Eternity) perceives everything, mortals cannot see God's form in this life, just as a mirror cannot shine without an external light.</summary>

# The Heart of Secrets

**"Now, master," said Placides.** "I do not believe that the High Shaper, who formed all the noble parts of man, is Himself without form." **"Placides," said Tymeo.** "The ancients said that He had a form / and he was very bold who dared to say it. They said that He has a round form <note>original: "forme ronde." In medieval philosophy, the sphere was considered the most perfect and eternal shape, symbolizing that which has no beginning and no end.</note> because no one can travel around it so much that they can find an end or a beginning. And so it is with God, that He never had a beginning nor will He ever have an end / nor was any other form ever given to the deity of the Creator. Nevertheless, He who possesses all forms and made them can certainly take whichever one He wishes."

**"Master," said Placides.** "Now you have done me a great kindness / but since God has everything within Himself and had it when all was together, tell me where He was and where He is." **Tymeo responded.**

**"Now, Placides," said Tymeo.** "By this you would be driven mad: for in the past, many philosophers were driven mad by such thoughts. **Emphitus** <note>This story is a variation of a famous legend usually attributed to St. Augustine of Hippo, who supposedly met a child on a beach trying to pour the ocean into a hole to illustrate the impossibility of understanding the Trinity.</note> the philosopher fell into such a fantasy and believed that he could find and know this. He went walking along the seashore / and the Creator, who knows all and can do all, put His holy spirit into a young child of a small age and made him know the foolish thought of **Emphitus** the philosopher. The child placed himself before the philosopher on the seashore and made a little pit in the gravel; he was taking the water of the sea with a tiny little spoon and putting it into that pit, as intently as if he wished to exhaust the entire sea. And while he was putting the water into the pit, the gravel drank it up and nothing remained of it. Then, when **Emphitus** saw this child working so, he said to him: 'Foolish child, what is this thing you are doing?' And the child answered him: 'As much a child and as foolish as I am / I am wiser than you are. And I would have sooner finished what I have begun to do than you would have finished what you have set your mind to.' 'Now I am truly a fool,' said **Emphitus**, 'to talk to you when you do not know what you are doing / and I can well see that you are a fool: for you do not even know what you are doing.' 'I do know,' said the child, 'I know well why I must put the whole sea into this pit.' 'That is what I was saying,' said **Emphitus**, 'it clearly appears that you are a total fool.' 'Why?' asked the child. 'Because you will never do it,' said **Emphitus**. The child replied: 'I told you before and I tell it to you again, that I will have done it before you have what you are thinking of.' 'And what is it that I am thinking?' asked **Emphitus**. 'What?' said the child, 'I will tell you. You want to know from where God came or where He was before He made everything.' And the philosopher, **Emphitus**, who heard this, was immediately so stunned that he did not know what to say. He looked at the child / and with great difficulty he stayed on his feet, nearly falling to the ground in a faint. And when the child saw him, he was greatly amazed. He said, laughing: 'God who made all has brought you great shame: for you thought to know the high secrets of God which do not belong to being known by any man or any creature. And He has held you in such little regard that He has shown your lack of power to a little child who never learned anything except from Him, just as He did with the ant <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Proverbs, where the ant is described as a humble teacher of wisdom and industry.</note> which is a very small beast / yet a master and teacher to the lazy and to you. Think then...'

# On Philosophy. Leaf.

...elsewhere: for in this you have no power / but nevertheless, because I have told you a little of your wickedness <note>original: "felonnie." In this context, it refers to the spiritual pride or "wickedness" of the philosopher attempting to grasp the infinite with a finite mind.</note> I will tell you what God has taught me of it. Then the little child said to Emphitus:

¶ What I will tell you, Emphitus, no one can say more, nor does God want anything else to be said of it / and whoever thinks further on it, his folly only increases / for it is exactly as I shall tell you. I forbid you—by the bond that exists between father and son and between master and disciple—that you think no deeper into these depths than what I shall tell you.

¶ Placides, I tell you that God made everything / and He is, was, and shall be without end and without beginning. And before He made anything, He was within Himself / and is, was, and shall be / and He is sufficient unto Himself to exist. And He is Being, and Being is in Him / and He is in Being. And from Himself comes all sustena<unclear>n</unclear>ce <note>original: "soustenance." The OCR shows an unclear 'n', likely referring to the medieval concept of God as the 'sustainer' or 'substance' of all reality.</note> / and He is sufficient for all sustenance, and sustenance is in Him / and of this, there is no more to say.

**"Master,"** said Placides, **"now, may you not be offended / but tell me why you have adjured me by the bond of father to son. Am I not your son?"**

**"Placides,"** said Tymeo, **"so you are: for you shall be my son if you wish to be."**

**"Master,"** said Placides, **"how could this be?"**

**"I will tell you,"** said Tymeo. **"There are four types of fathers by necessity and one by will.** The first father is God, who makes all things, and us as well. And He is the true father / He is the sovereign. He is the one for whom all others must be forsaken if need be, before He alone is turned away. The second father is the carnal father who begets children. To him, one must show honor and reverence after God: for God wills and commands it, and nature and reason agree. The third father is like the elderly men whom young men must call 'fathers' because they are older / and it is a force of nature that the elderly be called fathers / and that they be wise because they owe things to the world’s affairs that young men do not, for many good reasons which shall be told hereafter. Or, the 'third fathers' can be called those under whom we live, such as prelates or barons <note>The text offers two definitions for the 'third' father: either the elderly in general or social authorities like Church leaders (prelates) and lords (barons).</note>. The fourth manner of father is of great lordship: for these are those who beget the child into a man; I will make this word clear to you. When a child is born, he is as foolish by nature as a mute beast / except that he has a rational soul / so he is like a vessel in which there is nothing, and in which one could easily place something / or like the good earth of which I spoke to you before, which requires good seed. Therefore, that child is not begotten except unto life / for if his life is not good, then his begetting is worth nothing / so it is necessary to re-beget him to improve his first begetting so that his life may have value. And this act is beautiful and most marvelous for the one who does it rightly. This begetting is the teaching of wisdom, just as I do for you / and he who has ears, let him hear / and he who has a heart, let him understand. Therefore, I say that you are my son and I am your father / if you wish to retain wisdom from me. Now you have five manners of fathers, and they are by will and not by nature / as is the righteous establishment of men:"

God ordered these things by His pleasing ordinance. He made the firmament all around in a circle, and then placed all other things inside the firmament. He made the earth, which was first called Arida <note>Latin for "dry land," referencing Genesis 1:9.</note>, which means 'dry'; for it was divided from the moist things. Above the earth, the sea was first seated. Then above the waters was placed the air, which is lighter than any of the other elements beneath it. And above the air is the fire, which is lighter than any of the other elements beneath it. And above the fire it is so well partitioned and divided that there is just as much of one as there is of the other: as much earth as water, as much water as air, as much air as fire, and as much fire as air. And the ancients provided an example of this, saying that the world is just like an egg. The shell of the egg on the outside signifies the firmament. After the shell, there is a small white skin which is cold and dry, signifying the earth; for the earth by its nature is cold and dry. Beneath that skin is the egg white <note>original: "laubin." Related to the modern word albumen.</note>, which is cold and moist; this signifies the water that sits upon the earth, which is cold and moist. And after the egg white is another skin. And there, things are transposed according to the reason of the world: this other skin is the yolk <note>original: "moyeul."</note>, for the yolk signifies the air, which is soft, clear, and moist; and likewise that air is hot and moist. And that skin signifies the fire which is above everything, which is hot and dry. And inside the egg there is a germ; just so are the living creatures within the four elements: they take from all things living and substantial."**

And it pleases me greatly that you know how to ask so well: for in what you ask me so boldly, it is my opinion that you have a greed to possess the treasure of wisdom. For the philosophers say that there are in the world and on the earth two kinds of ill-fated people. The first is that God hates him who knows enough and yet will not teach. That one is unhappy and God hates him; and many good reasons can be found for this, but we will tell them to you another time, for now we have other things to attend to. The other unhappy person in the world is he who knows nothing and is ashamed to learn; that one is wicked and foolish and unhappy, and rightly so; and it cannot be that anyone understands well if he is ashamed to ask. And for this reason, I wish to answer you all, just as the secrets were answered to the philosophers."

"Placides," said Tymeo, "one water carries the other well and sustains it without the one mixing with the other, and this you can see. Does not the sea carry a ship, and it travels in the other water in vessels? <note>Tymeo is using the analogy of a ship carrying fresh water across the salt sea to explain how different layers of water coexist.</note> Thus does one water carry the other; and that water which is placed in the ship is there to serve a different purpose than the water of the sea, and that is for the use of the human body: for a human body could not use the sea water for a long time, as it is not its element. I also say that one earth carries the other by transposition and by the placement of something between the two. So I tell you, to speak broadly, there are two kinds of earth. One which is the element, and the other which is <term>elemented</term> <note>original: "elementee"; refers to physical, tangible matter composed of the four elements, as opposed to the pure, philosophical element itself.</note>, and it is called, to be broadly understood, the bearing earth and the fruit-bearing earth and...

# The Heart of Secrets

After the death of Solomon, those of Babylon came and wanted to build a city. And as they were laying the foundation of the walls, they found this vessel in the earth and coveted it <note>original: "cupitent"; they greedily desired it</note>, thinking that it was treasure; so they broke it. Then the devils issued forth from it, who were never again imprisoned, nor ever will be. ¶ At another time, it will be described to you how many kinds of spirits and how many kinds of souls there are; for because of the coarseness of our bodies, it is necessary for us first to know—after God—lowly things rather than high things. ¶ I tell you further that corporeal things are those that have a body; of these, some have an animated body—that is to say, with a soul—and others have a body without a soul. Soul <note>original: "Ame"</note> is named from this letter: "A," which means "without," and from *nomos* in Greek, which is as much as to say "blood" <note>The author provides a medieval folk etymology here. In Greek, "blood" is actually *haima*, while *nomos* means "law." The text is attempting to explain that a soul is an incorporeal, bloodless essence.</note>. This word "soul," then, is as much as to say "without blood"; for neither soul nor spirit has blood or body. The substances that have a body without a soul are the elements, the stones, and the wood <note>original: "fustz"</note>, which cannot move by themselves. The others that have body and soul are like men and women, mute beasts, birds, fish, and all corporeal things that can move by themselves.

Of the beasts, some are rational—that is to say, they have reason—the others have no reason. Those beasts that have reason are men and women, who are beasts. "Beast" is called *animal* in Latin; *animal* is derived from and said to be "soul" <note>Latin: "anima"</note>, and it means an "animated thing"—that is, a thing that has a soul. And because man has a soul, he is therefore called a beast, and for the sake of the body he is called man; for man was made of earth, and earth—as I have told you before—was called *hume* <note>Related to the Latin *humus* (earth) and *humidus* (moist).</note>, meaning "moist," because it was above the waters; but beneath is the true elemental earth which is called *sole* <note>Latin: *solum*, meaning foundation or soil.</note>, meaning "firm," just as I have told you before. Of the bodies that have souls of which I have spoken, which are called beasts, these are those where there is reason. The other kind is without reason and without speech, for they have no rational understanding, as we will tell you very soon hereafter. ¶ One kind of body exists that has a soul but is not at all called a beast, such as trees, which have souls, as we will clearly show you. Afterwards, we will tell you why they are not called beasts; and all things that can move by themselves are called beasts, as I have told you: man, horse, donkey, lion, and such things, small and large of whatever size they may be, and also the birds and the fish and the vermin <note>In the medieval sense, "vermine" referred to any small crawling animal, including insects and reptiles.</note>, of which we will speak to you in order; and we will tell you the reason for each thing and its nature, how it comes to be and from where.

¶ Because this matter can be more easily understood and answered as I have described it to you: a philosopher who was called Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD). His "Tree of Porphyry" was a standard medieval method for classifying species and genera.</note>, for the love of the fact that a stump (which is called in some places a "stalk"—that is, the foot of the tree) is the world, divides [everything] under God our Lord and our Creator into two manners: into substance and into <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that does not change the essence of a thing, such as its color or weight.</note>, just as I have told you and divided before in many ways. And its substance is divided like the substance of a tree in descending order. And in as many ways as substance branches into others, so too does accident branch within itself.

# The Heart of Secrets

"Master, for God's sake," said Placides, "You who speak to me of bodies, now tell me: what is a <term>body</term>? <note>In this context, "body" refers to physical matter or any three-dimensional substance, rather than just a human or animal body.</note>"

"Tymeo: Fair son, gladly. A body is anything that can occupy space, and anything that can fill a vessel, and anything that can be struck against another to make a sound—just as two stones sound against one another when they are hit, or two pieces of wood, and all types of physical matter."

"Fair, sweet master," said Placides, "you have told me that the elements have bodies."

Tymeo responds: "That is true, fair sweet son."

"How, master? I see that the sun goes through the air without being blocked, and the elements are high up and we are below, yet we see them clearly. If the air were a body, it seems to me that the sun would strike against it, and that the 'body' of the air would take away our sight. So, I pray that you teach me about this."

"Gladly," said Tymeo. "I tell you that the elements have bodies without souls <note>original: "corps sans ame" — meaning they are inanimate matter, lacking the 'vital spark' of living things.</note>. And first, I wish to prove this to you through several reasons. One of the reasons is that nothing can occupy space if it is not corporeal; but you know well that earth occupies space, and therefore you can know that the earth has a body. And there is another reason: nothing can strike another thing if it does not have a body. When one body encounters another, they strike each other; and there are some bodies that make a sound when striking, just as two stones make a sound when one is struck against the other, or two pieces of iron, or two pieces of wood and such things. And you know that one clod of earth can be struck with another clod; therefore, it is quite apparent that the earth has a body. And this is true, for otherwise it could not sustain any weight, nor could it carry or support anything if it had no body. Therefore, you can be certain that the earth has a body."

"Next, I will show you by similar reasons that water has a body: for water occupies space, and everyone knows this who finds water in a vessel; for if one put enough stones into a vessel once it was full of water, the water would have to leave and go out. This is because one body, which is larger, chases the other out of its place <note>An early description of the principle of displacement.</note>. Furthermore, as I told you, nothing can carry another thing if it has no body: but water carries ships, boats, wood, fish, and other things; for a fish, which has a body, can be supported on the water or between two depths of water. Therefore, it is clearly evident that water has a body. Furthermore, I told you that some bodies make a sound and a noise when they strike each other; therefore, it is apparent that water has a body and is a corporeal thing. Furthermore, I tell you that nothing, unless it is corporeal, can wear down or consume another body; but you can see that if drops of water fell often upon a stone, the stone would be worn down, and it would be visible there. And even though water is softer than stone, nevertheless, because that body [the water], through long use, wears down the stone. But because water is lighter than stone, for that reason the Creator placed water above the earth; and thus you can understand that water has a body."

Nature did not give this ability to know such things to man alone, but...

...to beasts and to birds. And I will tell you an example of this. ¶ There was a peasant who went to gather seeds in a desert, and he carried with him a large pitcher—big, long, deep, and narrow at the entrance and the mouth—and this vessel was full of water. This commoner <note>original: "villain" — in the Middle Ages, this referred to a non-noble country dweller rather than a "bad guy."</note> carried it every year to that desert when he went to gather his seeds. And he would drink from that water for his sustenance for three weeks or more sometimes. And this vessel was specially made to keep the peasant’s water: for in every direction in that desert, for five great leagues around, there was no water, river, nor spring from which that peasant could drink, except for the water he brought in that vessel. And he also carried his bread and his provisions and other supplies as he was able and as was necessary for him.

¶ Once it happened that for fifteen days the peasant had drunk his water such that the level in the vessel had greatly decreased and shrunk. During these things, a raven had placed himself in that desert out of fear of other birds of prey, and he was there for two days and two nights such that he never dared to leave. One day, during the great heat of the afternoon, that raven had such a great thirst that he did not know what to do, for he did not dare to leave that desert. He told himself once while the peasant was sleeping, and he came to the vessel where the water was and saw that he could not drink from it easily, for it was too large and too heavy <note>original: "pesant" — likely referring to the difficulty of tipping the vessel.</note>; for it was too strong, nor could he easily enter inside, for the entrance was narrow and the vessel was deep, so that if he entered, the peasant might wake up by chance and it might happen that harm would come to him. So the raven thought to himself how he might relieve his thirst and his distress. He took stones in his beak many times and put them inside the vessel, such that the vessel filled up and the water rose, so that he drank as much as he wanted. And by this he showed that what I said at the beginning is true: that <term>wit</term> <note>original: "sens" — meaning intelligence or cleverness.</note> is worth more than force; for what he could not do by force, he did by wit. And thus he showed that water has a physical body: for by another body, stronger and heavier, he made the water move from its place as I have told you before. Thus you can know, and it is true, that water has a body and that it is a corporeal thing. Just as the earth is, though water is more clear and lighter, as I have told you at other times. And if you wish to listen well to as many good reasons, I will be able to clearly show you that air likewise has a body, and fire as well.

...that if two bodies strike one against the other, they make a sound. And if you wish to know how, take a rod in your hand and move it swiftly through the air; the air will sound. This is because the rod cuts the air and strikes against it, and from this, the sound comes; otherwise, it would not sound at all. Therefore, it clearly appears that air has a body <note>In medieval science, "body" refers to physical matter or substance that occupies space.</note>. And for this reason, **Aristotle** says that nothing is empty; for all things are full, either of earth, or of water, or of air, or of fire. And just as stones displace water from a vessel because they are heavier, so when a vessel is empty—except for the air within—and one puts water into it, the water chases out the air and remains in its place. This is because, as I have told you, air is lighter than water, and therefore it stays above the water.

¶ There is another reason. No object could be so far away that it could not be clearly seen, provided no other body obstructed the view. You can take an example from water: you see that where water is shallow and low, because it has a clean and clear body, one can sometimes see the gravel. But when the water is very deep, it seems to be black or green or dark. This is because the body of the water is thicker. 

Also, just as you see that one can perceive the light of day through a cloth, yet if one were to put two cloths, one would see less of it, and there would be less light because the cloth is a body. So I tell you of water: the more water there is, the blacker and darker it is, because there is more "body" of water to look through. And I tell you exactly the same regarding the air: we see things well that are close, but the further away they are, the more of the thick body of air there is between us, and the less we see them. Everyone knows that the path will never be so straight, nor the weather so clear, that a very distant thing can be seen as well as one that is near. And this is not due to a defect of the eyesight, but rather, as I told you, because the further away it is, the thicker the body of air becomes. Therefore, you can certainly see and know that air has a body and is a physical thing.

"Master," said **Placides**, "now remember to continue your subject, and by your grace, answer a small request of mine in the meantime; for I have understood very well what you have told me. You told me that we can see things better when they are near than when they are far." "That is true," said **Tymeo**. Then **Placides** took a coin <term>denier: a small silver coin common in medieval France</term> from his purse and placed it so close to **Tymeo's** eye that it was touching his eyelashes, so that **Tymeo** could not recognize the shape of the coin at all, so close was it.

Then Placides said to Tymeo: "Master, what shape is on this <term>denier<note>A small silver coin common in medieval France, used here as a prop to discuss the physics of sight.</note></term>?" 

"Placides," said Tymeo, "it is already so close to my eye that I cannot see it." 

"How, sir?" said Placides. "You told me before that one sees things better when they are near than when they are far. And now you say that you cannot see the shape of the coin because it is too close. Thus, it seems that one sees things much better when they are far than when they are near. And so, I do not know which truth to believe." 

¶ Then Tymeo said to Placides: "You are mocking me; and through games and mockery one does not learn great wisdom. Now, hold your peace; for you shall have a different thought before I tell you anything more." 

When Placides saw his master angered, he said: "Oh, fair and most sweet master, do not be angry. I will make amends to you, and I faithfully promise you that I will never say anything to you that should displease you, insofar as I can help it."

"Placides," said Tymeo, "you understood poorly; for I did not tell you that things which are too close could be well seen; rather, it is necessary to be at a proper distance. I will tell you the reason why this may be, and how the fault lies neither with the eye nor with the coin that I do not recognize it; but I will tell you where it lies. That eye is just like the mirror of which I have spoken to you before. The mirror has no brightness except that which another brightness gives it: this is the daylight or a fire. And then, just as I have told you before, it shines back and represents the things that are placed before it. In just this way, the eye has no brightness of its own, except only as much as the daylight or another brightness gives it. This you know well: for if you are in a dark place at night, you cannot see a thing if there is no other light. # The Heart of Secrets

...another thing must be between the eye that sees and the thing that is seen; for that light which extends between the two represents [the image] just like a mirror. Regarding the form of the thing being seen: it is not at all appropriate for someone who wants to see something for it to be so close to the eye that no light can, in a measured and reasonable way, be placed between the eye and the thing one wants to see. And because you just now placed the <term>denier<note>A small silver coin common in medieval France.</note></term> so close to my eye, no sufficient light could be placed between the eye and the coin; thus the coin, by its own darkness, took away my sight of it and of others. So, I could not see at all nor recognize the shape of the coin you held; and this did not happen because of the eye nor because of the coin, but by a lack of light that could not be placed between the two things, just as I have told and explained to you. 

In the same way, you might have asked why an eye that can see a gold or silver <term>denier</term>, or one of copper, or any other thing made of thick and rough matter, cannot see when a small film <note>original: "pelecte"</note> happens to grow over the eye, which is called *macula* <note>original Latin: "spot" or "stain"</note>—in French this is a *maille* <note>A term for a cataract or a white speck on the eye.</note>. And this is for that same reason I told you before: because that film is so close to the eye and the pupil <note>original: "prunelle"</note> that no light can be placed between the two. For a human eye cannot see without light. I say "human," because there are some beasts that see better in a dark place than in the light—and some just as much, as you know—the wolf, the cat, and other beasts, of which we will tell you later when the time comes, and why this is, and of what nature they are. But if I stopped here on this, I would wander too far from my subject.

**E**n this manner you may know and understand that the earth has a body <note>meaning a physical, material substance</note>, and also the water, and also the air; and just so I tell you of fire. For just as much as the water is clearer than the earth, just as much clearer and more subtle is the air than the water. And understand well that I do not speak of a "shining" clarity, for none of the <term>elements<note>The four classic elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note></term> are shining of themselves; but I mean they are more thin and more subtle. And do not wonder if I tell you that none of the elements shine of themselves, for I will show you the reason and the nature of it hereafter. 

So I tell you further that just as much as the air is clearer than water or earth, so much is fire clearer, more subtle, and lighter; and therefore it is positioned above the air. And I tell you that fire has a body, and I will show it to you by right reason. I have told you that one thing will strike another to make a sound only if it has a body; but fire roars <note>original: "bruyt"</note> in the air and makes a sound as it grows, and this is because one body strikes another; and thus it appears that fire has a body. Furthermore, no thing can destroy another body unless it has a body itself; but fire destroys fuels and softens iron, and thus it is evident that it has a body. Furthermore, water is quite clear, and when one puts it into a bright fire, they make a noise and sound together and cannot endure each other; rather, they chase one another from their place. You see this when hot iron is wetted; it is extinguished, and the water chases the fire from its place. And this is because of the diverse natures they have together. And I tell you that a thing which moves another from its place is <term>corporel<note>Physical or material.</note></term>. And thus it is apparent that fire...

## On Philosophy. Folio xi.

...has a body. Moreover, just as sounds and noises are created; just as someone who strikes forcefully through a flame with a rod would cause sound and noise to come out, so it is apparent that fire has a body just like the other elements. But because it is clearer and lighter, it settles at the very top, as I have told you before, by the arrangement of the Creator.

"Master," said Placides, "you have told me that some bodies are animated—that is to say, they have souls. For God’s sake, tell me if the elements, which are corporeal, are animated." "Precisely so," said Tymeo. "Master," said Placides, "you have told me that everything which can move by itself has a soul. And I see the waters in the sea which move: for some go downward like rivers, and others spring from the earth higher than the sea, like fountains do. Therefore, it seems to me that the waters have a soul; it also seems to me that the flame of fire moves and stirs, one hour high, the other low; and for this reason, it seems to me that the elements have souls."

"Placides," said Tymeo, "he who asks well wishes to know well; and for this reason **Aristotle** says: that doubting each thing is not at all unprofitable, but profitable. And this is the reason: because you doubt, you ask, and he who asks knows, if he wishes to retain [the knowledge]. To what you ask me, I respond: Just as I told you before that this earth upon which we stand is not <term>elemented earth<note>A distinction made in medieval science between the everyday materials we touch and the pure, philosophical "Elements" (Earth, Air, Fire, Water) that make up the universe.</note></term>, so too the fountains and the rivers are not strictly elemental waters, nor is the fire we use here an element; rather, it partakes of the element and shares its nature. 

And just as the water of rivers, wells, and fountains is sweeter than the sea, so the earth where we are is milder than the elemental earth. And just as the fire we use here is softer than the fire above. I tell you that neither earth, nor air, nor fire ever move by themselves, but each tends to strive to reach its nature and its <term>center<note>In the medieval geocentric model, "heavy" elements like Earth and Water naturally move toward the center of the universe (the center of the Earth), while "light" elements like Fire and Air move upward.</note></term>. 

And you can see this if you throw earth into the sea; to quickly find its own kind, it will go to the bottom; and likewise a stone, which has more of the nature of stone than any other element; and also metal, whatever it may be—of which we shall speak of the cause and nature in due time and place. Just so, if you throw water on the earth, it will go straight down the valley to strive to reach the sea, of which nature it is; or if it cannot reach a valley, it will enter the earth as best it can, and it will seem that the earth <term>labors<note>original: "laboure"; here meaning to process or work the water into itself.</note></term>. This is because with all its power, it tends and strives to reach its element. The same is true for wine or oil or any other liquid, because they are comprised more of water than of any other element. 

Similarly, when a vessel is full of air and one puts earth or water into it, the air exits and goes to its element. Fire does the same, for because fire is lighter, the smoke that comes out of it is lighter than the air. And you see that the flame of fire always strives with all its power toward the heights, because its element is there. The Creator ordered this thing so: that is, that this earth where we are, which I tell you is not an element, sits upon the water; and just as one who...

<summary>Tymeo explains to Placides that the four elements do not have souls; their apparent self-movement is actually a natural striving to return to their "center" or their pure elemental source.</summary>
