...were a skin of parchment or a towel, they would be folded into wrinkles, high above and hollow and low beneath. Just so did the **Sovereign Creator of Nature** <note>original: "souverain naturien"</note> act through right nature. The earth above the water is wrinkled and humped in one place, and in another low; and these wrinkles and humps are the high lands and the mountains which are higher than the valleys. And where the earth is high above us, it is just as hollow underneath. And just as the earth is hollowed and pressured in certain places, the pressure of the water which is under the earth enters by force and by nature wherever it finds the earth hollowed and caved out. And when it finds a path or a hole, it leaps out, because where the earth is low, it presses and compresses the water beneath itself. And because the hollows of the caverns and the openings are beneath the mountains and the high lands, the waters also gather there more. And as I have told you, when it finds a path or an exit, it issues forth and leaps out because of the weight of the earth. It is just as if you put a vessel with a hole or a large opening at the bottom into the water; the water will enter it as if it were springing up. And you can see this in a ship when it is breached at the bottom: the water does exactly the same when it finds its path. And thus rivers and <term>fountains<note>In this context, "fountains" refers to natural springs where water bubbles out of the ground.</note></term> spring and are born upon the earth above. And do not say that they "spring" because they move by themselves, for that is not so at all; rather, they glide down toward the valley because they tend toward their <term>center<note>According to medieval Aristotelian physics, each element has a "natural place" or "center" it tries to reach: Earth at the bottom, then Water, then Air, then Fire.</note></term>, and because each center of the elements is attractive, everything that is of its nature enters therein. And for this reason, it is necessary by force that a spring emerges from higher ground than the other land around it, or otherwise no water would be flowing. But because it finds lower ground around it, or on some side lower than it is, it glides down to where its element attracts it. 

And likewise, fire does not move by itself, but rather it grows or diminishes as it goes and returns to its element. And as much as it grows in the air, it takes up just as much of the air's space. And do not think that the elements can grow or diminish in total; for they never grow nor diminish at all. For as much water as you put in one place, just as much decreases elsewhere. Just as one takes earth from one place and puts it in another: as much as one takes from there, one must put elsewhere. And though there is less here than there used to be, there is not any less in total, for there is just as much elsewhere. It is exactly the same with all the elements, like water and air. If one builds a great tower in the air, the air moves away from the place where the stone and mortar are put to make the tower, in the same amount that the tower takes up. And it is just the same with fire: the more fire grows here below, the more it chases the air from its place. And the air takes up just as much space above within the fire; never in the going or the returning will there be more or less of one or the other; and all this you will be able to understand further hereafter.

"Master, by your love," said Placides. "Tell me why the earth where we are, and the waters of the rivers, of the springs, and of the wells, are sweeter than those of the sea. And you also tell us that the fire we use is sweeter and more gentle than..."

<summary>Tymeo explains that mountains and valleys are like wrinkles in parchment and that water flows from springs due to the weight of the earth and the natural attraction of elements to their centers. He argues that the total amount of each element in the universe remains constant, even as they displace one another.</summary>

### Folio 12

# On Philosophy

...the one above, which is the pure element. Why are they of a gentler nature than the element from which they are formed?

Placides, said Tymeo: The pure elements exist without any share of each other’s nature, except in one specific way, as I have told you: For **earth** is cold and dry; **water** is cold and moist; **air** is hot and moist; and **fire** is hot and dry. Thus, each of the elements has a nature similar to one other, and no more so than to any other. And if one understands the relationship of each of the two elements, each element shares the nature of two others, and is the contrary of one. Earth and water resemble each other in one thing: earth is cold and water is cold; and in another thing they are contraries: earth is dry and water is moist. Furthermore, water resembles air in one thing, in that water is moist and air is moist; and in another they are contraries: for water is cold and air is hot. Furthermore, air resembles fire in one thing and in another they are contraries: for air is hot and fire is hot, but in this they are contraries: for fire is dry and air is moist. Furthermore, fire resembles earth in one thing: for fire is dry and earth is dry; and in another thing they are contraries: for earth is cold and fire is hot.

->¶ Here is the figure of how the elements are seated one upon the other.<-

<image-desc>A circular diagram within a square frame. The outer border of the circle features a swirling, wave-like pattern. Inside the circle is a landscape illustration showing a tree, mountains, and small plants or mushrooms on the ground, representing the terrestrial world.</image-desc>

By this you can know that there are as many points of agreement as there are discords, and there are two elements that are entirely contrary to one another. But between these two, there is always something that **tempers** <term>tempers<note>The original term is "attrempe," referring to the medieval concept of "temperance" or "temperamentum"—the balancing of opposing qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) to create a harmonious whole.</note></term> them. For if one were an absolute contrary to the other, the clash would be too harsh; but to create a **balance** <note>original: "attrempance"</note> between them, they are, by the disposition of the **Creator**, seated with a middle element between the two contraries. Air is placed between fire and water, which are absolute contraries: for fire is hot and dry and water is cold and moist, as I have told you. Air is hot and moist and earth is cold and dry: and dry and moist are contraries, and hot and cold are contraries. And likewise, the moisture that is in the air and the dryness that is in the earth are contraries, and the heat and the cold are contraries. And the same is true of fire and water.

<summary>Tymeo explains the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that define the four elements and describes how the Creator balanced the universe by placing "middle" elements between opposites to prevent a violent discord.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the medieval cosmological dialogue between Tymeo and Placides. Having established the relationship between the four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—the text now explains how God balanced these conflicting forces and uses the analogy of an egg to describe the structure of the universe.</meta>

<header>The Heart of Secrets</header>

...directly opposite; and air and earth are directly opposite. But to balance <note>original: *attremper*, meaning to moderate or bring into a state of equilibrium</note> the one with the other, God placed other opposites in between them in a mingled fashion, and to temper these opposites, he mixed them together so that one would balance the other. Fire and earth are the two on the outside <note>The OCR reads *dieux* (gods), but the context strongly suggests *deux* (two), referring to the two extreme elements of the four</note>, so that the cold of the one balances the heat of the other; for it is necessary that everything meant to create life be balanced, so that there is neither too much cold nor too much heat. For through excessive cold, a living nature <term>nature engendree</term> sometimes perishes, according to the natural disposition ordained for it, and by excessive heat as well; and thus many things perish. 

Just as you can see with an egg—and as I have told you before, certain philosophers, and specifically Ovid <note>The Roman poet Ovid, whose *Metamorphoses* describes the creation of the world from chaos</note>, say that the world was shaped like an egg. For just as an egg is formed around the central yolk, so it is necessary that the supporting earth—this earth where we are—be formed as a sphere and that it be in the middle of the world. And just as the membranes <note>original: *pelettes*</note> and the white <note>original: *laubun*, the albumen</note> provide nourishment to the yolk, so too must the elements provide nourishment to the world. And you know that if an egg were excessively cold, it would never be brought to such perfection that a chick could be created, nor if it were too hot. While it is true that the chick is formed by heat, that heat must be balanced; for if one put the egg in the fire, it would cook before it could improve or form into a chick. 

In this very way, the Creator placed the elements as intermingled opposites among the other opposite elements, so that the heat might balance without conflict through moderation, as well as the dry and the moist; for such are the elements: hot and cold, dry and moist. Thus it is that when certain fires are drawn to these lands by impact or by some force of the sun, the fire cannot descend as strongly as it exists above. For it must descend through the air, which is moist; and since fire is hot, it loses its strength in the air and becomes gentler and softer than the fire above, because it is moistened by the air. 

Furthermore, fire takes hold more quickly in fatty things than in lean ones: such as in oil or in hay <note>original: *fain*</note>, because they share more of the nature of earth than water does. They take their nature from either earth or air: hay from earth, and oil from air. And earth is dry and fire is hot; and every thing clings to its like, so fire clings to that which shares something of its nature. And oil takes part of its nature from the air, which is why it is clear and light. And because of this nature that oil takes from the air, if one puts oil in a bowl with water, the water stays below <note>The OCR reads *dessus* (above), but the text explains this is "because air is above water," indicating the author's logic that oil, being like air, sits on top</note> because air stays above water, and all fat takes part in the nature of air, as you will see more clearly another time. And because oil is partly made of air, and air is hot and fire is hot, they cling to one another. But in no way can fire be as harsh here below as it is above, as I have told you. And for the reason I have told you, we cannot see fire when it descends until it has struck something. And then, once it has struck, it fights against the thing it hit and destroys it completely. It casts light and shows its power in the air because of the violence it causes.

...and against the air and against the thing to which it clings. Fire tempers <note>original: *attrempe*, meaning to moderate or bring into equilibrium</note> all the air by the force of the heat that descends into it; and to temper the air, people build fires in winter. Even though air is hot by its own nature, it is also moist; thus, through its moisture, it draws to itself the coldness of the water and the earth. It then re-balances itself with the heat of the fire and the sun, and also with the heat of the air and the fire. For this reason, it is gentler than the elemental earth and is tempered by the moisture of water.

The water of the sea is also beneath this earth, and the fountains and rivers come and flow through the veins of the earth, which is dry, balanced, and sweet. Thus, the earth sweetens that water which flows and rises. But the water in the sea does not move from its place, so it remains as its element ought to be: bitter and harsh. And the more it lingers therein <note>original: *muse ens*</note>, the more harsh and bitter it becomes; and so it is with all the other elements. Here I have told you the reason why waters that come from the sea are sweet. And so say the philosophers Aristotle and the others. And Ovid, who was called "Naso" <note>The Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso</note> before he wrote of the egg and the world; and for this reason, he was called "Ovid," from *ovum* <note>original Latin: *ouium*</note> to "work" <note>The text creates a wordplay between the Latin *ovum* (egg) and the French *oeuvrer* (to work)</note>, which is to say "egg," and from "divide" <note>original Latin: *diuide*</note>, which means to divide, because he made the division of the world based on the egg, as I have told and described to you.

Master, said Placides: "For love's sake, now tell me something I shall ask you. I see that when one strikes two stones together, fire sparks <note>original: *fault*, in the sense of leaping out</note> and issues forth from them; and if one strikes iron against a stone or a piece of steel, the same happens. Yet I never saw two pieces of wood strike or hit each other so hard that fire could leap from them. Furthermore, I see that wood burns much more readily once the fire is there than stones or steel do; I marvel greatly at this."
Tymeo responds:

Placides, it is just as you say; it is the truth, and I will tell you what I think of it. Stones are more of the nature of earth than any other element, and so they follow their own nature. Know then that when one hits one against the other, because of their great hardness, they suddenly trap the air. By the trapping of the air, which is corporeal and becomes caught between these two hard things—and since air is hot, and stone is dry and hard—they engender from that collision and from such a blow a great fire. This is because the air is so struck by two such hard things that it suddenly attracts the fire, because within each of the elements there are traces of the other elements ready to be seized. And for this reason, Aristotle said that in each of the elements, all elements were present—that is to say, by potency <term>poeste; the Aristotelian concept of potentiality, where one substance contains the potential to be transformed into another</term>, meaning they are ready to be changed into another. And this is because they are attracted to one another to balance each other, as I told you before. Therefore, by the great hardness of two stones, or iron and stone, or two pieces of steel struck together in the air, fire is engendered with the air and leaps out. But it cannot stay there, for the stone is too hard in itself, as are the iron and steel; so the fire that comes through the air cannot cling to them. And by this, you may well know that fire moves through the air as you...

<meta>This page continues the cosmological dialogue between Tymeo and Placides. Following the discussion on the elements and the etymology of Ovid's name, Tymeo now elaborates on why certain materials like stone and wood react differently to fire based on their elemental composition, and explains the spherical nature of the universe.</meta>

# The Heart of Secrets

...heard before, and to understand and know more clearly. Again, stone and steel have more of the nature of earth than any other element, and the earth is cold; so too are stones, iron, steel, and metals. Because of their hardness and coldness, fire coming from the outside cannot remain there unless something else holds it. For this reason, stones, iron, and metal defend themselves better against fire than wood <term>fustz; meaning logs or timber</term> does, for wood reflects more of the common nature of the four elements than stones and metal do. This is because they are partly of the nature of earth, for they take their birth in the earth, emerge from the earth, and take on a coarse nature, as you will be able to understand more clearly hereafter. 

Wood also takes a great part of its nature from water; for otherwise, it could neither grow nor multiply if it were not for the moisture of the water that nourishes it. It is very apparent that when a tree dries out, it dies. You see this often; but as long as it has natural moisture, it lives and is nourished. It also takes part of its nature from the air, for it extends itself into the air and is nourished above the earth; this air is moist, and the nature of the water from which it is co-created and nourished is likewise moist by nature. 

Fire cannot be produced from wood by force alone without another element <note>The text argues that wood is too soft to strike fire out of the air compared to the hardness of stone</note>, nor is any wood so hard that it can strike or catch the air as forcefully as stone, for stone is exceedingly hard. For this reason, wood cannot defend itself against fire as well as water does, nor is it as cold as the other elements. Fire takes part of the air in which it is nourished and grows, and also part of the heat of the fire; for in summer and in hot weather, through the attraction of heat, trees grow more and spread out more than in any other season. Because wood possesses the two heats of the two elements <note>Likely referring to the heat of the sun/air and the internal heat that promotes growth</note>, and because they are not excessively hard, fire leaps and catches more quickly in wood than in stones. 

And you should know that fire is more quickly engendered by the force of flint or clear or grayish <note>original: *bises*</note> stones when they are struck together than by other stones of a coarse and heavy nature. Just as the flint or the clear or grayish stone does, it takes more of the nature of air than other stones. It is thus clearer and harder, and therefore it is hotter; for this reason, fire is engendered from it more quickly than from other stones of coarse nature. This is because there are other stones of subtle <note>original: *foutiues*, likely a variant of *soultives* meaning refined or subtle</note> natures which are called precious—such as crystal and others of which we will speak to you another time—from which fire would be engendered sooner than from those of coarse matter, and this is for the reason I have told you. 

Thus you can certainly know that the element has a round body, for each of the elements is round, as I have told you before. This is because no one could make any vessel so sound or so self-supporting as a round one; this you can see and know, for every round thing is supported on all sides by itself. For this reason, the Creator made everything round, and all the elements are also round, as I have told you.

¶ "Placides," said Tymeo, "I tell you that the Creator made many creatures. He made some creatures above all the elements, and he made many within them. He made some who have body and soul, and others who never had a body..."

...and never will have. Regarding creatures that have bodies, He made some movable, and others that do not move from their place. Those that have both soul and body and are movable are like the sun and the moon and some (indeed, many) of the stars which have bodies and souls, as we will show you hereafter. And there are some stars that do not move except by the will of the Creator, who ordained everything according to His pleasure. These stars the ancients called fixed stars <term>estoilles fischees; the "fixed" stars were believed to be set into a celestial sphere, maintaining a constant distance from one another</term>, because they never move from their positions. It is by these stars that wise mariners keep their watch and find their way at sea, so that they may not be deceived as to whether they must go to the right or to the left.

These creatures were called angels. *Angelus* <note>original Latin: "Angelus"</note> means messenger, because the philosophers say—and I agree with them—that they were and are messengers of God; and God made them marvelously beautiful. 

But as the ancients said, a portion of these, through their sin and their misdeed, fell and were cast down from the heavens and from above the elements, and He made them fall beneath the elements. Because they were once so beautiful, the Creator willed that they should now be all the more hideous and dark. And He gave them no power to ever rise above the elements again, but only to remain among the elements from which they come. Never since they fell have they done any good, nor ever will they, nor will they ever be mindful of the Creator; and for this reason, the ancients called them "evil angels." Others called them "filthy spirits," and others "messengers of evil." And the Hebrews call them Satan <note>original: "Sathan"</note>, which means "evil-doer," and we call them devils. *Diabolus* <note>original Latin: "Dyabolus"</note> means "two pieces." *Dia* means "two," and *bolo* means "piece" <note>The author uses a popular medieval folk etymology to explain that the devil's goal is to split the unity of man</note>; for we say that he makes two pieces of a man: one of the body and the other of the soul, because he strives to bring both body and soul to shame. This is because man was created to replace them following their misdeed and their fall. They have perceived that the Creator loves man more than any other creature He ever made, provided man does not turn away through filth or sin. Thus the devil remembers the joy and the beauty that he lost, and he is envious of the love that God has for man. And if you wish to know how the philosophers knew this, I will tell you.

The Creator has loved man so much—as we will tell you another time—that He gave and has given him sense and understanding. There have been some who have so loved and adored the Creator that the Creator sent certain angels to them to make these things known. And some had such great sense, by the grace of the Creator, that they through their wisdom so confounded the devils that the devils were forced to reveal the truth to them, just as...

**I** have told it to you; among those wise philosophers were King Solomon, Homer, Aegidius, and Darius, who spoke of it in several places and confirmed what the first father, Adam, had said. For he said that God the Creator had told him that if he did His will, He would give him the inheritance from which He had disinherited the wicked heirs who are called devils; and He announced to him what I told you before. Therefore, know that to serve the Creator is to reign, and whoever strives against the Creator, it will be necessary—if the wrath of the Creator falls upon him—that he descend below the elements <note>In the medieval worldview, "below the elements" refers to a place beneath the physical realms of earth, water, air, and fire, essentially the center of the universe where Hell was thought to be located.</note> where there is not, nor will there be, nor was there ever light, joy, or rest, nor any order, nor any measure, nor any repose. Here shall reign those who serve Him, who love, fear, and adore Him as the one who made everything from nothing. And he well affirms and assures us that just as serving Him is to reign and to live, so too to forget and abandon Him is to perish and die.

And of this you may have examples in many places, and by the testimony of many places. King Pharaoh and a great part of his people perished in the sea because he would not obey his Creator nor His commandments. King Nebuchadnezzar—strong, great, and exceedingly rich in the law of the Chaldeans—because he had people adore a metal image that he had made in his name, was for forty years in the deserts and woods, and went on four feet like a beast, and grazed on grass like a goat. King Saul, who was the first king of the children of Israel, was for his sin defeated and overcome before his time, and died a painful death. And for the sin of Solomon, the wealthy king, the kingdom was divided after his death, so that only a small part remained to his son. There are plenty of examples for anyone who would want to recount them all. But God showed these examples to man on earth because of the great love He had for him. For man is of such hard understanding that he would never believe he was but a man if God had not openly shown it on earth. For know this: more than a heart could think or a mouth could say, by a hundred and fifty thousand times over, the vengeance of the Creator is strong and hard and cruel when He makes those to whom He shows His wrath descend below the elements and beneath the world into a place called Hell. Hell <note>original: "Infernus"</note> is this place. *Infernus* is named for being lower <note>original: "inferius"</note>. "Lower" <note>original: "Inferius"</note> means beneath, because Hell is beneath the whole world, of which we will speak to you more clearly afterward.

¶ Regarding those creatures who have bodies, as I have told and described to you, no one could imagine the greatness of their bodies; for the philosophers tell us that the moon is nine times larger than the earth where we are. And the sun is nine times larger (or more) than the moon. And every single star, even the very smallest, is as large as the whole earth where we are. And the wise men prove this by certain reasons.

It is true, and you know it well, that if one places a great orb <note>The original "pommel" refers to a decorative sphere or rounded ornament.</note>—even the largest one that can be made—upon a very high tower, if the tower is very high, it seems to those who are below that the orb is small. And this thing is because it appears to be so high up.

### On Philosophy. Folio xv.

in the air. And for certain reasons that I am telling you. When I say that the air had a body—and the moon, which is entirely above the air and entirely above the fire, of which there is as much as there is of air, just as I have told you before. And as much further as these two things are high. Therefore it is evident to a soul that seeks to understand that the moon is much larger than one might think.

There is another reason. It is necessary that the body be very large when its glow <note>The original reads "sueur" (sweat), which is likely a transcription error or an archaic metaphor for "lueur" (light/glow), referring to the light visible from a great distance.</note> appears from so far away. Whoever sees a great fire from a distance, the further away they can see it, the larger it must be; the further away it is seen, the smaller it seems to be. Thus, by necessity, the thing must be very large if it can be seen from so far away. Therefore, you should well believe that the moon is much larger than it seems.

And again, I show you that by necessity it must be much larger than the earth where we are. You have heard it said (and it is true) that when the shadow of anything appears, that shadow is larger than the thing from which it comes; and the further that shadow is from the thing, the larger it is. Again, it is necessary by force that the thing to which this shadow clings must be significantly larger than that shadow. ¶ These are already two pairs of great magnitudes. And of this you can see an example: If your shadows pass and strike the ground or a wall beside you, your shadow is larger than you; and the ground or the wall upon which that shadow extends is also larger than that shadow is; or otherwise, that entire shadow could not be complete. In just this same manner, I tell you that it is necessary by force that the moon be much larger than the earth: for from so very wonderfully far as we are, the shadow of the earth appears on the moon <note>Tymeo is describing a lunar eclipse, where the Earth's shadow falls upon the moon's surface.</note>, as I will show you hereafter; and this is what you see—one place darker than another on the moon. Therefore, it is necessary by force that the moon be, as I have described to you, considerably larger than the earth. ¶ "Ah, Master," said Placides, "what kind of body is this moon-body, which you tell me is a living body that has a soul? For I see that this body fails <note>original: "fault"; referring to the moon's waning or disappearing during its monthly cycle.</note> every month; and when that body is gone, what then can become of the soul?" ¶ "Placides," said Tymeo, "listen to me. The sun and the moon have both soul and body; and since you wish to understand it, we will tell you about them in order."

The Creator made those spirits of whom I spoke to you—the angels—and he also made other spiritual powers <term>poestes: from the Latin 'potestates', referring to one of the traditional nine choirs of angels</term> who are higher and more worthy, and whose nature no other creature needs to know or understand except by the will of the Creator. Of these angels, some are called archangels; these are those who are holier and higher than the others and who know more of the secrets of God. They are called archangels from this Greek name *Archos* <note>original: "Archos", meaning "chief" or "prince"</note>, which means prince, and from *Angelus* <note>original: "Angelus", meaning "messenger"</note>: for archangel means "prince of the messengers." Of the powers and the angels of the Creator, one must not speak except when praying to that Creator who made and ordained them.

# The Heart of Secrets

The other creatures who possess animated bodies shall now be divided into classes. Once we have spoken of non-corporeal substances, such as spirits and souls, I tell you that the Creator made many kinds of souls. He made souls that shall never fail and will last forever without end, such as the angels. These souls include the souls of men and women, which shall never fail and will last forever without end. Others, which die when they depart from their bodies, are **corruptible souls**—that is to say, those that are capable of dying. I tell you that God made these in many different ways.

Some are **attractive**; these are those that have the power to attract. Others are **vegetative**; these are those that have the power to make bodies grow and expand. Others are **sensitive**; these are those that allow bodies to feel. Of the other souls, He made some without reason, and others that possess reason, called **rational**. And those that are rational possess all the virtues that the others have of which I have spoken to you. <note>In medieval philosophy, the "rational soul" (human) was thought to encompass the functions of the "vegetative soul" (plants) and the "sensitive soul" (animals).</note>

Of these souls, God—who made them for their sustenance and for the governance of bodies—placed some outside the body and others inside the body. Among those that are outside the bodies are the souls of the sun, the moon, and the stars; for the soul of the sun is on the outside of its body. Just as you might understand if a man pushed a wheel before him or pulled it behind him, so you can understand how the souls of the sun, the moon, and the stars act from the outside. But they act all around to govern the body, just as you might understand that if a round ball, perfectly shaped on all sides and in all parts, were set ablaze with fire and clear flames in every part, so is the soul of the sun and of the other things around their bodies. 

And because these souls are above the body, we do not say that these creatures are "beasts." <note>The author distinguishes celestial bodies from "beasts" (animals) because their souls govern them from the outside and they do not undergo biological growth.</note> These souls are not **vegetative**, nor do they provide growth, nor do they shrink; never, since these creatures were created, have they grown or diminished, even though it may appear that the moon grows or shrinks—but it is not so, as I shall tell you another time. These bodies and these souls exist outside the <term>elements</term> <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. The celestial spheres were considered to be made of a fifth element, or quintessence, and were thus immutable.</note>.

Afterward, the Creator made other creatures within the elements; He made those of which it is said that they live purely each within the place where they are born. And the ancient fathers, who found reason in this, said that in that element which is entirely above all the others—which is **fire**—there are beasts that are born in the fire, develop in fire, and live in fire. Although there are several kinds of these beasts, some are called **Salamanders**. Others have not been very well known, but two kinds of salamanders have been found. Some are small, like little <term>worms</term> <note>original: "vermisseaulx"</note>, and live in little cocoons <note>original: "buriaulx"</note> just like the worms that make silk. The others are shaped like mice. But their skin and hair are as shimmering as a mallard's neck when they are naturally of good quality; there are others that are a bit duller, but the shimmering kind is more valuable and more beautiful and

### On Philosophy. Leaf xvi.
L.iiii

...more strongly. And if you wish to ask how we can know this, I will tell you. It is the case that every thing that lives in a pure <term>element|In medieval science, the world was composed of four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. Most creatures were thought to be a mix, but some were believed to belong to one exclusively.</term>—as soon as it is outside of it, even by the slightest bit, it immediately dies. You can recognize this because it is exactly thus with the **herring**. The fish is called a **herring** which lives in a pure element [water], and the fishermen who catch them know well that as soon as it feels the air, it dies. This is for the reason that they cannot live except in a single element.

It is exactly the same with the **Salamander**: when it gapes too much, or fails even slightly by being outside its element—whether too low or too high—it immediately dies and then falls, and so they are found on the ground quite dead. And because they fall from on high, one knows well that they come from the fire above. <note>Medieval cosmology placed a "Sphere of Fire" above the atmosphere; Tymeo suggests salamanders live there and fall to earth when they stray from it.</note> This is for the good reason that one perceives that the skin of this beast is so strong and so durable that it is a marvel; it keeps it well from being wet, for wetting harms it more than anything else.

And it has another power that makes it well known that it comes from such an element as fire: it can neither burn nor be damaged by it; rather, the longer it is there, the more it improves. These beasts are of a cold nature, which keeps them alive outside the fire. <note>The author uses the theory of "complexions" or humors: the salamander is so intensely cold that it requires the heat of fire to survive, creating a balance.</note> And if you ask me why and how this can be, I tell you that later on we shall answer you regarding this nature and others—and also why the fish of the sea is sweeter than that of fresh water—but if I were to stop here now, I would stray too far from my subject. So, we shall speak of what we have begun.

These **Salamanders** of which we speak are more commonly found in the East, and in the regions of **Ethiopia** and **Greater India** than in any other part of the earth, and they fall there more readily than elsewhere. This is because fire is more present there than elsewhere, and because the fire is more "descending" there due to the appearance of the sun, which is born in that direction. Because of the sun's brilliance and the rise of joy they have from it, they are more amazed in that region and frequent it more than any other; and because they are too amazed by it, they meet their death there, just as I told you before.

The **Emperor of Greater India** <note>original: "Lemperiere Dinde la maiour." Likely a reference to the legendary Prester John.</note>, more than any other, customarily used to have these beasts in his land. No one dared find one without being required to hand it over to the Emperor; if anyone found one and did not hand it over, the Emperor would make him return it if he found out, and would punish his body severely according to the custom of the country. And from these little beasts that fall in clusters, the Emperor has cloths made to clothe himself. And from the skins of those that look like mice, he has garments made to wear over armor in war and in battle to defend himself from the fire that is thrown against his enemies. For fire cannot damage these garments; and when such a garment is dirty or soiled, it must be cleaned and washed in the strongest fire that can be made. They are placed inside it, and the longer they are there, the more they are improved, as I describe to you. As soon as the skin or the garment is put into the fire, it becomes the same color and appearance as the fire, and this is because of the nature of the element from which they are made, just as I told you before.

In the next element which is below fire, that is the air. There, so some say, is a type of bird called the <term>Gamalion|Likely a reference to the chameleon, which medieval naturalists often categorized as a bird or creature that lived solely on air.</term>. Some other philosophers said that the Gamalion did not come purely from the air because it sometimes consumes earthly food; but they said that these birds truly live on the air and behave in the air just like the **pelican**. For it [the pelican] makes its nest in the highest place it can find and in the highest tree, so that it lives on nothing but air. And because the father bird goes far to gather fresh and new air to nourish his chicks, he sometimes stays away longer than is right when he encounters corrupted air <note>Medieval science held that "corrupt air" was a source of disease and death; the father bird must search for "pure" air to sustain life.</note>. And when the father or the mother, by some mishap as I have told you, stays too long, the chicks die because they cannot fly or gather air for themselves. And when the father or mother return and find them dead, the parent strikes itself with its beak in the side under the wing so that the blood springs forth. And as soon as these birds are sprinkled with it, they return to life and are revived and fed with new air.

Next, in the other element which is the sea, mariners and those who know it well say that the one who lives most purely from it is the **herring**. For the herring consumes nothing else except the <term>froth|original: "cressumee"</term> and the foam of the sea. And the herring eats or uses nothing else, and thus cannot endure any other element; for as I have told you, as soon as it sees the air or smells it, it dies. And because of this, all those who know its nature are in agreement: that this is the sea fish that lives most purely in its own element.

Furthermore, the philosopher who investigates the nature of things and applies himself to the scriptures says that there are beasts that live from that single element [Earth]. And some who were mocked for it said it was the **mole**, because it is born under the earth and lives under the earth and sees not a drop. But those who contradicted them said that this meant nothing, for the dirt we see here is not the pure element [of Earth], as I have told you before. Rather, they said that the earth which is the pure element is beneath the ground, and it belongs to beasts of an extremely hard nature. For this reason, creatures like the **Salamanders** <note>Though usually associated with fire, the text here groups "Salamanders" or similar hard-bodied creatures with the element of Earth due to their dryness.</note> die: some of them have been found cast out dead by the sea, and some have been found in the nets of fishermen in such a form and variety that—since one can hardly find two that look alike—they did not know what proper name to give them. And some of those who first found the bodies of these beasts thought they were fish. But because these beasts had no fins <note>original: "nooueres"</note> by which it would seem they lived in the water, it was apparent they had come out of the earth. This was also evident from the extreme hardness and the great dryness found and perceived in them. And also, just as a sea fish senses the sea, they sensed the earth and their element with a full mouth. And no iron was or is as hard as they are. Nor do they have any moisture or sweetness in them, either inside or out, except only in the middle of the body, like a little <term>warm slime|original: "limonnee chauldete."</term>. The ancients named these beasts under the condition of **Solum** <note>original: "soubz laage de Solum." Solum is Latin for soil or ground.</note>—which is to say, as I have told you before /

...which comes from *born* <note>original: "genitus"</note>, which is to say "engendered," because these beasts are made from the earth, and in the earth they are made; they live in the earth and cannot live outside the earth, as I have told you. To these beasts, God gave souls according to their sensitive and vegetative nature. It is the same with herbs, by which it is apparent that they have souls, and this is the truth. Furthermore, no thing can grow or shrink by itself if it has no soul. But trees and herbs grow by themselves according to the season of the weather, as you plainly see. Therefore, it is a certain thing that they have a soul, and no one should doubt it; but they are not called "beasts" because of such souls, for they have only two virtues <note>Or "powers" of the soul.</note>, which are as one: one of these virtues is **attractive** and the other is **vegetative**. It is "attractive" because that soul attracts the humors of the earth by which the trees are nourished, and that soul exerts itself by nature to cast those humors it has found into the fruits and the growth of the tree: for just as other souls exert themselves with all their power to make their bodies grow. # Folio 18

## The Heart of Secrets

...and other creatures should be in service to this creature [Man]; and thus He gave him a soul such as no other creature possesses, having all the powers that any other soul has, and more: for it has power like that of the **angels**, because it has a **rational soul** <term>ame raisonnable: in medieval philosophy, the highest form of soul, capable of logic and divine contemplation</term> and yet he is also a **corporeal beast**. It is a great thing when an earthly beast has a rational soul that possesses reason and understanding. This soul is perpetual and will never die, but will endure forever. But it is not so with the human body, for it is **corruptible** <term>subject to decay, change, and death</term> just like the **elements** from which the body is made. 

This is despite the fact that **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose scientific views were often harmonized with Christian theology in the Middle Ages.</note> said that **generation** was perpetual; he was referring to that "generating generation" which is not engendered, but created—that is to say, commanded by God. For he says that if God the Creator had destroyed all beasts, each of their parts would return to the element from which it was made. And if He broke apart the elements, they would return to ash. And that ash, by its nature, would engender a balance among these parts, one heavier than the other. This thing is done at the will of the Creator and at His command. He meant this regarding creatures of one kind and another so that the elements neither grow nor diminish; we shall explain his meaning to you more clearly another time.

**L**es <note>original: decorative woodcut initial 'L'</note> Regarding the souls of men, which are endowed with reason and are perpetual, we will speak at greater length another time; but we must return to our first topic. Among these things, God made other corporeal things called **clouds**, which are not **animated** <note>original: "animees," meaning they do not possess a life-force or soul</note>; rather, they are moved through the air by **vapors** generated from the sea and the earth by the force of fire and the sun. These vapors are called **winds**, and they come from the four parts of the world. Each of those coming from the four parts of the world are called **principal winds**. The ancients gave them principal and proper names, as we will tell you another time. They are called "principal" because each of these winds has two other winds coming alongside it. These winds were named by scholars, and not by the common people. We will treat the winds, the clouds, their natures, and their power more at leisure and in proper order later, when it is time to return and give you this answer.

The Creator did one thing when He made that creature called the **Sun**. For in making the Sun, He made the **Day**. I shall tell you how and for what reason. First, one must know what "Day" is: for Day is only the brightness and the glow of the Sun. For I tell you—and do not be surprised by this—that nothing in the world has brightness or fire—neither the moon nor the stars—except from the Sun; and we will speak of this more clearly hereafter. 

Now listen and accept what I tell you. I tell you that God the Creator made the Day bright and shining in itself. All other things are obscure and dark by themselves, but they receive brightness from the Sun, just as I previously told you about the **Mirror**, which has no light except what the day gives it. Thus it is that the Sun and the Moon have an established path in the **firmament** <note>the heavens or the sky, then imagined as a series of transparent spheres</note> which we can see. Astronomers call that path the **Zodiac**, and it is this path which we mark <note>original: "saignons," likely a variant or error for "signons" (to mark or designate with signs)</note>...

# On Philosophy. Folio xviii

...whatever it may be: but to tell the truth, it [the path of the stars] is simply like the path of birds [through the air]. But we pretend that it is fixed because the sun and moon cannot travel by any other path; and so it is that when the sun is above the earth, it is day. And you should know that the sun and the moon go all around the firmament <term>firmament: in medieval cosmology, the vast sphere of the heavens that carries the celestial bodies</term> between day and night: so that when the sun is beneath [the earth], its brightness is not on the earth because it is night. For night is nothing other than darkness. But now listen to me closely so you may hear the answer to what you asked me: what kind of body the moon has, which each month renews and undoes itself.

The moon, as I have told you, goes beneath the elements <note>The moon's sphere was considered the lowest celestial circle, positioned just above the "sublunary" world of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> all around according to the roundness of the firmament, and the sun goes there as well. So I tell you that the moon neither grows nor shrinks; but as I have described the moon's body to you, it is large and round. The sun and moon go all around the firmament as if on paths, but they travel on different paths. Thus, what you ask about happens every month. 

Do you know why the moon has no brightness in itself? It is a shining body that reflects light when [the sun] strikes it. But the sun does not strike it all day when it rises beside it; and when it does not strike it—that is to say, when its light does not come directly to it—the moon does not shine and appears only pale. But for all that, the moon itself is neither more nor less; it simply does not shine because the sun's light does not strike it. And when it begins to strike, it shines a little. And when we call the moon "new" <note>original: "la lune prime" (the first moon), referring to the first visible crescent.</note>, it is because more light strikes it and it shines more, and we can see more of it. And when they are directly opposite one another, face to face, one is beneath the earth and the other is above. And when the sun is beneath the earth, it casts its brightness directly face-to-face against the moon. And the moon is high up so that we can see it well. Then we say the moon is "full"; but there is no more of the moon than there ever was, except for the glow and brightness that comes to it from the sun. 

And thus they come and go like those who travel by different paths. And we shall speak to you more clearly another time regarding what you ask about the body of the moon; you may know that it is round. And I tell you that the dark part which is in the middle of the moon, which is more shadowed than the rest of the moon, is the shadow of the earth, which is more dense than water or air; so that its shadow appears on the moon very clearly and plainly. <note>The author here explains the permanent dark markings on the moon's surface as a reflection of the Earth's shadow, a common medieval theory attempting to explain the "Man in the Moon."</note> And I have told you this before; and because the shadow of the earth appears from so far away on the moon, and there is more light than shadow, for this reason, you may well know that the moon is much larger than the earth. <note>This is a scientific error of the period; the Moon is significantly smaller than the Earth.</note> 

Regarding its soul, I tell you that the soul of the moon is outside its body, just like that of the sun. We will speak of these things another time; but as I have told you before, because we are earthly beings, it is proper for us to know earthly natures before celestial ones. But since you asked me, it is right for me to answer you. Now you may have understood what you asked about the moon; and do not marvel at anything I tell you, for I tell you the absolute truth, and everything will be proven to you by sound and natural reasons.

### The Heart of Secrets

...other creatures were in service to that creature <note>Refers to humanity, created in God's image as discussed on the previous page.</note>; and thus He gave them a soul such as no other creature possesses, containing all the powers that no other soul has: this soul has even more, for it has a power like that of the angels; it is a **rational soul** <term>rational soul: in medieval thought, the part of the human soul capable of logic and understanding, distinguishing humans from "sensitive" animal souls</term> and yet it is a corporeal beast. It is a great thing that an earthly beast has a rational soul which possesses reason and understanding. This soul is perpetual, so that it shall never die and will always endure. But it is not so with the human body: for it is corruptible, just like the elements from which the body is made. Although *Aristotle* said that generation was perpetual <note>original: "generation estoit perpetuelle." Aristotle argued that while individuals die, the cycle of birth and decay (generation) in the sublunary world is eternal.</note>, this referred to that "generating generation" which is not itself engendered but created—that is to say, commanded. For he says that if God the Creator had destroyed all beasts, each of the parts would return to the element from which it was made. And if He broke apart the elements, they would return to ash. And that ash would, by its nature, produce parts where one is heavier than the other. This thing is done by the will of the Creator and at His command. He meant this regarding creatures of both kinds, because the elements neither grow nor diminish; we will make his meaning more clearly understood to you another time.

Of the souls of men who are endowed with reason and are perpetual, we will speak to you at greater length another time; but we must return to our first subject. Among these things, God made other corporeal things that are called clouds, and yet they are not "animated" <note>Meaning they do not possess a "soul" or life-force like animals or plants.</note>; rather, they are moved through the air by the vapors which are engendered from the sea and the earth by the force of fire and the sun. These vapors are called winds, and they come from the four parts of the world. Each of those which come from the four parts of the world are called **principal winds**, and the ancients gave them principal and proper names, just as we will tell you another time. And they are "principal" because each of these winds has two other winds coming at its side <note>This refers to the classical 12-wind rose: four cardinal winds, each flanked by two collateral winds.</note>. These winds were named (not by the common people). Of the winds, the clouds, their natures, and their powers, we shall treat more at leisure hereafter and in proper order, as it is now necessary for us to return to giving you this answer.

The Creator did one thing when He made that creature which is called the sun: for in making the sun, He made the **day**. And I shall tell you how and for what reason. First, it is necessary to know what "day" is: for day is only the clarity and the glow of the sun. For I tell you—and do not marvel at this—that nothing in the world has brightness, neither fire, nor moon, nor star, except from the sun; and we will speak of this more clearly hereafter. Now listen and accept what I tell you. I tell you that God the Creator made the day bright and shining of itself; and all other things are obscure and dark of themselves. But they receive brightness from the sun, just as I have told you before regarding the **mirror**, which has no brightness except for as much as the day gives it. So it is that the sun and the moon have an established path in the firmament <term>firmament: the sphere of the heavens or the sky</term> which we can see. And that path the astronomers call the **zodiac**; and it is this path which we imagine...

### On Philosophy
#### Folio xviii

...whatever it may be: but to speak the truth, it is never fully like a path for birds. But we imagine that it is fixed because the sun cannot go by any other way, nor the moon either. And so it is that when the sun is above the earth, it is day. And you must know that the sun and moon go between day and night all around the firmament <term>firmament: in medieval cosmology, the spheres of the heavens that rotate around the Earth</term>: so that when the sun is underneath, it is night; its brightness is not on the earth because it is night: for night is nothing other than darkness. But now listen well to me and you will hear the answer to what you asked me: what kind of body the moon has, and why every month it remakes and unmasks itself <note>This refers to the moon's phases, which to the observer appear as the moon growing and shrinking.</note>.

The moon, as I have told you, goes below the elements <note>In the medieval geocentric model, the Moon's sphere is the lowest, positioned just below the sphere of fire and above the Earthly elements.</note> all around following the roundness of the firmament, and the sun goes there too. I tell you that the moon neither grows nor diminishes; rather, as I have described to you, the body of the moon is large and round. The sun and the moon go all around the firmament just like along paths, but they travel different paths. Thus happens every month what you ask about. Do you know why the moon has no brightness in itself? It is a shining body that reflects light when it is struck by it. But the sun does not strike it at all <note>original: "mpe," likely an OCR error or abbreviation for "mie," meaning "not at all."</note> all day when it rises beside it; and when it strikes it—that is to say, when its brightness does not come directly upon it—the moon does not shine and appears as nothing but the air. Yet because of this, there is neither more nor less of it, but it simply does not shine, because the brightness of the sun does not strike it at all, so it does not shine at all. And when it begins to strike, it shines a little. 

And when we call it the **new moon** <term>new moon: original "lune prime," the first appearance of the crescent</term>, it is according to how much more light strikes it; and the more it shines, the more we can see of it. And when they are one across from the other, face to face, one is beneath the earth and the other is above. When the sun is beneath the earth, it casts its brightness directly face-to-face against the moon. And the moon is high up so that we can see it well. Then we say that the moon is **full**, but there is no more of it than there always is, except for the glow and brightness that comes to it from the sun. And thus they come and go like those who travel by different paths. 

And we shall speak of this more clearly another time, concerning what you ask about what kind of body the moon has; you may know that it is round. And I tell you that this darkness which is in the middle of the moon, which is more shadowy than the rest of the moon, is the **shadow** <note>original: "lumbie," a variant of "l'ombre."</note> of the earth, which is more solid than water or air, so that the shadow appears on the moon very clearly and openly. And this I have told you before; and because the shadow of the earth appears from so far away upon the moon, and there is more of the bright part than the dark, you may well know from this that the moon is much larger than the earth <note>While modern science shows the Earth is much larger than the Moon, some medieval theorists misinterpreted the visual scale of shadows and celestial bodies in this way.</note>. Concerning the soul, I tell you that the soul of the moon is outside its body, just like that of the sun. We shall speak of these things another time. But as I have told you before, because we are earthly beings <note>original: "terriens"</note>, it is fitting for us to first understand earthly natures before celestial ones. But since you asked me, it is necessary that I answer you. Now you may have understood what you asked about the moon, and do not marvel at anything I tell you: for I tell you the absolute truth, and everything shall be proven to you by good and natural reasons.

# The Heart of Secrets

"Master," said Placides, "now tell me then, and answer and make me understand how it can be that you tell me nothing has light except the sun: for I marvel greatly at this thing, as I see that the brightness of fire illuminates and lights us, and it seems to me that fire is bright." 

¶ Placides, said Tymeo, "listen to me; know this, that nothing has light in itself except the sun; rather, there is darkness on earth, in sea, in air, and in fire, except only insofar as the sun provides natural light, and I shall demonstrate this to you."

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

"First, you know well that the earth is dark; in the earth there is no light, and because there is no light, almost no beasts can inhabit a dry place without losing their sight <note>original: "peulx," a variant spelling here for "yeux" (eyes).</note>. This is why there are few vermin who have sight that inhabit dark and dry earth. Because of the nature of the mole, it would have had eyes and sight were it not that it strives more to be inside the earth than outside. And as much as it strives more to remain there, so much does the dark nature of the earth strive to take away its eyes. If you ask why the toad, which lives underground, can see, I will tell you. The toad is not underground only to live: but to flee the cold, because it could not suffer the winter. For all venom, as we will tell you better another time, is cold by its nature and always seeks heat for tempering <term>tempering: "attrempance," the medieval medical concept of balancing the "qualities" (hot, cold, moist, dry) of a body</term>; for many things live by tempering. But everyone knows that as soon as the weather softens, the toad comes out of the earth with great joy and more willingly lives upon the earth and among the waters and in moist places and marshes. And because of this, there are more crystalline colors in its eyes. And the toad willingly returns to the sun, and so its sight is illuminated. And for this reason, the toad may well have sight, while the mole does not."

¶ "Just so, I tell you that the colubrine serpent, which is called a grass snake <note>original: "couleuure" (modern: couleuvre).</note>, enters into caves underground in the winter, and stays there until the summer time returns. Then it thinks to come outside. And when it comes out, because of the darkness of the earth's nature, it has lost its sight and sees nothing; it is not because it has no eyes, but because of the darkness of the earth which troubles and thickens its vision. And when it has come out, it seeks out thistles or fennel <note>original: "fanoil." According to medieval bestiaries and Pliny the Elder, serpents were believed to eat or rub against fennel to clear their sight after shedding their skin or emerging from hibernation.</note>, and it rubs its eyes against these herbs. And thus it recovers its strength through these herbs, about which we will speak another time regarding the light of its eyes. And by this you may know that some of these herbs show their power to the things that live near them. Just as the earth does to the colubrine serpent and the mole and many other vermin and reptiles that see nothing. And also the earth strives to give brightness to the light of the eyes of the beasts that lie most within it and who most strive to lie within it. Of these beasts, I shall declare and tell you further when I speak to you of those that see more clearly than other common kinds of beasts: such as the wolf, the cat, and the little owl <note>original: "cheuette" (modern: chouette).</note>, and such animals. And the reason is because such beasts strive more to have the secret of the night..."

This is because it is more specially extracted from them than from the others. It is just like crystal, which is extracted from water and is made of "true water," as we will tell you better and more clearly hereafter.

¶ For this reason, said Placides, since we see that the beasts who strive to make a home in the earth have weaker sight than others, we know certainly that the earth is dark by its own nature; no light is born from it, and there are many other reasons. And if the earth had any light of its own, it could not be that one who lived within it [would see less]; but rather, the further one enters, the less one sees. It is an easy enough thing to know and perceive that the earth has no light of its own.

¶ Of the water, you can know that it has no light of its own: but it is more glassy and subtle than the earth. It is a certain thing that if water had light of its own, it would illuminate the air when the nights are dark: but it does not do so at all, which is a good sign that it has none, and this is true. Furthermore, in some waters one sees the gravel at the bottom during the day; yet during a dark night one cannot see it. If the water were bright with a clarity that was within itself, it would hold its clarity by day and by night: but it cannot retain it. Therefore it appears clearly that it has no light of its own: nor, if you put water in a dark place at night, will it shine there; for to tell the truth, water has no light of its own.

# The Heart of Secrets

...subtle and lighter; fire is as much greater than air and water, and therefore it is above all the elements. The earth is thicker, heavier, and darker; and so it is that in some places water finds a path beneath this earth where we are, which is much lighter and more subtle than that which is underneath. And know that otherwise—if it were not more subtle and lighter than that which is elemental—it could not, without the command of the Creator who can do all things, remain upon the waters. Now it is thus, as I tell you further: that when water enters this earth (which is a hundred times lighter than the other) and carries with it a great conduit beneath the ground through which this water runs, it would seem that a great light <note>original: "clarte"</note> issues from the water. This is not at all because of light that the water has of itself, but because of the thinness, the lightness, and the primacy that it has over the earth. And because in its course it draws air with it—which is, as I have told you, thinner and lighter than the earth or water—because one weight makes a path for another lightness, and one thickness for another thinness, it therefore seems to have light, but it does not: for thinness is not at all light, nor is lightness.

->[Image: A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring floral and foliate patterns within a square frame.]<-

**T** <note>The text begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'T'.</note> Just as it seems with water and air in the earth, so it seems with fire in the air. For as I have often told you before, fire is thinner and lighter than any of the four elements; yet it is true that because the sun goes around the elements, and fire is the thinnest and the hottest of the elements, and the sun is also hot, fire retains more of the sun’s light <note>original: "clarte"</note> because one heat retains the other. And so, when it is down in the air, it makes a thinner path for the eyes than the air does; and it seems that it is light, but this is nothing but a thinning of the path in the air and a demonstration that fire is thinner than air. Thus it clearly shows its thinness and its lightness in the air, just as the air and water do in the earth. 

But know that fire has no light except for as much as it takes from the sun. Furthermore, if fire had light of itself, it would cast rays and brilliance everywhere just like the sun; but although it is as much an element as air and water, if fire does not enter the air, it cannot cast a ray of light. But when it enters there, it truly seems to be what I have told you: that is, that it produces light. But it does not; any more than water in the earth shows anything but thinness against thickness—which are contraries—and lightness against heaviness—which are also contraries, as we will show you more clearly another time in the *Book of Accidents* <term>Book of Accidents: Likely a reference to a specific section of this text or a related medieval treatise on Aristotelian "accidents," which are properties (like color or heat) that exist within a substance but are not its essence.</term>. 

And it is necessary by force that one contrary appears beside the other; and the closer two contrary things are to one another, the more clearly they appear. Thus the lightness of fire shows itself against the heaviness of water, and thinness against thickness, and so we judge it to be light. But it is not. I tell you that the darkest ray of the sun that exists is clearer than all the fire in the world. And take fire or a burning candle and place it in a ray of the sun that comes directly from it, and the fire will lose its prominence there. And know that no glow will arise from that fire outside the sun's ray; instead, the fire will seem like a physical thing, like a...

He concludes that all light originates from the sun, noting that even a candle's flame pales when held in direct sunlight.</summary>

The course of the moon and stars is such that they are made to receive brightness when it strikes them directly, just like a shining mirror. When the sun strikes the moon directly, the whole moon shines, as I have told you before; and then, from the reflection <note>original: "ressort"</note> of that light, the air is sometimes illuminated at night, according to whether the moon is full or empty, sometimes more and sometimes less.

As I have told you before, know that of all the creatures the Creator made and created, those are the ones in which he placed reasonable souls, such as man. This soul has all the virtues that all other souls have, and more; this is the creature that God loves most, provided it does what it ought. It is reasonable, possesses angelic reason, and is perpetual, such that it shall never fail nor have an end. The Creator made this creature for his own honor and gave him a sign to recognize him, in that he made his sight look upward <note>In medieval philosophy, the upright posture of humans was seen as a physical sign of their divine orientation toward heaven, unlike animals who look toward the earth.</note> as a sign that man must leave earthly things for heavenly ones. And of this, Ovid says in a verse that God made man’s face turned upward to see the sky, and commanded man to look at the stars, where he says these verses: <note>Tymeo refers here to Ovid's *Metamorphoses*: "Os homini sublime dedit caelumque tueri iussit" (He gave to man an uplifted face and bade him stand erect and turn his eyes to heaven).</note>

To this creature, Aristotle says, is the most worthy of reasonable creatures and a glorious vessel to receive all wisdom <term>sapience: spiritual wisdom or higher knowledge</term>, all worth, all science, all reason and all discretion, all sense, all understanding, all memory, all foresight, and all knowledge of good and evil, by the power of the soul which is reasonable and which has angelic reason and sense. For this creature, God made the elemental earth, and willed and commanded that every other creature serve it. No beast is reasonable except this one, and God loves it more than any other; it is the most beautiful and the most reasonable that exists, as I have told you before.

¶ "Master, for God's sake," said Placides, "you speak to me of the reasonable soul and tell me that the soul of man has reason, and you tell me that no other soul has it but man's; I pray you, tell me..."

...acts that are governed by reason. ¶ Placidus, said Timaeus, I have already told you that <term>reason</term> <note>original: "raison"</note> is the knowledge of good and evil, and the ability to distinguish one from the other. ¶ But, said Placidus, remember all that you have told me; you said that reason is to know good and evil and to know how to choose one over the other. <header>## Of Philosophy</header>
<sig>D iii</sig>
<meta>catchword: Die</meta>

...not by any sense or understanding he possesses, but by a natural <term>instinct</term> <note>original: "estimance," referring to the faculty of "estimative power" which medieval philosophers believed allowed animals to perceive intentions, like a lamb sensing a wolf is dangerous without prior experience</note> which teaches naturally in the work of life and of the brute; but this is not at all by the work of reason, for as I have told you, no beast has reason except for man. And for this cause, man has reason over all beasts, as well as strength and lordship—even over beasts much stronger than he is, such as the elephant, the horse, and many others which are well known. These animals certainly know how to seek and use the food they must live upon through instinct, according to their nature, and not at all through reason. Know that this instinct which beasts possess serves as a aid to nature; for you must know that if beasts had reason, many of them are so strong that man could never overcome them by any force he possessed. ¶ Regarding the soul of man, I tell you that it is the most precious soul, the highest and most worthy that exists. And because man is such a worthy beast, such a high creature, and so powerful, for this reason the philosophers said that man was a <term>Microcosmos</term> <note>The "Little World." This was a central idea in medieval thought, suggesting the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note>—from *micros* in Greek which means <note>original: "minus" in Latin</note> "lesser" and from *comos* in Greek which means <note>original: "mundus" in Latin</note> "world." Thus, "microcosmos" means "the lesser world," because within man all four elements can be understood. And know first that just as the world is round, so too a man of good proportion is round; for a man of upright stature should have as much span in the reach of his arms as he has length in his height to form a perfect circle.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral and foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>The ancient philosophers said that the head of man signifies the heavens and the fire; the chest signifies the air; the belly signifies the sea; and the lower parts of man signify the earth. As the throne of God is in the heavens, so too the lordship of man’s senses is in the head. In the heavens, there are two great lights <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> which illuminate the elements. Likewise, in the head of man are two lights which illuminate the whole world—that is to say, the whole body—and these are the two eyes. And just as fire is the lightest of the elements, so too the head of man is his lightest and highest part. ¶ The chest of man signifies the air; for just as clouds, winds, brightness, and darkness fly and gather through the air, so too thoughts, reflections, joys, and sorrows fly through the chest. Furthermore, just as the waters descend into the sea and return again, so too all the <term>humors</term> <note>The vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament</note> of man must return and descend to the belly; and blood and humors abound there more than in any other part of man. There are many other reasons one can find why the belly is similar to the sea.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>Furthermore, the final part of man is that upon which he sits, as well as the feet. Just as the elements are seated upon the earth, and just as the earth is dry and of a cold nature, so too are the feet of man; for the feet are cold and dry. And know that these are the members where one can most often certainy perform a <term>test</term> <note>original: "experimēt"</note> on a sick man to see if he shall die or not: for when the feet become too cold, it is a sign that the body wishes to take its leave, as the feet then most resemble the earth; and thus, it is a mortal sign.

<summary>Timaeus defines man as a "microcosm" or "lesser world," explaining how the human body symbolically mirrors the structure of the universe and its elements. He describes a system of symbolic anatomy where the head represents heaven, the chest represents air, and the feet represent the cold, dry earth.</summary>
