<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the teacher Timaeus and his student Placides. Following the previous page's discussion of man as a "microcosm" or "little world," Timaeus now moves from philosophical definitions to the biblical account of creation, blending theology with medieval linguistic mysticism.</meta>

# The Heart of Secrets

One can take a sufficient example from the fact that man is the whole world; regarding which thing we will speak to you another time more at length and more clearly, and in more ways than we have done here.

¶ "Master," said **Placides**, "is man made or engendered?"

"Placides," said **Timaeus**, "by the reasoning of the elements which rise and descend one and the other, just as we have told you before, **Aristotle** said that <term>generation</term> <note>The process of being born or created.</note> was eternal; and his understanding was such as I have previously told you, and it was good in its own right: but it is necessary for you to know a clearer way."

**Moses** the prophet wrote in his book, which book is called **Genesis**, from <term>genero</term> <note>Latin: *genero*, meaning "to beget" or "to produce."</note>, which is to say 'engendering' because it speaks of generations. There he spoke of the first man, and what he says of him is the absolute truth.

¶ The first man who was made by the hand of the Creator was made of the <term>slime of the earth</term> <note>original: "lymon de la terre," referring to the moist clay or dust mentioned in Genesis 2:7.</note>; and then when the Creator had made him, he breathed into him that breath of life—that is to say, he placed there a spiritual soul—and this was true. Afterwards came a time when that man was sleeping; the Creator made woman from his rib, and also breathed into her spirit and life, and then joined them together in companionship and granted them the power of natural engendering. 

The philosophers said, in agreement with **Moses**, that this first man was called **Adam**; and they said that the Creator sent four angels to the four parts of the world, and commanded them to bring the names of the first stars that they should find, and they did so. 
*   The first brought the name of a star which is called **Anathole** <note>original: "Anathole" (Greek: *Anatole*), meaning the East.</note>. 
*   And the next, the name of another which is called **Disis** <note>original: "Disis" (Greek: *Dysis*), meaning the West.</note>. 
*   And the third, the name of another which is called **Archos** <note>original: "Archos" (Greek: *Arktos*), meaning the North.</note>. 
*   And the fourth, the name of another which is called **Mensobrios** <note>original: "Mensobrios," likely a corruption of the Greek *Mesembria*, meaning the South.</note>. 

And from these four names the Creator took one letter from each name and joined them together and made a name from them. He took from **Anathole**, which was the first star, the first letter: that was **a**. From **Disis** the first letter: that was **d**. From **Archos** the first letter: that was **a**. From **Mensobrios** the first letter: that was **m**. And thus was made the name of the first man.

¶ Thus was he called **Adam**. And this bestowing of the name moved the Devil to envy toward man even more than toward any other; for it signified that as long as man did what he ought, he would be sovereign over all the creatures that are within the other elements. And after this, **Adam** called his companion and named her **Eve** <note>original: "Eue"</note>, from **E**, which is to say <term>extra</term>, and from <term>vado</term> <note>Latin: "extra" (outside) and "vado" (to go).</note>. Thus she was called **Eva**, as if he wished to say "going outside" <note>original: "extra vadens."</note>. And for this reason, the philosophers say that woman by nature willingly goes outside the way of wisdom. 

Others say that she was called **Eva** from this word **Ave** <note>Latin: "Ave," a greeting meaning "Hail" or "Welcome."</note>, because **Ave** is a salutation and is the name of **Eva** taken in reverse. And some say **Eva** comes from **Ave** because **Eve** was the contrary of salvation to man; for as I have told you, **Ave** is worth as much as "salvation" <note>This refers to the common medieval wordplay where "Eva" (the cause of the Fall) is reversed to "Ave" (the first word of the Annunciation to Mary, which began the Redemption).</note>. God commanded the other creatures to be male and female in every manner, each according to its nature; and from **Adam** and **Eve** came the whole human generation, from which we are both wise and foolish. And for this, God gave to...

He also explores the linguistic origins of Eve's name, contrasting her role in the Fall with the concept of salvation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the teacher Timaeus and his student Placides. Timaeus has just explained the creation of the first man and woman (Adam and Eve) from the book of Genesis. Now, he addresses the biological and metaphysical nature of human reproduction and the relationship between the soul and the body.</meta>

### Of Philosophy. Leaf xxii.
->D iiii<-

Adam and his wife were given the knowledge of procreation and natural childbearing, just as it is with the beasts. "Master," said **Placides**, "is it through the soul or through the body that man possesses sense and reason?" **Timaeus** said, "Placides, I have told you that it is by the soul and not by the body."

"Master," said **Placides**, "for the sake of love, when man or the soul is engendered, which is made first: the soul or the body?" **Timaeus** said, "Placides, sometimes I wish to test your sense and your understanding. Tell me: which do you think should be made first?" "Master," said **Placides**, "I will tell you my opinion. It seems to me, just as you yourself have told me, that the soul of man is within the body. Therefore, it seems to me that the body is the vessel to receive and keep the soul. And it seems to me that the vessel must be made before anything is put into it. Thus, it seems to me by necessity that the body must be completely finished before the soul is placed within it; and because of this, it seems to me that the body is made before the soul." 

**Timaeus** said, "**Placides**, this is very poor reasoning. For sometimes, and often, a thing is made before the vessel into which it is placed. Does one not put water into a pot or a pitcher? And before the pot or pitcher were made, the water was made. So too can one put the soul into the body after it is made; and by your reasoning, one could be made before the other, and that is quite true." "Ah, Master," said **Placides**, "do you mean to say then that all souls are made before the body is made?" 

"**Placides**," said **Timaeus**, "I do not say that at all. Thus it is necessary for me to tell you what you have asked; for it would be a difficult thing for you to weigh by yourself, without teaching, the answer to your question. **Placides**, I tell you that the soul is the <term>matter</term> <note>original: "matiere." In medieval philosophy, this refers to the essential "seed" or formal cause, rather than physical substance.</note> of the body—that is to say, the seed from which man is made—and so they are made all together, and I will tell you how. But first, I will declare and speak of something else briefly. I want you to know, **Placides**, that regarding this question you have asked, many philosophers have dwelled in folly and lost their senses; among them was a great scholar of great knowledge named **Pythagoras**. This **Pythagoras** was commonly with a sort of people who, among the Jews, were cursed, and among other people were held to be wise; they were called **Sadducees**, who did not want to believe that man should ever be resurrected. Many other people were astonished and troubled by this, of which thing we will speak to you very strongly another time.

¶ To that which you ask, I answer you—and have already done so—that the substance of the body and the soul are made together. Yet, to make this clearly understood, it is necessary for you to know and recognize another thing. It is necessary first, for a man to be engendered, that males and females live together according to the order of nature. We call "male" he who has two <term>genitoires</term> <note>Testicles; from the Latin *genitalia*.</note>, from <term>gigno</term> <note>Latin: *gigno*, meaning "to beget," "to produce," or "to bring forth."</note> which is the same as "to engender." For this reason, these have the power to engender, unless something else prevents it; for there are many kinds of males who cannot engender, of whom we will speak to you hereafter and provide the classification."

<summary>Timaeus explains to Placides that the soul and body are created simultaneously, using the analogy of a vessel and its contents to debate whether the container must precede the contained. He also critiques the views of Pythagoras and the Sadducees regarding the soul and resurrection.</summary>

Having discussed the creation of the soul and the body, Timaeus now turns to a detailed anatomical and philosophical explanation of the male reproductive system and the mechanics of generation.</meta>

### The Heart of Secrets
->iiii C<-

"Placides," said **Timaeus**, "it is necessary for the male to have his genitals, which we have told you are called by another name *testiculi* <note>original: "testiculi," the Latin term for testicles</note>: that is to say, 'little witnesses' <note>This reflects a common medieval etymology linking the word for 'testicles' to 'testimony,' as they were seen as proof of male sex</note>, because they are witnesses to a person's sex, to know if they are male or female. And it is also necessary that man have a penis <term>penis: the text uses the word 'verge,' meaning a rod or wand, which was the standard medical term in Middle French</term> which is the chief of all the members above it."

"This penis is called *priapus* <note>original: "priape," referring to Priapus, the Greek god of fertility</note> from *priamo*, which means 'firstly,' and from 'appearing' or 'highest,' meaning visible; therefore the ancients said that this is the thing one looks at first in a newborn child, to know if he has this penis. And when it is seen, it is the first sign that this child is male, and the two genitals bear witness to it. This penis, which by right provides the matter [of generation], should be squared with two corners; two corners above and a third below, and this is because of the three paths that are within."

"For you should know that in every penis of male beasts—which is called a *priapus* and in the common tongue a cock <term>cock: the original uses 'vit,' a common vernacular term in the Middle Ages</term>—there are three paths, and all three end in one at the tip of the penis. One of these three paths comes straight from the bladder, and through this path comes the urine, of which we will speak hereafter. Through the second path comes the superfluity of humors. When the body is too gay <note>In this context, 'gay' refers to being overly vigorous, lively, or full of humors</note>, it produces a kind of grease or foam which descends from the penis through this path. If the body and the flesh did not deliver themselves of this substance, which is conceived in man by the humors moved by the fatness of the flesh, the danger of disease could well come, either through the mouth or through other paths, as we will tell you another time."

"But it often happens that these superfluities descend through this second path; and this is what issues from a man while sleeping sometimes, when he is at ease of flesh <note>A reference to nocturnal emissions or 'wet dreams'</note>. From these humors, one could not create generation, for there is no seed and it does not come by the natural way. And through these paths sometimes, when a man thinks of lust and has a desire to 'dwell' with a woman <note>A common euphemism for sexual intercourse</note>, there comes a substance clear as oil and white as silver, which comes through the humors and because of the heating of the man's will. This substance could not lead to engendering, because there is no seed, as I told you before, and it does not come by the natural way, but by that of which I spoke before and will speak more clearly."

"The third path is that through which the engendering seed comes, which seed is called sperm <note>original: "esperme"</note>. And all these three paths end at the tip of the cock, as I have told you before, so that it seems there is only one path. And there are as many paths as there are in the penis of the cock. By necessity, man must find [a counterpart] in the nature of woman; for as **Aristotle** says, man is 'occasioning' <note>This refers to the Aristotelian idea of the male as the active 'cause' or 'occasion' of reproduction</note>. For whereas he must have his nature and penis as a witness—lest there be an 'occasion' of a defect in the nature of man—by this 'defect' <note>In medieval Aristotelian thought, woman was often described as a 'defective male' (mas occasionatus), a concept used here to explain how the female body is uniquely 'suited' to receive the male and act as the vessel for the child</note> she is ready and suited to receive and undergo the work of man's right according to nature, and to be the vessel of engendering."

"**Master**," said **Placides**, "now remember your word; and tell me, for the sake of love, what is sperm, and where does it issue from, and where does it come from, before you speak further? And what is the reason why there is more engendering seed in this thing [than the others]?"

<summary>Timaeus describes male reproductive anatomy, explaining the etymology of "testicles" as witnesses of sex and detailing three internal channels for urine, arousal fluids, and sperm. He invokes Aristotle to explain the complementary roles of men and women in the process of "engendering."</summary>

# On Philosophy. Leaf xxiiii.

"...clear to me what you say, which comes and descends by another path."

"Gladly," said **Timaeus**. "**Placides**," said **Timaeus**, "that which we call sperm <term>sperm: the text uses 'esparme,' referring to the reproductive seed</term>, which often contains the germ of engendering, comes—as **Aristotle** says (and he speaks the truth)—from the purest blood of a man, and this pure blood comes from the heart. And with this **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and many other philosophers agree; they say that it would be better for a man to lose a pound and a half of his blood through the veins of his arm or by a wound from an injury than it would be to surrender, beyond his rightful will, half an ounce of sperm by overexerting himself; and many philosophers agree on this."

"Master," said **Placides**, "is sperm then red like blood, since it is pure blood?"

"**Placides**," said **Timaeus**, "the philosophers say as I have told you: truly it is pure blood. But it is, as they say, whitened by the office of the testicles, which are called the 'genitories' <note>original: 'genitoires,' meaning the organs of generation</note>, as I have told you before. Other philosophers say that truly, because it is white, it must be—since it is pure blood—that it is whitened for some reason. They make a comparison between blood and sperm just like that of the sea and the macrocosm <note>The text uses 'macrocome' here to mean the universe</note>, which is the great world. It is named from *macros* <note>original Greek: 'makros,' meaning large</note> which is to say 'greater' <note>original Latin: 'maior'</note> and from *comos* <note>original Greek: 'kosmos,' meaning order or world</note> which is the same as 'world' <note>original Latin: 'mundus'</note>; and this is the great world. And it is so named to distinguish it from man. And for this reason, man is called a 'macrocosm' <note>The author uses 'macrocome' here, but means 'microcosm'—the 'little world'—as clarified by the next phrase</note>, that is to say, a little world. 

For just as from the sea, which is of a wild nature and flavor, there come—as I have told you before—those fresh waters that travel through the narrowness of the veins of the earth, so too from the blood of man there descends and comes through the veins of the flesh that which is divided into many parts; for one part rises and the other descends. That from the brain descends to the nose, and sometimes that from the heart rises to the eyes; and that from the lungs <term>lungs: the text uses 'pommon,' an old form of 'poumon'</term> to the mouth. That which rises to the eyes creates tears for many reasons: sometimes through sadness, sometimes through joy and through pity; regarding which we shall speak to you more clearly another time. 

The other blood, which rises through the wider paths from the stomach and the lungs to the mouth, is just like the scum of a cauldron. For the stomach is in the body of man and woman—the vessel that receives the food and where the food is cooked in the body, which is then divided into many other parts by the limbs, as we shall describe to you hereafter—it is just like the scum of a cauldron that rises to the top; in the same way, the scum of the stomach rises to the top and comes out through the mouth, and this is saliva; and that scum which comes from the lungs as well. 

The lungs are the vessel that draws in and rejects the air like a bellows, and it has its paths to the nose and the mouth. And because it draws in and puts out the air in this way, it is said that it causes one to speak. And the more a man speaks, provided he is naturally moist, the more he will have a wet mouth; and this moisture is called drool <note>original: 'baveure'</note>. This scum comes from the lungs; and while sleeping, when a man lies down uncomfortably, then the paths of the lungs become narrower than is right, and then the lungs are burdened, as when a man snores in his sleep. 

To the heart rises blood, and to the eyes as I have already told you, which through the narrowness of the paths and by the...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Timaeus and Placides from page 24. Having previously discussed how blood is "whitened" into sperm, Timaeus now expands on how blood is transformed into all other bodily fluids—tears, urine, and sweat—and how diet affects the nature of a person's blood.</meta>

# The Heart of Secrets

...[sub]tlety <note>original: 'soutiuete,' referring to the refining process of the blood</note> of the veins of the flesh becomes pure and clear, and these are the tears. Again, from the stomach descends blood which is changed into clear water, which water descends by very subtle ways into the bladder, and this is the urine. Again, by the distress of heat conceived within the body, blood goes out through all the extremities of the veins of man, which extremities are called <term>pori: the Latin term for pores, the tiny openings in the skin</term>, and these are those little holes that release the sweat when heat is conceived; and the sweat comes from the blood which, through the narrow ways, becomes clear. And where the sweat comes most naturally and by way of the path, hairs and little hairs grow more readily by nature, such as under the armpits and in the secret places, just like the grass that comes from the earth springs and is born more readily in moist and warm places than elsewhere, as you will see hereafter. And just so, hair grows readily in moist places, such as at the base of the belly and under the armpits of the arms, as I have told you, for these are the moistest places upon a man. And just as you see (and can frequently see) the dew rise up against the little leaves of the herbs, just so the sweat comes readily through the hairs; for there are many more hairs on a man than you think, which because of their delicacy <note>original: 'premierete,' meaning their primary or nascent state</note> and their subtlety cannot be seen; you can know this if you look at your flesh between yourself and the sweat of the day or the brightness of the sun.

NOW know that sweat comes from the blood: for blood is divided in many ways. One part of it becomes pure flesh, as I will show you clearly hereafter; and one part of it goes into water, as I have told you. And you can test this: for if you have yourself bled from a vein in the arm or elsewhere, and your blood is kept in a vessel, if you let it cool and settle, you will see the water <note>The "water" here refers to blood serum</note> come from it by itself on one part, and the other part is thick. And that which becomes water is that part which should have gone into sweat or into urine, as I have told you; and the other blood is what becomes flesh to sustain and nourish the limbs. Just as the blood from the stomach, the brain, or the lung—through the narrowness of the paths of the veins through which it makes its way for certain reasons, as I have told you—becomes water or white foam, just so the philosophers say (and it is true) that the blood which descends from the body when a man lies with a woman <note>original: 'habite a femme,' a common euphemism for sexual intercourse</note> becomes entirely white through the narrowness of the veins. And know that regarding the nourishment by which man and woman are fed, it is from meats <note>In Middle French, 'viandes' refers to food in general, not just animal flesh</note> that are tempered in the air of all the elements; and certain other beasts also. And because of this, it happens that when venom is able to mix with their blood, it kills them and extinguishes them suddenly, and many a worthy man has sometimes died from it. And know certainly that any beast which man and woman use for their eating could be nourished for a long time in such a manner that all its blood would be poisonous and would kill whoever ate of it. And do not marvel at this, for it is true of beasts and of birds; and of this we will tell you many marvels hereafter. Again, know that in the same way, a human creature, man or woman, could be nourished so that they would take on a nature contrary to their blood; therefore I tell you...

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the transmutation of bodily substances. Having established how diet and heat affect the blood and humors, the text now shifts into an extraordinary example of how human nature can be fundamentally altered through habit and "nourishment," specifically through the legend of the Poison Maiden—a story often associated with Aristotle’s advice to Alexander the Great in medieval lore.</meta>

# On Philosophy. Leaf 24.

...one could make a man or woman so venomous that they would kill people by their touch. Do not marvel at this, for it is true; and just as wine, which is hot by its true nature, takes on a contrary nature when it turns to vinegar—for vinegar is cold in itself—just so can the nature <note>original: 'sens,' here meaning the physical constitution or essence</note> of a man or woman take on a nature contrary to itself. Certain knowledge of this was given in the time of Alexander the Great, the king who was the son of Philip of Macedon.

When Alexander was born, there was a king who was his neighbor who greatly desired to disinherit Alexander’s father of his land. He had it seen through omens <note>original: 'sors,' referring to divination or the casting of lots to predict the future</note> what might become of that child; and it was found by the lot that if Alexander lived, he would defeat that king. Then that king considered how he might subtly cause him to die. So he took a young maiden of beautiful form and good lineage, and as soon as she was born from her mother's womb, he had her placed privately in a secret place and had her nourished on pure, mortal poison. And know that as it was later learned and known, he had more than one taken and nourished in this manner; but they all died except for one alone, who escaped death <note>original: 'desquitte,' meaning she survived the "trial" of the poison</note> and was clever and beautiful. And that king had her learn the art of harping to be more pleasing. When she came of age so that in appearance she could well endure a man, she was marvelously beautiful and pleasant, and knew how to harp exceedingly well. And she was so carefully guarded that it was a great wonder. This maiden was so poisoned that she corrupted the very air, so great was her venom. She even killed the animals with which she lived.

Long before Alexander was of age to bear arms, or to hold people in subjection, or to begin any war, that king who had caused those maidens to be nourished in the manner I have said (of whom only one remained) had a great war started against him by a king who was stronger in men-at-arms and artillery than he was. It happened that the king who had nourished the maiden was besieged and attacked by a very great army; so much so that this maiden was sent out by night, very well dressed, with two others who were not venomous. And she, along with her two companions, came before the king who led that host and began to play the harp. And when the king saw her so beautiful, he marveled and desired her greatly, and wished to lie with her. But he might well have done without it; for in the evening, when he sent for her privately to his pavilion because he wished to take solace with her, as soon as he had kissed her, he fell down stone dead. Many other knights of the host who had approached that maiden that day died that same evening. And before anyone took notice of this, the king who had nourished his maiden—who already knew through spies that the maiden was to sleep with the king that evening—came with great force to attack those who had besieged him. And those who were without a chief and without a lord were quickly defeated. Thus the king who had nourished the maiden delivered himself from his enemy by the venomous maiden. Then he took his maiden back with him and had her guarded better than before, and had her nourished then on purer poison than he had ever done before.

<summary>This page recounts the legend of the "Poison Maiden," a girl raised on venom from birth to be used as a biological weapon. It illustrates the medieval belief that human nature can be inverted, much like wine turning into vinegar, through extreme environmental conditioning.</summary>
<keywords>Poison Maiden, Alexander the Great, Philip of Macedon, alchemy, transmutation of nature, biological warfare, medieval legends</keywords>

<meta>The previous page introduced the legend of the Poison Maiden during the time of Alexander the Great. This page continues the physiological explanation of how bodily fluids—tears, urine, sweat, and reproductive seeds—are all derived and "refined" from blood, providing a pseudo-scientific basis for how a body might be "nourished" on poison to change its very nature.</meta>

# The Heart of Secrets

...[subtlety] of the veins of the flesh becomes pure and clear, and these are the tears. Furthermore, from the stomach descends blood that is transformed into clear water; this water descends through very subtle pathways into the bladder, and this is the urine. Again, by the pressure of heat generated within the body, blood issues from all the extremities of the human veins, which extremities are called **pores** <term>pori: the minute openings in the skin through which fluids and gasses pass</term>; and these are those small holes that release sweat when heat is generated. Sweat comes from the blood, which clarifies as it passes through narrow passages; and where sweat issues most naturally, there nature more readily produces hair and fine fuzz, such as under the armpits and in secret places, just as the grass of the earth rises and is born more readily in moist and hot places than elsewhere—as you shall see hereafter. And thus hair grows readily in moist places, such as at the base of the belly and under the armpits, as I have told you, for these are the moistest places upon a person. And just as you see (and can frequently see) the dew rise up along the leaves of herbs, so too sweat readily emerges through the fine hairs; for there are many more small hairs on a person than you might imagine, which because of their fineness and subtlety cannot be seen; you may know this if you look at your flesh between yourself and the daylight or the brightness of the sun.

Now know that sweat comes from the blood, for blood is divided in many ways: one part becomes pure flesh, as I will clearly show you hereafter; one part turns into water, as I have told you. You may test this: for if you are bled from a vein in the arm or elsewhere, and your blood is held in a vessel and you let it cool and settle, you will see the water come out of it on its own at the top, while the other part is thick. That which becomes water is the part that should have gone into sweat or urine, as I told you; and the other blood becomes flesh to sustain and nourish the limbs. Just as the blood from the stomach, the brain, or the lungs—through the narrowness of the pathways of the veins through which it travels for certain reasons, as I have told you—becomes water or white foam, so the philosophers <note>Referring to "natural philosophers," the scientists of the Middle Ages, who followed the teachings of Aristotle and Galen.</note> say (and it is true) that the blood which descends from the body when a man dwells with a woman <note>A common medieval euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note> becomes entirely white through the narrowness of the veins <note>The text refers to the theory that semen is "concocted" or highly refined blood.</note>.

And know that the nourishment by which man and woman are sustained comes from foods tempered by the air of all the elements; and certain other beasts likewise. Because of this, it happens that when venom is able to mix with their blood, it kills and extinguishes them suddenly, and many a worthy man has died from it. And know for certain that any beast that men and women use for food could be nourished for a long time in such a way that all its blood would be poisonous and would kill anyone who ate it. Do not marvel at this, for it is true of both beasts and birds; and of this we shall tell you many wonders hereafter. Again, know that a human creature, man or woman, can be nourished in such a way that they take on a nature contrary to their blood; therefore I tell you that...

### On Philosophy. Leaf xxiv.

...could make a man or woman so venomous that they would kill people by their touch; and do not wonder at it: for it is true. Just as wine, which is hot by its natural state, takes on a contrary nature when it sours (for vinegar is cold in itself), so too can the constitution of a man or woman take on a nature contrary to itself. Of this, certain knowledge was given in the time of Alexander the Great, the king who was the son of Philip of Macedonia.

When Alexander was born, there was a king who was his neighbor who greatly desired to disinherit Alexander’s father of his land. He had it examined through lots <note>the practice of "sors," or divination to predict the future</note> what might happen to that child, and it was found by the lot that if Alexander lived, he would defeat that king. Then that king considered how he might make him die subtly. He had a little maiden of beautiful form and of good lineage taken, and as soon as she was born from her mother’s womb, he had this maiden put in a secret place and had her nourished on pure mortal venom. And you should know, as it was later learned and known, he had more than one child taken and nourished in this manner, but they all died except for one; she survived and was clever and beautiful. And that king had her learn the art of harping <note>playing the harp</note> to be more pleasing. When she came to a fair age, such that by appearance she was ready for a man, she was marvelously beautiful and pleasant, and she knew very well how to harp. She was so carefully guarded that it was a great wonder. This maiden was so poisoned that she corrupted the air, so great was her envenomation. She even killed the beasts with which she lived.

After a long time, when Alexander was of an age to bear arms, to hold people in subjection, and to begin any war, that king who had the maidens nourished in the manner I told you before (of whom only one remained) had a great war started against him by another king who was stronger in men-at-arms and artillery <note>original: "artilleries"—referring to engines of war like catapults or early siege weapons</note> than he. It happened that the king who had nourished the maiden was besieged and attacked by a very great army. The maiden was sent out by night, very well adorned, with two others who were not venomous. She and her two companions came before the king who led that army and began to play the harp. When the king saw her so beautiful, he desired her marvelously and wished to lie with her; but he might well have done without it <note>meaning he should have abstained for his own safety</note>. For in the evening, when he sent for her to his pavilion privately because he wanted to take his pleasure with her, as soon as he had kissed her, he fell down stone dead. Many other knights of the army who had approached the maiden to feast with her that day also died that evening. And before anyone could take guard against this, the king who had nourished the maiden—who already knew through spies that the maiden was to sleep with the king that evening—came with great force before that hour to attack those who had besieged him. Those who were without a leader or lord were soon defeated. Thus, the king who had nourished the maiden delivered himself from his enemy by the venomous maiden; then he took his maiden back with him and had her better guarded than before, and had her nourished with purer venom than he had ever done before.

# The Heart of Secrets

¶ Afterwards, it happened that word became known that King Alexander had begun to wage war, and had already conquered and defeated <term>Darius</term><note>Daire in the original; refers to Darius III of Persia</note>, the powerful King of Persia. His name was already feared and doubted in a great part of the world.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'E' with floral and foliage patterns inside the letter frame.</image-desc>

**E**ventually, the king who had raised the maiden heard this news. He had four maidens dressed most richly, and the fifth was the **Venomous Maiden**, who surpassed all the others in beauty, charm, attire, and modesty. This king, who greatly feared—and had always feared—the life, the upbringing, and the renown of Alexander, sent these five maidens to Alexander as a sign of obedience and a sign of love (or so it seemed by right reason). They were sent as a gift along with five young pages, handsome and pious, with fine horses, great wealth, and beautiful jewels, the better to cover his treason. 

And when Alexander had received this gift, he saw these young ladies; he saw that particular maiden, so pleasing and so "serpentine" <note>original: "bien serpant," likely a play on her venomous nature or her graceful, winding movements</note>, and she pleased him marvelously. He could hardly restrain himself from running to embrace, kiss, and welcome her at once, for he was wonderfully tempted. 

But **Aristotle**, who was a wise and well-educated scholar of his court, and **Socrates**, his master <note>Medieval texts often grouped famous philosophers like Socrates, Aristotle, and Plato together as contemporaries or advisors to Alexander, regardless of historical chronology</note>, perceived the maiden's poison. They could not allow Alexander to touch her. When they told this to Alexander, he could not believe it; however, he greatly feared his master Socrates, so he did not dare contradict him. 

Socrates then had two servants, well and handsomely dressed, called before Alexander. He made one of them kiss the maiden, and immediately the man fell dead. Then he did the same with the other, and he also fell dead instantly. Thus Alexander saw and recognized clearly that what his master Socrates told him was true. Yet he did not stop there; he had her touch other animals, such as dogs and horses, which all died instantly. And so Alexander was delivered from death at that time by his master Socrates, who was of great value to him in many ways through his wisdom and his ingenuity.

¶ When Alexander had clearly perceived the maiden's venom, he had her head cut off and then had her body burned far away from people. That very same evening, many knights and barons died who had touched that maiden. For this reason, Alexander had a better excuse than he had before to wage war against the man who had sent him such a gift. We shall speak no more of this, but rather return to our main subject.

¶ The ancient philosophers and physicians called this kind of venom **Anapellis**. *Anapellis* is derived from *Ana*, which means to return or go back, and *pello*, which means to drive away <note>original: "Ana qui vault retourner... et de pello qui vault a dire deboute." This is a medieval folk etymology for a type of poison</note>. For this is a nature to be feared and shunned, just as it was in the maiden of whom I have spoken; and because this venom is so cruel, it must be driven back from all things. 

¶ You may also have heard how <term>sperm</term><note>esparme</note> is white, and yet it is made of the pure blood of a man or a woman, coming directly from the heart. And you should know that I say "man or woman" because a woman also has her desire just as a man does, and produces reproductive fluid as a man does, of which we will speak hereafter. **Placides**...

### Of Philosophy. Leaf xxv.

->E i<-

Timaeus said: just as there are three paths in the member <term>member</term><note>original: "verge," literally a rod or staff, used here for the male reproductive organ</note> of man, it is necessary that woman has a nature within that brings urine to the final orifice. We call it an "orifice," which is derived from the word for "mouth" <note>original: "os"</note>; these are the entrances of the woman (of which she has three, just as I told you of the three paths in the member of man). And just as the three paths of the member end in one, so the three paths in the woman end at the first orifice and the first entrance. One of these paths in the woman, just like in the man, brings out the urine; the second, the superfluity <note>refers to menstrual discharge or bodily waste</note>; the third, the true sperm <note>original: "esparme"</note>. ¶ There is a vessel in the woman called the <term>matrix</term><note>the uterus</note>; this is the womb, which is very dangerous regarding both illnesses and other matters. This matrix has an orifice called the "second" because it is the second entrance, and at this orifice the path where the sperm comes is joined; and this second path, which is called the second orifice, divides internally into seven paths, which are seven receptacles <note>the medieval "seven-chambered uterus" theory: three for boys, three for girls, and one for hermaphrodites</note> within the matrix to receive sperm or other things, whether according to nature or against nature, as we shall discuss hereafter.

Placides, said Timaeus, the second orifice is rightly called the <term>Vulva</term>: for it is called "second," though some philosophers called it *Volueus* <note>original: "Volueus," a folk etymology linking vulva to the Latin 'volvere' (to turn)</note>, meaning "turning," because this vulva sometimes turns within itself toward the path that brings the sperm; for this reason, that orifice is called the vulva. And that vessel to which this vulva is tied was collectively called the *matris*, from *matrix* in Latin. This *matris* is derived from *mater*, which is to say "mother": for these seven receptacles are the parts in which the mother can receive the fruit and the seed to be planted. Just as we call the "egg-producer" <note>original: "louuiere," likely referring to the ovary or oviduct in poultry</note> in birds that part in which the female bird can receive the seed of those birds to make eggs according to her nature. ¶ Placides, said Timaeus, so that you do not wander too far from your subject in understanding the question you asked me, I inform you that to engender a human body, whether male or female, so that it is conceived naturally, many things are required. Know that it is necessary that just as the man fulfills his desire until the child is conceived, the woman must also fulfill her own desire, and both together must release sperm <note>Medieval biology often followed the "two-seed" theory, which held that both parents contributed reproductive fluid</note>. ¶ Placides, said Timaeus, I do not tell you that one sperm begins to flow as soon as the other: but know that it is necessary for one to follow the other. I am speaking of when there is carnal procreation. And because when one follows the other, the matrix in its first orifice mixes and turns them together; for this reason, it was called *Vulva* from *voluo*, which means to turn or whirl like a <term>vortex</term><note>original: "vertillon"</note>. A vortex is the name for a kind of pit that makes the waters churn within themselves, then swallows them and casts them out again while turning, as many waters do—especially great rivers, and also in the gulf of the sea which is called the "navel of the sea" <note>the "nombul de la mer," a central oceanic whirlpool</note> because it is in the middle of the oceans, as the ancient mariners say, just as the navel is in the middle of the belly. This acts just like a type of sea-peril which is called <term>Charybdis</term><note>original: "Caribdis"; a legendary whirlpool from Greek mythology</note> in the sea.

Heat makes the veins stiffen and swell. That wind which is conceived within the body by the percussion / that is to say by the striking of the souls, is the most natural / that wind makes the sperm issue forth. And for this reason the sperm issues forth as if by turns and not all together: but as if by gulps <note>original: "gorgees," meaning spurts or mouthfuls</note>.

¶ When the sperm of the man comes all alone the matrix does not receive it: for the second orifice <term>orifice</term><note>an opening or entrance</note> is closed / because it draws toward the heart what the woman must do and intends still to do a thing that is to come from the woman and not to be received. ->## On Philosophy. Leaf xxvi.<-

the matrix <note>original: "marris"; the uterus</note> acts as a receptacle through several lines of nature / just like the painter who portrays the figure of the thing he wishes to make; and the germination of the sperm of every beast is made by nature to outline and portray the second matter of the beast from which it comes. And of this thing we shall speak to you quite soon and more hereafter. And so that your mind is not too burdened with words, I wish to respond to what you asked me: which is first, the body or the soul? I respond to you as Aristotle said, and he spoke the truth. In the founding <note>In the sense of casting metal in a mold.</note> of the sperm the soul is created if the matrix receives it / and in creating the soul, the sperms are founded if the matrix receives them / and of this I, who speak to you, will provide an example because I want you to understand it better.

I tell you that when one makes bells and chimes <note>original: "fains et campanes"</note> to ring / two things are necessary for this. The metal from which they are made / and it is also necessary that there be sound. In the same way, two things are necessary to make a man and every other creature. The matter to make the body / which is the sperm / and the soul which is in the body extends itself; and just as with the bells or the chime when they are made, the sound is made with them, and in making them the sound is made / so it is exactly with the man or the beast, for as I have said of the sound, in the founding of the sperm the soul is created / and in creating the soul the sperm is spread.

I will give you yet another example. Just as when one strikes two stones one against the other, two things are born which are both made together and in the same hour. What are these two things? One is the sound / and the other is the fire <note>referring to the spark</note> / so it is with the forming and co-creating of man or beast: for the soul and the body are made all together / and if man fails in nature / he fails in the working. I do not say that if the matter of the body is slightly deficient that the man fails entirely because of it: but he fails in part, as we shall speak to you more clearly hereafter and when we have more leisure.

"Fair sweet master," said Placides. "Now may it not displease you if I ask a question / and out of love, please answer me. You tell me that man or the living creature is made like the bell in which the body and the sound are made together. But I see clearly that the bell cannot ring when it is made if there is not something else, such as a hammer or a clapper <note>original: "bateil"</note> with which that bell is struck / and I see elsewhere that man and beast and living things can move as long as the soul is there. Therefore it seems to me, since you gave me the example of the bell, it ought to ring always just as man lives as long as the soul is in him."

"Placides," said Timaeus / "now I fear that from your bad thinking comes great peril and great pain in advising a young man. You are more foolish than I thought, or you ask through spiteful questions / and know that I marvel at it and consider myself ill-repaid by your question."

"Ha, fair sweet master," said Placides, "you told me at the beginning when I first came to you that I ought indeed to ask about that which I doubted / and know that I do not ask it out of pride nor out of bad thinking."

This is because a thing that is common is vile, but a thing found and known with difficulty is precious; and this is for the sake of the preciousness of the meaning understood by those who truly wish to know it. Know that when we have found this depth within you, we will speak to you of this matter. gathering that of which he perceives something of its sound; of a single penny or a single piece of metal, a sound of nature. Master, for God's sake, said Placides, now answer me one thing about which I am in very great dismay. I see that beasts have their assemblies and their natures at determined times—cows, sheep, pigs, and dogs—just as the time that they are in heat <note>the text lists various regional or technical terms for animals in heat: "en fault", "en luist", "en taist", and for dogs "en gest"</note>. When these beasts are outside of their terms, or when they have accomplished their natures, and they have conceived their young, their nature can no longer suffer that a male approach them, nor that they perform coitus, nor do the males pursue them strongly. And I see that a woman, even when full and pregnant, and a man at all times (and in all months, and in all seasons), willingly perform coitus together, and I marvel greatly how this goes.

Placides, said Tymeo, I will answer you where this comes from. It is true as you say: but I told you before that man and woman have reason and memory; and do you know what memory is? It is remembrance; and it is one of the beautiful gifts that ever the Creator gave to any creatures in the world. Wherefore the wise man says in this word that among the benefits of a single nature, nothing in the world is found more worthy than memory; it is a very great thing to understand well, and a marvelous thing to bring back to [mind]...

memory; and these are the four things that make a man perfectly wise when he can possess them. And I dare tell you that a man who possesses them would be wiser than any other, and yet they are not difficult to obtain for one who would be willing to put in the effort. ¶ The first is to willingly hear both good and evil; that is to say, to test all things <note>This is a common medieval reference to 1 Thessalonians 5:21: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."</note>. ¶ The second is to bring things back to memory, of which I spoke to you before; and this every man must do who truly wishes to know, for a man who has no remembrance is just like a brute beast, as I will tell you another time hereafter. ¶ The third is to choose the good from the evil; and understand well that he does not choose well who takes the worse part: but he is good and right who takes the better part, which is to say: take that which is good. ¶ The fourth is that after one has chosen the good part—that is, the good from the evil—that one actually performs the good. For good is worth nothing if it is not done, just as I have told you before: that knowing evil is not itself evil, but it is evil to do evil. Therefore, as the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, who discussed the knowledge of opposites in his works on logic and ethics.</note> says: of things that are opposites, there is one and the same discipline—that is to say, the same judgment—and since good and evil are opposites, to know evil is not evil; but it is evil to work evil. By such judgment I tell you that knowing good is nothing; but working good is a great good. And whatever other philosophers might say constitutes the sovereign good in life, I tell you for my part that the sovereign good in life is doing good.

In these four things—willingly hearing everything, bringing everything to memory, choosing one from the other, and doing what one has chosen—a man would be marvelous on earth and toward God. Some of the philosophers said that there is one virtue in man which greatly embellishes the others, and it is true, I agree: to have been given eloquence <note>original: "faconde"</note>, which is good speech. But not everyone can have this, except as nature gives it to them; and we will speak of this to you another time, for it is necessary to return to our subject, and I will answer what you asked before. ¶ "Placides," said Tymeo, "as I have told you, man and woman are rational by reason of the soul and they have memory; but other beasts do not. I tell you that when the flesh moves the beast, and it is in good health and great ease, it performs its <term>coitus (cohit): The act of sexual intercourse.</term>; and then beasts all do so, each according to its nature. And when they have finished and the flesh of one has cooled—that is to say, the flesh of the female is cooled of <term>lust (luxure): In this context, the physical heat or urge for reproduction.</term> or heavy with conception—and the flesh of the male is also cooled, they do not dwell one with the other; for the flesh does not require it, and when the flesh does not require it, the beast does not know how to seek it. But it is a different thing for a man or a woman; for according to what I have told you, they have the memory of dwelling one with the other. There is a delight of the flesh, such that man and woman remember that delight which they have in coitus; and by that remembrance the flesh is moved and heated so that man and woman perform coitus in all seasons, while the others do not, except when nature directly (and not at all by remembrance) summons them; and this is the direct reason for it."

"Willingly," the master answered him. "I tell you, Placides, that by many causes..."

# On Philosophy. Folio xxviii.

<margin>E iiii</margin>

sperm can enter the womb; but once it has entered and been naturally received, you should know that the internal orifice is as closed as if it were all naturally joined. Aristotle says (and the other philosophers agree, such as Empedocles, Mitrastius <note>Likely a corruption of a name like Metrodorus or similar, though often cited in medieval compilations alongside Aristotle.</note>, and many others) that this orifice is so tightly closed that the small point of a needle could not penetrate it, nor could a joint be divided. And after that, until the birth is completed and the child has come out, a woman has more distaste for intimacy with a man than at any other time. And when the sperm is gathered and mixed together and contained within its natural and proper vessel, it softens and heats up through the force of being retained and becomes thick, just like pure milk. And because man is the creature that God ever loved most, as I have told you before (and will tell you more of another time), we will first speak to you of the true nature of man: how he is formed in the womb and from what matter, according to the evidence of the ancient philosophers who speak of it in many ways and in many places.

¶ When it is received and retained—that is to say, the sperm, as I told you before—it remains in the manner of milk until the ninth day. Then there descends into the womb the blood with which women are marked monthly and which is accustomed to issue from them, which is called *maustre* <note>original: "maustre"</note>; this word comes from *mario* <note>original: "mario," meaning to flow</note> which means "to flow" and from *intra* <note>original: "intra," meaning inside</note> which means "within," because it flows inside. As long as the woman is not carrying a child, this blood, which descends through several veins into the womb, issues out through all the orifices because they are all open. But once the womb has retained the seed, as I told you, the orifice inside the womb is immediately closed, so that this blood called *maustre*—when it has entered and descended through subtle veins like sweat inside the womb—cannot leave because the womb is closed, as I told you. When women are not pregnant (and they experience this *maustre*), some courtly folk say that women are then "in their flowers" <note>A common medieval euphemism for menstruation, comparing the cycle to the seasonal blooming of plants.</note>; and know, Placides, that courtliness comes from wisdom, and generosity comes from worth. ¶ When the *maustre* has descended into the womb and finds no free path by which it can leave, it mixes with the sperm that is inside in the manner of milk, and then it becomes flesh.

Placides, Tymeo said this: in making a cheese, there are three things. There is the milk when the rennet is put in, and a thing called cream, and from that one makes butter or other things. And then it is put into the *casule* <note>original: "casule," a mold</note> which is called a cheese-vat; and it is called *casule* because of the word *casa* <note>original: "casa," meaning house</note> which means "house," and *casula* <note>original: "casula," meaning little house</note> "little house," because it is the little house in which the cheese is made. And from this *case* <note>original: "case"</note> comes the word *caseus* <note>original: "caseus," meaning cheese</note> which is to say, cheese. When the milk from which the cheese is made is pressed into this mold, the liquid issues from it like clear water, and that which is solid remains; and then the shape of that vat is impressed into the milk, whether it be round or square, or striped, or if one were to make one stripe lengthwise and another across, which figure Christians gladly make on top and call a cross.

# On Philosophy. Leaf xxviii.

...the sperm <note>original: "lesparme"</note> can enter the womb <note>original: "la marris"</note>: but when it has entered and been naturally received, know that the internal orifice is as closed as if it were entirely joined by nature. Then the shape of the mold is imprinted into that milk, whether it be round, square, or striped—or someone might make one stripe lengthwise and the other across, a figure which Christians gladly make on top and call a cross.

# The Heart of Secrets
### iii. j.

It is just so in the womb <note>original: "marris"</note> as blood is in a cheese mold <note>original: "foisselle," a wicker basket used to drain curds</note>: and the milky sperms <note>medieval science often held that both parents contributed a "seed" or sperm</note> are mixed, then a clear portion of this rises to the breasts which is converted into milk. From that which remains, the flesh is formed from one part and the bones from another, and the soul—which was placed and created with the sperm—strives to expand the flesh. The milk <note>referring here to the embryonic fluid or "seed"</note> is pressed into the shape of the womb just like cheese in a mold, which takes such a figure as the mold provides for it. And just as the milk rises more strongly to the breast and the fruit <note>the fetus</note> comes closer to its exit, the milk in the breast becomes thicker. But know that it will never be truly fine until the child is born.

¶ **"Master," said Placides.** "How can it be known that a woman dwells more willingly with a man when she has conceived than at other times? It is a marvel to know, and you put a great thing in my heart by placing this in my understanding."

¶ **"Placides," said Tymeo.** "I make you understand it more surely than it was done for me. I had great anxieties studying and seeking knowledge from whatever I could acquire, neither by heritage nor by conquest; one year ten marks, another twenty, in another year forty—or more or less as I was able to have. And know that concerning this matter and others, I will make you know and recognize as much in one year as I was able to extract from the counsel of masters in ten years with great difficulty. To such an extent did the rich man have a great advantage over the poor; for it is necessary that the poor man be able to know nothing except by his own wits, and to spend whatever he has to give to his masters. If a rich man gave his master the tenth part of his income for one year during his life, he would think he had purchased his knowledge too dearly. For this reason, there are more common people who are very wise than there are great lords, which is a great pity. For it is a very beautiful thing to be wise and rich, for it is said that riches embellish the virtues. From this, you must understand one who uses riches as he ought, and of this we shall speak another time. I know that you are of a good nature and that I will not lose my labor on you; and the better you reward <note>original: "guerdonnerez"</note> my pain and the service I do for you, the more you will work for your own profit and advantage. We must return to our subject and respond to what you have asked me."

"I tell you that a woman has a greater desire for a man when she is pregnant than at any other time. I will tell you how we know this. First, I tell you that there was a woman philosopher named Trotula <note>Trotula of Salerno, a famous 11th-century female physician and author of medical texts on women's health</note> who lived long and was very beautiful in her youth. All physicians <note>original: "physiciens"</note> who know anything hold many of her authorities and good teachings. She told us a portion of the nature of women. One part she could well tell us from what she felt in herself; the other part because, as she was a woman, all women revealed their conditions <note>original: "couenances"</note> to her more willingly than to any man and told her their natures. She looked into her books from the outside and found agreements with what nature described to her. And through her, we know a great part of the natures of women."

# On Philosophy. Leaf xxix.

The other secrets of women were discovered by a man who was wise of mind, but he was so lustful that his fleshly nature carried him away; he could never be satiated or weary of living with women. It so happened that because of the great heat of his body and his great desire for himself, and so that he might better have women at his will, he put on the clothes and likeness of a woman. He had his beard plucked and torn out by the strength of herbs and ointments, and then he went into strange places among ladies, women, and maidens. They willingly did what he wanted once they had become acquainted with him, for he maintained them and was wise, subtle, and full of great ingenuity, and very good at concealing private matters. And know this, Placides, that there is one thing women love above all else: a man who knows how to keep a secret. There are many reasons why, of which we shall speak to you another time if we find in you a reason to do so. 

This wise, lustful man of whom I speak inquired privately and through counsel in the various regions where he lived, in diverse ways, into the private natures of women; and he kept them with him at such leisure that they told him everything he wished to know. He did not wish to stay long in one land lest he be discovered, for he often placed himself in such situations that, had it been known he was interfering, he would have paid dearly for it; for this reason, he acted in secret. This wise man was named Hermaphroditus. <note>original: "Hermofrodites"</note> It was of him that Ovid <note>The Roman poet Ovid (43 BCE–17 CE), whose *Metamorphoses* contains the myth of Hermaphroditus. Here, the medieval author provides a "rationalized" version of the myth.</note> made a fable in his book, saying that their gods had changed him for a long period of time from a man into a woman, and then back from a woman into a man; this was because in his youth he acted as I have told you. And when he grew old and his body cooled, he left off the clothing of a woman and his beard returned to him according to his nature. 

This Hermaphroditus taught us much about the natures of women; and he, and Trotula <note>Trotula of Salerno, a famous 11th-century female physician and authority on women's medicine.</note>, and another woman philosopher, and another wise lady named Tyrenis, all agreed and said this: That when a woman has conceived—provided she has no other illness—she has a greater desire <note>original: "talent"</note> to dwell with a man than at any other time. Now I have told you in part how we know this. Next, it is necessary to answer why this is and from what nature it arises.

¶ **"Placides," said Tymeo.** "A woman is by her nature cold, and her blood is phlegmatic <note>original: "fleurbient," likely a corruption of "flegmatique." In medieval medicine, women were believed to be dominated by the "cold" and "moist" humors.</note> and cold. And when a woman dwells with a man, as I have told you before, the woman is warmed by the heat of the man, and the man is cooled by the coldness of the woman. From this it happens that once a woman has satisfied her will once, if one were to urge her a little more, she would be ready again; she would be ready even sooner than before, and then again, and again, until she was so exhausted that she could not sustain or help herself. Her face would become all dark and bruised <note>original: "pers," a blue-ish or livid color</note> and stained around the eyes. The more a woman feels the heat of a man, the more she warms and the more she desires it. Now it is as I told you before: when a woman has conceived and received [the seed], the orifice <note>the cervix</note> is closed and the blood that descends into the womb <note>original: "matris"</note> is cold. Because of that which is inside her, she requires the heat of a man, and a man can give her no help except by <term>confriquer</term> <note>original: "confriquer: cest a dire de frotter"; from the Latin *confricare*, to rub together. The text suggests that the physical friction provides the necessary warmth that the "cold" pregnant womb craves.</note>: that is to say, by rubbing.

### The Heart of Secrets

Just as a cheese mold <term>original: *foisselle*; a wicker basket used to drain curds and give cheese its shape</term> is to the blood, so it is in the womb <term>original: *marris*; the uterus</term>: and the milky juices <note>original: *lactius*; likely referring to chyle or nutritional fluids believed to circulate in the body</note> are mixed, then a clear part rises to the breasts which is converted into milk. From that which remains, the flesh is formed on one hand and the [bone] on another; and the soul, which was placed and created with the seed, exerts itself to expand the flesh. The milk is imprinted with the form of the womb just as the cheese in the mold takes such a shape as the mold provides for it. As the milk rises more strongly to the breast and the fruit <note>the developing fetus</note> comes closer to its term, the milk in the breast becomes thicker. But know that it will never be truly flowing until the child is born. 

**Master Placides said:** How can it be known that a woman dwells more willingly with a man <note>i.e., desires sexual intimacy</note> once she has conceived than at other times? It is a marvel to know, and you put great joy in my heart by placing this in my understanding. 

**Tymeo said, Placides:** I make you understand it more certainly than it was done for me. I had great anxieties in studying and [learning] from all that I could have, whether by inheritance or by acquisition: one time ten marks <note>a unit of weight for silver or gold used as currency</note>, another time twenty in another year, and forty in some years, or more or less as I was able to have it. And know that concerning this thing and others, I will make you know and understand as much in one year as I was able to draw [and] learn from the counsel of masters in ten years at great risk. To that extent did the rich man have a great advantage over the poor: for it is necessary that a poor man, to know anything and to conquer anything through his senses, must spend whatever he has to give to his masters. And if a rich man gave to his master during his life a tenth part of his income, in one year he would think he had bought his knowledge too dearly. For this reason, there are more humble people who are very wise than there are great lords, which is a great pity; for it is a very beautiful thing to be wise and rich, for to speak truly, riches embellish the virtues. And from this you must understand one who [uses] wealth as he ought; and of this we shall speak to you another time. I know that you are of a good nature and that I will not lose my labor on you; for as you reward my labor better and the service I do for you, so much more will you work for your own profit and advantage. To our subject we must return and answer what you have asked me.

I tell you that a woman has a greater desire for a man when she is pregnant than at any other time. I will tell you how we know it. First, I tell you that there was a woman who was a philosopher <note>in this context, a learned scholar or scientist</note> who was called Trotula <note>Trotula of Salerno, a famous 11th-century female physician and medical author</note>, who discovered much and was very beautiful in her youth; all the physicians who know anything hold many of her authorities and good teachings. And from those women, we know a great part of the nature of women.

# Of Philosophy. Leaf xxix.

The secrets of women were known by a man who was wise of mind, but he was so lecherous <note>original: *luxurieux*; in a medieval context, this refers specifically to the sin of lust or excessive sexual desire</note> that his flesh so moved him that he could never be satisfied nor weary of dwelling with a woman. It so happened that because of the great heat of his body and his great craving, and so that he might better have women at his will, he dressed himself in the clothes and appearance of a woman. He had his beard plucked and torn out by the strength of herbs and ointments, and then he went into foreign places among ladies, wives, and maidens. They willingly did what he wished once they had become acquainted with him, for he supported them; he was wise, subtle, full of great ingenuity, and very good at hiding secrets. And know this, Placides: that a man who knows how to keep secrets is a thing that women love dearly. There are many reasons why, of which we shall speak to you another time, if we find in you a reason to do so. 

This wise, lecherous man of whom I speak inquired privately and in counsel, in the various regions where he lived, into the private natures of women in various ways; he kept them with him at such leisure that they told him all his heart desired. He did not wish to stay long in any one land lest he be discovered, for he often put himself in such places that, had it been known he had meddled there, he would have soon paid dearly for it <note>original: *chieremēt comparé*; meaning he would have been severely punished or killed for infiltrating women's private spaces</note>; for this reason, he acted secretly. 

This wise man was named Hermaphroditus <note>original: *Hermofrodites*. In this medieval tradition, the mythological figure is reimagined as a human scholar who disguised himself to learn gynecological secrets</note>. It was of him that Ovid made a fable in his book, saying that their gods had transformed him for a great length of time from a man into a woman, and then back from a woman into a man; this was because in his youth he acted as I have told you. And when he grew old and cold, he left off the clothing of a woman and his beard returned to him according to his nature. 

This Hermaphroditus taught us much about the natures of women; and he, and Trotula <note>a famous 11th-century female physician from Salerno, Italy, to whom many medieval gynecological texts were attributed</note>, and another philosopher, and another wise lady who was named Cyrenis, all agreed together and said this: That when a woman has conceived, provided she has no other illness, she has a greater talent for dwelling with a man than at any other time. Now I have told you in part how we know this. Next, it is necessary to answer why this is and of what nature it comes.

¶ Placides, said Tymeo, a woman is by her nature cold, and the blood that flows from her is cold. And when a woman dwells with a man, as I have told you before, the woman warms herself from the heat of the man, and the man is cooled by the coldness of the woman. From this it happens that when a woman has once fulfilled her will, if one were to hasten her a little again, she would be ready even sooner than before, and then again, and then again, until she was so weary she could not sustain or help herself, and her face would be all dark and discolored around the eyes. The more a woman feels the heat of the man, the more she warms and the more she desires it. 

Now it is as I told you before: when a woman has conceived and received [the seed], the orifice <note>the cervix</note> is closed and the blood that descends into the womb <term>original: *matris*; the uterus</term> is cold; and because of that which is inside her, she requires the heat of a man, and a man can give her no help except by confrication <term>original: *confriquer*; to rub together, referring here to the friction of sexual intercourse</term>.

outside the <term>womb</term> <note>original: *marris*; the uterus</note>: for nothing can enter inside; so that whatever they do remains outside, and she always does and always requires more and more. And the womb always does its power to attract and receive when it feels the other nature grow warm; but it cannot, for it is closed just as I have told you. And always, as the <term>seed</term> <note>original: *germe*; the developing embryo or fetus</note> grows and swells in the womb, the more the seed receives tempering; nor, as long as she is pregnant from that hour when she took and received another seed, will she receive more until she is delivered of it in whatever manner it may be, whether for good or ill. And know that if the womb were to open even a little so that anything entered it after it has received the seed, that which was held within would perish. And this was one of the reasons why <term>Muhammad</term> <note>original: *Mahommet*; the medieval text attributes various dietary and sexual prohibitions to Islamic law as understood through a Western lens</note> forbade in his law that any man should dwell with a pregnant woman before she was delivered, because a man who dwells there loses his <term>seed</term> <note>original: *semence*; semen</note>: for she could retain nothing during that term, as I have said before.

Master, said Placides. And why do women have it more than men do? Placides, said Tymeo. And this was the creature of whom I have spoken to you before, whom God loved so much (and I shall speak more of him to you still). This was Man, to whom He gave flesh and body; so know certainly that Man has as much or more of this as Woman. Thus it seems by this reason that as the woman gives it out, the man ought also to give it out; but "what does not go lengthwise, goes breadthwise" <note>This is a proverbial expression meaning that if a substance is not expelled in one way, it is put to use in another.</note>. The blood which is called the *monthly course* which descends into the womb—if the womb is not closed, it delivers itself of it and gives it out by force from within; this is through the first entrance. And when the womb is closed, it goes to where I told you. And I tell you truly that a woman does not have this *monthly course* before she comes to the age to endure a man; and this is true. So know that man has other ways by which this substance departs, and I shall tell them to you. They are in the hair: for know this, that men by their rightful nature are hairier than women. And just as this *monthly course* flows by rightful nature before a woman comes to the age to endure a man, so a man has no beard before he comes to the age to dwell with a woman; and as that age comes to him, so the beard comes to him, and other hair grows around his breasts and around his thighs and on his chest and in various places according to his <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual's body.</note>. And for this reason, men are hairier than women: and for this reason, men have beards and women have none; and this is the rightful reason. And just as a man has no beard before he comes to the proper age, so it is with the woman, as I have told you. And know that the ancients found some reasons for why men do not have this as much as women, which reasons are not at all suitable: for they say that the ends of the veins were more open in women than in men. And that was of no account.

# Of Philosophy. Leaf xxx.

->### On the Nature of Men and Women<-

Some ancients said, and they spoke the truth, that there are some men who have this condition and suffer monthly courses and experience their **"flowers"** <note>original: *fleurs*; a common medieval euphemism for menstruation</note> at intervals just as women do; there are some of these men, but they are few. Afterwards we will show you the reason why and how this can be by nature. But first it is necessary to answer your entire question. You have the reason why women do this more than men. Tell me then: one must know the reason why women [have this] more than other female beasts.

Placides, said Tymeo, beasts other than men and women do not have such clear skin as man and woman; for nature provides for them either with scales, or hair, or wool, or feathers, with which they are naturally covered—and more so the males than the females of the land beasts. So it is that the blood which comes out of the females works within the beast and goes into the hair, or into scales, or horns, or feathers, or claws; and this is their purging. And so it expires at intervals according to what their time and nature require; and because nature is occupied in that part, they do not have monthly courses nor experience their "flowers."

And just as men are hotter than women and therefore are hairier, so too are the male beasts hairier or more horned than the females. A stag has more horns than a doe, and a boar has harder hair and larger tusks than a sow. A cock or a peacock has more feathers than a hen or a peahen; and so it is for all other things; and this is the reason for what you have asked.

Women have skin so tender and delicate that nature purges itself through the <term>womb</term> <note>original: *marris*; the uterus</note>, and the blood descends into the womb if that orifice is open at the first outer orifice as I have told you before. And just as the moon receives new light from the sun every month as I have previously told and shown you, so all living things receive a new growth of blood and an abundance more about once a month than at other times. And for this reason, women experience their "flowers" about once a month by right nature.

¶ Master, said Placides, it sometimes happens that some women have two children and some beasts have several young; tell me, if you please, whether they are conceived at once, or in two instances, or in several.

Placides, said Tymeo, did you not clearly understand what I told you? That once the orifice is closed, nothing can enter until the fruit held within is fully perfected. Therefore, no <term>conception</term> <note>original: *engendrement*</note> can happen one upon another; this is something that neither we nor nature could suffer. For otherwise, one would extinguish the other, and the female would die, and the womb would perish, and the nourishment for the <term>seed</term> <note>original: *germe*; the developing embryo</note> would perish. But I will tell you how this can be in beasts and in women who have the <term>womb</term> which has seven <term>receptacles</term> <note>original: *receptables*; this refers to the medieval medical belief in the "seven-chambered uterus"</note> and seven "beds." It happens that when the <term>seed</term> <note>original: *esparme*; sperm/semen</note> divides after it has been coiled together, it takes as much [space] as it finds nearest the receptacles; and sometimes it takes them all, as many as it can take; and if the matter is abundant and enough nourishment comes to it, then nature forms women...

...of beasts or of children; just as a channel, if there is enough metal, can by a single opening make its metal issue forth when it is melted and make it run into several parts, and thus many fruits are made. And when it is so, Nature outlines <note>original: *lignee*; to draw lines or shape</note> several parts and many fruits are made from them. And when it is así, Nature outlines, much like a carpenter who wants to make something; the womb <term>womb: *matrice*, the place of formation</term> is ready, and the soul <note>original: *lame* / *l’âme*</note> strives to expand itself within that body and extends through the limbs.
