And just as nourishment comes through the stem to the pear or the apple, so it comes to the fawn or the child by a "stem" <note>the umbilical cord</note> which holds them in the middle of the belly and nourishes them from all parts; and this is that gut which is called the navel <note>original: *nombril*</note>. When the apple is ripe, the stem breaks and it falls down. Likewise, when the child has reached its term, that gut breaks, and that child tends to go out just as the apple tends to fall down; for you will see that most flowers, as long as they are flowers, tend to hold their heads upwards, and then when the fruit comes, they begin to tend downwards, and the more it ripens, the more it lowers its head. Just so does the child or the fawn of beasts of which I have spoken to you before. And the more it ripens, the more it tends to go out.

"Fair sweet master," said Placides, "out of love, now let it not displease you; I marvel that you give me examples of various types of animate things <note>living things with souls</note> compared to things which do not seem animate to me at all." "Speak it, I wish it," said Tymeo. "Your mercy, master," said Placides. "Master, a pear or an apple has no soul at all; yet you have made a comparison between a form in infancy and a pear and an apple; and I tell you that I have well felt and understood that men and beasts and trees have souls such as you have described before. Fair sweet master, now do not be angry. But do children have souls?" "Yes," said Tymeo. "And yet you make a comparison of apples and pears to the fruit of men and beasts. What souls do pears and apples have? I do not believe at all that they have souls." "Placides," said Tymeo, "I wish that you were as wise as was Thimeuz <note>Timaeus of Locri, the Pythagorean philosopher and character in Plato's dialogues</note>, who was a good philosopher, of whom we will speak to you hereafter. If you wish, I will not be angry at all as long as you..."

...you should ask me with humility; but I would be angered if you asked me out of pride. "Master, God keep me from it," <note>Placides is responding to Tymeo's warning against intellectual pride.</note> said Placides.

"Placides, tell me how you know or why you think that apples, pears, the fruits of trees, grains, and wood do not have souls?" "Master," said Placides, "it seems to me that since they are out of the earth, or away from the tree or their roots, they have no souls, for they cannot die of themselves. And even if they did have a soul, it does not seem to me that their souls have any power <term>power: *vertu*; the inherent strength or functional ability of a soul</term>; for it seems to me you said that the souls of trees and herbs are 'attractive' of the humors <note>original: *humeurs*; the vital fluids or sap</note> which they catch and which rise as sap, by which the herbs and trees are nourished, returning a part of these humors into leaf, flower, and fruit. But I do not see this in pears, nor in apples, nor in the fruit of trees, nor in grains of wheat; for they neither catch nor expel anything. Therefore, fair master, it does not seem to me that they have souls."

"Placides, unless nature fails them, they have great nobility <note>original: *haulteur*; here meaning potential or status</note> if they do not turn to rot; and it is a sign of death in an apple and a pear when they begin to rot. Then they signify that they wish to die; I will make you understand this. You know that if one plants an apple, a pear, a walnut, or any other seed, if they find natural earth, they speak of it <note>original: *en dient*; perhaps 'respond to it' or a typo for *en devient*, 'become'</note> and there is born a pear tree, an apple tree, a grain of bean or pea or wheat, walnut trees, cherry trees, or great trees according to their nature. This is because of the soul <note>original: *lame* / *l'âme*</note> which is there; when it finds that which gives it the power to attract and to expel, it thus expands itself. But if an apple or a pear is in your mouth or in your hand, the soul cannot attract humor, for it does not have it nor find it near itself. Thus, it does not remain so because of a lack of soul, but because it finds no outlet through which it can achieve its expansion."

"Sometimes it happens with certain trees that one cuts them while they are all green and plants them elsewhere, and they grow again, just as one can do with the vine, the elder, the fig tree, and many other trees. And this is because they are planted while the souls are still in them; for know that nothing planted without a soul would return to life or bear fruit. Therefore, it is a certain and apparent thing that no dead or dry tree would return. Some plant those which seem to be dead and dry, but they are not; for there are some which are pithy or of a dry nature which retain their souls in a very small place. Thus, they are sometimes put in the earth when it is thought they are dry and dead, but they are not, and they sometimes return. Of such a nature are often vines, elders, willows, morsels <note>original: *morseaulx*; possibly a specific plant cutting or 'bits' of root</note>, and some others. And of this we shall speak more another time; we must return to our matter."

"Placides," said Tymeo, "there are some women who are very desirous of men, and when their flesh summons them either by day or by night, they experience a 'pollution' <note>original: *pollution*; a medieval term for nocturnal emission or female orgasm</note> just as men do, such that they release seed <term>seed: *esparme*; reproductive fluid</term> that is not natural, but bad; of which I have spoken to you before, that it comes by another way than the good does, as I have told you before. And it sometimes happens that when the woman is very desirous of a man, the womb <term>womb: *matrice*</term> receives that same bad seed along with windiness <note>original: *vētosite*; the presence of 'air' or gas in the body, often blamed for medical issues</note>, and when the bad seed and the wind have entered the womb..."

# The Heart of Secrets

...and force it to close. And then when the master <note>Likely referring to the "master" seed or the formative power of the male</note> descends there, it forms a shape and flesh just like good seed; but it is by no means good flesh, for the matter is bad and cannot perform good work. This matter grows, and some women believe themselves to be pregnant, but they are not. Physician-philosophers such as Hippocrates, Galen, Trotula <note>Trotula of Salerno was a famous 12th-century female physician; her inclusion here shows the text's reliance on classical and medieval medical authorities</note>, and others call this **Mola**: because it is neither fruit nor nature, it gives it no form nor any lineage of limbs; rather, it is round and frightening to see, and the woman carries it just as right nature makes her carry a right fruit. 

And when this mola is in the body, it is moved by its terms <note>The scheduled cycles or months of pregnancy</note> just as good fruit would be, and the women certainly believe they are pregnant and heavy with a true and good germ; but they are not. Many good physicians are often deceived by this, as we read; but the sign of this mola is such that the woman is heavier during that term than at any other, even more than she would be when giving birth. She swells and turns yellow as if she were dropsical <term>dropsical: *eutropisee*; suffering from edema or "dropsy," an accumulation of fluid in the body</term> and she cannot eat. 

And when she comes to the time of "birthing," she is in more anguish and more sick than she would be with a true child. If it happens that the mola wishes to come out all at once—I say "all at once" because it sometimes breaks apart and comes out like marsh-mud or dung and the rot of slime, or like white and red boils <note>original: *clou blanc et rouge*; likely referring to discharge of pus and blood</note> all together. This happens when the digestion <note>original: *decofite*; the internal breakdown or corruption of the mass</note> pierces it before it comes out; then it rots and does not cause nearly as much harm as when it comes out whole. For as I tell you, when it is born and comes out whole, the woman is in more anguish than with a true child. 

The reason for this is: when a woman carries a true child, just as nature gives shape to the true germ, so too does nature prepare the passages. And just as the rose blossoms by nature against the light of the sun, so too the passages open and blossom against the coming of a true birth or the true fruit of a beast. Therefore, you can clearly see that in women who carry true fruit, as soon as the proper terms approach, their loins widen, and all the passages, the veins, and their sight sharpens; all the outlets are more open to receive nourishment or to give back what is due to nature than at any other time—such as the nose, the ears, the lower passages, and the first orifice <term>first orifice: the cervix, the neck of the womb</term>. And for this reason, the mola causes greater pain in birth than a true child, because nature does not open the passages for it in its terms as she does for the true fruit.

"Master," said Placides, "tell me, if you please, why nature sometimes makes males and other times females." "Gladly," said Tymeo. "As I have told you, it is necessary before children or the fruit of beasts are engendered that both—that is, the male and the female—provide seed <term>seed: *esparme*; medieval medicine often followed the 'two-seed' theory, believing both parents contributed a reproductive substance</term>. Then, as I told you, the vulva gathers it and casts it into the matrix <note>The womb</note> so that the first orifice becomes as if it were completely dry. And many foolish women are amazed at what happens then. And there are some others who say that neither parent contributes anything to the child, but that is folly to say."

### On Philosophy. Folio xxxii.

f ii

...that of the man, it causes it all to turn toward the chambers of the womb <term>womb: *matrice*; the uterus</term> which are on the left; and in that part, the coldness of the woman is more abundant than elsewhere. Because of this coldness, it engenders a cold fruit, and the fruit remains to be fully perfected: for a woman is by no means a perfect fruit, but is rather partially failed. For that which should have been an instrument for working <note>Referring to the male reproductive organ</note> had to descend to receive <note>Referring to the female reproductive organ</note>. Aristotle agrees with this in his works on nature, where he says these words: that a woman is an accidental man <note>original: *hōme achoisonneux*; a translation of the Latin *mas occasionatus*, Aristotle's controversial theory that a female is a "misbegotten" or "incidental" male caused by a lack of formative heat</note>, which is to say failed or not at all perfect; and in this manner are females perfected and engendered.

Furthermore, when the sperm of the man or the male beast is more abundant than that of the woman or the female, it causes it all to turn to the right, directly to where there is more heat; and in that heat, a right and natural fruit is formed, and this fruit is male. ¶ Sometimes it happens that the sperm is so swift that it is sometimes cast out of the vulva to the right, and sometimes to the left; then the fruit is of diverse kinds. For when the germ falls into a cold place in the womb, it sometimes forms the shapes of men who are cold by nature and womanish <note>original: *famelins*</note>; and sometimes they resemble [men] in all things except that they have the testicles and penis of a man. ¶ It sometimes happens that the coldness turns into such bodies from the outside, and then such men are pale, green, and without beards. And yet, because the heat remains inside, the ancients say they can sometimes engender; but they say it rarely happens that the children of such men can live. When the heat turns outward, they certainly look like men and have plenty of beards, but they are cold by nature, and internally they cannot lie with a woman. And such men are called "chastes" <note>original: *chastres*; eunuchs or those naturally impotent</note> by the ancients, from the word *castratus* <note>Latin: castrated</note> which is as if to say *caste natus* <note>Latin: born chaste</note>; and these are those who are born so chaste that they have no power to lie with a woman. Sometimes the vulva casts the female sperm to the right. Thus are formed certain women who are conceived and nourished in heat; sometimes the heat turns inward and sometimes outward. When the heat turns inward, they are white or pale, except that they are fierce in their masculine gait or countenance; and then they cannot conceive by the heat of a man. And because she has a masculine nature in her body, she can neither be satisfied nor provide sperm nor live with a man. Others who are made of female sperm cast to the left, and the heat turns outward: these are black, bearded women; and when they have a good male, they habitually and willingly conceive beautiful, large, and strong male children.

Sometimes it happens by some chance that the human sperm of the man is more abundant than that of the woman, but it is cast to the left: thus there is sometimes engendered a form of man with two natures <note>A reference to hermaphroditism</note>: that is, one who has a penis and testicles, and also orifices just like women. And of such people there have been and will be [more]; and this is because the human germ strives to fulfill its right nature, which is a male thing, but the cold part strives to "accidentalize" <note>original: *achoisonner*; to make incidental or female</note> it—that is, to make it fail and turn into a female. Thus, they struggle one against the other. The ancient judges established that no one should allow such a person to use both natures...

Master, said Placides, may God keep us from such a beast! But for the sake of love, master, now tell me how it is that some are born without hands, and some without feet. Placides, said Tymeo, it is just as it is with those who have two heads, or twelve fingers—six on each hand—and twelve toes; and from this you can understand the reason why it is so. ¶ When a girdle-maker <note>original: *sceintier*; a maker of belts or girdles</note> makes a girdle and he has enough material, the material fills the vessel so much that it takes on all the shapes of the mold. It is exactly the same with the sperm and the womb <term>womb: *matrice*</term>; when there is enough or too much material, its bed <note>likely referring to the "cells" or divisions the medievals believed existed within the uterus</note> grows in the part where it abounds and overflows into the other bed; thus nature forms and outlines another limb—whether it be a foot, a head, or a hand—this is how it happens. ¶ Just so, you can understand from what I have told you that through an abundance of matter, limbs can double. I also tell you that nature works with as much matter as it finds; and just as if the womb did not fill the mold, some form would be missing; so when matter does not abound enough to fill the womb, a limb is missing. And this is not at all the fault of the woman; rather, it is a fault of nature. Now you have the reason for the nature of both cases. ¶ Master, said Placides, it happened in one of the regions of our land that two women were born who were two above the waist, but below they were only one thing, and they had only two feet; they had two heads and four arms, two breasts, two mouths, four eyes, one navel, and one belly. Placides, said Tymeo, I believe it well; and this can happen just as easily as two cherries can grow on a single stem.

Fair, sweet master, said Placides, now make me certain, if you please, of one thing I ask you. Regarding these two women formed in two shapes joined below: I say that they performed all their business above just like two separate women, and they walked on two feet, and what one wanted, the other wanted. I would very much like to know if they had one soul or two. Placides, said Tymeo, that is no small question; many times have the philosophers strove among themselves over this matter and about monsters <term>monsters: *monstres*; from the Latin *monstrum*, meaning a marvel or a sign</term>, such as that beast of which you spoke. ...among the philosophers concerning this knowledge and inquiry. When a monster was born who was named the **Minotaur**, this monster was born in Greece to a queen who was named **Pasiphae**. This queen was the mother of a strong and wise king who was named **Minos**, and this monster was half bull and half man—a bull from behind up to the navel, and a man in front. When he was born, some of the philosophers said that he had two souls, and some said no, but only one. All the philosophers did not agree together, but rather hurled great words at one another in proving and disproving, like champions who sometimes strike each other openly. However, most agree that no monsters born of beasts have more than one soul; and this is the truth, for two souls could not govern a single body once it is born upon the earth.

Master, said **Placides**, as for this monster who had a form other than a human body, I would gladly know, if it please you, how he could be born from a woman’s body. **Placides**, I will tell you, and how it came to be known. It happened that **Minos** was king from his childhood; he was brave, wise, courtly, and a good knight, feared and dreaded, and his land fell to him in his infancy. His mother, who was named **Pasiphae**, ruled <note>original: *regna*; she acted as regent while Minos was a child</note>, and she was a very beautiful lady and was desirous of men. She used to go often to a wood where she had a very great gathering of livestock—oxen, cows, and bulls. There was a very beautiful bull there who pushed all the others aside; he was strong and fat, and he bore himself with great pride among the cows and all the beasts. He was partly white as snow, except for the tip of his tail and a spot he had in the middle of his forehead, black with a bright face in the manner of a star. Why should I tell you a longer story? The lady saw him mounting the cows so often, and watched him so much, and he pleased her so much, that she fell into a fantasy and loved him like a madwoman, and she thought in her heart that she would like to be a cow. And the more often she watched him, the more he pleased her and the more she loved him; and her fantasy and her mad thoughts grew and multiplied, and she became jealous of that bull, just as **Ovid** himself tells us in the book of the *Art of Love* <note>Ovid’s *Ars Amatoria*, a famous Roman work on the practice of romance and seduction</note>. So, when the queen saw that this bull left the great company of cows for some cow that was more beautiful than the others, she immediately had her killed and slaughtered; and she herself would give that bull food with her own hand, and rub him, and scratch him, and stroke him. And she thought, like a fool, to draw this bull to her through some manner of lust <term>lust: *luxure*; in a medieval context, this specifically refers to the sin of lechery or disordered sexual desire</term>; but nature could not allow it, even though she handled his genitals at length <note>original: *a debalast*; likely meaning unrestrainedly or in an unbridled fashion</note>. And when she aroused him, he who was strong would escape her and go to the cows. And when she saw that she could not enjoy him, she sent for some of her private maids and told them her heart and her will. It is a light thing for a woman to consent to folly that comes from nature, so they should not be blamed for it. These maidens helped her, but they could never achieve the goal, for nature cannot allow a bull to perform his nature in her, even though they tried so many ways that it was a wonder—and it would be a shameful thing to relate.

# The Heart of Secrets

While the queen was in such anguish and in such foolish thought, one of her maidservants reminded her of the fame that was then spreading through all of Greece regarding the great ingenuity of a poor man who lived in the lady’s domain and in the land of her son, King **Minos**. This poor man was of such ingenuity <note>original: *soutiuete*; meaning cleverness, craftiness, or technical skill</note> that no one could imagine a thing that he did not know how to fashion and complete. This poor man was named **Daedalus**; it was he who through his ingenuity discovered many wonders, of which **Ovid** speaks in many ways. It often happens that clever men are rarely rich, and fortune rarely grants happiness in two ways: one is either clever and poor, or crude and rich; and if one had both virtues, fortune would surely take one away. 

The queen **Pasiphae** sent for this man of great renown to speak with her, and he came. When he had arrived, the queen, without shame or modesty and full of great folly, revealed her intent to him, showed him her treasures, and said: that if he knew how and was able to create some art or engine <note>original: *engin*; a mechanical device or clever contraption</note> by which the bull would desire to mate with her, she would grant him such wealth that he would never be poor again. And he, coveting knowledge and not thinking that it could turn to such great evil, agreed. But know this, **Placides**, that no evil exists that does not return upon the one who pursues it. The worthy man thought and pondered and set himself to great thinking, and then answered the lady: "My lady, if this thing is kept secret, I will do what you ask." The lady was joyful and presented and gave him great treasure immediately, and an agreement was made in the manner that I will tell you hereafter.

He observed the cow that the bull loved most and had her put in a strong house all by herself, and had her given food and drink. He also had the bull locked well in another house from which he could not leave, and had him given plenty to drink and eat. Then, from strong wood, he fashioned a hollow figure in the shape of a cow. When he had done this, he had the cow that had been locked up—the one the bull loved so much—killed, and with the hide, freshly flayed, he covered the figure he had made and placed it in the small house where the cow had long been kept. Then he had the queen enter inside the figure that was covered in the cow's hide. This figure was so ingeniously made that the queen’s anatomy <note>original: *sa nature*; referring here to her reproductive organs</note> could be positioned exactly where the cow’s was. 

When the queen was inside, the poor clever man, who turned his ingenuity toward wickedness, let the bull out from the house where he was into the small house where the figure and the queen were, and where the cow had lived. And the bull, willful, strong, hot, and eager, where he saw that figure wrapped in the cow’s hide, leaped upon it. And the queen, through and through <note>original: *que loing que pres*; literally "from far or near," meaning entirely or in every respect</note> like one foolish and out of her senses, received him. The bull followed his nature so that the lady conceived by him; and as each seed <note>original: *esparme*; the biological fluid/sperm from both parents that medieval science believed combined to form a child</note> followed its own nature, there came forth that monstrous figure of which I spoke to you before, half man and half bull. The lady carried him for her full term, and when he was born, it was not a hidden thing; nor was the lady wise enough to prevent people from thinking she had given birth to that beast. When King **Minos** learned of this marvel...

# The Heart of Secrets

...to be born from the first appearances—at the passing of winter and the entry of spring, it is windier than at other times, except at the passing of summer. And it rarely happens that at the passing of summer there is such a great wind; but at the passing of autumn, it happens by a force of nature that will be explained to you another time, if we can find the why and how. And I tell you: it is true that the torment, anguish, and harm to flowers and leaves is caused by the wind. This anyone can know, at least when the wind is too strong. And you know that the leaf and the vine are in the bud just as the chick is in the egg; and know that, commonly in all lands, the time when the buds of the trees are born is at the passing of winter. And then, know that it blows more than in any other season, except for the time I mentioned. Therefore, flowers and leaves have anguish and torment at their birth, for they emerge and are born into the wind.

Furthermore, wind is vapor; <term>vapor <note>original: "vapeur"</note></term> means wandering and moving. That is to say, moving through the <term>pores <note>the master defines these as tiny openings in the skin or surface of plants</note></term> just as I told you once before at the start of your instruction. These pores are the head and the ends of the veins—small holes through which the humors or the hair emerge. And know that trees also have pores just like animals do, according to their natures; and animals have them as well.

I have spoken to you before about the <term>dew <note>original: "rousee"</note></term> that rises upon the grass in the morning. Some people believe that it comes from the clouds like rain, but it is an error to say it does; rather, it is as I have told you. The plants catch it against the coming of the sun during the day; that which is drawn out by night through the sweetness of the weather strives to show itself against the attraction of the sun. For the sun, which is hot and dry, attracts moisture; this moisture that is attracted rises so much that it goes all the way to the end of the leaf. This is true dew, where the drop of water stays right at the tip of the leaf; this comes naturally from the earth. Many people have argued about this because they could not believe it. And if you do not believe me, I will tell you how you may know it for certain. At the time when the dews have gone, enter into a fine herb garden or a meadow and place a tile in the middle of it during the day. Return when the dew has fallen, and you will find the tile wet <insert>underneath</insert> and all dry on top. Thus you will be able to know well that if the dew came from above, the tile would be wet on top; but because it comes from the earth, it gets wet on the side facing the earth.

¶ "Placides," said Tymeo, "according to the common speech of the world, there are three kinds of dew, as some philosophers have said—some say more, some say less—but as for me, I will tell you my opinion. I say there are three: one of the three is natural dew, and this is called in the law of the Greeks the <term>fat of the earth <note>original: "gresse de terre"; a reference to the nutrient-rich moisture that fuels plant growth</note></term>; and the other is a fine rain, such as when people say in the spring that it is 'misting' <note>original: "rousille"</note>; and this is called the dew of heaven. For anciently the Jews said, and the Christians confirmed it—those who knew the two Testaments—that it had never rained on earth <note>This refers to a theological belief that before the Great Flood or in the early days of Creation, the earth was watered by a mist rather than rain</note>. But this is not according to the recently ordered nature, but according to the ordinance of <term>creative nature <note>original: "nature naturant"; a philosophical term for God as the creator of the natural order</note></term> which is God." Enough of that commentary; enough of that...

# On Philosophy. Folio .xxxv.

...understanding. May God grant you so much knowledge that on this and other matters you may know how to inquire and ask; for he who asks, learns, as I have told you before: he who teaches another, who records, or who studies, instructs himself. We must understand <term>art <note>The master refers to "art" here as a structured system of knowledge</note></term>, teaching, and doctrine as that which is taught by masters. And we must also understand practice, study, recording, and memory as belonging to oneself and to others. And he who looks well at all these things will see they are practice. Let us return to our subject.

¶ Placides, said Tymeo, that rain which came first—because it came and comes from the clouds by the order of the Creator—was called the <term>dew of heaven <note>original: "rousee du ciel"</note></term> until today. Of these two dews, a Jew named Jacob spoke when he gave his blessing to Joseph, his son <note>The text likely refers to the blessing in Genesis 27:28 ("God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth"), though in the Bible this is Isaac blessing Jacob</note>, and said these words: "The dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth." Some understand this as I have told you, and some understand it otherwise; but these other understandings belong only to the Jews and not to Christians.

¶ The third dew is a kind of vapor that is born from the earth, either at the departure of winter <note>original: "lyssir dpuet" / "l'issue d'hiver"</note> or at the entry of winter, and it rarely happens in summer. And when it happens then, it is not of a right nature. This vapor gathers willingly over waters, marshes, rivers, ponds, springs, and aquatic places. This vapor sometimes rises and sometimes descends. When it rises, it becomes rain for the reasons we will tell you later. When it descends in winter because of the coldness of the earth, it is frozen dew and is called <term>hoarfrost <note>original: "frimee"</note></term>. This frost does great good to the trees: for it constricts and "cooks" them from the outside so that they heat up on the inside and catch sweat and moisture. And then it puts great pressure on the bark, just as a good ointment would do to itchy flesh. And so say the wise philosophers.

Sometimes this hoarfrost descends without freezing and disperses so subtly that it becomes like a mist; then it returns willingly to the moist places from whence it came. This descent is dangerous to the bodies of men and beasts, for it gathers corruption and "strange natures" from the air. It can sometimes harm the bodies of men and women such that they receive illness and sometimes death. And when sometimes this hoarfrost descends and is changed in the air over herbs, vines, and trees, it shames, burns, cooks, and ruins them entirely; and this hoarfrost is called <term>mildew <note>original: "nieule" (modern French: nielle), referring to blight or agricultural smut</note></term>, and it is perilous to all things.

Sometimes it happens that when this hoarfrost strives to rise into the air, the sun preserves and overcomes it and forces it back down; then it falls to the ground in the manner of rain, and this is properly called dew. But it is neither as good, nor as true, nor as natural as that which comes from the earth. Let us return to our subject: we will tell you how wind is everything to trees and flowers. I tell you that wind, which is vapor, goes through the pores of the trees; it constricts them from the outside and shrinks them so that the buds emerge with more difficulty; for every thing by nature has a defense against that which is contrary to its nature, and for defense against bad weather they have the...

# The Heart of Secrets

...listen. The more the wind enters among the trees, the thicker their bark becomes; and the thicker the bark, the more reluctantly and with greater pain the buds are born. Thus they are born in suffering. Know this for certain, Placides: they are born at that time more than any other, except for when they fall. Everyone knows that the wind knocks down the leaves at the onset of winter, and the cold sears and weakens them. It is therefore a certain thing that every living thing is born in anguish in this world, and in anguish it also ends.

"Fair, sweet master," said Placides, "you have spoken to me of wind both at the beginning and the end of my instruction, but you never told me what wind actually is." "Placides," said Thymeo, "did I not tell you that it is vapor raised from the earth? For the love of learning, now clarify this for me: is that vapor corporeal? Do the winds have bodies or not?" "Placides," said Thymeo, "dear son, yes. And to better satisfy your desire, I shall speak of it further."

I have told you previously that there are four principal winds: one is called <term>Eurus <note>The East wind</note></term>, another <term>Auster <note>The South wind</note></term>, another <term>Aquilo <note>The North wind</note></term>, and the other <term>Boreas <note>Also a North wind, often used interchangeably with Aquilo in medieval texts</note></term>. I tell you they are corporeal; they are vapors engendered in the <term>elemental earth <note>The physical world composed of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire</note></term> by the force of the sun's heat. When the sun passes beneath, it impresses its heat into the earth. When the earth heats up, it draws in the moisture of the waters above. Thus, these vapors are created just as if you were to place a hot stone in cold water: a vapor would emerge that is called smoke. In just this way, from the four parts of the world, vapor arises from the elemental earth and is called wind. 

Sometimes it thrusts itself into the sea, one body pushing against the other. When it pushes the sea, the sea pushes and strikes the air. Since the air is thin and clear, it makes way for the wind and drives it forward with force. Sometimes the wind flies with excessive force, sometimes very little; sometimes the wind flies high, and sometimes low. When it flies low, it encounters bodies stronger and heavier than itself, such as a mountain or a deep, sturdy tower; it strikes them and recoils, creating noise and turmoil. Sometimes, when it is too strong, it flies across the rebound, and quite often it breaks apart and divides into small portions, so that the vapors settle into the earth and water; thus the winds end. When they fly too high, it is sometimes when you believe the weather is clear <note>original: "serp temps," likely "serain temps" meaning fair/clear weather</note> but you see the clouds racing. Know then that the wind is flying four times higher, until it dissipates by itself and, like smoke, departs.

Many people name these four winds I have mentioned differently. Some call them Eurus, <term>Subsolanus <note>The East wind, literally "beneath the sun"</note></term>, <term>Meridianus <note>The South wind, related to midday</note></term>, and Boreas. Others say that Boreas and Aquilo are one and the same. They say <term>Aquilo <note>original: "Aquilo... est dit de aquas et de ligo"</note></term> is named from the words for <gloss>waters <note>Latin: *aquas*</note></gloss> and <gloss>to bind <note>Latin: *ligo*</note></gloss>, because it binds the waters. It is the wind that is so cold it freezes the waters, and for this reason, it is said to "bind" them. This is both Boreas and Aquilo, for they are one and the same; however, others claim they are not, saying that...

The philosophers say that each principal wind has two <term>sergeants <note>Attendants or collateral winds that flank the main wind</note></term>; to hear of this now would be a long matter for you. ¶ "Fair, sweet master," said Placides, "if it pleases you, tell me now what clouds are made of." "Listen to this," said Tymeo: "Cloud is <term>nubes <note>Latin for cloud</note></term>, and <term>nubes</term> means 'cloud'; it is so named, as some say, from <term>nubsice <note>likely a corruption of "nubere," to cover or veil</note></term> which means 'obscure.' I shall tell you and make you understand how, just as vapors dry, they are born and issue from the sea and the waters. Just as you see that when one sets a full cauldron of water to heat upon the fire, a thick and dark vapor is created and rises above it; just so, by the power of the sun—which rises from beneath the earth and heats the earth and sea—there issues forth a vapor: a dry vapor from the earth, a moist one from the waters, and from both earth and water together, a thick and moist vapor. And just as you see the vapors of hot water rising from the fire, gathering together and then dividing and departing; just so do the clouds rise, and likewise they depart and return to nothingness. And when some have gone, others are born, just like the generations of the elements; and these are the 'bodily waters.' But just as flour can be so finely divided in all its parts that no one could find any of it, or as one could boil water so much that the fire would draw it so subtly to itself that no one would know what had become of it and none would remain; in such a manner the body of the cloud wastes away and disperses into the air, just like the wind of which I spoke to you."

# The Heart of Secrets

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a rainbow (L'arc du ciel) as a series of concentric semi-circular bands arching over a stylized landscape of rolling hills or waves.</image-desc>

->The Rainbow.<-

---

It signifies a great continuation of rains for the duration of two, three, or four years—so much so that the lands of the country where this occurs become so raw, so cold, and so soaked that no <term>winter seeds <note>Original: "yueinages." Refers to crops sown in winter or the winter agricultural season.</note></term> can bear fruit or prosper. Because of this, there have sometimes been great famines, especially in the western regions <note>Original: "parties d'occident."</note> which are colder than those in the east. This is because the power of the sun’s heat is greater and more abundant in the east <note>Original: "orient."</note> than in the west. And take careful note of the rainbow: for you will always find it opposite the sun. When the sun is toward its rising, the rainbow is in the west; if the sun is in the west, the rainbow appears in the east; if the sun is at <term>midday <note>The South.</note></term>, the rainbow is in the <term>north <note>Original: "septentrion."</note></term>. 

And through the four elements—that is to say, by the gathering of the four elements from which it takes its body and shape—it takes the four colors it possesses, along with the splendor of the sun which illuminates it and gives light to its colors. For by the <term>intensity <note>Original: "acciaturete," likely meaning the sharp brilliance or focus of the light.</note></term> of the sun, the rainbow is formed; this is quite apparent, for if the sun were not there, you would not see the rainbow in the sky.

"Master," said Placides, "I do not understand where these four colors come from. You tell me they come from the brightness of the sun; the sun seems to me to be entirely and purely bright, yet the rainbow has four colors."

"Placides, I told you before that it is formed from the four bodies of the four elements; this is true. The redness comes to it from fire, as does the yellowness; the greenness comes from the water; the <term>blue <note>Original: "lince," likely a transcription of "l'inde" (indigo/blue) or a related term for the color of the air.</note></term> from the air; and the darkness from the earth. 

Nevertheless, some philosophers say that it forms and takes a body because one cloud is higher than another; for the one less burdened with rain stays higher, and the heavier one stays below. The lighter one is the clearest, and the heavier is the darkest, according to whether there is more water in one than the other. They create various shapes: for one stays round, another oblong <note>Original: "belongue."</note>, another hanging as they move. One is thin, the other thick. When there is one that is very round, very thick, and very heavy with water, the sun, which is of another..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the master Tymeo and his student Placides. Following the explanation of how the sun's light interacts with the elements to form the rainbow, the text transitions into medieval meteorology (the nature of "dry vapors" or shooting stars) and astrology (the influence of planets and the zodiac on earthly life).</meta>

### Of philosophy. Leaf xxxvii.

[The sun's light] strikes against the cloud and shines in the water of the cloud which receives the sun’s arrival; it reflects a flaming brilliance in the water against the sun. This appears just as if you put water in a cup in a room and the sun's ray strikes it—the water receives the light, and the wall receives that light and is illuminated. And just as the sun creates such light in the water, such light is reflected back toward the sun. The moon also gives off a similar light from the air; it happens just as if one mirror were held against another—the form that appears in one is represented in the other. We shall say no more of this art.

¶ "Master, what kind of beast is a <term>vapor <note>The student is asking about "shooting stars" or meteors, which medieval science classified as "dry vapors" rather than astronomical bodies.</note></term>?"

"Placides, it is neither beast nor bird; rather, it is a dry vapor that gathers in a great mass so close to the <term>element of fire <note>In the medieval geocentric model, the sphere of fire sat just below the moon and above the air.</note></term> that it catches fire from the heat, due to its own dryness. And when it is ignited, it travels as straight as it can, like fire being hurled toward the earth. This flying fire continues until it finally becomes nothing. These vapors are much like those white <term>gossamer threads <note>Original: "filandres blanches." These are the fine spider silks often seen floating in the air on sunny days, which medieval observers linked to atmospheric phenomena.</note></term> that appear during the March sowing when the weather is clear."

¶ "Master," said Placides, "do the stars of the firmament serve only to light the sky?"

"Placides," said Tymeo, "the Creator of all creatures gave them many virtues other than lighting the sky. You should know well that there is no star in the sky that does not provide <term>influence <note>Original: "inclination." The celestial "leaning" or pull that stars exert on earthly nature.</note></term> in some manner to the creatures here below—whether to herbs, trees, vermin, beasts, fish, birds, men, or women. For among all creatures, there are masculine and feminine types. We will tell you about some of them, and speak especially of the <term>seven planets <note>The Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the Sun.</note></term>, which affect the natures of men and women more than others, along with the twelve stars called the **twelve signs** <note>The Zodiac.</note>. Together with the seven planets, these signify the qualities and the fates of children, male or female, according to the planet, the sign, and the point where they are located. From these seven planets, the seven days of the week take their names:

*   **Monday**, which is named for the **Moon** <note>Original: "Luna."</note>.
*   **Tuesday**, for **Mars**.
*   **Wednesday**, for **Mercury** <note>Original: "Mercurius."</note>.
*   **Thursday**, named for **Jupiter**.
*   **Friday**, for **Venus**.
*   **Saturday**, for **Saturn**.
*   **Sunday**, for the **Sun**; for this is the day of the week when one must most carefully avoid angering one’s Creator, as it is the day one must thank God and his saints without ceasing, and avoid sin."

¶ "Master," said Placides, "how are these seven planets arranged in the firmament?"

"Placides," said Tymeo, "the seven stars are not together; rather, each is in its own circle or its own heaven. A 'circle' is understood to be a heaven—one higher than the other—and each has its own movement as it pleases the decree of the Creator. Each has its own time to travel through the twelve signs, which are twelve stars in the **zodiac** through which the seven planets pass. In passing through, they are in their 'reign' <note>A position of astrological strength.</note>. In their 'descent' <note>Original: "abaissement." Also known as a planet's "fall," where its influence is weakened or altered.</note>, they change their qualities and temper their virtues. We will speak more clearly to you of the tempering of these twelve signs regarding the birth of male and female children later, but we must now return to our subject."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the master Tymeo and his student Placides. After discussing the nature of light, mirrors, and atmospheric vapors (shooting stars), the master now explains the celestial hierarchy of the seven planets and the mechanics of the lunar and solar cycles within the zodiac.</meta>

### The Heart of Secrets

Placides, the seven <term>planets <note>In the medieval geocentric model, the "planets" included the Sun and the Moon, as they were "wandering" stars compared to the fixed constellations.</note></term> are situated one higher than the other, just as I told you before. The Moon, which is the smallest of the seven, is the closest to us. And because she is closest to us, she appears to our sight to be the largest; she completes her course through the twelve signs in one month, for she <term>reigns <note>The "reign" here refers to the period of waxing or increasing in light/elevation.</note></term> for fifteen days, and for the other fifteen days she goes into decline. "Master," said Placides, "now remember your word and tell me how she reigns." Tymeo said, "Placides, the Moon renews herself in a sign, beginning with the first, which is called **Aries** <note>original: "Aries"; the sign of the Ram</note>. And in each of these signs there are thirty degrees, of which thirty she reigns from the moment she enters the first degree, and from degree to degree until she has ascended to the fifteenth. This is from the first day she is waxing, and she goes on filling with brightness until she is called the full moon. Then she goes declining through the signs in which she takes her descent and the loss of her brightness, and she diminishes from day to day until her light has failed, which the common people call the <term>waning <note>original: "decours"</note></term>, and she completes her course in twenty-five <term>artificial days <note>A medieval term usually referring to the time from sunrise to sunset, though here used to calculate the lunar cycle.</note></term>."

"Placides," said Tymeo, "**Mercury** is above the Moon and has his common path while he reigns and declines just as the Moon does through the twelve signs. And then **Venus** will go her way, doing just as the Moon does. After Venus is the **Sun**, who in one year completes his course through the twelve signs, and remains in each sign for one month and reigns for half a year, and in half a year declines. It should be known that he begins to reign in the middle of March when he enters **Aries**; and through these signs—**Aries**, **Taurus** <note>the Bull</note>, **Gemini** <note>the Twins</note>, **Cancer** <note>the Crab</note>, **Leo** <note>the Lion</note>, **Virgo** <note>the Virgin</note>—he makes his course and finishes his reign at the entry of **Libra** <note>the Scales</note>; and he declines in **Libra**, **Scorpio** <note>the Scorpion</note>, **Sagittarius** <note>the Archer</note>, **Capricorn** <note>the Goat</note>, **Aquarius** <note>the Water-Bearer</note>, and **Pisces** <note>the Fish</note>."

"Placides, they say **Mars** is next, who is the god of battle, of whom we shall speak more clearly hereafter. And of **Jupiter**, who has his reign in his circle between Mars and **Saturn**. **Saturn** is the one who is at the highest point and who takes thirty years <note>original: "vingt ans" (twenty years), though the text immediately contradicts this with the following math</note> to run through the twelve signs; that is to say, to run for twelve and a half years <note>This likely refers to a specific phase, as the text then changes the figures again</note> and he is in his reign for fifteen years as he travels through six signs, and fifteen years which make up his decline; and thus the seven planets reign and decline along the path they take through the twelve signs that make up the **zodiac**. "My fair, sweet master," said Placides, "sometimes I have heard it said that when the Moon was full and the sky was clear and pure and without the obscurity of clouds, she changed her brightness into several colors, and at the last lost her light and her color; what could this be?" "Placides," said Tymeo, "I will tell you what I can understand of it. According to the sayings of the ancient philosophers, the seven planets suffer an **eclipse** according to how they encounter one another and take the light from one another. Especially two suffer eclipses which are more apparent to us and better known than the other five: these are the Sun and the Moon, which eclipses are natural. This is despite the fact that there have been some that were against nature, such as when our Lord suffered pain and death on the cross to redeem sinners from the death of Hell where they were."

He concludes by distinguishing between natural eclipses caused by planetary alignment and the miraculous eclipse recorded during the Crucifixion.</summary>

Folio 38.

# On Philosophy.

G iii

...fallen through the sin of Eve and Adam, who was our first human father, because they trespassed against the commandment of their Creator, just as Saint Dionysius <note>Saint Dionysius (or Denis) the Areopagite, an Athenian judge converted by Saint Paul. In the Middle Ages, he was legendary as both a great astronomer and a mystical theologian.</note>—who was one of the great scholars among the pagans and a fine astronomer—witnesses and spoke of to my lord Saint Paul. When my lord Saint Paul went to Athens, where Saint Dionysius was born, he preached the faith of Jesus Christ; Saint Dionysius disputed with him until Saint Paul asked him to show him the arrangement of his temple. 

And then Saint Dionysius led him to his temple and showed him seven altars he had made in honor of the seven planets, which he held to be gods because of the powers and <term>inclinations <note>In medieval astrology, "inclinations" refer to the way planets influence earthly events and human temperaments.</note></term> they exerted over all earthly things—of which the Sun was most honored. He described the power of these gods until Saint Paul saw and looked upon an altar behind the other altars of this temple. Then Saint Paul said to Saint Dionysius: "What purpose does that altar serve, and how is it named?" And then Saint Dionysius said to Saint Paul: "It is in honor of the **Unknown God** <note>original: "dieu mescogneu"; a reference to the "Ignoto Deo" mentioned in Acts 17:23.</note>. Do you not remember a day when the sun lost its brightness around the hour of noon and became eclipsed? That eclipse was not by nature nor by reason." Then Saint Dionysius said that the God of Nature suffered a wrong upon the earth, or else the world was preparing to end. Thus he perceived that He was a great God who had power over all other gods (for he believed in many other gods). He told Saint Paul that he had made this altar in honor of that very God, "and no one approaches it but me." And then Saint Paul told him that he was preaching to him about that very God, and thus Saint Paul converted him; and he who was then a pagan became a good Christian. The other eclipse that shall occur against nature will be full of evil fortune, and it shall be a sign of unbelief, for it shall occur against the birth of the son of perdition—that is, the **Antichrist**. Now it is necessary for us to return to our subject.

Placides said: "Tymeo, I will tell you briefly to make you understand, and so that I may learn other things." 

The sun makes one complete circuit around the earth between day and night. And as long as it remains above the earth, the day lasts. And when the sun is beneath the earth, it is night. It is just as if someone had a candle around his head, or a burning fire in his fist, or around a <term>pommel <note>A small, rounded knob or ball used here as a physical model for the Earth.</note></term>; the part that was closest to the candle would be directly illuminated, and the part that was further behind would be dark. In this way, the sun by its nature causes night and day to be born beneath the earth. Day is always with the sun, and on the other side, it leaves the shadow and the earth which is dark; and on that side, it leaves the shadow where it cannot see. And it is this shadow that makes the night, and not the day itself. 

And because the sun is larger than the earth, its shadow goes on <term>diminishing <note>original: "appetissant"; meaning to taper or grow smaller.</note></term> until it comes to nothing at the end, in the manner of a pointed **steeple** upon a monastery. But if the earth and the sun were of the same size, the shadow would have no end, but would continue forever without fail. And if the earth were larger, the shadow would go on widening, as you can see in these three figures.

# The Heart of Secrets

Placides, the seven planets are situated one higher than the other, just as I told you before. The moon, which is the smallest of the seven, is the closest to us. And because it is closer to us, it appears to our sight to be the largest. It completes its course through the twelve signs in one month; for it <term>reigns<note>In this context, "reigns" refers to the period during which a celestial body is ascending in the sky or increasing in its light and influence.</note></term> for fifteen days, and for the other fifteen days it goes descending.

"Master," said Placides, "now remember your word and tell me how it reigns."

Placides, said Tymeo, the moon renews itself in a sign, and so it begins at the first, which is called **Aries**. And in each of these signs there are thirty degrees; of which thirty, it reigns from the moment it enters the first degree, and from degree to degree until it has ascended to the fifteenth. This is from the first day that it is waxing, and it goes on filling with brightness until it is called the full moon. Then it goes descending through the signs in which it takes its decline and the loss of its brightness, and it diminishes from day to day until its light has failed—which the common people call the <term>waning<note>original: "decours"</note></term>—and it completes its course in twenty-five <term>artificial days<note>In medieval science, "artificial days" often referred to the period of daylight, but here it is used as a technical unit for calculating the lunar cycle.</note></term>.

Placides, said Tymeo, Mercury is above the moon and has its common path just as it reigns and as it descends, like the moon does through the twelve signs. And then Venus will go her way to do just as the moon does. After Venus is the Sun, which in one year completes its course through the twelve signs; it stays in each sign for one month and reigns for half a year, and for half a year it descends. It should be known that it begins to reign in the middle of **March**, when it enters **Aries**; and through these signs—**Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo**—it completes its course and ends its reign at the entry of **Libra**. It then descends through **Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius**, and **Pisces**.

Placides, **Mars** sits next, who is the god of battle, of whom we shall speak more clearly hereafter. And then Jupiter, who has his reign in his circle between **Mars** and **Saturn**. **Saturn** is the one which is at the highest, and which takes twenty <note>The text says "twenty," but the subsequent math of 15 + 15 suggests thirty years, which is the actual orbital period of Saturn.</note> years to run through the twelve signs; that is to say, to run through the twelve <insert>signs</insert> and a half; and it is in its reign for fifteen years, which it takes to go through six signs, and fifteen years which make up its descent. And so the seven planets reign and descend along the path they take through the twelve signs that make up the zodiac.

"Fair, sweet master," said Placides, "sometimes I have heard it said that when the moon was full and the sky was clear and pure, without the obscurity of clouds, she changed her brightness into several colors, and at last lost her light and her color. What could that be?"

Placides, said Tymeo, I will tell you what I can understand of it. According to the sayings of the ancient philosophers, the seven planets suffer eclipses according to how they encounter one another and take away the light from one another. Especially two suffer eclipses, which are more apparent to us and better known than the other five: these are the Sun and the Moon, and these eclipses are natural. However, there have been those that were against nature <note>Meaning "supernatural" or "miraculous."</note>, such as when our Lord suffered pain and death on the cross to redeem sinners from the death of hell where they were...

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram illustrating a solar eclipse or the casting of shadows in space. It shows three celestial bodies aligned within a conical frame. And you can also prove this without a diagram. If you take any opaque object that can block light / such as iron / stone / wood <note>original: "fust"; archaic term for wood or a wooden staff</note> or any other thing through which one cannot see, and you place it before your eyes against what you wish to see—either the earth or the sky. If that object is larger than the space between your two eyes, it will obstruct your view both near and far in its direction more than its actual size. And if the object is equal to and as large as the space between your two eyes, it will deprive you of as much vision as the object is large. If the object is smaller than the width between your two eyes, it will take away less from your sight than its distance from what you wish to see beyond / and the closer you place the object to your eyes, the further you will be able to see around the object until you can see it all <note>This describes the principle of parallax and how the distance of an object relative to the observer's eyes changes the field of vision.</note>. 

But to understand this better and more easily / take a candle in your right fist / then place your left fist between the candle and the wall / or your arm / or your back. And if what you place there is larger than the flame of the candle / the shadow of the object hitting the wall behind it will be wider than the object itself / and the further it is from the object causing the shadow, the larger the shadow will grow compared to the flame. Or if the shadow hits the wall / you can never place it so close to the wall that the shadow is not longer and wider than the thing blocking the light. 

And if the flame were exactly as large as the body whose shadow is on the wall / the shadow would be equal to the flame and to the body of the thing casting the shadow / nor could you ever move it so far away that all three would not be of one size. 

If the flame is larger than the body / then it follows that the shadow must be smaller than the body casting the shadow / and you could never place it so far or so near that the shadow is not smaller than the body that makes it / and you could move it so far from the wall that there would be no shadow at all <note>This explains the formation of the "umbra" or a tapering shadow cone. When the light source is larger than the object, the shadow eventually comes to a point and disappears.</note> / and the wall is just as well illuminated in the spot where the object previously cast a shadow as elsewhere where the object casts no shadow. 

You can likewise understand this regarding all things that give light and everything that can cast a shadow. Thus you must understand that the sun is larger than the earth which circles the sky, and it gives brightness to all the stars of the sky night and day, above and below. But those stars that are below <note>Referring to the stars on the other side of the Earth or those obscured by the sun's daytime glare.</note> we cannot easily see by day. This is caused by the brightness of the sun:

### On Philosophy. Leaf 39.

For the brightness [of stars] is as great as that of burning candles that you see at night. If between you and them there were a great fire, it would prevent you from seeing their brightness. And if one were then to put that light behind your back, you would immediately be able to see the light [of the candles]. In this way, you must understand that the stars cannot be seen by day as long as the sun is shining upon the earth; but when the sun is beneath the earth and the earth casts a shadow for us, so that the sun does not give us its light, then we can see them. And those stars that are above us in summer are beneath us in winter; because the sun shines around us, it soon follows them when they are in the part where the sun shines until it moves away from there. But they are always illuminated wherever they may be, both night and day, and the whole firmament <term>firmament: the sphere of the heavens where the stars are fixed</term> above and to the sides, except for that which is near the earth, as far as that shadow reaches where the sun is not. It is always day somewhere in the world, except for where the shadow of the earth falls, just as we can understand by the diagram and also recognize how the shadow decreases, because the sun is larger than the earth and [the shadow] ends in a point <note>original: "finist en coing"; this describes the conical shape of the Earth's shadow, or umbra</note> and lasts further away from the earth than where the moon sits on high; but it fails before reaching the sun. The earth is what prevents you from seeing the daylight that the sun gives us. If the earth were itself clear so that one could see through it, one would always see the sun both above the earth and below; but because it is inherently dark, it prevents us from seeing it and casts a shadow between us and the sun. And the shadow also follows its course just like the sun, which always goes alongside it; when the sun rises in the morning, the shadow begins in the West. And when it rises toward midday, the shadow is beneath the earth. And when it is in the West, the shadow is in the East. And when the sun is beneath us, then the shadow is toward us, which always goes on lowering its point toward the West until the sun shines again, which gives the day and the night.

Since you, Placides, understand what night and day are, it is fitting that hereafter you understand the moon and how she receives light from the sun; for in whatever place she may be, she is always illuminated by it. And so, when we say she is "full" in her roundness, the further she is from the sun, the more she is full of brightness. And when she is beneath, we cannot see her. That is when she is between the earth and the sun, so that she is bright on the side toward the sun and dark on the side toward us; and for that reason, we see nothing of her. And when she has passed the point where she moves above the sun, then a horned <note>original: "cornue"; referring to the crescent shape</note> light appears. And as she moves further away and the light of the sun strikes her more, she appears half-bright. Then she is in the middle of her circle where she makes one revolution each month, and then she goes on moving away from that quarter, her brightness increasing until she is beautiful and clear all over. And then she is as far from the sun as she can possibly be. And the sun is on the other side, from which she takes her light, and she is turned toward us. Then the earth is between the sun and the moon, so that one can see them only a very little, and not [both] upon the earth. But one of them can be seen while one is beneath and the other above; for this reason, one cannot see them both together morning and evening; but the moon, having completed half of—

"Placides," said Tymeo, "it is necessary for her to lose brightness when she is at her fullest, and she goes little by little darkening, just as you have heard before how she receives her light from the sun. And when it is necessary for her to <term>eclipse: the obscuring of a celestial body's light when another body passes between it and the observer or its source of light</term>, her brightness comes to her from nowhere; and this does not happen to her before she turns half of her course toward the sun so that she is continuously illuminated. But when she has entered into alignment <note>original: "entree en ligne"</note>, just as she goes failing, so her course is most shining <note>referring to the moon being full at the moment the eclipse begins</note>. Then the sun strikes her with its rays and gives her brightness; and the less she passes through the shadow <note>original: "lumbre"</note> of the earth, the less she loses the brightness she receives from the sun. But when she is caught in the shadow, you can understand it thus: if a line were drawn through the center point of the earth and out both sides, and passed through the body of the sun to the other part, the end of that line passing from the earth would go as far through the point of the shadow <note>original: "coing de lumbre"; refers to the apex of the Earth's conical shadow, the umbra</note> as the day through the moon, which passes near here or there each month; and sometimes she passes right through the middle. Then she falls inside the shadow and becomes all pale, and [the earth] obstructs the brightness of the sun so that it cannot reach her. And the more she is directly on that line, the more her brightness declines. Thus one must sometimes [see] in the middle of the month the moon, which is at its fullest and most dark—

# On Philosophy. Folio 40.

...entirely and within three hours regain her brightness. Thus you can understand that the moon eclipses because of the earth, which casts a shadow against the sun so that its brightness cannot shine upon the moon, and she becomes dark and shadowy.

Placides, Tymeo said this: it happens similarly to the sun, which sometimes at midday goes into a decline which is called in Latin an *eclipse* <note>original: "eclipse"</note> and in French a *failing of light* <note>original: "deffault de lumiere"</note>. It happens in this manner: when the moon, which is below, comes between us and the sun, directly on the line of sight, she takes away the brightness of the sun from above, so that it seems to us that it fails. For the moon is not of such a pure body that the sun can shine through it, as if through another star. It is just like one candle placed far from another; if you held your palm in front of the candle, it would take away the brightness so that you could not see that part. And the more you placed your hand in front of the candle, the less brightness you would see, until you saw none at all. 

And you can also understand about the eclipse that occurs between the sun and the moon: they do not share the same path; rather, the moon goes another way that deviates. And for this reason, you can imagine it as if you stretched a thread from your gaze all the way to the sun; likewise, understand that line from which the moon deviates sometimes here or there each month as she travels beneath the sun. But when she is near that line and passes through it, she prevents those of us who are below her from seeing the sun for as long as she is at that point. For then she casts a shadow upon the earth so that the sight of the sun does not reach the earth. And those who are in that part then have shadow before their eyes, but this is not across the whole world; for the moon is not nearly as large as the sun, and therefore the shadow falls only where it lands on the path of the line that lies between the sun and the earth. 

Because of this, philosophers used to travel to where they knew it would occur, having sought it through their senses and the cases they had observed, of which they had many proofs; thus they praised God all the more for His powers <note>original: "vertus", referring to divine strengths or the natural properties of the universe</note> which they had confirmed. And just as we see here below the failing of the sun upon us while the moon is directly beneath it—and the lower the moon is—then the sun passes beyond it, and they continue moving apart in such a way that it appears, as before, that the moon (which is always moving) appears horned <note>crescent-shaped</note> three days after the eclipse.

# The Heart of Secrets

You can understand what I tell you: just as the moon takes light from you, so also the earth often takes the brightness from the moon, as you have heard before. However, an eclipse of the moon could never happen except when it is at its full phase, nor an eclipse of the sun except at the failing of the moon <note>original: "deffault de la lune"; this refers to the New Moon, the phase when the moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun.</note>, unless God—who makes all things change according to His will—caused it to happen otherwise. He did this once when He died on the cross for us, when the light of day failed between noon and mid-afternoon <note>original: "midy et nonne"; Nones was the traditional prayer hour for 3:00 PM.</note>. At that time, the moon was positioned above the sun as far as could be, and it was known that she was full, yet she was below the earth <note>This highlights the miraculous nature of the event: a solar eclipse usually requires a New Moon, but according to tradition, the moon was full and on the opposite side of the world during the Crucifixion.</note>. Then the day was darkened, as I told you before regarding Saint Paul, through whom Saint Denis was converted by the grace of God <note>This refers to the legend of Dionysius the Areopagite (Saint Denis), who supposedly witnessed the miraculous eclipse in Egypt and concluded that the "Unknown God" was suffering.</note>.

Placides, Tymeo said this: "Now you have heard about the eclipses of the sun and the moon."
"Master," said Placides, "what profit do they bring to the world?"
"Placides, I will tell you. These are demonstrations from God; such as the loss of some good, the coming of war, the death of kings or princes, or the lightning-strikes of cities that collapse through earthquakes <note>original: "crosset"; likely referring to fissures or the breaking of the earth.</note>. That eclipse which was so great signified the death of Jesus Christ. It happened differently than it does for earthly kings, for it occurred against nature; but other eclipses happen by nature, holding their influence on earth regarding events that must happen in this world where everything must end in a brief time. God did not make the firmament or the stars for nothing; rather, He gave them force and power over us, falling upon the earth and in the sky, each according to its power. This applies also to things that are born on the earth. There is nothing that does not have such power as it ought to have, of which we shall speak more clearly further on if we remember it or if you wish to ask. But first, we must return to our subject."

¶ Placides. The Creator, who created and made all things through His marvelous science, ordained the heavens and made and placed there the stars, which are the <term>instruments of nature</term> <note>The text views nature as a machine or craft, where the stars are the tools God uses to shape physical reality.</note> through which nature works every day. Nature has such power that it makes known the influence of the stars in the heaven, which have their virtues on earth—virtues that God gave to the sun and the moon, which provide brightness, heat, and moderation <note>original: "attrempance"</note>. For the heat of the sun is moderated in part by the moon, by some of the seven planets, and by some of the twelve signs <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>. And their coldness is also moderated by the heat of the sun, of which we will speak to you more clearly, for we must return to our subject.

¶ For through these things all living things enter into life and return to corruption, because they have an end and a beginning. For by the power that the Creator gave to the stars, there are created in people and in beasts, in trees, herbs, fish, birds, and in all things, diverse appearances and qualities of spirit <note>original: "courage"; here meaning the inner disposition or vital spirit.</note>. Each of these things in this world is inclined toward its planet, or its sign, or the star by which it is governed through the power God gave them when He first created the world. And He placed them by nature so that He made them go around the world against the turn of the firmament by their power and their course; and...

-> ## Of Philosophy. Leaf xli. <-

...by their movement is born everything that God placed in this world. And know that if it pleased God to make the firmament hold still and not turn around the world, there would be nothing living in this world that could move, nor have sense or knowledge, any more than a dead man who feels nothing and has no sense nor movement; and everyone would be like a stone statue. If there were no movement in the heavens, there is nothing that could live on earth: for God, who established everything by right and formed all the world, gave to everything He made such power <term>virtue: translated from "vertu," referring to an inherent astrological power or "property" that influences earthly matter</term> as belonged to it. 

He created the stars in the heavens and to all gave power. You can clearly see that the moon gives us the brightness <note>original: "larte", likely a printer's error or OCR mistake for "clarté" (light/brightness)</note> by which we see it entirely full; and there is no man with bones or veins that are not fuller of humors <term>humors: "humeurs," the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which medieval medicine believed were governed by the phases of the moon</term> when the moon is full than when it is waning <term>waning: "decours," the period after the full moon when the visible surface decreases</term>. 

It is the same for all beasts, which are fuller of blood and marrow; and the sea itself swells at the full moon, and likewise subsides in the waning, so much so that when a month passes, those who live near the sea go to live in high places when the moon is full; each takes his household <term>mesgnie: a term for a family, including their servants and retinue</term> and moves away from his house and goes to stay in a high place until the sea has retreated. And when the moon grows small and falls into its waning—and this happens every month—it is all because of the moon, which is one of the seven planets <note>In the medieval geocentric system, the seven "planets" were the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>.

And so one sees of the sun also that when it approaches us, it causes the earth to bear fruit, and also the trees to turn green again. The birds begin to sing for the sweetness of the new season <note>Spring</note>; and when it begins to lower and move away from us, then begins the winter which makes everything [fail] <note>original: "fleurir" (to bloom); this is almost certainly a printer's error for "fremir" (to shiver/shake) or "faillir" (to fail), as it is contrasted with the leaves withering</note> and leaves wither. And since these two stars have these powers, the others were not made for nothing; rather, each has its power according to its nature, causing so many diversities on earth and mutations of the weather—one early and the other late—so that in one year the goods are riper than in another time. 

Hail and frosts cause enough grievances, so that one summer is hot and moist, and the other dry and full of wind. It often happens with winters that they change, so that one is cold and rainy, and the other is cold and dry; and one time things are expensive and another time many things are cheap; and while there was little of something this year, in the other there was a great abundance, and they return for better or worse in the year that follows. 

All these diversities are caused by the stars that are in the sky, where they run their courses naturally, each in a different manner. For if no other star in the sky had power except the sun and the moon—which travel equally each year through the firmament and rise as much in one summer as in another, and always go steadily until the next year returns to the same point as it was before—everything would be different. Good astronomers know that as the sun goes around the sky, where it is today, it will be a year from today. By this we know that if there were no other stars that had power, everything would happen differently: for all years would resemble each other, and each year would be just like the previous year was. And the months would be similar without changing their movements each year without fail: for the sun goes just the same in a month in this year as it did last year, and so it will do again. And when this month and today would resemble the day and the month that will be a year from today in cold, in dryness, and in...

Just as you have heard of the sun, it is the most powerful of the other stars and the most virtuous over all things. And the other stars each have power according to what they are. "Master," said Placides, "it seems to me that the sky is made like an oven for baking bread, where it joins to the earth all around, and is high in the middle."

Therefore you can see the nature of it by a square figure that you might place beneath a round figure, or another that is not round; if you make them turn, which of them would take up the space beneath it like the one that is round? # On Philosophy

...to fill from every side: for He <note>God, the Creator</note> wishes to leave nothing empty, and willed that it should turn night and day; for it is necessary for the heavens to have movement, which causes all things to move. And I shall tell you the reason why the heavens turn all around. God, who created everything from nothing, said that nothing could exist on earth beneath the firmament <term>firmament: the vast, solid dome of the sky that separates the Earth from the upper heavens</term>—which exists by nature—if it did not have heat within it; and heat could not exist without movement.
