And the sun always turns in such a way that it returns to the point from which it first departed, and it does this every day; for between day and night, it completes one turn. And it is right by reason that all things formed within it should return to their first form; for all was nothing and all shall become nothing <note>This refers to the cyclical nature of material existence, contrasting with the eternal soul</note>, so let each person watch what they shall be, so that the spirit which comes from God may return to Him.

And whoever wishes to know what stars are, let them know that they are certain parts of the sky that are brighter than elsewhere, and which, through the course they take as they encounter one another, seem like burning candles, just as one sees on earth in many places. Whoever would search there for certain parts that are brighter than others would find that they are not made of gold or silver or any other shining metal that one sees on earth in many places; but none but God knows what they are. Nor can one find their size or their height by instruments, nor prove their movement by lively reason <term>lively reason: logical arguments or proofs based on observation</term>. For in this, nothing can ever endure; but from what one can see with the eyes, one can certainly inquire into the truth, at least of the things that are beneath the heavens. But regarding the things that are within the sky, which shall never be seen on earth in their own likeness—such as God and angels—there is no one who knows the truth of them. Nor is it in our power to know, for these are the secrets of God. It is not wisdom to inquire into them; rather, we ought to praise the Creator when He shows us the sky and the stars, whose virtues <term>virtues: the inherent powers or astrological influences of celestial bodies</term> and movement we may safely and boldly inquire about, for which we must praise, serve, and love Him; and for the fact that He gives us the sea, the earth, and the sky. If we do His will well, He has promised us this when we pass away.

Some say that it is great folly to inquire into the secrets of God, whether in heaven or on earth. And they say that the work of nature is among the secrets of God, and because they do not understand the work of nature, to excuse their own ignorance <note>original: "rudesse", meaning lack of education or refinement</note>, they say that one should not meddle with it. But the work of the stars, which are works of nature, He truly wished for the human lineage to inquire about and know; for these are not His high secrets, which are of a more exalted matter than the heavens and the stars, or anything that rises within them. This He clearly shows to some of His beloved ones on earth so they may learn. Concerning those high secrets, no corporeal man can or should inquire. And therefore we shall speak of this great world, which is made of the four elements and of the heavens within, which all other things produce by nature, except for God, through whom all things endure. ### On Philosophy. Folio 44.

Master, said **Placides**: "Tell me why man, who is formed of the **four elements**, does not live as long as the four elements themselves? For you have told me that he is made of these four." "Do you not know what I told you regarding the **four qualities** <note>The qualities are Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness, which correspond to the four elements.</note> in a man or a woman? Within them, one of these four always overcomes the other three. Because this one is stronger than the others, it must by necessity—and sometimes by nature—happen that the weakest of the four is destroyed by the power of the other three, against which it cannot stand. And as soon as it is destroyed, man must die. For if there is more **heat** than **moisture**, the heat dries up the moisture. And if there is more moisture than heat, the moisture extinguishes the heat. Likewise, if there is more **heat** than **cold**, the heat annihilates the cold. And if there is more **dryness** than **moisture**, the dryness drinks up the moisture. And if there is more moisture than dryness, the moisture drowns the dryness. And when any of these qualities fails in a man, his nature is corrupted; thus man or woman dies, and it is necessary for the soul to depart from the body."

Now that you have heard how the world was made, we will tell you of the height and the greatness of the stars, just as **Ptolemy** <note>original: "Ptholomee." Claudius Ptolemy was a 2nd-century astronomer. In the Middle Ages, he was often mistakenly called the "King of Egypt" because of his name.</note>, the good king, inquired and proved; many others found it to be true after him and marveled at his wisdom. We shall tell you how they knew these things. First, they measured the **Earth**. By this, they proved the size and the height of the **firmament** <term>firmament: the sphere of the fixed stars that medieval scholars believed rotated around the Earth</term> and the stars. Once they had measured the Earth and found how thick it was, they then inquired about the **Moon**, because it is closest to the Earth. Then they asked about the **Sun**, how far it is from the Earth, and they found it to be much larger than the Earth. Once they had measured the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth, they could more easily inquire about the other stars—which ones are closer or further away—and the size of each. They found that every star is larger than the entire Earth, except for three, each of which is smaller than the Earth. Every man who knows the art of **necromancy** <term>necromancy: here used to mean "astral science" or hidden knowledge of the heavens, rather than modern "spirit summoning"</term> and **astronomy** must know this. But because common folk are not such clerks or masters that they can prove this themselves, I wish to recount for you how large the Earth is and how thick it is; how far the Moon is from the Earth; and how large each star is, just as Ptolemy proved it, and how great and high the firmament is. And we shall begin with the Earth.

"Placides," said **Tymeo**, "now listen. When they had measured the Earth by an art they had proven through divine reason, they found that the Earth was twenty thousand, four hundred and twenty-eight **leagues** <note>original: "lieues"</note> all the way around. Each league contains one thousand **paces**, and the pace has five **feet**, and the foot is twelve **inches** <note>original: "pounces"</note> long. And if the Earth were split through the middle, one would find that it is six thousand, five hundred leagues thick through the center. By this last measurement, one knows well how high the firmament is from the Earth; they could find no more accurate measurement. Thus they 'pierced' through the middle of the Earth, by which they measured the firmament, the stars, and the planets. They foun—

### The Heart of Secrets

[They] found that the body of the Earth is more than twenty-nine and a quarter times larger than the Moon. And from the Earth up to the Moon, the distance is twenty-four and a half times—plus five times twenty times—the thickness of the Earth through its center. Of the Sun, they said by this same reasoning that it was one hundred and seventy times larger than the Earth. **But** he who does not know this hardly believes it; and yet it is proved by geometry, which is the true science by which it can best be proven. Many philosophers have since troubled themselves, doubting whether this was true or not, until they found through reason that this king <note>Referring to Ptolemy, whom the medieval author considers a king of Egypt.</note> had spoken the truth regarding the height and the greatness. Thus one can well know that the Sun is very far from us when it seems so small; but it is so high up that one cannot know from down here how much [land/distance] there is from the Earth to the Sun. It is five hundred and fifty-five times the thickness of the Earth to the heaven where the stars are fixed <note>In the medieval model, stars were thought to be embedded in a physical crystalline sphere.</note>, which is ten thousand and fifty-five times as much as the Earth’s thickness. And he who knows how to calculate will find how many inches and how many feet, how many leagues, how many thousands, and how many days' journey there are from here to heaven. But there is so much that if a man could go there by a straight path and traveled every day without stopping for twenty-five leagues for a duration of six thousand and fifty-six and a half years, that time would be passed before he went from here to heaven. Or if the first man whom God made <note>Adam</note> had walked continuously from the moment he was created and had traveled twenty leagues every day, he would not be there yet. Rather, he would still have to travel for seven hundred and twelve years from the time this book was first made—which was written in the year one thousand two hundred and forty-seven, on the day of the Epiphany <note>original: "l’apparition," the feast celebrating the manifestation of Christ.</note>. So much time would Adam have spent if he had moved from the moment he was made and formed. And he would still have so far to go as I told you before. And if a lead weight <note>original: "plombee."</note> were there and took a hundred years to fall, it would have to descend seventy-four and a half leagues every hour of the day before it reached the ground.

The number of planets is such that there are one thousand and twenty-nine in total <note>The author uses "planets" here to refer to the catalog of fixed stars, as 1029 is the number of stars listed in Ptolemy's Almagest.</note>, and there may well be more. **But** one cannot see more than can be clearly discerned, nor can their movement be known. **But** it is the opinion of many people that there are more than I say; but it is because they are so far from us that it prevents us from discerning them. It is like candles: if one lit many of them in one place, it would seem from a distance that there were many more because of the rays of their light reaching from one to the other; and he who saw them from further away would think there were even more. And so it is with the stars: looking up at the sky, there are fewer than it seems because one sees them all together. **But** if one knew how to discern each one individually, fewer would be counted. But not everyone knows what this amounts to; and no one could count them except by seven instruments that King Ptolemy made, by which they are known and one knows how to count, and where each one sits, and how far it is from one to another, whether they are near or far from each other. And he gave us the knowledge of their figures and the entire greatness of the firmament: the stars, their names, and the shape by which they are known. And especially forty-five of the most powerful <note>original: "vertueuses," referring to their astrological influence or "virtue."</note>, among which are the twelve signs <note>The Zodiac</note> that make a circle where the seven planets pass. And we are so far from heaven...

### On Philosophy. Folio xiiii.

...that whoever is caught in sin, his sinful soul will never leave that state. And the soul that is caught in a state of grace will have gone there <note>Meaning to Paradise.</note> in less than an hour. And furthermore, it climbs so high into paradise that no one in this world could calculate the height to which souls ascend, nor the joy where the soul goes; no one could imagine or compare the height of the "up above" and the lowliness of the "down here." There is as much distance as there is from the earth to the firmament. For the firmament is so much greater, higher, and wider that one could hardly imagine or count the number of houses on earth that would be needed to fill it. For if they were all placed in a single mountain, and each house was as large as the whole earth—and if the earth were a hundred thousand times larger than it is—and if there were a hundred thousand times as many people as there are—and if everyone did their best to procreate from now for a thousand years, and each person was as large as a giant, and each had a residence so great that no king ever had the like, with woods, bird-filled groves, ovens, mills, meadows, vineyards, and gardens around each house for their sustenance so that each could provide for his whole household—even then, they could all easily dwell within the firmament. And there would still be more empty space than they would require for their enjoyment if they wished to frolic. From this, people can well reflect that God is truly powerful, He who knows how to make such noble things as the sun, the heavens, and the firmament.

But since I have told you of the greatness of the firmament, which always moves and where the stars follow their courses, now hear of the heaven above where they do not move at all, but are always in one spot. Just as a man who moves from one place to go to another: the first place would not move, but the man would go along as if around a circle and return to the first place from which he departed before; but the place itself would not move at all, but rather stay in one spot. You must understand the heaven in this way: that nothing is shifted within the firmament or the stars, but rather they hold fast. And it is this heaven that seems blue to us, which extends forward into the air that we see when the air is pure all around, and it cannot suffer corruption. This heaven encloses the firmament.

**Placides** said to **Tymeo**: "Now it is necessary that I tell you about the heavens that are above this firmament, and what they are. But man cannot see them, for human senses have no power there. But above the heaven of which we have told you, there is another, beautiful and round and the color of crystal <note>original: "couleur de cristal"; this refers to the Crystalline Heaven of medieval cosmology.</note>. Above that one, there is another which is purple in color, and it is called the **Imperial Heaven** <note>original: "ciel imperial"; often referred to as the Empyrean, the highest heaven and the dwelling place of God.</note>. And there are the holy orders of angels and the holy souls who see God; night and day, there is nothing that bothers them because they see paradise."

You wish to hear of paradise to understand what I have said above; you may do so without sin. For that heaven is blessed, and by right there can be nothing there but goodness and all beauties; for there is no man who could write down the number of good things that are there. And God truly promises it to those who wish to be His friends, as is their right. And it is so common <note>Meaning accessible or manifest.</note> everywhere that everyone who has served Him can see it. Like He who sees everything here and there, as He who reigns everywhere. And of this you can...

# The Heart of Secrets

You can take an example from some whom you hear speaking, and likewise how every person listens to their own words. ¶ Thus you can understand through a single word what many say: that all good must be, and God must reign everywhere. For His power is in all places, like the light of the sun in clear weather which illuminates the world wherever it pleases, as quickly in one thing as in another. For if you were to put many things together, the light would come as quickly to the thing in the middle as to the one in front or the one to the side. ¶ Since these created things have such virtues, how much more must He have who created them from Himself and who has all goodness within Him? His paradise extends everywhere, as He is the lord of all creatures. In paradise are all the angels and the archangels and all the saints who sing praise and glory before God. There is such delight there that there is no one who could understand by example, nor know, nor learn what paradise is, nor the great joy that those have to whom God has granted it. Even if the best scholar in all the world—possessing the deepest knowledge, and being the most subtle and best-spoken person who was ever seen on earth or who could ever be—had a thousand tongues, each speaking on its own, and had a thousand hearts and more to think as best they could at all times to describe what paradise is, and if each tongue could speak the thoughts of each heart, they still could not describe in any heart the great joy that the poorest person has there. There is no one so poor in paradise who would wish to be king of the whole world down here—even if everyone obeyed him without contradiction—at the cost of being out of paradise for a single day. There is life everlasting and stability everywhere, so that nothing is lacking; may God wish to place us there. Amen.

"Master," said Placides to Tymeo, "by your mercy you have answered me well according to my wishes regarding everything I have asked you about <term>natured nature</term> <note>original: "nature naturee"; referring to the created world and its physical laws</note> and <term>naturing nature</term> <note>original: "nature naturant"; referring to God as the creative force or the impulse of creation</note>, and how man is conceived until birth. But there is one thing I marvel at concerning all men: I see none who perfectly resemble one another without some difference. ¶ Master, I would like to pray you—provided it does not weary you—to tell me the causes so that I might understand it." "Placides," said Tymeo, "I have told you before that he who wishes to know enough must inquire enough; and it pleases me much that you have committed this to memory so well, and I will answer you according to my opinion and the science that God has lent me."

"Placides, the diversity of appearances that you can see in men and women is caused by the points of their <term>nativities</term> <note>The specific moment and astrological conditions of one's birth.</note> and by the movement of the planets and the signs as they encounter and pass one another. We will tell you a little of what we think of it. ¶ Placides," said Tymeo, "if you wish to know under which planet a person was born, and the cause why, and why they are of various appearances and various <term>dispositions</term> <note>original: "courages"; in this context meaning temperament, inner character, or spirit</note>, it is all through the nature of the planet that was rising or setting at the hour of their birth, and by the virtue of the sign in which the planet was at the hour they were born. We shall speak of this more clearly hereafter. Now we must return to our subject."

# On Philosophy. Folio xlv.

->h.iii.<-

Should all those who are born under a single planet not be of one likeness, of one nature, of one manner, and of one quality? "Placides," said Tymeo, "I will indeed tell you the reason for this. There are seven planets in the sky which all seven pass along a single path called the zodiac <note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</note>, in which there are the twelve signs; and the seven planets pass through these twelve signs. And when any planet enters into any sign—for example, if Saturn enters Aries, which is the first of the twelve signs—it runs through it for two and a half years. That is to say, fifteen months in its reign <term>regne: the period of a planet's strongest influence</term> and fifteen months in its debasement <term>abaissement: the period where a planet's influence weakens</term>."

"Now tell me, master, what is its reign and its debasement?" "Placides," said Tymeo, "I will tell you. And first of Saturn <note>original: 'Saturnus'</note>, which is the highest planet of the others and which takes the longest to complete its course through all the twelve signs. For you must know that it remains for two and a half years in each sign, which constitutes its reign; and it begins in Aries from the hour it enters there until it leaves the sign of Virgo and enters Libra; and immediately its debasement begins until it leaves Pisces. And you can understand the same of all seven planets: as soon as they enter Aries, their reign begins until they enter Libra. And then, when they enter there, their debasement begins and their powers <term>vertus: the inherent qualities or strengths of the celestial body</term> diminish. And because of this, men and women are of many manners and diverse qualities, through the encounters of the planets and the signs they meet as they pass through the zodiac, which is their path in the sky—the path where there are twelve signs through which the seven planets pass. By the power of these signs, the qualities are transformed and tempered in the planets. For instance, Saturn is cold and dry <note>original: 'freste'</note> when it enters Aries, which is a hot, moist, and gentle sign. Thus, it is tempered by the virtues of Aries. For the malice <note>original: 'felonnie'</note> of Saturn is tempered by the gentleness of Aries, its coldness by its heat, and its dryness by the moisture of Aries. And in this same way, the other seven planets are tempered by the encounters with the twelve signs, of which I shall speak to you more clearly hereafter."

"Master," said Placides to Tymeo, "now tell me, if it pleases you, about the children who are born during the reign of Saturn and during its debasement." "The child who is born under this planet called Saturn will be troublesome to raise and will be in danger of being imprisoned <note>original: 'enferre', literally 'put in irons'</note> in their youth. He will be cruel and a great eater but a small drinker, and will be diligent in finishing what he has undertaken to do. He will willingly do what pleases people and will love strangers more than those of his own country. He will love money and be envious <note>original: 'avieux'</note>, but his anger will pass easily. He will be pensive and secretive. He will have strong loins but a weak head. He will be fearful and <unclear>denupt</unclear> <note>This word is obscure; it may suggest being 'stripped' or 'destitute'</note>. The humors <term>coles: choler or bile, associated with a bitter or irritable temperament</term> will rule in his body. Wearing black clothing will be good for him. The best day of the week for him will be Saturday, and the worst will be Friday. And of the months, September will be the best for him and March the worst. And the child will be of this same condition if it is female."

"Master," said Placides to Tymeo, "are all those who are born during the reign of this planet <note>Referring to Saturn</note> and during its debasement <term>abaissement: the period where a planet's influence is weakened</term> of this same nature?"

"Placides," said Tymeo, "you are playing the wise fool, or you do not understand what I have told you of Saturn: how it is tempered <term>attrempee: balanced or modified by external influences</term> in its nature and loves its qualities when it passes through the twelve signs. It is through these signs that the planets love their natures and their qualities, and temper their coldness and their heat, their moisture and their dryness <note>The four primary qualities of medieval science which combined to form the temperaments</note>. So we shall tell you more about it."

He will be chaste, piteous, and of good faith. He will often be sick in the eyes and will often lose his possessions. He will willingly travel to foreign places and will have a mark on his face. He will be in danger of falling from a height. And if he escapes this, he will live a long time and have a good end. And if the child is female, she will be a beautiful woman, between dark and fair. She will have black eyes, slow speech, and be well-proportioned. She will be clever with her hands, and will be courteous and comely of body. She will often be sick. She will be of average means, good, and chaste. She will have one man in her life and several children. She will have a mark on her breast and will be in danger from a venomous beast. And if she escapes this, she will live a short time.

¶ If **Pisces** is at the birth of the child, he will be worldly and of beautiful speech; he will be wise and courteous. He will have slender limbs and will be weak in the loins. He will be lustful and outrageous, of poor faith, and knowledgeable in evil. He will be a slanderer and will often annoy <note>original: "engraingnera" — to provoke or aggravate</note> people. He will have knowledge of arms and will be generous. He will willingly move from one country to another. He will have a mark on his neck and will be in danger of the sword. And if he escapes this, he will live a long time and die in a foreign land. And if the child is female, she will be a good woman, tall and beautiful, dark-skinned and loyal. She will have two husbands and several children. She will have a mark on her loins and will be in danger of a house falling upon her. And if she escapes this, she will live a short time.

"Master," said **Placides** to **Tymeo**, "of all these signs through which this planet passes, I see no two judgments that resemble each other."
"Placides," said Tymeo, "this is because of the various movements of the planet as it runs through the twelve signs, which are of different qualities and different movements. Now let us leave that and return to our subject."

# The Heart of Secrets

Placides, now listen, and I will tell you about Jupiter, which is less high <note>meaning lower in the celestial spheres than Saturn</note>. It takes longer to travel through the twelve signs than Saturn, for Saturn takes only fifty-nine years, while Jupiter takes eighty-three years to complete its revolution. <note>The text provides "Great Years" or recurrence cycles used in medieval astrology rather than the actual orbital periods we recognize today (Saturn ~29 years, Jupiter ~12 years).</note> And this is because it is retrograde <note>term: retrograde; appearing to move backward in the sky due to the relative positions of the Earth and the planet</note> from one place to another, as do all the other planets, some more and some less. This you may know through the great tables of astronomy. We shall say no more of that, but return to our matter concerning Jupiter: for the child born under the planet Jupiter will be a handsome man, fair-skinned, and a gentle child; wise and perfect, he will love to amass money and will be very stingy. He will willingly work to earn a profit; his best days of the week will be Thursday and Saturday. And if the child is female, she will be of the same condition in matters concerning women.

¶ If **Aries** is encountered with Jupiter, he will be a tall man and lean; wicked and of an evil wit; stingy, covetous, and he will have tender eyes. He will have knowledge of the labor of the earth <note>farming or agriculture</note>, and for the greater part of his life, he will be poor; he will have two marks on his arms and will be in danger of water. If he escapes this, he will live a common lifespan. And if the child is female, she will be a brown-skinned woman and short; of a foolish body <note>original: "folle de corps" — likely meaning promiscuous or lacking self-restraint</note>, and she will often be sick in all her affairs, and she will have a mark on her private parts.

¶ If **Taurus** is encountered with Jupiter at the birth of the child, he will die as a small child without any learning; and he will have his birthmark at the place of peril, whether male or female.

¶ If **Gemini** is there, he will be a small child but grow into a stout man with thick legs, and he will be a good and loyal man. He will have knowledge of arms, but he will have a weak head. He will have a mark on the neck. And if the child is female, she will be a stout woman and coarse in all her works; she will be poor rather than rich, and she will live a short time.

¶ If **Cancer** is encountered with Jupiter, he will be a subtle man of many sciences; he will be wicked and melancholy; a great eater and a great drinker, and very sleepy. His birthmark will be near his foundation <note>euphemism for the buttocks or anus</note>. And if the child is female, she will be a beautiful woman, courtly and gentle, but of a foolish body; slender of limb, and she will die in wealth.

¶ If **Leo** is there, he will be a tall man, strong in all his limbs; he will have knowledge of arms and will be a poor man, but very loyal, and he will strongly wish to keep his word. He will be in danger of dying by weapons. And if the child is female, she will die without skill and in her youth.

Master, said Placides to Tymeo, what if **Virgo** is there? The answer: If Virgo is there, he will not live long and will have a mark on the belly. And if the child is female, she will be skillful with her hands and will die young.

¶ If **Libra** is there, he will be a handsome man, neither too tall nor too small, but he will have no craft; yet he will be as rich as he is able. He will be base of body and lustful, and will be in danger of the sword. If he escapes this, he will live a long time. And if the child is female, she will be a beautiful woman and foolish with her body; she will love musical instruments and will be a great drinker.

[in] this planet, its **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person’s health and personality</term> will be tempered by the power of the aforementioned sign; its quality will be neither as cold, nor as dry, nor as healthy as it would have been if the planet had not been in that sign. It is the same for every planet and every sign when children are born: for they are given their complexions through the tempering they receive by virtue of the movement of the planets. When a planet enters a sign (each sign being divided into thirty degrees), it then enters its reign and its power. And when it has traveled through the twelve signs, by the last six it departs from its reign and its power diminishes; its qualities change and weaken as it travels through the other signs. It is just so for the other planets and signs according to their qualities.

**Placides**, said **Tymeo**: now I wish to tell you what the **triplicity** <term>triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water)</term> of the signs is. Triplicity is named for "three," just as I will tell you of many things in groups of three; thus I will now begin to speak to you of the triplicity of the twelve signs, for you must know that there are three signs of a single quality. That is to say: the **Ram** <note>Aries</note>, the **Lion** <note>Leo</note>, and the **Archer** <note>Sagittarius</note>, which are hot and of the element of fire. The other three signs are cold and dry like earth: these are the **Bull** <note>Taurus</note>, the **Virgin** <note>Virgo</note>, and the **Goat** <note>Capricorn</note>. The other three are moist and hot, as are the **Scales** <note>Libra</note>, the **Twins** <note>Gemini</note>, and the **Water-bearer** <note>Aquarius</note>. And the others are cold and moist: such as the **Crab** <note>Cancer</note>, the **Scorpion** <note>Scorpio</note>, and the **Fish** <note>Pisces</note>.

**Placides**, now I have told you of the four triplicities of the twelve signs; those which belong to one triplicity are of the same complexion. The ancient philosophers perceived this through experience: for when a planet enters its own sign, if it is hot, its heat doubles; and if the planet is hot and moist and enters a sign that is hot and moist, its heat and moisture double. And if the planet is cold and moist and the sign it enters is cold and moist, its coldness and moisture double. But when hot and cold or moist [and dry] meet, they temper one another; and likewise when hot and moist meet cold and dry, it is another kind of tempering. From these four qualities are engendered four other qualities that are less powerful than those mentioned before.

"Master," said **Placides**, "why are these last four qualities less powerful than the first four?" "Because," said **Tymeo**, "the four aforementioned qualities are created during the reign of each planet. This occurs when the planet enters the sign of thirty degrees: for it ascends for fifteen degrees, and its reign consists of this ascending. Then it descends for the other fifteen degrees; and as soon as it begins to descend in its sign, it departs from its reign and its power diminishes. It is thus for all seven planets." "Master," said **Placides** to **Tymeo**, "how can it be that some planets are cold and dry, others hot and moist, others dry and hot, and others cold and moist?"

**Placides**, said **Tymeo**, I will tell you what **Aristotle** says of this: for he says that all things that are movable by force are brought back to a single cause which gives movement to all other causes, and yet it does not move itself <note>Aristotle's concept of the "Unmoved Mover" (Primum Mobile)</note>.

->### The Heart of Secrets<-

...for otherwise there would be no stability or purpose in things, and all the world would be without order and all science lost. And for this reason, all things in this world that provide cold or heat, dryness or moisture—whether they be the four elements or other things—are by necessity traced back to other causes that are neither cold nor hot, dry nor moist in their own substances. But by their **virtue** <term>virtue: in this context, the inherent power or spiritual influence of a celestial body</term>, they bestow these qualities upon the four elements and all other things: heat and moisture, cold and dryness. And these causes are the celestial bodies, such as the heavens, the stars, and the twelve signs, which are neither hot nor cold; but by their virtue, they bestow all these qualities, just as the element draws fire to itself, and the sun by its virtue gives heat. 

Even though it [the sun] is not hot in its own substance; and just as **Saturn** gives cold and yet is not cold itself. For if the planets were hot, cold, dry, or moist in their own substance, they would contain **corruption** <term>corruption: in medieval philosophy, the process of decay or change caused by the conflict of opposing physical qualities</term> within themselves; and since they cannot have corruption within them, it is for this reason they are neither hot nor cold, nor dry nor moist. For heat is corrupted by cold, and moisture by dryness. By this, you can see that in the celestial bodies are found these four qualities through which they transmute the bodies here below, according to how the celestial bodies are in different locations and how they have different "aspects" <note>original: "regardz", referring to the geometric angles between planets</note>, just as with the twelve signs of which I spoke to you before, which create various qualities. And they have their virtues and power over various things here below in men and women, of which I have spoken to you before in many and various ways.

"Master," said **Placides**, "it seems to me you told me before that the twelve signs had movement. I pray you to tell me what movement they have."

**Placides**, now listen. I tell you that four are **movable** <note>today called "Cardinal" signs</note>, like the **Ram** <note>Aries</note>, the **Crab** <note>Cancer</note>, the **Scales** <note>Libra</note>, and the **Goat** <note>Capricorn</note>. For when the sun is beneath any of these four signs, then the weather is changeable in its qualities and does not remain in one state; for in these four signs begin the four quarters of the year <note>original: "parties du monde", referring here to the transition into the four seasons</note> in which the weather shifts. 

The **stable** signs <note>today called "Fixed" signs</note> are the **Bull** <note>Taurus</note>, the **Lion** <note>Leo</note>, the **Water-Bearer** <note>Aquarius</note>, and the **Scorpion** <note>Scorpio</note>. And they are called stable because when the sun places itself beneath these four signs, the weather is stable in its qualities. 

The other four are **indifferent** <note>today called "Mutable" signs</note>, such as the **Twins** <note>Gemini</note>, the **Virgin** <note>Virgo</note>, the **Archer** <note>Sagittarius</note>, and the **Fish** <note>Pisces</note>, which hold the middle way; for they are neither entirely movable nor entirely stable. And when the sun is in these four signs, then the weather is of a middle quality. Anyone who does not know this disposition of the signs will not know at all what the nature should be of the works that are begun under these signs; for a work begun under the movable signs must be movable <note>i.e., subject to change or quick results</note>, unless an impediment comes to it from the condition of some planet.

"Master," said **Placides**, "you tell me that some signs are masculine and some feminine." 

**Placides**, I tell you that a sign is called masculine because when a sign has influence, and especially over any thing...

<meta>This page continues the instructional dialogue between the master Tymeo and his student Placides. Building on the previous discussion of masculine and feminine signs, the text now explores the metaphysical nature of celestial bodies as "first causes" and categorizes the zodiac signs by their "movement"—what modern astrologers call the quadruplicities (Cardinal, Fixed, and Mutable signs).</meta>

<header># The Heart of Secrets</header>

...for otherwise there would be no stability or purpose in things, and the whole world would be without order and all science would be lost. And because of this, all things in this world that provide coldness or heat, dryness or moisture—whether they be the four elements or other things—are by necessity traced back to other causes that are neither cold, nor hot, nor dry, nor moist in their **substances** <term>substance: the essential, unchanging nature of a thing, as opposed to its outward qualities</term>. But by their **virtue** <term>virtue: the inherent spiritual power or influence exerted by a celestial body</term>, they grant these qualities to the four elements and to all other things: heat, moisture, coldness, and dryness.

And these causes are the celestial bodies, such as the heavens, the stars, and the twelve signs, which are neither hot nor cold; but by their virtue, they grant all these qualities. Just as an element draws fire to itself, so the sun by its virtue grants heat, even though it is not hot in its own substance. It is just the same with **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnus"</note>, which grants coldness and yet is not cold. For if the planets were hot, cold, dry, or moist in their substance, they would contain **corruption** <term>corruption: in medieval science, the process of decay, change, or breaking down that affects all earthly matter</term> within them. And since they cannot have corruption within them, they are neither hot nor cold, nor dry nor moist; for heat is corrupted by cold, and moisture by dryness.

Therefore, you can see that in the celestial bodies are found these four qualities by which they transform the bodies here below, according to how the celestial bodies are in different places and how they have different **regards** <term>regard: the "look" or astrological aspect a planet or sign casts upon the Earth</term>, such as the twelve signs I spoke of before, which have different qualities. And they have their virtues and power over various things here below in men and women, of which I have spoken to you before in many and various ways.

"Master," said Placides, "it seems to me that you told me before that the twelve signs had movement. I pray you to tell me what movement they have."

"Placides, now listen. I tell you that four are **movable** <note>These are now known as the Cardinal signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn.</note>, such as the Ram, the Crab, the Scales, and the Goat. For when the sun is beneath any of these four signs, then the weather is movable in its qualities and does not remain in one state; for in these four signs begin the four quarters of the world in which the weather changes. The **stable** <note>These are now known as the Fixed signs: Taurus, Leo, Aquarius, and Scorpio.</note> signs are the Bull, the Lion, the Water-Bearer, and the Scorpion. And they are called stable because when the sun places itself beneath these four signs, the weather is stable in its qualities. The other four are **indifferent** <note>These are now known as the Mutable signs: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces.</note>, such as the Twins, the Virgin, the Archer, and the Fish, which hold the middle way; for they are neither entirely movable nor entirely stable. And when the sun is in these four signs, then the weather is of a middling quality. Whoever does not know this disposition of the signs will not know what nature the works started under these signs ought to have. For a work started under the movable signs must be movable, unless an impediment comes to it from the condition of some planet."

"Master," said Placides, "you told me that some signs are masculine and some feminine."

"Placides, I tell you that the masculine sign is so named because when any sign has a regard, and especially upon any thing..."

...and if that sign is masculine, then the thing is of a stronger **complexion** <term>complexion: in medieval science, the specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—that determines a person’s temperament and physical nature</term>. And if it is a thing that is born under that sign or is conceived, it will have a male nature. It is just the same for the feminine signs; for a masculine sign has greater power by day than by night, and a feminine sign has greater power by night than by day. And this is because **Aries** <note>original: "le mouton"</note>, **Gemini** <note>original: "Gemini"</note>, **Leo** <note>original: "le lyon"</note>, **Libra** <note>original: "Libra"</note>, **Sagittarius** <note>original: "le sagittaire"</note>, and **Aquarius** <note>original: "Aquarius"</note>—of these six signs, three are of a hot and dry quality: namely Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius. "Placides," said Tymeo, "I tell you further that Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Leo, Libra, and Sagittarius have voices and instruments of speech, by which you should know that those men and women who have their natures under these signs cannot be **mute** <note>original: "muez"</note>, but rather have great power in speaking and in deceiving. And you will find the complete opposite in Scorpio, Cancer, and Pisces; for these three signs have no voice nor any **harshness** <note>original: "duresne"</note> to produce speech. However, Virgo, Capricorn, and Aquarius have the nature of the other six mentioned before, for they are neither too much nor too little talkative."

"Master," said Placides to Tymeo, "Tell me why it is that many men engender easily and many women conceive easily, yet some men cannot engender nor women conceive?" "Placides, I will tell you according to what I can understand of it. Of the twelve signs, there are three signs that cause great **generation** <term>generation: the act of producing offspring or procreating</term>, such as Scorpio, Cancer, and Pisces. And some cause a total lack of generation, such as Aries, Virgo, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, and Capricorn. And the other three hold a **tempered** <note>original: "attrempee"</note> nature, for they cause sufficient generation but not too much: such as Taurus, Gemini, and Aquarius. "Master," said Placides to Tymeo, "I pray you that you tell me the certain movement of the planets."
Tymeo said to Placides: "You must know that they are **erratic** <note>original: "erraticques"; meaning wandering</note>, which is to say they are wandering and movable—that is, going and coming—for they go against the movement of the heaven in which the stars are situated. Therefore, you must know that the seven planets have two movements: namely, that of the first heaven <note>The "Primum Mobile" or first moved sphere in medieval cosmology, which carries everything from East to West once a day</note> which carries them from the East to the West, and the movement which belongs to them naturally, which is from West to East; and by this latter movement they are called wandering planets. And you should also know that all the planets are sometimes **retrograde** <note>original: "retrogradees"; the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky</note>, except for the sun which is always rising high, which is the same as being **stationary** <note>original: "stacionnaire"</note>. For being stationary is the same as rising high, or being at its highest point; for then its influence is stronger than when it is retrograde, for then its influence is very weak and very small. And the planets have all these conditions within them by reason of their movement in their **epicycles** <term>epicycles: small circular orbits centered on the circumference of a larger orbit, used by ancient astronomers to explain the complex paths of planets</term>, which is nothing other than a small circle by which the planet moves according to its nature. And in this epicycle, the planet is according to its right and natural movement, which is from West to East, whether in retrograde or in stationary."

# The Heart of Secrets

### Concerning the Fortunes of the Seven Planets

Placides, now I have told you of the general properties of the seven planets; now I shall tell you of their fortune. First, **Saturn** and **Mars** are of ill fortune. **Jupiter** and **Venus** are of good fortune. And although others may be of good fortune, these two are the primary ones. It is the **Sun** and the **Moon** who are the luminaries of the world, of which one illuminates the day, such as the Sun, and the other the night, such as the Moon. And **Mercury** adopts the temperament of those with whom he is joined, whether for good or for evil.

¶ Placides, said Tymeo: The strengthening of the seven planets in their influence is such that each planet can be fortified by five things. First by its **house**; second by its **exaltation**; third by its **triplicity**; fourth by its **term**; and fifth by its **face**.

¶ "Now listen," said Tymeo to Placides, "you must know that when any of the planets is in its **house**, it is like a king who is at the height of his throne and his glory. And when it is in its **exaltation**, it is just like a king when he is being crowned. And when it is in its **triplicity**, it is just like a king among his friends and his allies. And when it is in its **term**, it is just like a king among his relatives and his brothers. But when it is in its **face**, it is like a master among his disciples. Therefore, you can see that the **face** gives the planets only one degree of strength; the **term** two; the **triplicity** three; the **exaltation** four; and the **house** five.

And you must know that each of the planets has two houses, except for the Sun and the Moon, which each have only one house. The houses of **Saturn** are **Capricorn** and **Aquarius** <note>original: "aquaire"</note>. The houses of **Jupiter** are **Sagittarius** <note>original: "le Sagittaire"</note> and **Pisces** <note>original: "le Poisson"</note>. <meta>This page continues the instructional dialogue between the master Tymeo and his student Placides. # The Heart of Secrets

The artificial day <term>artificial day</term> <note>In medieval science, the "artificial day" refers to the full 24-hour cycle of day and night, whereas the "natural day" referred only to the hours of sunlight.</note> has twenty-four hours and begins at midnight according to certain philosophers of Egypt, and according to the Romans at noon. And from the moment it begins to rise, it begins to dawn and rises from midnight until noon; and from noon the sun begins to lower itself until midnight. Each planet has a greater lordship over the artificial day from which it takes its name, as you will hear hereafter. For the hour in which each planet reigns has the greatest lordship—that is to say, the first hour of the day which is named after that planet. 

For example, Saturday <note>original: "samedy"</note> is named after **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnus"</note>, who rules the first hour of Saturday, which is stronger than the other hours because he is its lord. **Jupiter** <note>original: "Juppiter"</note> rules the second; **Mars** the third; the **Sun** <note>original: "Soleil"</note> the fourth; **Venus** the fifth; **Mercury** <note>original: "mercure"</note> the sixth; and the **Moon** <note>original: "lune"</note> the seventh. Then returning to **Saturn** in the eighth hour; **Jupiter** in the ninth; **Mars** in the tenth; the **Sun** in the eleventh; **Venus** in the twelfth; **Mercury** in the thirteenth; and the **Moon** in the fourteenth. And again returning to **Saturn** in the fifteenth; **Jupiter** in the sixteenth; **Mars** in the seventeenth; the **Sun** in the eighteenth; **Venus** in the nineteenth; **Mercury** in the twentieth; the **Moon** in the twenty-first. And returning to **Saturn** in the twenty-second; **Jupiter** in the twenty-third; and **Mars** in the twenty-fourth. 

And thus is finished the day of Saturday which has twenty-four hours, by which you can clearly see that **Mars** has lordship in the last hour of Saturday; the **Sun** in the first hour of Sunday; the **Moon** in the first hour of Monday; **Mars** of Tuesday; **Mercury** in the first hour of Wednesday; **Jupiter** of Thursday; **Venus** of Friday; and **Saturn** in the first hour of Saturday. And for this reason are the days named and called according to the planets. Therefore, you may know that each planet reigns in each hour of the day.

"Listen again to this," said **Tymeo** to **Placides**. "You must know and understand that the planets have among them principally four aspects <term>aspects</term> <note>original: "regardz" — literally 'gazes,' referring to the way planets 'look' at each other from specific angular distances.</note>, of which the first is **conjunction**; the second is called the **sextile** aspect <note>original: "sixte regard"</note>; the third is called the aspect of **squares** <note>original: "regard des quartes"</note>; and the fourth is called the aspect of **opposition** and contrariety. 

We shall speak to you of the first aspect, which is called **conjunction**, of which you should know this: it is when one of the planets is joined to another as closely as it possibly can be, so that the rays of the one above are mixed with the rays of the one below. Then occurs the true aspect and stir by which the strength of the planet grows where it was smaller. And when two planets are joined and are of one goodness and one temperament <term>complexion</term> <note>Refers to the qualities of hot, cold, moist, or dry associated with a planet.</note>, that goodness and temperament is doubled in strength. But when a good planet is joined to a malicious one, then the malicious one is diminished in its malice, and the goodness of the good one is also lessened because of the malice of the evil one. And when it happens that a planet approaches so close to the Sun that it is within fifteen degrees, then it is called the planet all "burnt" or **combust** <term>combust</term> <note>original: "arse & bruslee" — a planet so close to the sun that its own influence is overwhelmed or 'scorched' by the sun’s power.</note>. At the time of such a conjunction, rains are willingly engendered; and such an aspect is of mastery and benevo— <note>Text cuts off at bottom of page.</note>

# On Philosophy

...influence: for when a good planet is joined with another good one, it holds a strong and thick good influence. And when it is joined to a malicious one, it then tempers the malice. For this reason, it is fitting that he who wishes to begin any good work should watch the **Moon** <note>original: "lune"</note>, so that it is not conjoined with a malicious planet.

The **second regard** <note>In astrology, a "regard" or aspect refers to the angular distance between planets, which was believed to determine how their energies blended.</note> you should know is when one of the planets is far from another by one-sixth of the zodiac: that is to say, by two signs <note>The OCR reads "douzes" (twelve), but "one-sixth" of the twelve-sign zodiac is two signs; the text likely intended "deux" (two).</note>, just as if the **Sun** was at the beginning, the end, or the middle of the **Ram** <term>Ram</term> <note>The zodiac sign Aries.</note>, and the **Moon** was in **Gemini**. **Taurus** <note>original: "Thorel"</note> for two days / and if the illness begins in this sign / the Moon will be on the seventh day in the sign of **Leo**, which is opposite to Taurus <note>In medieval astrology, the "opposite" here likely refers to the "square" aspect or the critical turning point in the lunar cycle (roughly 7 days), rather than a literal 180-degree opposition.</note> / and also through all the signs by which the condition of the seventh day appears clearly. **Prades** <note>Likely a character in a philosophical dialogue or a reference to a specific authority.</note> said to **Timaeus** <note>original: "Thymeo"; likely referring to the speaker in Plato's dialogue regarding the nature of the physical world.</note>: in this science there are two things without which no one can work within this field. The first is **theory**, which is for learning the science and how one ought to work. The second is **practice**, through which one works and creates medicines or decides how they should be made. And because this practice cannot be properly performed without observing the planets and the signs: yet since one cannot have knowledge every day of all the planets nor of the signs: at the very least you must observe the **Moon**, which has special power over the **humors** <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</note> of the body, and over the conditions of the sick; and he who does not observe the condition of the Moon can neither well care for nor cure the patient. Nor can he give medicine to the healthy to preserve their health; to understand this more clearly, you must understand that within the body of man and woman there are **three virtues** <term>three virtues</term> <note>Biological faculties believed to govern how the body processes nutrients and waste.</note>, of which we must now speak.

The first is named **Retentive** <note>original: "retenue"</note>; and this is the one by which each limb retains for itself what it needs to sustain itself. The second virtue is **Expulsive** <note>original: "expulsue"</note>; and this is the one that puts out of the body the superfluities and that which is contrary to the health and life of the body of man and woman. The third is called **Attractive** <note>original: "attractiue"</note>; and this is the one that draws to each limb what it requires.

Now we see by reason that "attraction" is achieved through **heat and dryness**, according to what **Aristotle** says: for heat and dryness attract moisture. Therefore, physicians who wish to strengthen the attractive virtue—which has become somewhat weakened—must ensure that their medicine is appropriately **hot and dry**. And above all things, the Moon must be in a **hot and dry sign** <note>These are the Fire signs: Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius.</note>: for medicine can neither work nor be of any profit if the movement of the heavens and their course are contrary to it; and especially the Moon. 

I also say that the **retentive virtue**, which is achieved through **coldness and dryness** according to **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, if the physician wishes to strengthen it, he must strengthen it with **cold and dry medicine** while the Moon is in a **cold and dry sign** <note>These are the Earth signs: Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn.</note>: for otherwise he would cause more discomfort than comfort. Regarding the **expulsive virtue**, I tell you also that it is achieved, according to the masters, through **moisture and heat**; for if the physician wishes to comfort the patient, he must do so with **hot and moist medicine**. And let the Moon be in a **hot and moist sign** <note>These are the Air signs: Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius.</note> if he wishes to give medicine more perfectly. 

If the medicine is to strengthen the attractive virtue, see that it is made of things that are reasonably hot and dry, and let it be made at the time when the Moon is in an ascending hot and dry sign without any hindrance. I also say, to perfectly strengthen the retentive virtue, let the medicine be made while the Moon is in the **Ascendant** of a cold and dry sign: and at that time let the medicine be made, such as **diap-based medicines** <note>original: "diappier"; likely referring to *diaprunum* (a plum-based electuary) or other "dia-" prefixed compound medicines common in medieval pharmacopeias.</note> and those other medicines. And this manner being observed...

Prides <note>Likely a corruption of a classical name, such as Porphyry or Proclus, addressing the character Timaeus from Plato's dialogues.</note> said to **Timaeus**: in this science there are two things without which no one can work. The first is **theory**, which is for learning the science and how one ought to work. The second is **practice**, through which one works to make medicines or determines how they should be made. And because this practice cannot be properly performed without observing the **planets** and the **signs**—and since one cannot have knowledge every day of all the planets and signs—you must at least keep watch over the **Moon**. The Moon has a special power over the **humors** <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that medieval doctors believed controlled health and temperament.</note> of the body and over the matter of the sick; whoever does not watch the condition of the Moon cannot properly cure or heal the patient, nor give medicine to the healthy to preserve their health. 

To understand this more clearly, you must understand that within the bodies of men and women there are three **virtues** <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the natural biological powers or faculties of the body.</note> of which we must now speak. The first is named **retentive**, and it is that by which each limb retains for itself what it needs to sustain itself. The second virtue is **expulsive**, and it is that which casts out of the body superfluities and anything contrary to the health and life of the body. The third is called **attractive**, and it is that which draws to each limb what it requires. 

Now we see by reason that **attraction** is caused by heat and dryness, according to what **Aristotle** says: for heat and dryness attract moisture. Therefore, physicians who wish to strengthen the attractive virtue when it is somewhat weakened must ensure that their medicine is appropriately hot and dry. And above all, they must ensure the Moon is in a hot and dry sign <note>The "fire" signs: Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius.</note>; for the medicine cannot work or provide any benefit if the movement of the heavens and its course are contrary—especially the Moon. 

I also say that the **retentive virtue**, which is governed by cold and dryness according to **Galen**, must be strengthened by the physician using cold and dry medicine while the Moon is in a cold and dry sign <note>The "earth" signs: Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn.</note>; otherwise, he would cause more discomfort than comfort. Regarding the **expulsive virtue**, I tell you that it is governed, according to the masters, by moisture and heat; if the physician wishes to comfort the patient, he must do so with hot and moist medicine. And let the Moon be in a hot and moist sign <note>The "air" signs: Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius.</note> if he wishes to give medicine most perfectly. 

If the medicine is to strengthen the attractive virtue, see that it is made of hot and dry things, and let it be made at a time when the Moon is in an **ascendant** <term>ascendant</term> <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time the medicine is prepared or administered.</note> that is hot and dry, and without any planetary hindrance. Likewise, I say that to perfectly strengthen the retentive virtue, the medicine should be made while the Moon is in a cold and dry ascendant; at that time, let medicines such as **plum-based electuaries** <note>original: "diappier," likely referring to *diaprunum*, a common medicinal paste made from plums used as a laxative or digestive aid.</note> and others be prepared. # The Heart of Secrets

Physicians can wisely administer these medicines, heal the sick, and keep the healthy in good health. However, because the planets govern diverse humors <note>The "four humors"—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were believed to control human health and temperament.</note>, a wise physician must observe which humor needs to be expelled (which we call medicine) until the planet governing that humor is weakened and hindered. For if the planet were at full strength, it would retain the humor inside the body and multiply it, thereby hindering the medicine; for the influence of its planet is much stronger for retaining than the medicine is for expelling.

And here is an example for you: It is true that Saturn governs the humor of melancholy <note>original: "cole de melencolie"; black bile</note>; for he is the cause of generation, and all melancholic creatures are under Saturn. Therefore, whoever wishes to purge melancholy should do so when Saturn is weak and hindered; otherwise, the planet will not allow the medicine to work. And this rule must be observed for the planet Mars, which especially governs yellow bile <note>original: "la couleur," a likely variant of "colere" or choler</note>, and the Moon, which governs phlegm <note>original: "le fleuve," likely a corruption of "le flegme"</note>.

**M** <note>Large decorative woodcut initial featuring floral and foliate patterns.</note>

But having said this, asks Placidus <note>Placides, likely a fictional or legendary figure used in medieval dialogue-based teaching texts</note>, should one take medicine at all times and at all hours without peril? 

Placidus, said Timaeus <note>original: "Tymeo"; a reference to the speaker in Plato's dialogue, though here used in a medieval context</note>, to know at what time one should take medicine, you must know that there are two kinds of medicine: one is purged through the mouth, which is by vomiting; and the other through the bowels <note>original: "fondement"</note>, which is by going to the chamber. 

The first, which is purged through the mouth, should not be given when the Moon is in the sign of **Leo** <note>original: "Lyon"</note>; for it would be harmful to the stomach and the throat in such a way that it would cause [excessive] vomiting. Nor should one undergo bloodletting <term>bloodletting|The surgical removal of blood to balance the humors, a staple of medieval medicine</term> at that time, nor when the Moon is in the "Burned Way" <term>Combust Way|original: "voye bruslee"; a specific section of the zodiac, roughly the last 15 degrees of Libra and first 15 of Scorpio, considered unlucky or debilitating in astrology</term>, as it is at the end of Libra for fifteen degrees. 

But when the Moon is in **Cancer** <note>original: "Lescrevice" (the crayfish)</note> and it is retrograde <term>retrograde|When a planet appears to move backward across the sky; in astrology, this often changes the planet's influence to be more internal or reversed</term>, then it is a good time to give medicine for vomiting. And there are certain signs, like **Taurus** <note>original: "Torell"</note> and **Capricorn**, in which, if the medicine is given for vomiting, it will be expelled through the mouth. And for that reason, in those times, one should not give medicine that purges from below, but only that which purges through the mouth.

Generally speaking, when the lord of the Ascendant <term>Ascendant|The zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment; it was considered vital for determining the "health" of an undertaking</term> is in a good sign and is fortunate and free from all evils and hindrances—and the Moon is also in its aforementioned condition without hindrance, and the "house" is well-disposed by good fortune—then the physician should give his medicine. He must also consider the shifting causes and the substance of the medicine. The physician must take care not to medicate a man or woman when the Moon is in a bad aspect to Mars or to Saturn, who is very malicious.

Furthermore, you should know that if the Moon is in a "movable" <term>Movable sign|Also known as Cardinal signs (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn), which initiate change</term> sign when a person falls ill, the disease will be changeable and will soon reach its end. If it is in a "stable" and firm sign <term>Fixed sign|Signs like Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius, associated with stability and persistence</term>, the illness will be long and enduring. And if it is in signs that are neither movable nor stable <note>Commonly called "mutable" signs: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces</note>, the illness will follow that condition. You should also note that the best time for medicating is when the Moon is in the sign of **Pisces** <note>original: "poissons"</note>, free of all evil and all hindrances.

"Master," said Placidus, "since man is made of the four elements, it seems to me that he ought to live as long as the four elements, which will last as long as the world lasts." "Placidus, remember that the Authority <note>original: "le Boap"; likely a corruption of a specific author's name, possibly Boethius or a similar philosophical source</note> says that all four elements are subject to corruption. Each element has a type of creature that lives in its own element without the mixing of any other, just as the salamanders <note>In medieval lore, the salamander was a mythical lizard believed to live in and even extinguish fire.</note> do, who live by fire alone; if they tasted or felt any of the other elements besides fire, they would die instantly. The same is true for the creatures of the other three elements. Therefore, you must know that since man is formed and made of the four elements which are corruptible, so too is man. For when any of the elements in a man becomes corrupted—either by the corruption of too much drinking or eating, or too much heat, cold, or moisture—it is like someone putting a little water into a great fire: the fire would overcome it and waste it away through its dryness and heat. And whoever put a great quantity of water into the fire would overcome the fire and extinguish it through its coldness and moisture. It is the same for the other elements according to their nature. You must also understand this regarding men and women who are made of the four elements: if even one element is corrupted in any way, then the man or woman must be corrupted by some sickness due to the failure of that element. It is then inevitable that they die suddenly, for as soon as any of the four elements fails in a man or woman, their balance <term>attrempance: the proper mixing or "tempering" of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—to maintain health</term> must also fail. And this balance is nothing other than life itself, so that when the balance fails, life fails."

"Master," said Placidus, "when a man is in balance, where does the imbalance come from, and how can it be?" "Placidus," said Timaeus, "I will tell you how one can balance the four qualities of man and woman when they are corrupted in any way."

"Placidus," said Timaeus: "They can remove themselves from this corruption and protect themselves by these ways that I will tell you. First, how you shall guard yourself against this corruption and its significance; the signs of how you are falling into it, and how you have already fallen. And we shall begin with how you might fall into it if you do not take care."

"Placidus, there are four elements and four humors <note>original: "coles"; referring to the biles or humors of the body</note> caused by each element. These four humors contain the four temperaments <term>complexions: the physical and mental constitution of a person determined by the dominant humor</term> of the four elements: like fire, which is hot and dry; air, which is hot and moist; earth, which is dry and cold; and water, which is cold and moist. All these temperaments are in men and women, but not equally. For a man or woman always has one of these four qualities that rules over the other three, as one follows the other, weakening each other in turn. Thus, one person is choleric <note>The "choleric" temperament was associated with yellow bile and a fiery, ambitious, or irritable nature.</note> and of the nature of fire: he is hot, dry, hasty, and long-lived. If he can pass sixty years, then by the heat of his constitution <note>original: "cetuel"; likely a reference to the animal heat or brain</note> he will become bald and pale and have little hair. The sanguine <note>The "sanguine" temperament was associated with blood and a courageous, hopeful, or amorous nature.</note> person will be hot..."

...is called ecchymosis <term>Equimece|A discoloration of the skin resulting from bleeding underneath, typically caused by bruising</term>, or by a great flow from the nose, or an affliction of the eyes which remain all red or swollen, or having a great flux of the bowels <note>original: "menoison"; a historical term for diarrhea or dysentery</note> through the body, or having red spots <note>original: "dessies"</note> on the body in several places. Placidus, all these diseases and several others come from a superabundance of blood: and in all these diseases one must be bled at the first appearance of such signs as are mentioned above.

Placidus, if your mouth feels sour and unpleasant: or if you sleep poorly: if you have many ill-ordered thoughts: or if your heart urges you to do something <note>Likely referring to impulsive or intrusive thoughts</note>: or if your face is dry and dark: or if you feel a tightness in the pit of your stomach <term>forcelle|The scrobiculus cordis or epigastrium</term>: and if your dreams are terrifying and horrible and make you afraid: or if you dream that someone wants to put you in a stinking and dark place. And you should eat good fresh bread, pork, capon, mutton, or young chicken; eat little fish that have many bones <note>original: "harettes"</note>, and you should drink good white or red wine diluted with clear spring water. In this way, you can defend yourself against the diseases mentioned above.

If you see that any of your limbs are more affected by heat or by cold than they used to be, such heat or cold signifies the advancement of a "hot" disease or a "cold" one.

# The Heart of Secrets

Placidus, Timaeus said: the pain that comes from an excess of blood is strongest from the hour of Nones <term>Nones|The ninth hour of the day, approximately 3:00 PM</term> and throughout the night until the hour of Terce <term>Terce|The third hour of the day, approximately 9:00 AM</term>. This pain is more acute in the front part of the head, and the whites of the patient's eyes appear red; the head is hot, the mouth tastes sweet, and the patient does not suffer from excessive thirst. This pain often occurs in the spring while one is sleeping. For this pain, one must be bled from the cephalic vein <note>original: "veine du chief"; the vein in the arm traditionally associated with treating the head</note>, and one must take care to avoid drinking wine and eating "hot" meats <note>In humoral theory, foods were classified by temperament; red meats were considered "hot" and "moist," which would worsen a blood imbalance</note>. If the pain does not cease, one should have cupping glasses <term>ventoser|The practice of "cupping," applying heated glass jars to the skin to create a vacuum and draw out "bad" humors</term> applied very well to the "horns" <note>The temples or the upper back of the head</note> at the back of the head. If the illness persists, take borage and crush it, and make poultices for the head. Take also the lung of a cat and place it upon the painful part of the head—it should be split open and wrapped in the skin of the cat just as it is flayed, applying it while still warm against the flesh. Keep your head wrapped in this skin for a day and a night. If this does not heal you, take the juice of ground ivy <note>original: "herbe terrestre"</note>, the juice of nightshade <note>original: "morelle"</note>, and the juice of the white-seeded poppy, equal parts of each; soak a linen cloth in this and wrap it around the painful area, doing this often. This type of poultice induces sleep and is good against all pains coming from the head.

The headache which comes from phlegm <term>flume|Phlegm, the cold and moist humor</term> is dominant in the back part of the head and holds most strongly from nightfall until the hour of midnight. The patient sleeps too deeply and for too long, and sees white things and rain in their dreams. The patient feels exactly as if they were drunk and lacks their proper senses. To remove this pain, one must receive an enema <term>clistoire|A clyster or enema, used to purge the bowels of excess humors</term> or two, and must avoid sleeping in a cold place. One should wash the head with warm water in which anise or the herb called Nepeta <note>original: "Nepita"; likely Catmint or Catnip</note> has been cooked; this herb is the best there is against pain coming from phlegm. For this, one can also take another herb named Blessed Thistle <note>original: "Cardobeny"; from the Latin *Carduus benedictus*</note>. If the patient does not recover, one must bind the calves of their legs very tightly, and then take powder of pellitory <note>original: "popure"; likely *pyrethrum*, used to induce sneezing and clear the head</note> and put it in the nostrils to make them sneeze. The patient must not sleep too much; rather, one must wake them so that they do not fall into a lethargy <term>litargie|A state of pathological, death-like sleep or coma associated with an excess of cold phlegm in the brain</term>. If the patient still does not recover, take alum, rue, and ground ivy, equal parts of each, and crush them all together with two egg whites <note>original: "oubins deufz"</note> and a little honey. Make a poultice and place it upon the pain, and they will truly be healed.

Placidus, Timaeus said: The pain that comes from melancholy <note>Black bile, the cold and dry humor</note> in the head is a little stronger in the back part of the head or on the left side, from the hour of Nones until Terce the next morning. The patient is anxious and sleeps little; their ears ring and they see black things in their dreams, and these dreams are terrifying. To remove this pain, one must anoint the patient's head with a good decoction <note>original: "bonne diete"; here likely referring to a medicinal wash</note> or with woman's milk mixed with oil of violets. If he does not have regular bowel movements <note>original: "va bien en chambre"</note>, he must take pills or enemas. He may well eat chicks and partridge or mutton, and drink watered-down wine. And he must have in his company...

And they should not be too salty: and one should drink good old wine, not too strong: and eat no "hot" & "dry" things: such as leeks/ garlic/ onions and all other things of their nature: but cold and moist things such as lettuce/ borage/ fish: rye bread and drink cold water with one's wine: but let it be newly drawn: and wash one's head in water that comes through pipes: and anoint one's head with oil of roses and oil of myrtle.

# The Heart of Secrets

Placidus told Timaeus: the pain that comes from a superfluity of blood is strongest from the hour of Nones <note>Nones: about 3:00 PM</note> and through the night until the hour of Terce <note>Terce: about 9:00 AM</note> the next day.
