# The Heart of Secrets

**Placidus said to Timaeus:** One must keep the eyes in health. Although the body can live well without the eyes, nonetheless the body can live better with the eyes than without them to govern and lead itself in all circumstances. For this reason and for several others, it is good to know how one can guard them for the ease of the body and to sustain its beauty: for through the eyes one can avoid dangerous situations where the body could perish and be brought to nothing. For as **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician (c. 980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in medieval Europe.</note> says, the eyes were placed in the highest part to see all things that could grieve and harm; and for their nobility, God gave them natural covers to defend them and avoid things that could harm and grieve them.

**Placidus, said Timaeus:** It is necessary to guard the eyes from dust, from smoke, and from the sun in summer when it is too hot: and from things that have too great a brightness. For this is a thing that greatly destroys the sight. And therefore the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often cited simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> says that too much brightness quickly takes the sight and too much sound quickly takes the hearing. It is also bad to look at a thing for a long time without blinking, and especially to look at books with tiny letters and other things where the sight works too hard by looking; and also too much weeping, too much yawning, and too much sleeping. Especially the sleep that one takes immediately after eating. Consorting with women <note>original: "le hanter femmes"; a common medieval medical warning was that excessive sexual activity depleted the body's vital spirits and dimmed the vision.</note> causes more harm than all other things. And you can see this in those who do it too much: for they have eyes more afflicted than all their other members. And it is good to guard oneself from all beverages and all heavy meats. Such as garlic, leeks, onions, olives, myrtle <note>original: "mitres"; likely referring to myrtle berries or possibly a transcription error for "mures" (mulberries).</note>, dates, cabbage, lentils, and basil <term>basilicum|basil; medieval herbalists often believed basil had properties that could affect the humors of the head</term>, which especially takes the sight for a small cause; and one should be pure and use vomiting. And although vomiting is good for purging the humors of the stomach, from which vapors could be engendered, nonetheless it does harm in that it stirs up the vapors and humors of the head and makes them come to the eyes. And to speak more briefly, all things that fill and burden the head too much grieve the sight.

**Placidus, we shall tell you what you must use to guard the sight and keep it in health.** The first point is to plunge one's head into a full bucket of clear and cold water, and to close and open the eyes inside that cold water; and to use fennel water <note>original: "eaue de fanoil"</note> in the manner made like rose water; or take ceruse <term>ceruse|white lead; a white powder used in ancient and medieval medicine, though now known to be highly toxic</term> made into a powder of the sword <note>original: "despee"; possibly referring to scrapings or a specific refinement process</note> soaked in the juice of calamint <term>calemente|calamint; an aromatic herb used to treat various ailments in the Middle Ages</term>: but let it remain there for six days and then put it in the eyes: for this guards the sight marvelously and lets no humor come there that could grieve them. Or take the juice of a sweet pomegranate and the juice of another that is sour, and let them be put in two vials, each by itself; and let them be well stopped and remain so for fifteen days. Then one must remove the juice from the top and throw away the thick part, and afterwards make a powder of aloes, of black pepper <note>original: "popure noir"</note>, and of long pepper, and of sal ammoniac <term>sel armoniac|sal ammoniac; ammonium chloride, used as a flux and in various medicinal preparations</term>, one dram of each; and let them be finely ground and tempered with the juice of the aforementioned pomegranates, and the...

Guard the ears from the cold, from the wind, and from loud sounds, for these things destroy the hearing. # The Treasury of Secrets

**Food:** For Constantine <note>Constantine the African (c. 1020–1087), a physician who translated Arabic medical texts into Latin.</note> says that Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for over 1,000 years.</note> was once asked why he weighed his food every day. He replied that it was to lengthen his life, and that he did not have a time to live just for eating. Because of this, you should understand that no one should eat so much that the pit of the stomach <note>original: "forcelle"; referring to the epigastric region or the hollow of the chest.</note> swells or feels crushed; rather, one must eat in an orderly manner.

Placides, Timaeus said: the liver is one of the four principal members where the blood of the whole body is engendered, which is why it is good to set one's mind to keeping it healthy. You must know that the food which comes from the pit of the stomach could not "cook" <note>Medieval medicine viewed digestion as a process of "coction," where the body’s internal heat literally cooked food to transform it into nutrients.</note> without the heat of the liver. For this reason, nature gave the liver five "mouths" <note>This refers to the lobes of the liver, which were thought to wrap around the stomach like a hand to provide warmth.</note> to better grasp the bottom of the stomach to provide better heat. So, when the food is cooked and purified, it becomes like barley water in the stomach; then this water leaves the stomach and travels through veins that physicians call "mesenteric" <note>original: "Mezariches"; these are the veins connecting the intestines to the liver.</note> and is thus received. When it is well-cooked in that part, it becomes blood and goes through all the veins of the body, from which every limb receives nourishment. 

The other part, which is cooked to excess, becomes choler <note>original: "colle"; also known as yellow bile, one of the four humors.</note>; dry nature has a vessel for this, which is a branch of the liver called the gall <note>original: "lamer"; literally "the bitter," referring to the gallbladder.</note>. Another part is like the dregs of blood, which is called melancholy <note>black bile</note>, and it goes to another part; and that which is in the root and does not cook well is called phlegm <note>original: "fignie"; likely a variant or corruption of "flegme" or "pituite."</note>, which goes with the blood throughout the body. Because blood is lacking, nature receives this and gives it as nourishment to the limbs. From this food where the humors are created, there comes a superfluity that nature drives out through the kidneys, and this is urine. Although these are called "superfluities," they are sometimes necessary for the human body to live; therefore, nature gave them their own place to be used when there was a need for them.

Placides, you must know that the signs of a **hot complexion** <note>In this context, "complexion" refers to a person's physical and psychological constitution based on their dominant humors.</note> are such that one should have wide and swollen veins, a hairy chest, a great talent for eating and drinking, and a body color that leans toward yellow because of the abundance of choler produced in the liver. Those who have this complexion should use "cold" things <note>Medieval dietetics classified foods as hot, cold, moist, or dry to balance the body's humors.</note> and guard themselves against "hot" things, and drink wine mixed with water, especially a tart wine <note>original: "vin verdelet"; a young, sharp, or slightly acidic wine.</note>.

The signs of a **cold complexion** are the opposite; they make all the body's virtues weak and the person always sickly. They must use things contrary to what we said before. The sign of a **naturally dry complexion** is to have small veins with little blood and a dry body, to have much hair—and curly—and to have a greater talent for drinking than for eating; such a person should use "moist" foods. Those who have a **naturally hot and moist liver** <note>The "sanguine" temperament.</note> have signs opposite to those with a dry complexion and should use "dry" things. You must understand that if these complexions become more abundant than they should be, one must use things contrary to that complexion; but if they are not in excess, one should use similar things. And know that the way to destroy the health of the liver is to put one meal on top of another before <insert>the first is digested</insert>.

¶ The sign of a cold complexion is to have a narrow chest, unless other members contradict this; that is to say, the heart could be situated so high that the chest could not be wide despite the heart's heat; rather it would be narrow because of the coldness of the pit of the stomach <note>original: "forcelle"; the hollow area at the base of the sternum.</note>. Namely: hyacinths <term>iagonces: precious stones often ground into medicinal powders</term>, gold, silver, bugloss <term>briglose: a flowering plant used to treat melancholy</term>, and basil <term>basilicum</term> which bears a black flower. ### The Heart of Secrets

"Master, I pray you to tell me of the veins that are in the body of man and woman." Timaeus said: "Placides, just as through the earth—which is one of the four elements—there are bitter springs that run through it, as is found by those who dig wells, for there is no place in the earth where, if one dug deep enough, one would not find water. So it is with the body of man and woman. You could not wound any part without blood coming out; and all this is because of the veins, which are conduits for the blood running through the body, just as water runs through the conduits of the earth. From this, it happens that when one of the earth's conduits becomes blocked by soil falling into it—when it is stopped up so that the water cannot have its course— the conduit of that water swells until, by the force of that water and of the air and the wind which fight together, the earth bursts and [the water] issues forth. Or, if the earth is so strong that it cannot burst, it happens that the water—by its own force and that of the air and the pushing they do in that conduit—breaks the earth to find a way so violently that all the earth shakes, so much so that sometimes towers, castles, and towns fall because of this movement <note>This is a medieval explanation for earthquakes, suggesting they are caused by subterranean pressure of water and air.</note>.

In just this way, you can understand that whether it be man or woman, through the excesses they commit—either in drinking or eating, or sleeping too much or staying awake too much, or through other excesses—one can so block the veins of a man or woman that the blood loses its natural course through which it is accustomed to go to restore the limbs of the body, each according to its nature. From this it often happens that through this blockage many diseases occur in these conduits that we call veins, which are obstructed by certain humors <term>humeurs: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which medieval doctors believed governed health and temperament</term> that mix with one another, such as the hot with the cold, or the dry with the moist in too great abundance; for by the superfluity of both, corruptions come to man and woman. 

So we will tell you of these conduits, how they should be emptied by bloodletting <term>saigner: the medical practice of withdrawing blood to balance the humors</term> and set free so that they may have their natural course without hindrance to keep the body in health. The evil humors that are inside the body are emptied by bloodletting from the veins. And no one should perform such emptyings except for two things: the first, when the blood is too abundant; the second, when the man is sick. 

So we will tell you of the first: as for those who are nourished on good and delicious meats and those who are at rest, for these people bloodletting is good. And you can recognize one who has need of it in this manner: his urine will be red and thick and dark; his pulse will throb much more than it used to, and he will have a full and black pulse; and he will have pain in the forehead, more on the right side <gloss>dextre</gloss> than on the left <gloss>senestre</gloss>; he will have sweet saliva, his face and the whites of his eyes will be red; and while sleeping he will dream of seeing red things, and he will have a red and black color throughout his whole body. 

But for other people—such as those [under] fourteen years old, or a man of great age, or one who is rising from sickness, or a pregnant woman, or a drunken man, or one who has just lain with a woman, or one who has too much flux <term>menoisone: a term usually referring to diarrhea or a flux of the bowels</term>, or one whose body is exhausted from labor—such people have no business being bled unless there is a very great necessity. And if they do it...</term>

Placides, you should know that in the year the weather changes four times according to the four seasons of the year. That is to say: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter; for at the change of these four seasons, as **Hippocrates** <note>original: "ypocras"; the ancient Greek physician</note> says, new natures or new qualities are engendered. But before we tell you what must be done, we will describe these four seasons in which the weather changes according to the doctrine of medicine <note>original: "phisique"; in the Middle Ages, this referred to the study of natural science and the practice of medicine</note> and astronomy. You know that the sun performs its natural course in one year. And in this course, the sun goes through the twelve signs, and remains in each sign for one month. And the signs are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. These are the signs through which the sun passes, of which the astronomers say that in each of the four seasons of the year the sun passes through three of its signs. They say that the sun enters into Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, and thus in the middle of March, Spring begins. And it enters into Cancer and passes through Leo and Virgo; thus in the middle of May it is Summer, and this is the second part of the year. And when the sun comes to the middle of September, it then enters into Libra and passes through Scorpio and Sagittarius, and this is the third part of the year. And when it comes to the middle of December, the sun then enters into Capricorn and passes through Aquarius and Pisces; and this is the fourth part of the year, which we call Winter. And such is the correct division of the year according to the four seasons, as the astronomers say.

But according to the physicians, who speak more generally <note>original: "grossement"; meaning in a practical or broad sense rather than a mathematical one</note>, they say that Spring is when the trees begin to bloom and have leaves, and it lasts until the sun begins to grow hot. And that time is Spring, for it is hot and moist. And when the heat begins to grow strong, then Summer begins, which lasts until the cold of winter. And that time is hot and dry. Then, around September, it begins to grow cold—not yet greatly—and the leaves of the trees begin to fall, and it lasts until Winter has come and the great cold. And that time is called Autumn; it is cold and dry. And afterward Winter begins when the cold strengthens and grows and when the sun is low so that it cannot give heat; and it lasts until Spring. And that time is cold and moist.

Tymeo said, "Placides, now we will say how one must guard oneself in these four seasons. And know well that just as I have told you before that there are four seasons in the year, there are also four <term>complexions</term> <note>In medieval medicine, a 'complexion' or temperament was the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual, determining their health and personality.</note> in man and woman similar to them. There are the **Sanguine**, who are hot and moist and are similar to Spring. And the **Choleric**, who are hot and dry and are similar to Summer. The **Melancholic**, who are cold and dry, are similar to the season of Autumn. The **Phlegmatic** <note>original: "flumatiques"</note>, who are cold and moist, are similar to Winter. And each of these complexions is good, healthy, and well-proportioned in man and woman. And one feels best during the season to which their nature is similar."

...than in another: but because one cannot find the body so perfectly balanced <note>original: "complexionne apoint"; referring to the balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>. Thus we tell you what generally each person should do in these four seasons.

¶ In spring, man and woman should wear clothes that are neither too hot nor too cold; and one should purge and bleed <note>original: "saigner"; bloodletting was a standard medical practice used to remove excess humors</note> to remove the humors that may partly arise and which could generate vapors <note>original: "fumees"; internal gases thought to rise to the head and cause illness</note>, from which fevers and other illnesses might result due to the heat of the summer season which causes the humors to boil <note>original: "abolir" (ebullir)</note>. For although illnesses occur in spring, they do not come from its nature, but from the winter in which they were engendered. For this is the most temperate time to take medicines, and those who are fleshy and full of gross <note>thick or excessive</note> humors should do so. And it is proper to use light foods <note>original: "viandes"; in this period, the term referred to food or sustenance in general, not just meat</note> that cool, such as chicks with verjuice <note>original: "verius"; a highly acidic juice made from unripe grapes</note>, lamb, mutton, pottages of orach <note>original: "arraches"; a leafy green vegetable similar to spinach</note>, borage, chard, broth of egg yolks with verjuice, and all scaled fish. Drink good, tempered wine that is not at all sweet, because in this time one must guard against all sweet things; and one should sleep in the morning, but one must not sleep at all during the day.

¶ And in summer, one should wear cool and light clothes, and should eat light foods, such as chicks with verjuice, purslane <note>original: "porcelaine"; a succulent leafy green</note>, plums, apples, and the fish we have named for you, bread in water, and all other things that cool. One should eat little and often: that is to say, in the early morning when the sun rises and in the evening when it sets. And one must guard against eating things that are too salty, sweet, or fatty; and one should use, as much as possible, these foods with sour things. Drink syrup in the morning and violet sugar <note>original: "succre violat"; sugar infused with violet flowers, used as a cooling medicinal sweetener</note> in cold water in the evening, or sugar with water that has been boiled and then cooled. And this should be done whenever one wishes to drink outside of meal times. For at meal times, one should drink weak and young wine <note>original: "verdelet"; a sharp, slightly acidic wine</note> mixed with water, until it has more the flavor of water than of wine. One should often bathe in cold water to reinforce the internal heat that is weak within the body. And one must avoid lying with women <note>sexual intercourse was believed to be physically draining and dehydrating, making it dangerous in the heat of summer</note> and labor the body as little as possible, for labor in this time is the thing that most weakens and dries out a person's body.

In autumn, one should be dressed as in spring, but with the cloth being a little warmer, and one should hasten to bleed and purge the humors; for this is the unhealthiest season of the year, when the most perilous diseases occur. And therefore it is proper to use good foods: such as capons, young chicks, and pigeons that are beginning to fly, and pork, and to drink good wine; and one should not overfill oneself. One must guard against all fruits, for that is the thing that most causes fever to stir and be engendered, just as **Galen** <note>a prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years</note> says: that he never had a fever because he never ate fruit. And one should guard against drinking water and washing oneself with cold water; but one may well wash with warm water. And one should protect one's head from the cold at night, and not sleep in the sun at noon, nor should one labor or think too much, nor suffer hunger or thirst.

Eat bread soaked in water and all other cooling things. One should eat little and often: specifically, in the early morning as the sun rises, and in the evening as it sets. One should often bathe in cold water to reinforce the internal heat that is weakened by the external summer weather. One must also refrain from lying with women and should exert the body as little as possible; for labor in this season is the thing that most weakens and dries out a person's body.

In autumn, one should dress as in spring, but with cloth that is a little warmer. One must be quick to perform bloodletting and purge the humors, for this is the most sickly season of the year, when the most perilous illnesses occur. Therefore, it is necessary to eat good meats: such as capons, young chicks, and pigeons that are just beginning to fly, as well as pork. Drink good wine, but do not overfill yourself. One must avoid all fruit, for fruit is the thing that most stirs up and breeds fever—as Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, a 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories on the humors formed the basis of European medicine for 1,500 years.</note> said, he never had a fever because he never ate fruit. One should not work or worry too much, nor suffer hunger or thirst.

But Placides said to Tymeo: "In this preceding chapter, you spoke to me of purging through bloodletting <term>bloodletting: the practice of withdrawing blood to prevent or cure illness by balancing the body’s humors</term> and light medicines; I would therefore pray that you teach me how one ought to purge themselves, and when, and in what season." 

"Placides," said Tymeo, "this question still pertains to our primary subject. We will tell you how one should be purged, for it is an essential thing for those who do it as they ought. It allows the body to be maintained healthily and avoids diseases. Therefore, we will speak to you according to the teachings of the Authors of **Medicine** <note>original: "Phisique." In the Middle Ages, 'physics' referred to the study of nature and the medical arts.</note> regarding what one must do before being purged, when one will purge, and after one has been purged. 

And before we speak of purging, you must know about the **four humors** <term>humors: the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to determine a person's health and temperament</term> that make up the human body: 
1. The first is **blood**, which is hot and moist. 
2. The second is **phlegm**, which is cold and moist. 
3. The third is **red bile** <note>original: "cole rouge." Also known as yellow bile or choler.</note>, which is hot and dry. 
4. The fourth is **black bile**, which is cold and dry. 

This last one is the final humor, but **phlegm** is divided within the body into five types: 
*   The first is called **salty phlegm**, which is hot and the driest of all the phlegms because it is mixed with red bile. 
*   The second is phlegm that is hot and moist because it is mixed with blood. 
*   There is another type that medicine calls phlegm that is cold and dry because it is mixed with **melancholy** <note>original: "melencolie," another term for black bile.</note>. 
*   The fourth type is what medicine calls **deteriorated phlegm** <note>original: "fleume diterion."</note>, which comes from coldness as seen in people of great age. 
*   The fifth type is **natural phlegm**, which is cold and moist and has no flavor. 

**Red bile** also exists in five types: 
1. The first is **natural red bile**, which is hot and comes from the liver, as we have told you. 
2. The second is **citrine** <note>original: "citerne."</note>, which has the color of the fruit named citron and is not as hot as the first. 
3. The third type is **vitelline bile** <note>original: "cole lenceline."</note>, which resembles egg yolks; it is made of phlegm coming from great cold and clear red bile, and is the least hot of the others. 
4. The fourth type is bile that is green like the juice of herbs, which medicine calls **prassine** <note>original: "prasule."</note>, and it is found especially in the stomach. 
5. The fifth is called **aeruginous** <note>original: "arrougine."</note>, which has the appearance of copper rust; it comes from excessive heat and is naturally poisonous. 

Of **black bile**, there are two types: 
1. The first is **natural**, which is the dregs of the blood; this is truly dry and cold. 
2. The second is that which comes from the excessive burning of heat; this is truly called black bile <note>original: "cole noire." Likely referring to "burnt" or adust bile, considered more dangerous.</note> and is hotter than the other.

These are the humors that can abound in the human body and which must be purged and medicated. Regarding the first complexion, which is **blood**, we have told you how it must be purged: such as by purging with a medicine of four leaves of **mallows**, **violet**, and **borage flowers**. However, **bloodletting** is more appropriate because the place where the blood remains is always within its veins, whereas the other humors are...

### On Philosophy. Leaf 69.

...their place outside the veins. And do not think that these humors can be mixed with the blood inside the veins; for these three humors <note>The three humors besides blood: phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> that we have named for you are always mixed with the blood inside the veins. These can be well-expelled along with the blood through **bloodletting** <term>bloodletting: the surgical removal of blood to balance the humors</term>. But when a humor is outside the veins, it is necessary that it be purged by medicines. However, before we teach you how you must purge them when they abound too much, you must first know how you will recognize which ones are in excess throughout the body.

The sign of **phlegm** <note>original: "fleume"</note> when it overabounds in the body can be known easily by the fact that the urine will be white and thick. In another case of great coldness, the urine will be white and the substance will be between thick and clear; this indicates an abundance of "sour" phlegm. And if the urine is colored in this substance, it will be "salty" phlegm. If it is thick and colored, it will be "sweet" phlegm. Along with such urine, the patient will have a pain in the head on the left side from the **third hour of the night** <note>approximately 3:00 AM</note> onwards. He will have a pale face and sleep poorly, and will dream of rains and being in rivers. He will have an abundance of spit, and according to the nature of the phlegm, his belly will rumble and he will digest his **food** <note>original: "viande." In Middle French, this refers to food in general, not just meat.</note> poorly. He will be heavy and slow of body, and will crave cold foods. You must know that all these signs are signs of phlegm.

The sign of **bile** <term>bile: also called choler, the hot and dry humor associated with fire</term> that abounds too much throughout the body is when the urine is clear and red and of thin consistency. This is despite the fact that it can sometimes be of thick consistency if "vitelline" bile <note>original: "cole Vitelline." Bile the color of egg yolks.</note> abounds. And if **citrine bile** <note>original: "cole cretiue." Likely a variant of "citrine" (lemon-colored) bile.</note> abounds, then fear comes quickly and a pain in the forehead arrives, as if inside the eyes. The greatest pain lasts from the **third hour of the day** <note>approximately 9:00 AM</note> until **vespers** <note>sunset or early evening</note>. The face of this person and the whites of the eyes turn yellow, as does the whole body. He will have a bitter mouth and a rough, dry tongue; he will have an appetite to eat but a great craving to drink. He will always dream of fire and red things.

The sign of **melancholy** <term>melancholy: black bile, the cold and dry humor associated with the earth</term> is black bile. The urine is white and clear, and at other times yellow, and it is thin and full of foam. Occasionally, when the bile is being expelled, the urine is thick. The pulse will be slow and heavy. The face and the whites of the eyes will be pale, bluish-livid, and bleary. The taste of his burps will be like sour wine, and his dreams will be strange and fearful. The pain in the head will be heavy and more in the left part toward the back than anywhere else. The pain will always be worse around the evening; he will always be heavy, slow, and of poor color.

For according to the diversity of these things, one must purge as you shall hear. The ancient Greek physician regarded as the father of western medicine.</note>, for these are the two most temperate parts of the year. # The Heart of Secrets

...heating without smoke. And know that in this season, one must consider when the medicine should be given at night; for if the spring takes on the nature of winter—namely, being cold—it is better to give it by day than by night because of the night’s chill, unless it is a medicine of heavy substance, such as pills. And September takes on the nature of summer—namely, heat—so it is better to give it by night than by day because of the great heat of the day.

NOW listen to what Tymeo says to Placides: we will tell you the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors in an individual, determining their temperament and health</term> of the **choleric** <note>original: "colericque." Those dominated by yellow bile, traditionally associated with a fire-like nature.</note>: that is to say, hot, dry, and thin. For to these people it is proper to give light medicines, because their **humors** <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that medieval medicine believed governed health</term> are light. Thus one can purge them with light medicines, and one can easily purge them by vomiting, provided that the man or woman has a broad chest.

¶ Placides, I tell you further that for those who are **sanguine** <note>original: "sanguins." Those dominated by blood, usually considered cheerful and robust.</note>, light medicines are proper; for they suffer more from them than the choleric. The **phlegmatic** <note>original: "fleumaticques"</note> and **melancholic** <note>original: "melencolicques"</note> can be purged from below <note>i.e., through the bowels using laxatives or enemas</note> because their humors are heavy. Furthermore, whoever wishes to purge correctly must look at the age: for the young child and the one of great age do not at all endure strong medicines because of the weakness of their **complexion**. But those who are thirty or forty years old endure stronger medicines because the nature within them is stronger. Furthermore, one must look at the build of the body: for those who are large and fleshy endure strong medicines better than those who are thin and bony <note>original: "alix"</note>, to whom it is proper to give light medicines. And above all things, one must hesitate to give or take medicines in a weak body. And one must also know if the person vomits more willingly than they go from below. Furthermore, one must consider whether it is a man or a woman who wishes to be purged; for the nature of a woman is colder than that of a man, and for this reason light medicines are proper for them; and they are purged more readily from above than from below. But in a cold country, one must give colder medicines for the humors which are heavy, and one can purge them more readily from below than from above. And after what we have told you, one must observe whether the matter is small or great, whether it is hot or cold, and in what quantity; and according to the location, one must vary the medicine given. And look before these things we have named to you that they are not contrary—such as the virtues and other things—for without these things, no one can operate safely except by guesswork, as many physicians do today. It is necessary to know how you must **ripen** <term>ripen (meuter): the medical process of "coctio" or "cooking," where raw, diseased humors are brought to a state where the body can expel them</term> the matter; for according to the commandment of **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Dyppocras," the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>, it is necessary to ripen the raw matter before it can be purged. And therefore, whoever recognizes that **red bile** <note>original: "cole rouge." In this period, yellow bile was frequently called "red bile" or "choler."</note> abounds by the signs we have told you, it must be ripened in such a manner: First of all, it is necessary that he refrain from eating salty and roasted things and all other dry meats. And it is necessary that he use soft things, such as chicken broth, soft eggs, pottages of borage and beets. For as Hippocrates says: "Whoever wishes to purge the body must first soften it." One must refrain from drinking strong wine and eating hot spices, and one should eat little.

# The Heart of Secrets

<meta>catchword: The figure</meta>

...by its movement and by its influence. And it is "improperly" so called: for it cannot be divided or broken. It is also amply filled with light in every part, whether thick or in pieces: for the star is the thickest part of its sphere or its heaven, and yet no star or other part can be added or taken away. It does not grow or shrink, nor does it take another shape, nor alter, nor change, nor worsen, nor grow old, nor be corrupted, nor altered in any manner—except somewhat in its light alone, as appears during an eclipse of the moon. It cannot be stopped, nor rest, nor return in any other way, nor go faster or slower, in whole or in part; it cannot behave otherwise than according to its first and common ordained course, unless it were by a divine miracle. For this reason, the heaven and the stars are of a different manner and nature than the four elements and the things composed of them: for those are transmutable and <term>corruptible: subject to decay, change, and death</term>. And Aristotle <note>original: "Aristote"; referencing the Greek philosopher whose geocentric views dominated medieval science</note> says that everything corruptible will one day be corrupted according to the course of nature.

The entire mass of the four elements and the things within them is called the "Sphere of Corruptible Things." It is enclosed in the heaven just as the yolk of an egg is enclosed in the white. And all the heaven above is divided into several parts or spheres. First, and closest to the elements, is the sphere of the moon, which directly encloses the sphere of fire. The body of the moon that we see is contained and fixed within that sphere and is moved by the motion of that sphere, just like a nail fixed in a ship; the other planets and the stars fixed in their spheres behave in the same way. Next above is the sphere of Mercury, then Venus, then the Sun, then Mars, then Jupiter, and then Saturn. Thus are the spheres of the seven planets arranged according to their order. And beyond, above them, is the starry heaven. This is the eighth sphere where the fixed stars are located, which are called such not because the others are not fixed each in its own sphere, but because they are moved more regularly, all in the same manner, following the first movement more than the others. Then, according to the <term>astronomers: the text uses "astrologiens," but in this period the study of the stars and the study of their influence were often the same discipline</term>, there is above everything the ninth sphere, in which no star appears. The reason they say it exists is because more than one movement appears in the eighth sphere, so there must be one above it that is moved by only a single, simple motion. Furthermore, some say that above there is an immovable heaven, then a crystalline heaven, and then the <term>Empyrean heaven: the highest, fiery heaven, traditionally considered the dwelling place of God and the angels</term> or the Throne of Solomon and such things which do not belong to the knowledge of natural philosophy or astronomy. Therefore, it is enough for now to speak of the nine spheres mentioned above. One should take good note of the marvelous distribution of these stars: for in the ninth and sovereign sphere there is no star; in the eighth, there are so many they cannot be numbered; and in the others, descending, there is only one in each—calling the sun and the moon "stars."

# The Heart of Secrets

...[ima]gine anything in the world more round, nor better turned, nor more polished. And each sphere is <term>concentric: sharing the same center</term> with the world: that is to say, the center is the middle of the world, or where the center of the earth is in the middle / and the center of each of these spheres of the heavens and their aforementioned surfaces is the same. Each of these spheres touches and encloses or surrounds another / and is itself enclosed by another, except for the first and the last. For example, the sphere of Mercury encloses the sphere of the Moon within its <term>concave surface: the inner, hollow side</term> and is itself enclosed within the concave surface of the sphere of Venus, which it touches with its <term>convex surface: the outer, curving-outward side</term> / and so it goes for the others, except for the last, which is enclosed by nothing. For outside and above it, there is neither body nor place / neither fullness nor void, according to what **Aristotle** says. And the sphere of the moon, where the body of the Moon resides, encloses no other sphere of the heavens. Instead, it encloses the sphere of fire / and fire encloses the air / and the air encloses the water / and the water encloses the earth, except that the sphere of water is, as it were, divided where the earth is uncovered <note>This refers to the "dry land" emerging from the global ocean</note>. And the sphere of the earth has no concave surface as the others do: for it is the first to begin at the bottom / and is entirely solid and has its center within itself. And the others are hollow / and have their center in the earth as has been said / and such is the arrangement of the world.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

**W**e see clearly that the entire sky is moved from east to west / and this is called the <term>diurnal movement: the daily rotation of the heavens</term>. And because of this, one must imagine that a straight line passes through the middle of the earth / and that it has two ends at two points in the sky: these two points do not move and are called the **poles of the world**. One of these is near the North Star, which is always visible to us / and is called the <term>arctic or northern pole</term> / for this part of the sky is called "Septentrion" because of the seven stars found there that people call the "Wain" <note>The Big Dipper or Great Bear</note> / as does **Ptolemy**. **Y**ou should know that halfway between these two aforementioned poles, on the convex surface of the world in the final sphere, one must imagine a circle equidistant from these two poles: that is to say, that every part or every point is just as near to one pole as the other part / and the same for the other pole. And according to how this circle is made, it measures the diurnal movement / and is called the <term>equinoctial circle: the celestial equator</term>. # On Philosophy

<sig>N i</sig>

->[Image: A circular diagram representing the celestial spheres. A large circle is bisected by a horizontal line labeled "Equinoctial." A diagonal line intersects the circle, labeled "oblique" on the upper left and "oblique" on the lower right, representing the ecliptic or slanted path of the planets.]<-

Although the entire heaven together is moved from day to day from East to West—as if the **ninth sphere** <note>In medieval cosmology, the ninth sphere or "Primum Mobile" was thought to drive the daily rotation of all lower spheres</note> drags the other spheres beneath it along with it—nevertheless, each of the **seven planets** is also moved in another manner by its own movement, which is in the opposite direction. However, I will remain silent for now regarding the specific movement of the ninth sphere.

Anyone who wishes to know **philosophy** or **astrology** <note>At this time, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to mean the study of the stars</note> must necessarily understand these two movements, which I wish to explain.

First, by way of example: we see that a ship can be moved in the water, coming from the East and going toward the West; and a man who is inside that ship can walk by his own movement toward the East, or across the deck. And so, although in truth this man is always getting closer to the West <note>because the ship is carrying him there</note>, he does not do so as much as he would if he stayed still in the ship. Therefore, this man is moved by a **double movement**: one of which is the movement of the ship and himself together, and the other is his own movement.

Similarly, the **sphere of the moon** is transported with the entire heaven from East to West by the **daily motion**; but it moves more slowly and differently than a **fixed star** because it has its own movement in the opposite direction. And because of this, in one month, the moon makes one fewer turn around the earth than a fixed star does. And the **sun** makes only one turn in a year, and the other planets each in a certain time according to the speed of their own movement.

Furthermore, this is visible to the senses: for if you look at the moon one evening near a **fixed star**, and look the following evening, you will see it further away from that star, and it will be further back, more toward the East. And the next night, it will be even further back, and so on.

Also, imagine if the entire Heaven ceased its daily motion, and the other movements remained. I say that then the moon would make one turn or circuit, as if going from East to West <note>The author likely means West to East here, as he is describing the "own movement" which he previously called "contrary"</note>, and would do it in the time that now lasts twenty-seven days and eight hours. And **Mercury**, **Venus**, and the **sun** would make one turn going from West to East, and returning to the West, over the span of one year. And **Mars** in two years or thereabouts. And **Jupiter** in twelve years or thereabouts. And **Saturn** in thirty years or thereabouts; for they currently make their turn and their revolution and accomplish their own movements in the spaces of time that I have named here.

The proper movement of the aforementioned planets is not straight from West to East, nor the exact opposite of the first daily motion; instead, it is <term>oblique: on a slant or diagonal</term>, and this can be clearly seen: for if you look at the moon...

<header>The Heart of Secrets</header>

...[heaven], but if you observe a planet near a **fixed star** <note>original: "estoille fixe"; these are stars that appear to stay in fixed positions relative to each other, unlike the "wandering" planets</note>, you will find it on the second or third night away from that star. It will not have moved directly toward the East; instead, its path will be drawn toward the **North** <note>original: "septentrion"</note> or toward the **South** <note>original: "midy"</note>.

And for this reason, just as the **daily movement** <note>The rotation of the entire sky every 24 hours</note> is made and measured according to the **equinoctial circle** <term>equinoctial circle: The celestial equator, an imaginary line in the sky directly above the Earth's equator</term>—as it appears in the fifth chapter—so too is the specific movement of the planets made according to another circle which is called the **zodiac**. 

This circle crosses and intersects the equinoctial at two opposite points, and each of these two circles divides the other into two halves at these two points. One half of the zodiac slopes and moves toward the **North**, and the other toward the **South**. Likewise, the poles of the zodiac slope and move away from the **poles of the world** <note>The North and South celestial poles</note>, and the movements of the planets are performed upon or near the two poles of the zodiac. This zodiac must be imagined in the **ninth sphere** <note>In this model of the universe, the ninth sphere was the outermost moving layer that carried the others</note> or the final one, just as the equinoctial is, and the planets are moved upon this circle.

# On Philosophy.

There are in the **zodiac** four principal points: namely, the two aforementioned points where it intersects the **equinoctial** <term>equinoctial: the celestial equator</term> and two other points where it is furthest away and declines from the equinoctial, of which one is toward the **North** <note>original: "septentrion"</note> and the other toward the **South** <note>original: "midy"</note>. ¶ And the zodiac is divided into four equal parts by these four points. ¶ Likewise, each of these four quarters of the zodiac is divided into three equal parts; and thus they make twelve parts which are called **signs**. The signs are named: **Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn** <note>original: "Capicornus"</note>, **Aquarius, and Pisces**. There is no need to name them in French <note>original: "en francoys"</note>, for their names possess no specific property that has any effect regarding the **science of judgments** <term>science of judgments: judicial astrology, or the practice of predicting the future and human character based on the heavens</term>. The first-named sign, namely **Aries**, begins at the point where the zodiac intersects the equinoctial, at which point the sun begins to decline toward the North, and this sign extends toward the East, and so on for the others following. ¶ Likewise, each of these signs is divided into thirty parts which are called **degrees**. And thus there are three hundred and sixty degrees in the zodiac. ¶ Likewise, each degree is divided into sixty **minutes**; and each minute into sixty **seconds**; and each second into sixty **thirds**; and each third into sixty **fourths**. And this is sufficient, although one could proceed further to fifths and sixths, and so on as much as one might please. Similarly, each of the circles of the **sphere** <note>the celestial sphere</note>, or any other circle whether large or small, is imagined to be divided into three hundred and sixty degrees, and further as has been said. And also each hour into sixty minutes, and further as has been said.

For had someone wished it so, they could have said that each sign has sixty degrees and each circle four hundred degrees, or some other number. # The Heart of Secrets

->ii ii<-

whether each sign be divided into so many degrees, this was a matter of choice; for there is no more natural difference between the last degree of **Aries** <note>The Ram</note> and the first degree of **Taurus** <note>The Bull</note> than there is between the second and third degrees of Taurus. And so it is with the other parts of the heavens, except only when the **Sun** <note>original: "Soleil"</note> has some relation to a certain fixed star or another; then it has a different significance than when it is otherwise. But these stars are not always in the same degree or in the same sign. Because of this, many rules of the **judgments of astrology** <term>judgments of astrology: also known as judicial astrology, the practice of predicting events based on planetary positions</term> are false, having been written primarily by those who did not understand **natural philosophy** <term>natural philosophy: the study of nature and the physical universe, a precursor to modern science</term>, or who had not recognized or perceived the movements of the fixed stars, or who were too bold in their pronouncements. Consequently, one should see, and it is commonly seen, that those who presume to judge by such rules fail to speak the truth.

¶ Every circle of the sphere is imagined as a slender line or as a thin thread without width, except for the **zodiac** alone, which is like a wide circlet <note>original: "chappel," referring to a circular headband or crown</note>. It has three hundred and sixty degrees in its longitude or circumference, and about twelve degrees in its width or latitude. Likewise, each sign has thirty degrees in length and twelve in width. The Sun is moved, and has its course and its view, through the middle of this circle along a slender line which is called the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the Sun's apparent path across the sky; the "line of eclipses"</term>. And the reason why the zodiac is so wide is because the other **planets** do not have their courses or their paths directly under the ecliptic line through the middle of the zodiac as the Sun does; rather, they decline and draw more toward the **South** <note>original: "midy"</note> on one side and toward the **North** <note>original: "septētrion"</note> on the other. From this it happens, and one can clearly see, that the **Moon** <note>original: "lune"</note> sometimes comes higher toward our heads than the Sun ever did, and also she descends lower and draws further toward the South; and so it is with the other planets. For just as the zodiac declines from the **equinoctial** <term>equinoctial: the celestial equator</term>, as was said in the seventh chapter, so too do the circles of the planets decline from the path of the Sun—which is called the ecliptic because there can be no **eclipse** of the Sun or Moon except when the Moon is in that path or very near it, as will appear more fully hereafter.

"Sign," in its proper meaning, is a surface or a part of the zodiac in the **outermost sphere** <term>outermost sphere: the highest heaven or Primum Mobile in the medieval geocentric model</term>; this part is thirty degrees long and twelve wide, as has been said. Thus, when it is said that a planet is "in" Aries or another sign, it means that it is beneath Aries or beneath such a sign. ¶ In the second meaning, one can understand a "sign" to be everything that is beneath that surface or part or sign taken in the first meaning. This wedge has four sides, two of which are wider than the others. ...point. And if he goes straight toward the north or toward the south without deviating to the east or to the west, he still always has the same **meridian**; however, he cannot move without continually having a different **zenith** <note>the point in the sky directly above an observer</note>.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a scholar or astronomer holding an armillary sphere or globe, surrounded by foliage.</image-desc>Furthermore, there is another circle in the sphere which is called the **horizon** <note>Middle French: *orizon*</note>, which divides the part of the sky that we see above us from that which we do not see and which is as if below us. And because the earth is nothing but a small point in comparison to the sky, it follows that whenever a man is in open country, he can see half of the sky. And this half is called our **hemisphere** <note>Middle French: *emispere*</note>, which is to say our "half-sphere." And thus this circle called the horizon divides the sky into two halves; and this circle and the meridian intersect and divide each other in a cross into two halves at that point of the meridian which is above us called the **zenith** and the pole of the horizon; and each person is at the center of their own horizon. And because whenever a man moves from one place to another, he is in another part of the sky and has another zenith, he also has a new horizon wherever he goes, whether toward the east, the west, the south, or elsewhere.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>Although in every place on earth there is always a different horizon, every horizon is either **right** or **oblique**. Those have a **right horizon** who live under the **equinoctial** <note>the celestial equator</note>, for they have their zenith on the equinoctial, since their horizon intersects and divides the equinoctial in a cross at right angles. And the two **poles of the world** <note>the north and south celestial poles</note> are on their horizon, in such a way that neither of these two poles is raised above their horizon, nor hidden <note>original: *despere*</note> beneath it. But other people who live elsewhere than under the equinoctial have an **oblique horizon**; for their horizon intersects and divides the equinoctial diagonally <note>Middle French: *de bies*</note>, not straight in a cross, but at oblique angles that are not equal. And one of the poles of the world always appears to them raised above their horizon, and the other is always hidden <note>original: *muce*</note> and depressed below their horizon, more or less according to various locations, as will appear more fully. And for this reason, there are two circles in the **material sphere** <term>material sphere: a physical model of the heavens, like an armillary sphere or astrolabe</term>, one of which represents the right horizon and the other the oblique, and one can move it and make it more or less oblique according to various locations.

Leaf 76.

# On Philosophy.

n iiii

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram representing the celestial sphere. It features a central horizontal band labeled **zodiac** <note>original: *zodiacus*</note> containing astrological symbols (Gemini, Taurus, Aries, Pisces, Aquarius, Capricorn, Sagittarius, Scorpio, Libra, Virgo, Leo, Cancer). As it appears from the previous chapter, neither of the world's poles is raised above the **horizon** <note>Middle French: *orizon*</note> for those who live under the **equinoctial** <note>the celestial equator</note> and who have a "straight sphere." But everywhere else, one of the poles is raised above the oblique horizon; and the more the pole is raised, the more the horizon is tilted or "oblique." And just as the horizon is more oblique, the pole is higher, and the other pole is correspondingly depressed further below the horizon. And it should be known that however much the pole is raised above the horizon, there is an equal distance between the **zenith** <note>the point directly overhead</note> and the equinoctial. This rule is clear because from the horizon to the zenith (which is the pole of the horizon), the distance is a quarter part of the **meridian** <note>90 degrees</note>.

¶ Also, from the pole of the world to the equinoctial, the distance is likewise a quarter part of the meridian; and these two quarters are equal. Therefore, if one subtracted from each an equal amount, the remaining parts would be equal. Let us therefore subtract from each of these two quarters the section that lies between the pole and the zenith; thus the remaining parts of the meridian are equal: namely, the part between the horizon and the pole (which is called the **elevation of the pole** <note>what we now call latitude</note>) and the part between the zenith and the equinoctial.

¶ Also, I show this by example in the horizon of **Paris**, where the pole is raised by about 49 degrees. I say, therefore, that there are 49 degrees between the zenith of Paris and the equinoctial, and here is the proof: Because from the horizon to the zenith there are 90 degrees (which is a quarter of the circle); now, subtract the elevation of the pole [49 degrees], and there will remain 41 degrees between the pole and the zenith. And from the pole to the equinoctial there are 90 degrees. Therefore, subtract these 41 degrees that are between the pole and the zenith, and there will remain 49 degrees between the zenith and the equinoctial.

¶ Also, there are 90 degrees from the zenith to the horizon along the equinoctial; from which, if you subtract the distance from the zenith to the equinoctial (which is 49 degrees), there will remain 41 degrees. This is the elevation of the equinoctial above the horizon of Paris, which is necessarily equal to the distance between the pole and the zenith.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "minor circles" of the celestial sphere. The previous page ended while introducing the two tropics (the solstices). This page defines the various types of "days" and explains how the tilt of the horizon affects the length of daylight across different regions of the world.</meta>

### On Philosophy. Leaf lxxvii. ###

The **natural day** <note>a full 24-hour cycle</note> is the span of time in which the sun makes one entire revolution around the earth; that is, from the moment it reaches the **meridian** <note>the imaginary line representing noon</note> until it returns to that same spot. The **artificial day** is the time between sunrise and sunset, and the night is the remainder. Therefore, in each natural day, the sun describes something like a circle, though it is not strictly a circle, but misses it by a small margin; for the sun does not return to the exact same point of the meridian from which it started, but rather a little higher or lower, in the manner of a screw or a thread wound around a **spindle** <note>original: "fusee." The author is describing the sun's spiral path between the tropics over the course of the year.</note>. These circles here are called **parallels** <note>original: "parables." These are circles of latitude on the celestial sphere.</note>, and there are only three of them marked and described on the **material sphere** <note>an armillary sphere, a physical model used for teaching astronomy</note> because they are the most important: these are the two **tropics** and the **equinoctial** <note>the celestial equator</note>.

Of these aforementioned circles, or of each of them, the part which is above the horizon is called the **diurnal arc** <note>the "arc of the day"</note>; for as long as the sun is there or passing through it, it is day. The part which is below is called the **nocturnal arc**. Consequently, the larger the portion of one of these circles is above the horizon, the longer the artificial day is and the shorter the night; and conversely, the smaller the portion, the shorter the day and the longer the night. Now it appears clearly enough that the **right horizon** <note>the horizon as seen from the Earth's equator</note> intersects and cuts all these circles through the middle. From this it follows that all those who live under such a horizon—that is, upon the equinoctial—have days and nights of equal length at all times. Likewise, it also appears clearly that the **oblique horizon** <note>the horizon as seen from any latitude other than the equator</note>, however it may be positioned, can only divide the equinoctial into two equal halves; and for this reason, when the sun is there (which happens twice a year: once at the entry of **Aries** <note>the spring equinox</note> and the other at the entry of **Libra** <note>the autumn equinox</note>), it is then the **equinox**, and the days and nights are made equal throughout the whole world. Likewise, all the other aforementioned parallels—that is to say, all of them generally except the equinoctial—the oblique horizon divides them into two unequal parts <note>original: "trois parties non egalles." This appears to be a scribal error, as a horizon circle divides a parallel into two parts: day and night.</note>. The more oblique the horizon is, the more unequal these parts become; and therefore, at all times except for the two aforementioned dates, the days and nights are unequal in an oblique horizon. The more oblique it is, the greater the difference. For this reason, in **Sweden** <note>original: "sueste," likely referring to Suecia</note> and **Norway**, the days are longer in summer and shorter in winter than they are in France, and longer in France than they are in **Jerusalem**; and so it is in various regions according to whether the horizon is more or less oblique.

The entire **zodiac** rises and sets in one natural day over every horizon on the habitable earth. And because it is an oblique circle, it does not rise regularly in its parts as the equinoctial does; rather, one part rises sooner and the other at leisure or more slowly in varying ways. This variation occurs four times in a right horizon at the four principal points of the zodiac: for the fourth part of the zodiac which is from the first point of **Aries** until the end of **Gemini**, and the fourth of the equinoctial which corresponds to it, begin to rise at the same moment and finish at the same moment; and so it is with the other three quarters of the zodiac and the other three quarters of the equinoctial: but...

¶ Every circle that divides its sphere into two halves and has its center at the center of the world <note>the Earth, which was considered the center of the universe</note> is called **concentric**. Now, it is the case that the circle the Sun describes in its sphere upon the zodiac is not concentric; rather, its center is located elsewhere than at the center of the world, and thus it is eccentric, as appears by way of example in this figure which follows.

# On Philosophy. Leaf LXXX.
## D ii

The sun in its **eccentric orbit** <note>A circular path that is off-center relative to the Earth</note> moves regularly, and passes through almost one degree each day. If one were to draw a line from the diameter of the first point of **Aries** <note>The Ram; the spring equinox</note> to the first point of **Libra** <note>The Scales; the autumn equinox</note> passing through the center of the world, it appears clearly that more than half of the Sun’s eccentric circle lies toward **Cancer** <note>The Crab; the summer solstice</note>. Therefore, the sun must pass through more than half of its eccentric orbit during the time it travels from the first point of Aries to the first point of Libra (or the end of **Virgo**). Because of this, it must take more than exactly half of the year. This period is called the "greater half" of the year and is longer than the other. If one wished to call this entire part "summer" and the other part "winter," as some authors do, it would follow that summer would be that much longer than winter.

-><image-desc>A circular diagram representing the celestial sphere. A horizontal line is labeled "Equinoctial" <note>The celestial equator</note>. A diagonal line intersecting it is labeled "oblique" on the upper left and "Horizon" on the lower right.</image-desc><-

The <term>natural day</term> <note>The 24-hour period of the Earth's rotation relative to the sun</note> is from one sunrise until the next sunrise, or from noon until noon. In that space of time, the Heavens make one full turn. Along with that turn, the sun moves as far as it has traveled through the Heavens by its own motion—which is contrary to the daily motion measured by the **equinoctial** <note>The celestial equator</note>, as was stated in the second chapter. Now, it is the case that the sun moves through the heavens by its own motion more in one natural day and less in another for two principal reasons. One is because some <term>signs</term> <note>Signs of the zodiac</note> rise "straight" and others rise "obliquely," both because of the tilt of the zodiac and the tilt of the horizon. The other reason is the nature of the Sun’s eccentric orbit. To make this matter appear more clearly: let us suppose that the sun, in its own motion, passed through one sign every natural day. I say that the day it passed through Aries would be shorter than the day it passed through Libra on an **oblique horizon** <note>An observer's horizon that is not at the equator</note> like ours. For on that day, it would be necessary for the entire equinoctial to rise above the horizon, and then as much again as rises with Aries. And because Aries rises obliquely, it does not carry the full twelfth part of the equinoctial with it, but less. But on the day the sun passed through Libra, the entire equinoctial would have to rise, and then even more than a twelfth part, because Libra rises "straight." Therefore, the natural day would be notably longer when the sun passes through Libra than when it passes through Aries. And because the sun now passes through about one degree of the zodiac each day...

### The Heart of Secrets

...and one degree rises faster than the other, more at leisure. And one degree carries with it more of the **equinoctial** <note>The celestial equator</note> and the other less. I say that although there is less difference than if the sun passed through an entire sign in one day, nevertheless, there is a difference; and for this reason, they cause **natural days** <note>The full 24-hour cycle from one noon to the next</note> to be longer toward the end of September than toward the end of March.

-><image-desc>A circular diagram divided into four quadrants by a vertical and horizontal line. The vertical line is labeled "straight" at the top. The horizontal line is labeled "The Eccentric" across the middle. The bottom vertical segment is labeled "Horizon." The circle represents an eccentric orbit—one whose center does not align with the center of the Earth—in a cosmological context.</image-desc><-

To understand another cause: Suppose that one draws two lines from the **eccentric** of the sun that pass to the **zodiac** through two **apogees** <note>original: "Aux solis"; the point in the sun's orbit furthest from the Earth</note>; and suppose that between these two lines lies the twelfth part of the eccentric. Likewise, suppose that one has two other lines on the opposite side which similarly encompass a twelfth part of the eccentric on the other side of the figure. I say that the two lines toward the **apogee** encompass less than a twelfth part of the zodiac, and the two which are toward the **perigee** <note>original: "oppositum augis"; the point in the orbit closest to the Earth</note> encompass more than a twelfth part. This is to be assumed as a thing demonstrated by geometry. Therefore, it follows by necessity that when the sun is near its apogee and it passes a twelfth part of its eccentric, it passes less than a twelfth part of the zodiac—that is to say, less than one sign. And thus, when it passes one degree of its eccentric, it passes less than one degree of the zodiac. On the other hand, toward the perigee, it is quite the opposite: for when it passes one degree of its eccentric, it passes more than one degree of the zodiac. 

Now, it is so that the sun passes about one degree of its eccentric regularly every day. Because of this, it does not pass through the zodiac regularly. For this reason, natural days would be longer when the sun is toward the **perigee**; for then the entire zodiac rises in one natural day plus more than one degree, and when it is toward the **apogee**, it is not so. And thus, according to this cause, the **artificial days** <note>The period of daylight from sunrise to sunset</note> would be longer in winter than in summer; but sometimes the other cause mentioned in the previous chapter works to the contrary. Nevertheless, for both of these reasons, they are longer toward the end of September than toward the end of March. Nonetheless, the half of the year toward winter is the shorter one, as was said in the fourteenth chapter: for the increase of these natural days in quantity is not as great as the increase of the other half in the number of days.

It concludes that while individual winter days might be longer in duration, the winter half of the year contains fewer days in total.</summary>

As was stated in the first chapter, the Earth is effectively completely round; and therefore, as one goes from one country to another, one has a different **horizon** and a different part of the sky appears. And if a man went from the **North** <note>original: "Septentrion"</note> straight toward the **South** <note>original: "midy"</note>, the **Arctic pole** <note>The North Star or celestial North Pole</note> would be continually less elevated; if he went in the opposite direction, it would be more elevated. And therefore, if he went straight toward the south along a **meridian** until the Arctic pole was less elevated above his horizon by a twelfth part of the meridian, he would have traveled a twelfth part of the circuit of the Earth. And if he went until the pole was less elevated by only one degree—or on the contrary, until it was more elevated by one degree—he would have traveled one degree of the Earth, which has three hundred and sixty such spaces. And in this manner is found the measurement of the Earth: for the elevation of the pole or of a star is easy to find by the **astrolabe** or by the **quadrant** <note>Two primary medieval instruments used for measuring the altitude of celestial bodies</note>.

¶ It is thus found by experience that if a man went straight toward the North until the pole was elevated one degree more, or straight toward the South until it was elevated one degree less, he would have traveled seven hundred **stades** <note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</note> according to the author of the Sphere <note>Referring to Johannes de Sacrobosco, whose "De sphaera mundi" was the standard astronomical textbook of the era</note>. Therefore, repeat and multiply this number by 360, and thus we find that the circuit of the Earth, going all the way around, is 252,000 stades, which are worth fifteen thousand seven hundred and fifty **leagues**; for one league is worth two miles, and one mile is worth eight stades, and one stade is 125 **paces**. And one pace is five feet, and one foot is worth four **palms**, and one palm is four **fingers** <note>A breakdown of medieval units of measure: fingers, palms, feet, paces, stades, miles, and leagues</note>. And thus, someone who could circle the entire Earth traveling exactly ten leagues every day would have finished his turn in one thousand five hundred and 75 days, which equals four years, 16 weeks, and two days.

¶ Item, to find the **diameter** of a circle from its circumference, use this rule: take away from the circle (or its circumference) a 7th part, and let the remainder be divided into three parts. The diameter is as large as the third part of that remainder. Therefore, according to this rule, the diameter of the Earth is about five thousand eleven leagues and six stades. And thus the **semi-diameter** <note>The radius</note> is two thousand five hundred leagues and fourteen stades. And it is this far, or thereabouts, to the center of the world: which is the lowest thing that exists, and if one were there, one could not move in any direction without going up. And it should be known that one cannot state the aforementioned measurements precisely and to the exact point; but it is sufficient and a beautiful thing to reach near the true measure without there being...

and one degree rises sooner than the other more at leisure. And one degree carries with it more of the **equinoctial** <note>original: "lequinoctial"; the celestial equator</note> and the other less. I say that although there is less difference than if the sun passed an entire line in one day, there is nevertheless a difference; and for this reason, **natural days** <note>The full 24-hour cycle from noon to noon, as opposed to just the daylight hours</note> are longer toward the end of September than toward the end of March.

<image-desc>A circular diagram divided into four quadrants by a vertical and horizontal line. The quadrants and lines are labeled with text. Top left: "straight". Bottom left: "Horizon". The horizontal line is labeled "The ec-cent-" on the left and "-ric" on the right, forming the word "The eccentric".</image-desc>

To understand the other cause: Suppose that two lines are drawn from the **eccentric circle** <note>original: "lepcentrics"; the sun's orbital path which, in medieval astronomy, was thought to be a circle whose center is not the Earth</note> of the sun, extending to the **zodiac** toward the **solar apogee** <note>original: "Aux solis"; the point where the sun is farthest from the Earth</note>; and suppose there is a twelfth part of the eccentric circle between these two lines. ¶ Item, suppose there are two other lines on the opposite side which similarly encompass a twelfth part of the eccentric circle on the other side of the figure. ¶ I say that the two lines toward the solar apogee encompass less than a twelfth part of the zodiac, and the two toward the **perigee** <note>original: "oppositum augis"; the point where the sun is closest to Earth</note> encompass more than a twelfth part. This is to be assumed as a thing demonstrated by **geometry**. Therefore, it follows by necessity that when the sun is toward the solar apogee and passes a twelfth part of its eccentric path, it passes less than a twelfth part of the zodiac—that is to say, less than one **sign** <note>One of the twelve 30-degree divisions of the zodiac, such as Aries or Leo</note>. And thus, when it passes one degree of its eccentric path, it passes less than one degree of the zodiac. On the other hand, toward the perigee, it is quite the opposite: for when it passes one degree of its eccentric path, it passes more than one degree of the zodiac. Now, it happens that the sun passes about one degree of its eccentric path regularly every day. Because of this, it does not pass through the zodiac regularly. For this reason, natural days would be longer when the sun is toward the perigee; for then the whole zodiac rises in one natural day plus more than one degree, while when it is toward the solar apogee, it is not so. And thus, according to this cause, **artificial days** <note>original: "iours artificielz"; the hours of daylight from sunrise to sunset</note> would be longer in winter than in summer; but sometimes the other cause mentioned in the previous chapter works to the contrary. Nevertheless, because of both these causes, they are longer toward the end of September than toward the end of March. Nevertheless, the half of the year toward winter is the shortest, as was stated in the fourteenth chapter; for the increase in the length of these natural days in quantity is not as great as the increase of the other half in the number of days.

...there would be a notably great defect. ¶ Suppose that the earth were or is inhabited all around. Secondly, those who live under the Tropic of Summer <term>Tropic of Summer: the Tropic of Cancer</term> have the Sun directly overhead at noon on the day of the summer solstice. And thus, if one calls "day" the entire continuous time the Sun is above the horizon, or from sunrise until sunset, they have only one night and one day in the whole year. And the manner described for this half of the earth which is toward the Arctic pole is to be understood for the other half and for those dwellings toward the [Antarctic] pole.
