### Of Philosophy. Leaf 82.

There are five parts or zones or regions on the earth. The first and the last are too far from the sun and are uninhabitable due to excessive cold. The third and middle one is too close to the sun, under the third zone which is called the **torrid** or scorched zone, and is uninhabitable because of extreme heat. The other two—namely the second and the fourth—are neither too close to the sun nor too far, and would be habitable and temperate in heat and cold according to this consideration, if there were no other obstacle. 

And according to Aristotle, the <term>pole antarticque: the South Pole</term> is the top of the world: for the part of the earth that is habitable is like the face, and is the front of the earth and the world. Thus it is the [top] part of the sky: for it faces the front of the sky, namely the part toward the south <note>original: "midy"</note> from the middle of the habitable earth. 

¶ Also, the east of the first horizon of the habitable earth is the right-hand side: for from there begins the movement of the <term>artificial day: the period from sunrise to sunset</term> in the habitable earth. He says thus: that if a man had his face and front toward the south <note>midy</note> and his back toward the ground and his right hand toward the east, it would follow that he would have his left hand toward the west <note>original: "occident"</note>, and his head toward the Antarctic pole, and his feet toward the <term>pole articque: the North Pole</term>; and thus the east is the right-hand part of the sky and the world, and the Antarctic pole is above, the south is in front, the west is on the left, and the Arctic pole is below, at midnight, and behind. 

And according to this consideration, we <term>Latins: Western Europeans</term> are in the lower and left-hand part of the world: for we live toward the west and toward the Arctic pole. But if we consider the proper movement which follows the <term>zodiaque: the path of the sun and planets</term>, it is as if it were the opposite. The Arctic pole is on top, and the west is on the right, and the south is always in front; and perhaps this movement is the most noble, or the spheres that are moved in this way. 

¶ Also, a greater multitude and more beautiful stars are in the northern part of the sky toward the Arctic pole than in the other half which is beyond the <term>equinoctial: the celestial equator</term>: and according to this, we would be in the upper part of the world, and on the right, and in the most noble; and the first zone would be around the Arctic pole, as I shall set out at the beginning of this chapter.

Some say that the earthly region which is under the path of the sun between the two <term>tropicqs: the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</term> is uninhabitable, as was said: but others say that it is a very good and very noble and very temperate habitation, especially toward the middle under the equator. And this was the opinion of <term>Auicenne: Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath (980–1037)</term>. And those who now maintain this argue thus: If it were uninhabitable, it would be because of excessive heat as was said: but it is not so. 

Firstly: because one cause of great heat in our habitation is that summer is long, and therefore it is hotter toward the end. And in that region, summer is very short, for they have two summers in a year, as it appears in the twenty-fifth chapter. 

¶ Also, another cause of great heat for us is the length of summer days, and for this reason, it is commonly hotter in the afternoon than before. And under the equator they always have the <term>equinocte: the equinox, when day and night are equal</term>, as was said in the twenty-sixth chapter, and they do not have days as long in summer as we do.

...a more direct reflection of light, which is the cause of heat. The second cause is when the sun is closer to the earth or to our heads <note>meaning the zenith</note> and at a shorter distance; and this is when it is in the opposition of the <term>apogee: the point in an orbit furthest from Earth</term> <note>original: "opposition augis." And then it heats more strongly than if the other factors were the same; for as <term>Albumazar: Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a highly influential Persian astrologer and astronomer</term> says in the *Book of Impressions*: "The heat of the planets is stronger the closer they are to the air." Now it is so that the sun is in its apogee <note>original: "aux solis"</note> around our summer. And thus, the first cause of heat <note>the directness of the sun's rays</note> is strong, and the second <note>proximity to the earth</note> is weak. For this reason, we have a sufficiently temperate heat in summer. And in winter, the sun is near the earth (near us) and in the opposition of the apogee. And thus, the first cause of heat is weak, and therefore we have a sufficiently temperate cold. But those who would inhabit the fourth region <note>the southern temperate zone</note> would have it differently; for in their summer, when we have winter, the three causes of heat are all strong: the sun is near the earth and high above the horizon, so there is excessive heat there.

<image-desc>A simple line diagram showing two intersecting circles or arcs, representing the intersection of celestial or terrestrial circles described in the text.</image-desc>

One must imagine a circle on the surface of the earth beneath the <term>equinoctial: the celestial equator</term>, and another circle which intersects this one in a cross and which passes through the East and the West of the habitable earth. These two circles here divide the earth into four equal quarters, of which only the quarter where we are is habitable, and not even all of it; for there is a part toward the equinoctial that is not well inhabited because of too great heat, and another toward the Arctic Pole that is poorly inhabited or uninhabitable because of too great cold. Whereby it appears that the habitable land is not round nor in the manner of a circle. And Aristotle says that it is like a quarter of the surface of a sphere: the quarter is cut off at two ends, or like a wide, curved or concave shield that is cut off at the bottom end. And the <term>mappa mundi: a medieval world map</term> cannot be very properly represented on a flat thing, but only on a rounded thing in the manner of a part of a sphere. And the habitable earth has four corners which are called the four angles of the habitable earth, of which one can be called the angle of the Summer East, another the angle of the Winter East, another the Summer West, and another the angle of the Winter West. And it should be known that one can understand by "East" every part where the sun rises on any horizon. And thus every place is "East" with respect to some horizon, and every place is "West." But "East" can be understood differently as the first part of the habitable land toward the rising sun, and "West" also as that of the last horizon toward the setting sun. And thus, at the beginning of this chapter, returning to our purpose, the aforementioned portion which is the habitable land can be divided in a certain way according to the historians...

...of the second [climate], the longest day is thirteen hours and 45 minutes. At the beginning of the third, the longest day is 13 hours and 45 minutes. At the beginning of the seventh, it is 15 hours and 45 minutes; at the end of the seventh, it is 16 hours and 15 minutes. From this, it appears that in each <term>climate</term> <note>In ancient and medieval geography, a "climate" was a latitudinal zone of the Earth defined by the duration of the longest day of summer, rather than by weather patterns.</note>, from the beginning to the end, there is a difference of half an hour in the length of the longest day. **And from the beginning of the first climate until the end of the seventh, there is a total difference of three and a half hours. This is established in regard to this cause and to the seven planets <note>Medieval cosmology often linked the seven known "planets" (including the Sun and Moon) to the seven habitable zones of the Earth.</note> upon the habitable earth thus divided into seven climates. For this reason, the first climate is longer <note>Here "longer" refers to the physical width of the zone on the ground, not the duration of the day.</note> than the second, and the second than the third. And so it follows, as it appears in the preceding chapter: For to find the longest day increased by four hours <note>Original: *quatre heures*. This may be a scribal error for *quart d'heure* (a quarter-hour), as the logic follows that smaller increments of time require different distances of travel.</note>, one must travel a greater distance when heading toward the <term>north</term> <note>Original: *septentrion*, the traditional term for the North, named after the seven stars of the Big Dipper.</note> when one is near the <term>equator</term> <note>Original: *equinoctial*, the celestial or terrestrial equator.</note>. This distance is greater in the first climate than the second, and in the second than the third. This continues thereafter, and it is due to the roundness of the earth and the obliquity of the <term>horizon</term> and that of the <term>zodiac</term>.**

¶ Also, some authors state that the longest day in the middle of the first climate is 13 hours; in the middle of the second, 13 and a half; in the third, 14 hours; in the fourth, 14 and a half; in the fifth, 15; in the sixth, 15 and a half; and in the seventh, 16. However, the "middle" is not well-assigned this way. As touched upon before, to find the longest day increased by half an hour or by a quarter of an hour—and specifically to find the longest day's increase of a quarter-hour at the beginning or in the first part of the first climate—one must travel over more land than at the end of that same climate. Therefore, it follows that the place where the longest day is 13 hours is closer to the end of the first climate than to its beginning. Thus, one must use the subtleties of <term>geometry</term> if one wishes to assign these zones according to the quantity of the longest day.

The <term>elevation of the pole</term> <note>In medieval astronomy, the "elevation of the pole" above the horizon is equivalent to what we now call latitude.</note> above each horizon is as great as the distance between the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly overhead.</note> and the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note>. And it appears by the thirty-third chapter that the zenith at the beginning of the first <term>climate</term> <note>A latitudinal zone of the Earth.</note> is elevated by thirteen degrees and forty-five minutes <note>The text says "thirteen" (treize), but the following sentence and the table below use "twelve" (douze), which is the mathematically consistent figure for this system.</note>. Wherefore it follows that the pole is elevated at the beginning of the first climate twelve degrees and forty-five minutes. ¶ Item: add to this the latitude <note>Here meaning the "width" or span of the zone itself.</note> of the first climate, which is seven degrees and forty-five minutes; you will then have the distance between the equinoctial and the zenith at the end of the first climate. And consequently, the elevation of the pole at the end of the first climate and the beginning of the second is twenty degrees and thirty minutes. ¶ Item: add to this the latitude of the second climate, and you will have the elevation of the pole at the end of the second climate and the beginning of the third: and it is twenty-seven degrees and thirty minutes. ¶ Item: by this same method you will find the elevation of the pole at the beginning of the fourth climate to be thirty-three degrees and forty minutes. ¶ Item: at the beginning of the fifth, thirty-nine degrees. ¶ Item: at the beginning of the sixth, forty-three degrees and thirty minutes. ¶ Item: at the beginning of the seventh, forty-seven degrees and fifteen minutes. You will find that the elevation of the pole at the middle of the first climate is sixteen degrees, thirty-seven minutes and thirty seconds. ¶ Item: at the middle of the second climate, twenty-four degrees. According to the astronomers, the length or <term>longitude</term> <note>In medieval geography, "longitude" often referred to the east-west extent of the known world, while "latitude" or "breadth" referred to the north-south extent.</note> of the earth—as was stated in the thirtieth chapter—compared to the <term>latitude</term> is the sum of all the <term>climates</term> <note>The seven latitudinal zones of the habitable world.</note> together, which is 28 degrees and 45 minutes. And according to <term>Albategni</term> <note>Al-Battani (c. 858–929), a famous Arab astronomer and mathematician whose work was foundational to medieval European science.</note>, there is still habitation beyond the climates toward the south as far as the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The equator.</note> and toward the north, such that the latitude of the habitable earth is from beneath the equinoctial up to 60 degrees toward the north; this is the sixtieth <note>The text says "sixtiesme" (60th), though mathematically 60 degrees is the *sixth* part of a 360-degree circle. The author's subsequent logic uses the "sixth part," suggesting a scribal error in the original French.</note> part of the circuit of the earth. And by this, Albategni wishes to conclude that only the twelfth part of the earth is habitable: for he who takes half of a thing in length and the sixth part in width, such a portion is the twelfth part. Just as one who would take half of a field in length and the sixth part in width, it would be the twelfth part. But, with all due respect to him, although this rule holds and has its place on a flat and straight surface, it does not prove his point on the surface of a round object—and the habitable earth is part of such a surface. ¶ Item: by consideration of the 31st chapter, the habitable earth is in one of the four quarters of the earth. And so Albategni posits: for whoever takes the entire length of this quarter and sixty degrees of width starting from the equinoctial, as Albategni does, it clearly appears that this is more than half of the quarter of the earth's surface; whereby it follows that significantly more than the eighth part of the earth is habitable. ¶ Item: Albategni places as habitable two parts or two-thirds of the latitude of the fourth part of the earth—and specifically in the area where that fourth part is at its widest. Whereby it follows by necessity that more than two parts or two-thirds of that fourth part are habitable; and two-thirds of a quarter make a sixth. Thus, more than the sixth part of the earth is habitable, and consequently more than two-twelfths; but the certain measurement cannot be properly known, as was said regarding the longitude of the climates.

¶ The climates taken together are bounded by four lines, as appears by the figure in the 21st chapter. One of these lines begins the first climate and is twelve and a half degrees on this side of the equinoctial. Near this line, the Authors place several habitations; and especially the last known habitation beyond is called an island, <term>Taprobane</term> <note>Ancient name for Sri Lanka.</note>. It is opposite India toward the east according to Albategni, and according to the historians it is beyond and past the equinoctial: for when the inhabitants of that island look toward their midday, they have the sun rising in the east on their right and setting in the west on their left, and we have the contrary. Furthermore, they cannot see the North Star nor those near it, and they see the stars that are perpetually hidden from us. Among these, there is a bright one called <term>Canepos</term> <note>Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky, visible in the Southern Hemisphere.</note> according to <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of "Natural History."</note> and <term>Solinus</term> <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler of geographical wonders.</note>; it is large and white, and not too "burning" <note>In the sense of twinkling or harsh radiance.</note> according to <term>Albumazar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astronomer/astrologer in Baghdad.</note>, who mentions it and calls <note>original: "sicut fas regionem zinigo"</note> the region of the Zanj <note>The "Zinigo" or Zanj refers to the people of the East African coast; the Latin phrase implies this is the "rightful" or "divine" name for the region.</note>. And King Alexander sent a legate to this island, which Pliny, Solinus, and <term>Pomponius</term> <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer.</note> describe sufficiently, and they place many other islands and habitations in that direction or outside of the climates.

...habitations, or perhaps none at all, unless there are some small islands. For there is called the Great Ocean Sea, and there, according to <term>Haly</term> <note>Likely referring to the Arab astrologer and geographer Haly Abenragel (Ibn Abi al-Rijal).</note>, were three statues or idols on three islands. Each of these statues held a key, signifying that there is no further habitation beyond. Haly says they are near the "Passage of Hercules," which we call the <term>Strait of Morocco</term> <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note>. Hercules had these idols made, and they are called Edeas, or guardians, or the <term>Pillars of Hercules</term>. Some say he also placed idols toward the East. <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a prominent Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval science.</note> mentions one of these idols at the end of the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*, saying it was near Spain, marking a straight path outward; it was later destroyed and removed by the <term>Barbarians</term> <note>Refers here to the Almoravid or Almohad conquests in al-Andalus.</note> who fought the people of that island. This occurred in the 430th year of the preaching of Muhammad, which was around the year 1051 of the incarnation of Jesus Christ.

¶ Likewise, there are many habitations beyond the line that marks the end of the "climates" toward the north, such as England, <term>Dace</term> <note>Dacia, a term frequently used in medieval texts to refer to Denmark.</note>, Norway, and several other regions.

¶ Furthermore, according to Aristotle and Averroes at the end of the second book of *On the Heavens and the Earth*, the end of the habitable land in the East and the end of the habitable land in the West are very close to one another, and there is only a sea between them that is not very wide. Because of this, traveling from one end to the other by way of the habitable land involves a much greater distance than half the circumference of the earth. Therefore, if the climates are drawn toward the Western end (as the Authors suggest) and they do not find more than half the circumference of the earth in a year, it follows according to Averroes that the climates do not extend all the way to the end of the East. This implies there is a vast habitation beyond the climates toward the East, or that the climates (or some of them) must be much longer than the astronomers state.

Let us suppose that, according to the <term>longitude</term> of the climates, one could circumnavigate or travel around the earth, or go straight ahead toward the East or West until returning to the place from which one first departed. According to Aristotle and Averroes, one is very nearly able to make this circuit or pilgrimage, as was mentioned in the previous chapter. Now, let us pose for the sake of example that a man or a bird made this circuit in twelve <term>natural days</term> <note>A "natural day" (jour naturel) refers to a full 24-hour cycle of day and night.</note> by traveling steadily toward the West, starting now at noon. It is clearly apparent that each natural day he would pass the twelfth part of the earth's circuit, which is thirty degrees. Therefore, the sun would have to complete one full circuit around the earth plus an additional thirty degrees before it returned the next day to that man's <term>meridian</term> <note>The highest point of the sun at noon.</note>. Thus, this man would find his "day and night" to last 26 hours. It would be longer by a twelfth part of a natural day than if he had stayed still. Consequently, it follows by necessity that in these twelve natural days, that man would have experienced only eleven days and eleven nights, and the sun would have risen for him only eleven times. For eleven days and nights, each lasting 26 hours, make twelve [natural days]...

I say, then, that if this man <note>John, in the following example.</note> made that circuit going toward the West, and Pierre went toward the East, and they set off at the same time and returned or finished at the same time, Pierre would have, in this same span of time, two days and two nights more than John. And Robert, who stayed at rest <note>Meaning he remained stationary at the starting point.</note>, would have one day more than John and one day less than Peter, regardless of how long they took to make the circuit—whether they took twelve days, or a hundred days, or ten years, or however long they took. ¶ Item, it is a beautiful thing to consider how, if John and Pierre arrived on the same day—such as on a Sunday, for example—nonetheless John would say he had arrived on Saturday, and Pierre would say he had arrived on Monday. There would be great debate regarding the assignment of the days and their naming. And as for how this affects the influence of the planets according to the hours of the day and other matters, I leave them for the sake of brevity.

...the earth. And there are three principal causes why any part of the habitable earth—even at a suitable distance from the path of the sun and within the <term>climates</term> <note>In medieval geography, "climates" were seven latitudinal zones of the habitable world.</note>—may be uninhabitable. One is when that part is covered by the sea or obstructed by water. The second is when it is sterile and bears no good fruit, or is occupied by serpents or evil beasts, as are some deserts. The third is the disposition, the site, and the shape of certain mountainous places or valleys that are uninhabitable due to extreme cold or extreme heat, or because the air is too thin or too thick, or some other condition of the air that is not suitable for human nature. ¶ Likewise, regarding the distance of <term>distemperature</term> <note>An imbalance of qualities like heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note> from the sun's path which would normally be uninhabitable: it is possible that three special causes, contrary and opposite to the three causes mentioned above, may coincide or surround a place together; because of this, such a place becomes habitable. And so the historians say that the **Hyperborean mountains** <note>Legendary mountains in the far North, believed by some to have a perfect climate despite their location.</note> are of great temperance, and people live there for a very long time—some so long that they must be killed <note>A reference to the myth that Hyperboreans, tired of immortality, would jump from a cliff to their deaths.</note>. And yet they are far away and outside the climates toward the **North**. And <term>Lincomense</term> <note>Robert Grosseteste, the Bishop of Lincoln (c. 1175–1253), a famous scientist and philosopher.</note> declares the cause and says it is because of the shape and the disposition of these mountains. For they have a surface or a part facing the sun that is flat or well-polished and concave, whereby they suitably receive and retain the light and the heat of the sun; and they cast a shadow or provide shelter, defending the inhabitants from the **north wind**. And for these two reasons, they do not suffer great cold. ¶ Likewise, if these special causes of good habitation were to coincide and concur with the governance [of the stars]: if the land is fertile enough and well-situated to one’s liking with a good view of the heavens, then such a region would be very temperate. And perhaps such is the place that the poets, according to **Aristotle**, call the **Blessed Isles**, and it may be that such is the **Earthly Paradise**.

The four lines that form the boundaries and extremities of the habitable earth were touched upon in the 38th chapter; the extremity toward the **South** and that toward the **North** are "distempered" <note>Imbalanced or extreme in climate.</note>, as I have often said. And for this reason, **Ptolemy** says in his *Quadripartitum*, as do **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> and others, that in these two extremities there are savage men who eat people, and who have faces and countenances that are corrupted and deformed. And the cause, according to Haly, is the "distempered" nature of these regions in heat and cold: whereby their bodies are of a discordant and evil and ugly <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) which determined physical and mental traits.</note>; and because of this, they are of very evil, strange, and savage behavior. And there are people there of horrible appearance, and monsters or beasts, such that one can hardly tell if they are men or not, as **Saint Augustine** relates. ¶ Likewise, Haly says specifically of those toward the South that they are black and very <term>sallow</term> <note>original: "tressors" - likely meaning reddish-brown or tawny, common in medieval descriptions of people in hot climates.</note> under the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The Equator.</note> where they are governed [by the sun]; for there is greater temperance there, as was said before. ¶ Likewise, Haly relates that <term>Linius</term> <note>Likely a misspelling of Pliny the Elder (Plinius).</note> says that in the two aforementioned extremities dwell evil spirits and beasts that harm men. And it should be known that the two other extremities of habitation—that of the **East** and that of the **West**—are not so "distempered" in this way, except insofar as they participate with the other two: that is to say, in the four corners of the habitable earth.

of which I have already spoken. For these two extremities in the other parts are at a moderate and tempered distance from the path of the sun.
¶ In the habitable earth elsewhere than the aforementioned extremities, there is a difference according to **longitude** and according to **latitude**; but the greatest difference is according to latitude. For those who are further toward the **South** <note>original: "Midy"</note>, as **Aristotle** says in the seventh book of the *Politics*, are of much greater understanding and of greater prudence, but are less courageous, less strong, and less daring; for this reason, they are subjects. And on the contrary and otherwise, those who inhabit the **North** <note>original: "Septentrion"</note> are stronger, bolder, and more courageous, but of less prudence; they hold and keep to their liberties. And Aristotle says that the **Greeks** are in the middle and have sufficient strength and prudence. And for this reason, he says that they are by nature suited to have lordship over the others who are further toward the south or toward the north. But it seems to me that the Greeks have not continually held such lordship, but have been tributaries to the **Romans** and **Italians** according to the historians. And I believe that once the aforementioned cause for maintaining royal lordship and good <term>policy</term> <note>In this context, "policy" (pollice) refers to the organized government or civil order of a state.</note> are stronger, as perhaps by the movement of the <term>solar apogee</term> <note>original: "aux solis"; the point in the sun's orbit farthest from the earth. Medieval thinkers believed its movement influenced the rise and fall of empires.</note> and of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars in the Ptolemaic model of the universe.</note> or some other movement which can be the cause of the ennobling of a kingdom, or of a failure of good governance and a turning toward tyranny, whereby there follows a disposition toward division or a transfer of lordship. And it is not my intention that this be a necessary cause, but only that the body of the heavens inclines us toward various things.
¶ Likewise, **Ptolemy** in his *Quadripartitum* <note>original: "quadripertiti"; Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology, also known as the *Tetrabiblos*.</note> says similarly that those who inhabit further toward the south are of greater understanding and more skilled and of greater virtue in knowing the sciences of the stars and the mathematical arts. And **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel or Haly Heben Rodan, influential Arabic commentators on Ptolemy.</note> says that the wisest have been from the third, fourth, and fifth **climates**, and that Aristotle and **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher.</note> were from the fifth, and Ptolemy and several others were from the third. And this rule or difference mentioned above is understood regarding the many, commonly and according to the common course of things.

The other difference of the well-inhabited parts is according to the **longitude** of the climates, and it is not as great nor as notable as the difference of the **latitude**. And of this, Ptolemy says that those from the **East** <note>original: "Orient"</note> are more masculine and of stronger heart and show their courage quickly. And Haly says that they do not know how to hide or cover their deeds in any way, and have greater power in marvelous things and in the knowledge of **astrology**. For they are in the East, which is the right-hand part of the world and they are more of the nature of the **sun**. And on the contrary, the part toward the **West** <note>original: "Occident"</note> is more of the nature of the **moon**. And those of these parts, according to their courage, are willingly contentious in the manner of women. And when they have victory over their enemies or adversaries, they slay and kill them; and they do it only out of cowardice and for the great fear they have that [their enemies] might otherwise rise against them again and take revenge. And Haly adds that this is to be understood regarding the many. For

# The Heart of Secrets

After having spoken of the earth, I wish to return to speaking of the heavens and describe the causes of eclipses. However, I first want to explain how the **Moon** is illuminated; that is to say, she has no light of her own, but is illuminated by the **Sun**. And this is also true of all the other stars, according to what **Averroes** <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "auerrois". Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval science.</note> says. The Moon is round and spherical, in the manner of an apple or a ball. And it is the same for the other stars. For this reason, it can clearly be seen that the part of the Moon which faces the Sun is illuminated, and the other side is not, because the light and rays of the Sun cannot reach there. And because the Moon is spherical, nearly half of its surface is turned toward our sight. This is the case for all spherical things.

¶ Likewise, the Moon—which by her own movement is carried beneath the **zodiac** faster than the Sun—is sometimes in **conjunction** <term>conjunction</term> <note>When two celestial bodies appear in the same part of the sky from the perspective of Earth.</note> with the Sun, when they are at the exact same point in the zodiac. And sometimes the Moon is in **opposition**, which is when she and the Sun are at opposite degrees. And sometimes she is in opposition and conjunction and other aspects.

I say, therefore, that when the Moon is in conjunction or near it, she is positioned between the Sun and us. Thus, the part of her that is above and facing the Sun is illuminated. But the other part is below, facing us and our sight, and is not illuminated; for this reason, we cannot see the Moon when she is in conjunction or near conjunction.

¶ Likewise, when she is in opposition, we are then positioned between the Sun and the Moon. At that time, the part of the Moon facing the Sun (which is illuminated) is also facing our sight, and so she is seen in full.

¶ Likewise, when there is only a small part of the Moon facing the Sun that is also facing our sight, the Moon appears small; and the more of that part there is, the larger she appears. She appears first as **horned** <note>original: "cornue". This refers to the crescent shape, which medieval writers often described as having horns.</note> and then nearly in other shapes, because she is spherical, as was said. And according to what **the Commentator** <note>Referring again to Averroes, who was known simply as "The Commentator" in university settings because of his extensive work on Aristotle.</note> says, one should imagine two circles: one which divides and separates the part of the Moon that is illuminated from the part that is not, and another circle that divides and separates the part of the Moon facing our sight from the other part.

As the Moon approaches conjunction and moves away from opposition, these two circles overlap less. This is the reason why the Moon appears to wax and wane in light; and because of this, she is called by a name in **Greek** <note>The author likely refers to the Greek name *Selēnē*, or perhaps a term related to her phases like *mēnē* (crescent).</note> among us, but it is not necessary to know it. The meaning of this chapter can be seen in the figure that follows.

# The Heart of Secrets

After having spoken of the earth, I wish to return to speaking of the sky and state the causes of **eclipses** / But first I want to say how the **moon** is illuminated / that is to say, that it has no light of its own / but is illuminated by the **sun**. Medieval scholars relied heavily on his commentaries on Aristotle to understand the natural world.</note> says / and the moon is round and **spherical** in the manner of an apple or a ball. And it is similarly so for the other stars: whereby it can clearly appear that the part of the moon which is toward the sun is illuminated & the other is not, for the light and rays of the sun cannot reach there. And because the moon is spherical, almost half of its surface is toward our sight. And so it is with all spherical things.

¶ Item: the moon, which by its own motion is led through the **zodiac** faster than the sun, is sometimes in **conjunction** <term>conjunction</term> <note>original: "conionction". When two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky as seen from Earth.</note> with the sun, being at the same point of the zodiac. And sometimes the moon is in **opposition** <term>opposition</term> <note>original: "opposition". When two celestial bodies are on opposite sides of the sky (180 degrees apart).</note> / that is when it and the sun are in opposite degrees. And sometimes it is in opposition & conjunction and in other aspects <note>original: "regardz". The geometric angles between planets that were thought to influence earthly events.</note>. I say then that when the moon is in conjunction or near it, then it is as if it were between the sun and us. Then the part of it which is above and toward the sun is illuminated. And the other part is below and toward us and toward our sight, which is not illuminated: and therefore we cannot see the moon when it is in conjunction or near conjunction.

¶ Item: when it is in opposition: then we are as if between the sun and the moon: and then the part of the moon that is toward the sun and which is illuminated is toward our sight & it is seen in full.

¶ Item: when there is a small part of the moon that is toward the sun which is also toward our sight: then the moon appears small: & the more there is, the larger it appears. And it appears first **horned** <note>original: "cornue". This refers to the crescent shape of the moon immediately following a new moon.</note> / & then in other shapes / because it is spherical as was said. # The Heart of Secrets

The line of the **mean movement of the epicycle** is that which proceeds from the center of the world <note>the Earth</note> through the center of the **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a small circle on which a planet moves, while the circle's center itself orbits Earth</term> to the zodiac. The line of the **true place** or of the movement of the planet is that which is drawn from the center of the world through the center of the planet's body to the zodiac. The **mean movement** of the planet or of the epicycle is the arc of the zodiac from the beginning of Aries <note>the vernal equinox point</note> according to the succession of signs <note>the standard counter-clockwise direction</note> up to the line of the mean movement of the planet; however, the **true movement of the epicycle** is counted up to the line of the true movement of the epicycle. And the **true movement of the planet** is counted up to the line of the true movement of the planet. The **mean center** of the planet is the arc of the zodiac from the line of the **altitude** <note>original: "haultesse", referring here to the apogee or highest point of the orbit</note> to the line of the mean movement of the epicycle. The **true center** or the **equation** <term>equation: in medieval astronomy, this is the "correction" value added or subtracted to the mean movement to find the true position</term> is numbered from the line of the altitude to the line of the altitude of the true movement of the epicycle. The **equation of the center** on the zodiac is the arc of the zodiac between the line of the mean movement of the epicycle and the line of its true movement. This is zero at the center of the epicycle when it is at the altitude <note>the apogee</note> of the **deferent** <note>original: "differant", the main orbital circle</note> or at its opposite <note>the perigee</note>; but the equation will be at its greatest at the **mean longitudes**. When the mean center is less than six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, the mean center is greater than the true center. ¶ Similarly, the mean movement of the planet is greater than the true movement of the planet. Therefore, the equation of the center is **subtracted** on the zodiac from the mean center, and likewise from the mean movement of the epicycle, so that the true center and the true movement of the epicycle remain. ¶ But the opposite occurs when the mean center is more than six signs. The **equation of the center** in the epicycle is the arc of the epicycle lying between the mean altitude and the true altitude of that same epicycle. Similarly, this is zero when the center of the epicycle is at the altitude of the deferent or at its opposite, but it is at its greatest at the mean longitude of the deferent.

Whenever a **spherical** <note>original: "spertique"</note> body that is larger illuminates another smaller spherical body, it illuminates more than half of it. Also, the closer these two spherical bodies are to one another, the larger the portion of the smaller body that is illuminated; and all this is demonstrated and proven in the **science of perspective** <note>original: "perspectiue", referring to medieval optics</note>. ¶ Now, it is the case that the **Sun** is marvelously larger than the **Moon**, and they are both spherical bodies; therefore, it follows that the Sun illuminates more than half of the Moon. And because the Moon is closer to the Sun <note>at certain points in its orbit</note>, it follows then that a larger part of it is illuminated than when it is in **opposition** <note>the full moon phase, when the Earth is between the Sun and Moon</note> or at other times. ¶ Item: it follows that the more of the Moon appears illuminated to us, the less of it <note>the total surface</note> is actually illuminated; and the less appears to us, the more is illuminated. ¶ Item: according to perspective, for any spherical object that is larger than the space between our two eyes, one can see only less than half of it. For of such a thing, less than half is turned toward our gaze. Therefore, it follows that even if the Moon were illuminated all the way around, we still could not see more than half of it.

<vocab>zodiac, epicycle, planet, altitude (apogee), equation, longitude, spherical, Sun, Moon, perspective (optics)</vocab>

And because of this, it is impossible for us to see as much of the Moon as is actually illuminated. ¶ Furthermore, if we define "full moon" as being when everything facing our gaze and which can appear to us is illuminated, it can well be a full moon notwithstanding that it is not in [perfect] **opposition** <term>opposition: the astronomical alignment where the Earth is directly between the Sun and the Moon</term>; but it must be close enough to true opposition. Now it appears from what has been said how the Moon is illuminated, and how it neither grows nor shrinks in the manner it appears to grow and shrink <note>The author clarifies that the Moon’s physical size is constant; only the visible portion of its lit side changes from our vantage point.</note>. And concerning the other stars or planets, one should know that even though they are illuminated by the Sun, which is the fountain of light, they do not appear to grow or shrink in light as they approach or move away from the Sun like the Moon does. The reason is: because they are higher up than the Sun; and also, the part of them facing the Sun is illuminated and is simultaneously facing us in our view. And if some planets are below or lower than the Sun, such as **Venus** and **Mercury** according to many, they nevertheless do not appear to grow or shrink in light like the Moon; either because they appear small compared to the Moon, or because they hardly ever distance themselves far from the Sun, or because the light of the Sun enters inside them and they are not opaque or dark bodies as much as the Moon is. Instead, they are **transparent bodies** like crystal, so that the light of the Sun enters deep inside them just like a lamp full of clear oil; and they are not only illuminated on the outside or on the surface as the Moon is. And for this reason, they do not appear with a **horned shape** <note>original: "figure cornue", referring to a crescent</note>, nor do they grow or shrink in light as was said; and perhaps they even shine and have light of their own.

Anyone who has reason within themselves can see clearly that since the Earth is at the center of the **zodiac** <term>zodiac: the circular belt of the heavens where the Sun, Moon, and planets appear to travel</term> and at the center of the **ecliptic line** <term>ecliptic line: the specific path the Sun follows against the background of stars</term> of which I spoke before, it follows that if the Moon and the Sun were both moved exactly upon that ecliptic line, it would be necessary at every **conjunction** <term>conjunction: when the Moon and Sun align on the same side of the Earth</term> of the Moon and the Sun that the Moon be between the Earth and the Sun. And thus, at every conjunction, there would be a solar eclipse; for a solar eclipse is caused by the Moon being positioned between the Earth and the Sun, and between us and the Sun.

¶ Likewise, it would be necessary that at every **opposition** <term>opposition: when the Moon and Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth</term> the Earth would be between the Moon and the Sun, and this is the cause of a lunar eclipse. And so it would follow that at every opposition there would be a lunar eclipse; yet it is not so. And for this reason, one must know—as was said before—that the Sun moves through the middle of the zodiac along the ecliptic line, but the other planets are not on that same line. Instead, they deviate and pull more toward the North <note>original: "septentrion"</note> on one side, and more toward the South <note>original: "midy"</note> on the other side, according to the **latitude** <term>latitude: in this context, the vertical distance of a planet above or below the Sun’s ecliptic path</term> of the zodiac. ¶ And especially

Q iii

I wish to speak and explain regarding the Moon: for she has her own movement along a line that intersects and divides the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the apparent path the Sun follows against the background of stars</term> into two opposite points. And the point where the Moon begins to deviate away from the ecliptic toward the **North** <note>original Middle French: "septētrion"</note> is called the **Dragon’s Head** <note>original Latin: "caput draconis"; the ascending node where the Moon’s path crosses the Sun’s from South to North</note>; and the other point where she begins to deviate away from the ecliptic toward the **South** <note>original Middle French: "midy"</note> is called the **Dragon’s Tail** <note>original Latin: "cauda draconis"; the descending node where the Moon crosses from North to South</note>. This can be shown in a diagram. From these things it is apparent that when there is a **conjunction** <term>conjunction: when the Moon and Sun align on the same side of the Earth, known as a New Moon</term>, if the Moon is not at either of these two points—even though the Sun and the Moon are at the exact same degree or minute of the **zodiac** <term>zodiac: the circular belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs</term> and on the same **meridian** <term>meridian: here referring to a line of celestial longitude</term>—the Moon is nevertheless further in **latitude** <term>latitude: the angular distance of a celestial body North or South of the ecliptic</term> toward the North or the South than the Sun. And thus, she is not positioned directly between the Sun and the Earth, and for this reason, there is no **solar eclipse**. Similarly, when they are in **opposition** <term>opposition: when the Moon and Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth, known as a Full Moon</term> and she is not at or near one of these two aforementioned points, the Earth is not directly between the Moon and the Sun. Therefore, no **lunar eclipse** occurs at that time.

¶ Below, you may see in the figure the two points where the Moon begins to deviate, along with the proper names of these two points.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from leaf 93 regarding the celestial mechanics of the Moon. The moon, insofar as she is by herself a dark body, is illuminated by the sun on her surface: as is said in the eighteenth chapter: wherefore it is necessary that she casts a shadow behind her. And because the moon is smaller than the sun, that shadow proceeds far from the moon and always goes along narrowing in the manner of a **gable** <note>original Middle French: "pignon," referring to the triangular top of a wall</note> or a church steeple/ and that shadow does not extend nor reach as far as the sky on the opposite side. And for this reason, that shadow cannot touch or reach the stars nor eclipse them: that is to say, to cause an eclipse in them: but that shadow extends quite as far as, or further than, the distance between the Earth and the moon. 

And therefore, when it happens that at the hour of the **conjunction** <term>conjunction: when the Moon and Sun align on the same side of the Earth, marking a New Moon</term> the moon is in one of these two points that are called the **Head and Tail of the Dragon** <note>original Latin: "Caput a cauda draconis," referring to the lunar nodes</note> or near them, then her shadow touches and covers some part of the earth/ and then there is an eclipse of the sun in that part of the earth. And just as the shadow of the moon covers a part of the earth at the time of the solar eclipse: so also the moon **hides** <note>original Middle French: "musse," meaning to conceal or stash away</note> the sun in whole or in part/ and covers it with respect to our sight. 

And it should be known that when there is an eclipse of the sun in some place, it is not necessary that it be an eclipse everywhere/ nor that it be as large one time as another/ nor in the same way that it be as large in one place as in another: for in one place the shadow of the moon sometimes covers and **hides** <note>original: "musse"</note>/ or is between a part [of the sun] and us/ and at other times in another place it covers a larger or smaller part according to whether the moon is more or less near these two points mentioned above/ and according to the different **aspects** <note>original Middle French: "regardz," an astrological term for the angular relationship between celestial bodies</note> that the moon has toward different dwellings or different places. And this diversity of aspect can be known through the **theory of the planets** <term>theory of the planets: the medieval study of planetary models and motions, often based on Ptolemaic systems</term>/ and through the tables of astrology/ **theory** is the speculative science of the movements of the circles and the aspects.

### Eclipse of the sun.

<note>The heading "Eclipse of the sun" appears just above the text block, though the text and diagram primarily discuss the lunar eclipse and the Earth's shadow. This may be a printer's error or a general heading for the section on eclipses.</note>

Because the earth is much smaller than the sun, its shadow proceeds behind it and goes on narrowing and tapering <note>original Middle French: "appetissant & en agressissant," describing the conical shape of the shadow</note> just as was said of the shadow of the moon in the preceding chapter. And the point and the end of that shadow is always at the opposite side of the sun / and that point opposite the sun is called the **nadir of the sun** <term>nadir solis: the point on the celestial sphere directly opposite the sun's position</term> / and the shadow of the earth extends as far as the sphere of the moon. And therefore, whenever the moon falls into the **shadow** <note>original: "lorbe," here referring to the orbital path or the volume of the shadow</note> of the earth / and into eclipse, it is necessary that she be beneath the **ecliptic** <term>ecliptic: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky; for an eclipse to occur, the Moon must cross this plane</term> or near it / and thus it is necessary that she be in or near one of the two points mentioned above <note>referring to the "Head and Tail of the Dragon" or lunar nodes mentioned on leaf 93</note>. And because of this, it happens that sometimes part of the moon is eclipsed—sometimes a small amount, sometimes a large amount / sometimes on one side, other times on the other. And sometimes she is entirely eclipsed / sometimes for longer, sometimes for less, according to how she enters fully into the shadow of the earth from one side or the other, either entirely / or partially / and more or less. And it can be seen in this figure here that you see.

Furthermore, one can clearly see from the things said above that when the moon is eclipsed, it lacks light within itself / and the eclipse is of the same magnitude and manner throughout all lands, as much in one place as in another. This is despite the fact that it is seen at one hour in one place / and at another hour in another / and yet within the same movement of time: for when it is sunset in one place, it is night in another place further toward the **East** <note>original French: "Orient"</note>. But to return to the point, the sun during its eclipse has no lack of light within itself: for its brightness lasts forever, perpetually without fail. And therefore, when we say that it is an eclipse of the Sun, we should better say and speak properly that it is an eclipse of the earth. For just as the earth in an eclipse of the moon casts a shadow on the moon / just so the moon in an eclipse of the sun casts a shadow on the earth / except that the earth brings hindrance of light to the moon more often than the moon does to the earth in a certain part, such as at Paris and at Rome. And it happens often that the shadow of the earth covers the whole moon: but the shadow of the moon can never cover the whole earth.

The moon, when it is eclipsed, retains within itself some color in its light. And the cause is because the sun illuminates the sphere of the **four elements** <term>the four elements: in medieval science, these are Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, which occupy the space between the Earth and the Moon</term> which are made of thick or dense matter. For which reason the sphere of fire and the sphere of air receive light from the sun and return or reflect it into the shadow of the earth / and onto the moon at the time of an eclipse. And also the other planets and stars shine upon the moon when it is eclipsed. And similarly, the earth is illuminated at night without the moon for the reasons stated above: except when there is hindrance from clouds / or from the darkness of the weather caused by vapors. Furthermore, the moon at the time of an eclipse appears of one color at one time / and at another time of another. And I **believe** <note>original: "cuyde"</note> that the cause is the light it receives from the planets and the stars and from the reflection of the air as has been said. This light is sometimes of one manner and sometimes of another / according to the various **aspects** <term>regardz: the relative angular positions of celestial bodies which were thought to influence their effects</term> that the moon has toward the other stars at different times: and according to the reflection caused by the air or by certain vapors / according to this, it is sometimes of one color and sometimes of another. And it also changes color according to whether it is more or less deep within the shadow of the earth.

Likewise, an eclipse, to speak properly, is a deficiency of light / and thus the moon is sometimes eclipsed / and the other [the sun] is also partially eclipsed / when we say there is an eclipse of the sun / and no other planet or star can be eclipsed, as was stated in the 45th chapter. But an eclipse can be understood differently in regards to us / for a thing is eclipsed when another thing is between us and it, which prevents us from seeing it and causes it to be eclipsed as far as we are concerned / and in this manner the moon can eclipse the sun / and it also sometimes eclipses another planet / or one or several stars. And in this manner, one planet can eclipse another planet or star which is above it / and in a higher heaven: But this is not properly called an eclipse <note>The author distinguishes between a "true" eclipse (loss of light, like the moon in Earth's shadow) and an "occultation" (one object blocking another from view).</note>.

I wish to make an end here / for I do not wish to speak here of epicycles <note>small circles followed by planets while moving along a larger circle</note> nor of the eccentrics of the planets <note>circles where the center is not the Earth</note> nor of difficult matters / because it would be too long a thing / and would not be easily treated sufficiently in French / and it seems to me that it is better to remain silent about them than to speak of them without showing the causes and the reasoning / and why such things were discovered and the possibility or the manner in which they can be. Likewise, my purpose was not to enter further into such subtleties / nor to provide astrology in French. Rather, I only intended to explain roughly the general disposition of the sphere of the world <note>the universe or celestial sphere</note> / and that which is honorable for every man to know, and especially for a prince of noble mind <note>original: "noble engin," meaning high intelligence or character</note>, except that he has nothing to do in the heavens that pertains to his office or status / and to the government of the public wealth <note>original: "chose publique," the commonwealth or state</note>. And if he wished to delve deeper into the speculative study of movements, it would be a matter of curiosity for him: and something in which he should not place his intent. And if he affectionately desired to know or inquire regarding the practice of the judgments of fortunes <note>judicial astrology or horoscopes used to predict the future</note> / it would be an uncertain thing, irrelevant to him / and perilous before God and the world / and he would put himself in danger of losing soul and body and goods and honor / just as I have more fully declared and proved in a small book in French that I made for this purpose and on this matter.

Likewise, I have spoken in this treatise in some places at great length / and have been wordy so that everyone of good understanding might easily understand what I have said / and without need for commentators. And furthermore, for this reason, I have made here at the end a table of strange words which are in this treatise / in which table I mark the chapters where such words are explained, and I have put them in order so that one can have recourse to easily find the chapter where such a word was previously explained: for every word is explained by definition in the chapter where it is first found.

The second aspect is called the **quartile aspect** <note>original: "quart regard"; an aspect of 90 degrees, often considered challenging in astrology</note>, which is the one that looks at the fourth sign ahead of itself and the fourth sign near itself; for instance, **Aries** will look at its planet that is in **Cancer** ahead of it and **Capricorn** behind it. The third aspect is called the **trine aspect** <note>original: "trine regard"; an aspect of 120 degrees, traditionally considered harmonious</note>; for example, **Cancer** looks at the planet that is in **Scorpio** ahead of it and **Pisces** behind it. The fourth aspect is called the **opposition** <note>original: "opposite regard"; an aspect of 180 degrees</note>, such as between **Aries** and **Libra**. The other aspect is called **mean or true conjunction**. The **mean conjunction** of the planets occurs when the lines of their mean motions are joined in the zodiac according to longitude. And the **true conjunction** occurs when the lines of their true motions coincide in the manner aforementioned.

# The Heart of Secrets
a

### The Heart of Secrets

On the first day, God created the heavens, the angels, the earth, the air, and the water out of nothing. On that same day, a light was created from nothing, which was like a bright and shining cloud; it illuminated the earth and circled all around, just as the sun does now, and it made day before the sun was formed on the fourth day. The heaven I spoke of is up there, above the firmament; no man can see it, and it is made of fire. And the angels are there, who also have the nature of fire. And when God wishes to send any of them to the world to announce something to men, they take the form and likeness of a man. And from what do they take this? Not from earth, but from air; and in that form they appear to men and speak to them. We read that the angels ate with Abraham <note>Referring to Genesis 18, where three visitors—often interpreted as angels or the Trinity—visit Abraham</note>. If you ask what became of the food, it became nothing while being eaten, just as water diminishes and becomes nothing when it boils in a pot over the fire. For as I say, the angels are of the nature of fire. If you ask what becomes of the forms in which they appear when they have delivered their message, they return to their first nature and become air, just as a ring loses its shape in the fire and becomes the gold or silver it was before. Thus it was with the dove in which the Holy Spirit appeared at the baptism of Jesus Christ. The Holy Spirit formed it from air for his service, and afterward, it became air again. In that baptism, the entire Trinity appeared: the Father in his voice, which said, "This is my beloved son" <note>original: "Cestuy est mon filz ayme"</note>; the Son appeared there in human form; and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, which is simple and has no gall <note>Medieval natural history believed the dove lacked a gallbladder, making it a symbol of purity and a lack of bitterness or malice</note>. 

On the second day, God formed the firmament and all the stars that are fixed within it, and he placed it between the waters that are above and the waters that are below. On the third day, God gathered the waters from below, which were spread over the earth like a bright cloud, and he called that gathering of waters the Sea. On that same day, God made the earth sprout and bring forth trees and herbs. On the fourth day, he made the sun and the moon from the light that was created on the first day. On the fifth day, he made the fish and the birds, and he made them from water. On the sixth day, he made the beasts and man, all from earth, except that the soul of man was created from nothing. When man was formed in the gardens of Damascus <note>A common medieval tradition held that Adam was created in the "Field of Damascus" before being placed in Eden</note>, God placed him in the Earthly Paradise, which he had planted by his simple word. For he spoke, and it was done. On the seventh day, God rested. Was he tired from working? Not at all; his rest was nothing other than that he ceased creating new creatures. For he has not since made anything of which he had not already created some likeness.

The world is a single entity composed of heaven, earth, and the four elements, and it is round. The first element is fire, from which all the stars of heaven shine. Air is the second element, through which all living things here below breathe <note>The original French "aspirement" refers to the act of drawing breath or inspiration.</note>. Water is the third element, which surrounds, pierces through, waters, and provides for all the earth. Earth is the fourth element, which is in the middle of the firmament, and it can there be entirely surrounded by water and air.

The form of the world can be seen in an egg. The yolk <note>original: "moeuf"</note> is the earth; the egg-white <note>original: "aubin"</note> is the white that surrounds the yolk, which is like the air around the earth; the shell <note>original: "escaille"</note> which is on the outside is the firmament, which encloses everything—both air and earth.

The word "World" <term>monde: Derived from the Latin "mundus," which means both "the universe" and "clean" or "neat."</term> sounds the same as a "clean thing": and it is so named for its noble adornment. Fire is hot and dry. Air is hot and moist. Water is cold and moist. Earth is cold and dry. From these four elements comes the constitution <term>complexion: In medieval medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four humors within an individual's body.</term> of man; bile <term>cole: Also known as choler or yellow bile, the humor associated with a fiery temperament.</term> takes the place of fire,

...blood in place of air, phlegm in place of water, and melancholy in place of earth. And these four things follow the nature of the four elements, as has been stated previously. 

The firmament is round and is made of water hardened and solidified more than crystal, and it always rotates from east to west so swiftly that if the sun and the moon and five other great stars that are called planets did not run against it to temper its speed, it would collapse <note>The original "tresbuscheroit" implies a stumbling or falling, suggesting the cosmic order would break without the balancing motion of the planets.</note>. For the philosophers observed this long ago in Egypt, where it never rains and where one can best perceive these things because of the clarity of the air. 

Right here one can see seven stars fixed in the firmament that people call "The Chariot" <note>The OCR reads "le chat" (the cat), but this is a common transcription error for "le char" (the chariot), referring to the Big Dipper or Ursa Major.</note>; they always turn in the same manner because they are fixed there. And whoever watches them in the evening and morning can clearly perceive how they turn. These seven stars are only seen for fifteen days a year by those who are in Judea because they are situated lower than we are; but we can see them every day of the year. Wise men call these seven stars one of the hinges <term>charnieres: In medieval cosmology, the poles or pivot points around which the celestial sphere was believed to rotate.</term> upon which the firmament turns; for the other hinge is below, so that no man ever sees it. 

Above the firmament is a heaven that is entirely made of fire; in this heaven are the angels and the sovereign virtues. God made it on the first day, perfectly round. Waters formed like crystal are between this [fiery] heaven and the firmament; for otherwise the great heat of that heaven would burn both the firmament and the four elements below it. The fact that the firmament rotates continually also helps, for because of its movement, the fire cannot harm it as easily. Regarding these waters, God said: "Let there be a firmament, and let it divide the waters from the waters" <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis 1:6.</note>. 

The world has five zones <note>original: "environnemēs," referring to the five climate zones: the torrid, two temperate, and two frigid.</note>: of which one is hot and two are cold, and the other two are in between, caught between heat and cold, so that one can inhabit them in this form and likeness.

The world has four parts: East, West, South <note>original: "Midy," literally "Midday."</note>, and North <note>original: "Septentrion," the traditional name for the North based on the seven stars of the Great Bear.</note>. All the stars are fixed in the firmament, except for the sun and the moon and five other great stars. One is named Saturn, the other Jupiter, the other Mars, the other Venus, and the other Mercury. The stars receive their light from the brightness of the sun and turn with the firmament. As for the sparks that sometimes appear in the air like stars <note>A reference to meteors or "shooting stars."</note>, this happens from some movement of the air; for truly they are not stars, for no star...

Saturn <note>original: "Saturnus"</note> has a white color; Jupiter is bright; Mars is red like fire; Venus has a joyful and resplendent color; Mercury a radiant color; the Moon is blue; the Sun is burning in the morning and afterward becomes brighter as the day grows. The Moon is significantly larger than the earth, which is why it happens that it seems to be of a great size in all lands. The Sun is eight times larger than the moon, and according to how it varies its course, it divides the days, the months, the seasons, and the years, and tempers the air according to the time, both by approaching and by moving away; for if it always remained in one place, one part of the world would perish from cold and the other from heat. The Moon does not grow or diminish of its own accord, but because the Sun gives it brightness according to how near it is to it, it is brighter on that side where the sun's ray touches it, and on the other side less bright according to how much less the sun touches it. On the night that the moon is last and first <note>The transition night between the old lunar cycle and the new one.</note>, it will never be seen in any of the signs except the Ram <note>Aries.</note>.

**A**n eclipse is the failure <note>original: "deffaultre" (default), used here to describe the temporary loss or obscuring of celestial light.</note> of the Sun and of the Moon when the Sun is secluded and darkened to us because of the Moon which places itself between the Earth and it; or the Moon similarly when it goes so low that some part of the Earth is between us and its brightness. The eclipse of the Sun never occurs except at the time of the old moon and the new <note>original: "en la derniere Lune & en la premiere," referring to the end of one lunar cycle and the start of the next (the New Moon phase).</note>, during the conjunction <term>conjunction: An astronomical event where two celestial bodies appear in the same area of the sky as seen from Earth.</term> of it and the Sun. The eclipse of the Moon only happens when it is full. And if the Earth were larger than the Moon, the eclipse of the Sun would not be seen across the whole Earth at once; but because the Moon is larger than the Earth <note>The author incorrectly asserts that the Moon is larger than the Earth. While we now know the Earth is much larger, this claim was used in some medieval texts to explain why the Moon could block the Sun’s light so effectively.</note>, it happens that it can withdraw the brightness of the Sun from the whole world when it places itself between the Sun and the Earth. This failure of the Sun and the Moon which occurs in this manner, which is called an eclipse, happens every year on certain days and at certain hours, either below the Earth or above. An eclipse is a deficit of the sun and the Moon when the Sun is hidden and obscured from us by the Moon, which places itself between the earth and the sun; or the Moon similarly when it goes so low that some part of the earth is between us and its brightness <note>A description of the Earth's shadow causing a lunar eclipse.</note>. An eclipse of the sun never happens except during the time of the "last moon" and the "first moon" <note>The New Moon phase, when the Moon is in conjunction with the Sun.</note> at the conjunction of the moon and the sun. An eclipse of the moon only happens when it is full. If the earth were larger than the moon, the eclipse of the sun would not be seen across the whole earth at once; but because the moon is larger than the earth <note>As noted on the previous page, this is a common medieval scientific error; the Earth is actually much larger than the Moon. The author uses this logic to explain how the Moon's shadow could cover the world.</note>, it happens that it can take away the brightness of the sun from all the world when it places itself between the sun and the earth. This deficit of the sun and the moon which is created in this manner, which we call an eclipse, happens every year on certain days and at certain hours, either below the earth or above. -># The Heart of Secrets.<-

...that which is named Olympus <note>Mount Olympus was often cited in medieval texts as being so high that its summit reached above the wind and clouds.</note>. For sometimes letters have been written in the sand at the summit and were found entirely intact at the end of the year; and those who climbed there carried water in vials near their mouths and noses, otherwise they could not breathe because of the thinness of the air. Wind is nothing other than air moved and driven little by little until it becomes a great blast of Wind. Just as God has ordained it, and to cause fruits to fall quickly by tempering the heat. It can be proven well enough with a small bellows that wind is nothing other than air moved; move the bellows and you will feel the Wind. There are twelve Winds, of which four are principal, coming directly from the four parts of the world; each of these four has two others, one to the right and the other to the left. The first of the four is the Northwest Wind <note>original: "Galerne," a traditional name for the moist, cold wind from the northwest.</note>, the second is the East Wind <note>original: "Solerne," likely referring to the solar or rising sun direction.</note>, the third is the Rainy Wind <note>original: "Pluiol," associated with the rainy South wind.</note>, and the fourth is the West Wind <note>original: "flauonies," from the Latin *Favonius*, the gentle west wind.</note>. The names of the others are not much used in French, except for the North Wind <note>original: "bise," the cold, dry wind from the north or northeast.</note>.

### On thunder and lightning bolts.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' with floral and foliate patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>

Thunder comes from the fact that winds sometimes get inside the clouds. And when they break out of the clouds by force, they make that crash <note>original: "escrois"</note> that we call thunder; this can easily be seen with a bladder <note>original: "vessie"</note>, for when it is full of air and the air is forced out by squeezing it, it gives off its sound or crash. And also when a man forces air out of his body <note>A common, if crude, medieval analogy comparing thunder to flatulence.</note>, lightning bolts can be born in two ways: either from the clouds clashing together, which strikes fire like stones do; especially at the hour when the thunder happens; or from the meeting of the winds. For fire naturally strikes out from all things that clash together too harshly: and one perceives the flash sooner than the sound, even though both happen together. Some say that thunder is born sometimes from the battle of fire and water that the air attracts to itself from above and below; and when the fire comes, the fruits of the earth are spoiled, but when the water comes, they are improved. The fire of lightning is more piercing than our fire, for it is of a more subtle element. It does not fall as often in winter or summer as it does in Spring <note>original: "Ver"</note> and Autumn. Why? Because the air is cold in winter, so it more easily resists the fire; and in summer, those hot mists <note>original: "niellees," often referring to blights or thick mists.</note> are not made in the air, for they are all thickened into clouds, and without those clouds, thunder does not often happen.

### On the rainbow and rains.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' with floral and foliate patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>

When the sun casts itself against a dense <note>original: "chiesne," likely meaning thick or hoary.</note> cloud, following the shape of the cloud which is round and hollowed—that is to say, concave—then the rainbow appears. And it is of four colors according to the four elements: fire gives it the red color; water, purple; air, blue; and earth, green. Rain is born in this manner: the air raises thin vapors <note>original: "fumees," literally "smokes."</note> from the sea and the earth; as these vapors are light and thin, they run through the air. And when they gather together in such a great cloud that the air can no longer support them, they fall and drop down here below, just as the wind drives them down or the force of the sun. Those waters that come from the sea, when they have traveled somewhat through the air, they are sweetened <note>original: "adoulcies," meaning the salt is removed through the atmospheric process.</note>...

# On Philosophy. Folio 101.

...[drops] fall upon the plants of the earth to give nourishment to the plants growing there; and those waters that come from the earth fall back into the sea.

### On hailstones and snows, and signs, and storms.

Hailstones are nothing other than raindrops frozen in the air by the force of a cold wind; they dissolve and melt sooner than snow. Hail falls more often by day than by night. When the mist or vapor of the waters has not yet thickened into drops, and the cold catches it, it becomes snow. It never snows on the high seas. When the sun rises, if it is hidden beneath a cloud, it is a sign of rain. If it glows red, it brings clear weather; if it is pale, a storm. If it appears hollow or concave, so that its rays extend toward the North Wind <note>original: "bise"</note> and toward the South Wind <note>original: "pluiol"</note>, it signifies a moist storm full of wind. If it is pale and sets within a black cloud, it brings a swift wind from the north named *aquilo* <note>original Latin: "aquilo," the North wind</note>. If the sky glows red in the evening, it is a sign of a clear day tomorrow; if it glows red in the morning, it is a storm. If it glows red toward the North, it is a brilliance at the "solar window" <note>likely referring to a break in the clouds or a parhelion</note>, which signifies a storm; if toward the South, it signifies heat. When the moon is four days old, if it is red like gold, it signifies wind. Similarly, on the fourth day, if there are black spots at the tip of the upper horn, it means rain at the beginning of the month. If these spots appear during a full moon, it is a sign of clear weather. When one rows <note>original: "naige," meaning to navigate or row a boat</note> at night, if the water sparks against the oars, there will be a storm. And when the porpoises <note>original: "tumbareux," literally "tumblers," referring to dolphins or porpoises leaping from the water</note> appear, the wind will come from the direction where they are leaping.

### Where pestilence is born.

Because of the sins of the people, the air sometimes becomes corrupted; this happens through an imbalance <note>original: "destrempement," an improper mixing or lack of moderation</note> of heat, or of dryness, or of rain. This corruption is called pestilence, for when one receives this corrupted air, either by breathing it in or by eating, one dies from it.

### Why the sea does not grow from any fresh waters, and why these waters are salty.

The sea would overflow were it not that the saltiness consumes and wastes the fresh water that falls into the sea, or because the wind and the sun dry it out. It may also be that the fresh waters return to their proper sources <note>original: "droitz"</note> through underground conduits, resting places, and hidden passages. The waters of the sea could be sweetened by the rivers and rains that fall into them, if the sun and the winds—as we have already said—did not drive away the fresh waters.

### On the Red Sea and the river that waters Egypt.

The Red Sea is one hundred and fifteen feet <note>In medieval geography, these distances were often symbolic or copied from older, misunderstood sources</note> away from the Egyptian Sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>. It is not naturally red, but rather it is red because of the sand on its shores, which is vermilion; this sand mixes with the water and makes it red. There, one can find cinnabar <note>original: "sinopre," a red mineral pigment</note> and gemstones in marvelous abundance <note>original: "plante"</note>.
