# The Heart of Secrets

In Egypt, where it never rains <note>Medieval scholars often believed Egypt experienced no rainfall, relying entirely on the river for water.</note>, there is a river named the Nile. When it is windy in May, gravel accumulates in the place where the river flows into the sea. Then, the river backs up because of the high mounds of gravel and sand it encounters, and it spreads throughout Egypt, watering the seeds of the earth. And when the wind ceases and the sand is no longer dispersed, the river returns to its channel.

<image-desc>A woodcut T-O map (mappa mundi) enclosed in a square frame. The circular world is surrounded by an outer ring representing the ocean. The interior is divided into three sections by a T-shaped body of water. The top section is labeled "Asia" and features a large castle with multiple towers. The bottom left section is labeled "Africa" and shows a smaller castle on a hill. The bottom right section is labeled "Europe" and depicts rolling hills. The orientation places East at the top.</image-desc>

An <term>earthquake</term> <note>original: "Terremote"</note> comes from the wind, especially across the sea where the earth is filled with openings and caverns within. For when the wind is trapped in these caverns and is so powerful that the earth breaks apart, the settling that follows causes a rupture. It then seems to those who are there that all the earth is being moved, and sometimes churches and houses fall down. The circle of the earth is surrounded by the sea and is divided into three parts, namely:

### On Philosophy. Folio Cii.

...in Europe, Asia, and Africa. Europe extends from the West to the North. And Asia extends from the North to the South through the East. And Africa extends from the South to the West. But Asia alone contains as much land as the other two parts combined. <note>This reflects the medieval T-O map worldview, where Asia occupied the entire top half of the circle of the world.</note>

Here ends the ordering of the world. And here begins the arrangement of the <term>Compost</term> <note>original: "compost." This refers to the "computus," the medieval science of calculating time and the dates of moveable church feasts like Easter.</note> and the Calendar, and the names of those who created it: such as Master Simon of Compiegne, who was a monk of Saint-Riquier in Ponthieu, who translated it from Latin into French, following the work of Master Aignan <note>Likely referring to Anianus, a 13th-century author famous for a mnemonic poem used to teach calendar calculation.</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the general introduction of the "Compost" to a historical and technical explanation of the calendar's origins, moving from the legendary founders of Rome to the medieval scholars who refined the system.</meta>

<header>The Heart of Secrets</header>

Romulus, a prince who founded Rome, was the first among those who knew Latin to treat the <term>compost</term> <note>original: "compost"; the medieval science of timekeeping and calendar calculation</note> and the calendar. He established his year of ten months and decreed that the year should begin in the month of March, which he named as such because he believed himself to be the son of a man named Mars, who was believed to be the god of battle according to the folly of the pagans. Numa Pompilius, another prince who came after him, added these two months: January and February. Romulus established the year of ten months for two reasons: either because every woman carries her child for nine months and delivers in the tenth, or because every woman remained in her home in black clothing, in sadness and in widowhood, for ten full months after the death of her lord, after which she could remarry. For after ten months, it was well known that she was not pregnant by her first lord. Julius Caesar, the first Emperor of Rome, who was very learned in reading, discovered the <term>bissextile day</term> <note>The leap day added every four years</note> long afterward and gave it a certain place in the calendar; he also found a number that extends from one to nineteen to know when the moon is new. This number is called the <term>Golden Number</term>, either for the value it has in itself or because the Romans used to write it in letters of gold. But now it is written in many colors in all calendars, and it is the first number one finds on the left in each month throughout the calendar. And if anyone wishes to know the reason why Numa Pompilius added two months to the year of Romulus and began his month in January, it is as we have said: because he had found in many books that the sun then begins to climb and the days to lengthen. And because the firmament is divided into twelve signs <note>The Zodiac</note>, and the sun cannot circle these twelve signs in less than 365 days and six hours—that is to say, in no less than 12 months. After the coming of Jesus Christ, Dionysius <note>Dionysius Exiguus, the 6th-century monk who started the Anno Domini dating system</note>, an abbot of Rome, was the first to treat the compost and the calendar and made a table of five hundred and thirty-two years. After him, Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk</note> added many things. And then an abbot named Helpetin <note>Likely Helperic of Auxerre, a 9th-century author on the computus</note>; these two were English. Afterward, Gerland <note>Gerlandus of Besançon, an 11th-century scholar</note>, a man from Lorraine, and many other good clerks spoke of these quantities. We shall set down here the summary of the benefits.

### Why the year is so named and into how many parts it is divided.

The year is called <term>air</term> <note>original: "air"; likely a play on the Latin word "annus" (year) and "annulus" (ring)</note> because it goes around like a ring. And because of this, when the Romans wished to depict it in ancient times, they painted a serpent holding its tail in its mouth in a circle <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of eternity and the cyclical nature of time</note>. The year is divided into four seasons. The four seasons contain twelve months; a month contains four weeks and a little more. The week has seven natural days; the day has four <term>quadrants</term> <note>A six-hour period</note>; the quadrant has six hours; the hour has four <term>points</term>; the point has ten <term>moments</term>; the moment has twelve <term>ounces</term>; an ounce has forty-seven <term>minutes</term>, which are so small they cannot be divided. Because of this, the Greek calls them <term>Athomos</term> <note>original: "Athomos"; meaning an "atom," the smallest possible unit of time in medieval science</note>: that is to say, a thing without division, for it cannot be divided further due to its smallness.

S i

### ¶ On the kinds of days.

There are two kinds of days: one is called the **natural day** of twenty-four hours, which includes both day and night. The other is called the **usable or artificial day**: this is the day without the night. Regarding these days, the wise Egyptians established what we call <term>avoided days</term> <note>original: "iours deuez"; traditionally unlucky or "perilous" days in the medieval calendar</note> or perilous days, while others are not. The **Egyptian days** are those on which God sent plagues upon Egypt; there were several of these among the ten famous ones with which the Egyptians were struck, according to the testimony of **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note>; but **Moses** speaks only of ten, because those were the greatest. Holy Church announces these avoided days in the **Calendars**, not because she believes that anyone must stop **bloodletting** <note>original: "seigner"; the common medieval medical practice of phlebotomy</note> or doing anything else on these days more than others, but solely for the remembrance of God's miracles. Each month contains two of these days, one toward the beginning and the other toward the end. Each of these days is called "Egyptian" for a single hour. We shall demonstrate hereafter both the Egyptian days and hours for each month, for we are writing the twelve months in order. And at the tail of each month there will be four numbers. The first two numbers will show the Egyptian day and hour that falls at the beginning of the month. The [latter] two numbers will show the Egyptian day and hour that falls toward the end of the month.

### ¶ How the days of each month are named.

One must know that every day is named either for the <term>Kalends</term>, the <term>Nones</term>, or the <term>Ides</term> <note>The three marker days in the ancient Roman calendar from which all other days were counted backward</note>. The first day of every month is always called the **Kalends**. And the days that fall at the end of each month are named after the Kalends of the month that follows, in this manner: "Four [days before the] Kalends of February," or "Three [days before the] Kalends of February." If it is the fourth day, the third day, or another day at the end of January, you shall say it thus: the fourth day before the Kalends of February.

-># The Collection of Secrets<-

on the third day or any other day toward the end of the month. In this manner, one describes the others. And if one were making a charter or other authentic letter on the fourth or third day toward the end of January, one would write the day in the manner we have written above: namely, <term>four Kalends</term> or <term>three Kalends</term> <note>The Roman system counted backwards from fixed points. "Four Kalends of February" would be January 29th, counting January 29, 30, 31, and February 1 inclusively.</note> or otherwise, according to whether the day of writing is closer or further from the end of the month. The fifth day or the seventh day, which are at the head of the month, are called the **Nones** of that same month to which they belong; and all the other days that fall between the **Kalends**—that is to say, from the first day of the month until the Nones (meaning until the fifth or seventh day)—are named after the Nones in this form: "four Nones," "three Nones." The thirteenth or the fifteenth day of the month is called the **Ides**, and all the days from the Nones until the Ides are named after the Ides in this form: "four Ides," "three Ides," which is to say the fourth day or the third day before the Ides.

**Kalendes** <note>Kalends</note> signifies the same as "calls" or "summons"; for this word <term>Kalon</term> <note>original: "Kalon"; from the Greek *kalein* (καλεῖν), meaning "to call"</note> spoken in Greek means the same in French as "call." For formerly, on the first day of each month, the priest would climb to a high place in his temple and cry out with a loud voice, "Kalon!" as many times as there were days to come from the Kalends until the Nones. This was because at that time—namely, on the day of the Nones—the **fairs** <note>original: "foires"; these were market days and public gatherings</note> began, and they were announced to the Romans just as the feasts of the saints are announced in the church. And the first day of each month is not named "Kalende" in the singular, but "Kalendes" in the plural, because the priest cried "Kalon, Kalon!" many times. And he called the people to the fair; likewise, the ancients honored the beginnings of the months and made a feast of them. For this reason, the first days of the months can be called Kalendes, as "Kalende" can sound like and be said to mean "cultivation" or "observance."

**Nones** mean and signify the same as "fair." And for this reason, the fairs are named <term>nundine</term> <note>original: "nundine"; from the Latin *nundinae*, the market day held every ninth day</note> in Latin, for the Romans call them Nones. On such a day in the calendar the fairs begin; or one may call the Nones thus because that day is the **ninth day before the Ides**. **Ides** sound like and signify "departures" or "divisions," for on such days the fairs were dissolved and the people departed.

If one asks why some months have only four days before the Nones and others have seven, two answers can be given. Either because the Romans held a double feast in some months and could not go to the fairs as early as they did in others when they had only a simple feast at the start of the month—and therefore, during double feasts, the Nones were further from the beginning of the month—or because **thieves** would lie in wait for merchants as they went to the fairs to rob them. It was not desired that they should be certain of the day of the fairs, and so the Nones were placed differently in the months, some closer and others further from the start. We shall set down hereafter how many Nones, how many Ides, how many Kalendes, and how many days each month has.

"Month" <note>original: "Moys"</note> can sound like or be said to mean "measure" <note>original: "mesure"</note>: because the year is measured into twelve months, or because <term>Moyse</term> <note>original: "Moyse"; a Middle French derivation from the Latin *mensa* (table)</note> and "table" are one and the same. The year is a measure and is divided into twelve months because a circle of the firmament which is named the **Zodiac** is divided into twelve signs, which the sun passes through and circles in three hundred sixty-five days and six hours; this is within the space of twelve months: for after so many days the sun returns to that same point from which it departed at the...

The Hebrews begin their year in March / and the reason why is: because spring begins to be born / that is to say the springtime which begins in March and at this time all things renew / that is to say that all types of trees and flowers begin to turn green again. ...the solar cycle is the calculation of the sun's course by whole years / by weeks & days. This number—that is to say, 28—by which the dominical letters, the ferial numbers, and the leap years <term>leap year; original: "bissexte"</term> follow their sequence, is called the solar cycle. These are located at the joints of the four fingers / which, when all are taken together, make 28 joints. And the first joint of the first finger / that is to say the index finger where "f" is placed, is on the inside part of the hand / And the part of the joint in which "d" is placed is also inside, at the thick root of the said finger. And two letters are always placed on the little finger to denote the leap year, which is positioned according to this verse: **Be a son of God; accept the good heaven freely.** <note>original: "filius esto dei celum bonus accipe gratis." This is a mnemonic where the first letter of each word (F, E, D, C, B, A, G) represents the Dominical letters in descending order to help track the leap year cycle.</note>

### ¶ How one can know without looking at the Calendar on which day each month begins.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>To know on which day each month begins, two numbers must be known. One is named the "regular," because it guides a person straight like a ruler and never fails. The other is named the "concurrent," because it "runs with" the regulars. To show on which day the months begin, we shall speak hereafter: but first we will note the number of the regulars and the concurrents.

### ¶ How many regulars each month has.

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| March | **V.** | September | **vii.** |
| April | **i.** | October | **ii.** |
| May | **iii.** | November | **V.** |
| June | **vi.** | December | **vii.** |
| July | **i.** | January | **iii.** |
| August | **iiii.** | February | **vi.** |

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' with floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>We have written March at the beginning: for these regulars begin there / nor will they ever change until the end of the world. But the concurrents change every year: for when Sunday runs by **A**, the concurrent is **vi.**; when it runs by **B**, the concurrent is **v.**; when Sunday runs by **C**, the concurrent is **iiii.**; when it runs by **D**, the concurrent is **iii.**; when it runs by **E**, the concurrent is **ii.**; when it runs by **F**, the concurrent is **i.**; when it runs by **G**, it is **vii.** And this will never fail. But to demonstrate it more easily, we have noted a small table here. <note>In medieval time-keeping, adding the "Regular" number of a month to the "Concurrent" number of the year allowed one to calculate the day of the week for the first of that month.</note>

The cycle of the sun <note>original: "cile du soleil" is likely an OCR error or variant for "cercle du soleil."</note> is the calculation of the sun’s course by whole years / by weeks and days. This number—namely twenty-eight—by which follow the Dominical letters, the ferial letters, and the leap year, is called the solar cycle <term>Solar Cycle; a 28-year cycle after which the days of the week return to the same days of the month</term> / and they are located at the joints of the four fingers / which, all taken together, make twenty-eight joints. And the first joint of the first finger / namely the index where **F** is placed, is on the inside part of the hand / And the part of the joint in which **D** is placed is also inside, at the thick base of the said finger. And always on the little finger, two letters are placed to denote the leap year <term>bissexte; the extra day added during a leap year</term>, which is situated by this verse: **Son, be of God, receive heaven freely as a good man.** <note>original Latin: "filius esto dei celum bonus accipe gratis." This is a mnemonic where the first letter of each word (F, E, D, C, B, A, G) represents the Dominical letters in descending order.</note>

**Leaf C. viii.**

# Of Philosophy

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>This table written here above has twenty-eight points in length and seven in width; it has twenty-eight points in length because there is a cycle that extends to twenty-eight years and is named the solar cycle <term>Solar Cycle; a 28-year cycle after which the days of the week return to the same calendar dates</term>. This means that once the count has gone from one to twenty-eight, it returns again to one. And because it always goes around from one to twenty-eight, and from twenty-eight returns to one, it is called a cycle. It is called "solar" because the leap year <term>bissexte; the extra day added to the calendar in a leap year</term>, the concurrents <term>concurrents; numbers from 1 to 7 used to find the day of the week for March 1st</term>, and the letters for Sunday <note>Known as Dominical Letters, these were used to track which day of the week every date in the year would fall on</note> and the other days that the sun brings forth all occur within it.

Look above at the head of the table and you will find written in English <note>original: "francois" (French)</note> all the things contained therein, in their proper order. If you wish to know the letter by which Sunday runs, along with the concurrent and the leap year: look first to see which year of the solar cycle you are in, whether the first, the second, or another. If you are in the first year, look for a number on the left side of the table, searching downwards; where you find "1" written, that is the number showing the first year of the solar cycle. The number "2" shows the second year, and so on for the other numbers in order. 

When you have found in this manner which year of the solar cycle you are in, look across horizontally from the number showing that year, and you will immediately see the letters that show Sunday and the other days, the concurrents of the year, and the leap years. But before you search in the table, you must first know which year of the solar cycle you are currently in. If you are in doubt, take the years of the Incarnation <note>The "years of the Incarnation" refers to the current year A.D.</note> and add nine to them. This is because nine years of the cycle had already passed when Jesus Christ took incarnation. 

Divide that total sum of years by twenty-eight as many times as you can. For example, twelve hundred and sixty <note>1260 is a useful landmark because it is a perfect multiple of 28 (28 x 45)</note> can be divided equally by twenty-eight. If one remains after the division, it will be the first year of the cycle. If two remain, it will be the second year, and so on for the others up to twenty-eight. If nothing remains beyond twenty-eight, it is the twenty-eighth year. Then, according to this result, look for the number on the left side of the table, and it will show you beside it the days and the concurrents.

<vocab>cercle solaire, bissepte, concurrens, dimanche, lincarnation, Jesuchrist, tablette</vocab>

<term>Manus sinistra</term>: Latin for "left hand." In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, the left hand was often associated with more "passive" or "hidden" knowledge compared to the active right hand.

<term>Chiromancy</term>: The practice of reading the lines and mounts of the palm. While this diagram uses the hand for memory, the choice of the hand as a canvas is rooted in the belief that the body reflects the structure of the universe.

<term>Griffin</term>: A mythical creature with the body of a lion and the head of an eagle, often symbolizing strength, watchfulness, or the dual nature of Christ (human and divine).

...a certain instrument called an <term>astrolabe</term> <note>A handheld astronomical instrument used by navigators and astronomers to tell time and determine the position of celestial bodies.</note> and found that the sun made its course in the first year, and he found it at the first point, proceeding in this manner until twenty-eight years and twenty points. <note>The "twenty points" likely refers to the fractional hours (approximately 6 hours per year) that accumulate over the 28-year cycle.</note> And then he said that the sun went no further, but returned to its first point. A scholar who calculates the dates of the calendar and movable feasts.</note> among the Latins, and began his year in March.

### How the regulars and the concurrents teach on which day each month begins.

If you wish to know the beginning of each month, join together the concurrents of the year and the regulars of the months; and if the concurrents and the regulars joined together fall within seven, in such a number as they fall, on that day of the week shall enter the month you seek. If the concurrents and the regulars joined together exceed seven, cast out the seven, and by such a day of the week as the number that remains above seven, the month shall begin. Now let us take an example. March has five regulars, as is written hereafter. Now, let the concurrent be one; join five to one and that makes six. On the sixth day of the week, March shall therefore enter: that is, on Friday; for Sunday is the first day of the week. Similarly, April has one regular; if the concurrent is one, add one with one together and they will be two. On the second day of the week April shall therefore enter; that is, on Monday. If the concurrent is five, put together the five regulars of March and five concurrents, which makes ten; take away seven and three will remain. On the third day of the week March shall therefore enter: that is, on Tuesday. If the concurrent is seven [and you add] six to five, that makes eleven; take away the seven and four will remain. On the fourth day of the week March shall therefore enter: that is, on Wednesday. In this manner, do for the other months and take care that if the number exceeds seven when you have put together the concurrents and the regulars, you always cast out the seven, and the number that remains will demonstrate to you on which day and month it will enter, as I have said. And if the number of the regulars and the concurrents together remains at seven or within seven, on that day of the week the month shall begin.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the calendar, moving from the specific calculation of days (concurrents and regulars) to a broader history of the solar and lunar years, the origins of the calendar under figures like Romulus and Numa Pompilius, and the religious significance of the four seasons.</meta>

# The Heart of Secrets

We have previously stated why the year is so named. Next, we shall say that there are two kinds of years: namely, the solar year and the lunar year. The solar year is as long as it takes the Sun to travel through the twelve signs of the firmament, which is three hundred sixty-five days and six hours. Romulus, the first prince of Rome, established his year as ten months and began it in March, as we have said, because the world began then. And for this reason, the Greeks still begin their year in March. The Latins begin their year in January, as did Numa Pompilius, who added two months to the year of Romulus. Those of Egypt begin their year in September, for they believe that the world began then because the earth brought forth herbs and fruits such as they usually are in Autumn. We Christians follow each of these in certain things. We follow Romulus in that we begin the <term>concurrents</term> and the <term>solar regulars</term> <note>These are numerical values used to calculate the day of the week for any given date.</note> in March. We follow Numa Pompilius in that we begin in January the <term>golden number</term> <note>A number from 1 to 19 used to track the phases of the moon and determine the date of Easter.</note>, which shows when the moon is <term>new</term> <note>original: prime</note>, and the keys to the dates of Septuagesima—when the Alleluia ceases <note>Referring to the liturgical practice where the word "Alleluia" is omitted from church services starting seventy days before Easter.</note>—and of Lent, Easter, Rogation days, and Pentecost. We also follow the Egyptians in that we begin in September the <term>lunar regulars</term> and the long number called <term>epacts</term> <note>The age of the moon in days on the first day of the year; used to synchronize the solar and lunar calendars.</note>, by which one finds the state of the moon at the start of each month.

### On the four seasons of the year.

The year is divided into four seasons: <term>Spring</term> <note>original: Ver</note>, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. The shift or change of these four seasons occurs either because of the distance or the approach of the sun. Some say that Spring begins on the feast of Saint Peter in February <note>February 22, the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter.</note>, and Summer on the feast of Saint Urban in May <note>May 25.</note>, and Autumn on the feast of Saint Symphorian in August <note>August 22.</note>, and Winter on the feast of Saint Clement <note>November 23.</note>. Others say that Spring begins twelve days before the <term>Kalends</term> <note>The first day of the month in the Roman calendar; twelve days before April 1st is March 21st, the equinox.</note> of April; Summer twelve days before the Kalends of June; Autumn twelve days before the Kalends of October; and Winter twelve days before the Kalends of January. We fast for three days in each of these four seasons to restrain the impulses of sin, because these three days signify faith in the Holy Trinity, or because the soul has within itself three natural powers that have need of right direction through fasting: these are the power of reason, of will, and of <term>judgment</term> <note>original: prix. This refers to the tripartite soul, often categorized as the rational, irascible (spirited), and concupiscible (desiring) faculties.</note>. This is also done in four seasons because the body is made of four elements: namely fire, air, water, and earth. One fasts in Spring during the first week of March, because it falls in Lent, and the Sunday closest to the Kalends is the first day of that week. The fasts of Summer are during the weeks of Pentecost. Those of Autumn are in the third week of September. I call that week the "third" because it is the third after the first Sunday closest to the Kalends. Those of the winter season are in the week before Christmas Eve; for Christmas Eve and the Saturday of these fasts must never fall on

### ¶ When the Advents of Christmas begin:

One should know that there are always at least three full weeks in <term>Advent</term> <note>The liturgical season of preparation before Christmas.</note>, and sometimes one or more days extra, but it never exceeds four weeks. The first day of Advent is always the Sunday closest to the feast of Saint Andrew, whether before, after, or on the day of the feast itself when it falls on a Sunday. <note>Saint Andrew's Day is November 30th.</note>

### ¶ Where the leap year originates, and why it is so named.

The <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the heavens or the sky.</note> is divided into twelve signs. The sun remains in each sign for thirty days, ten hours, and half an hour. Twelve times thirty days makes three hundred sixty days. Twelve times ten hours makes one hundred and twenty hours, which, when divided by twenty-four, makes five days. Twelve times half an hour makes six hours. These six hours, collected over four years, make one day of twenty-four hours in the fourth year, which is called a <term>bissexte</term> <note>A leap year. The term comes from the Roman practice of counting the "sixth" day before March twice.</note>. 

If one asks how these hours that have passed by cannot be retained until the fourth year to make a day, we say that the year has its beginning and end at the rising of the sun; and these six hours that have already passed cannot be moved. But the first year delivers six hours to the second year, and the second year begins with those six hours. The second year delivers six hours to the third. Similarly, the third year delivers eighteen hours to the fourth, which has six of its own, making twenty-four in total; these create the leap day in the fourth year. It is called *bissexte* because *bis* in Latin means "twice" in English. <note>original: "bis en latin est a dire en francoys par deux fois"</note> And that day is pronounced and counted twice on the sixth day before the <term>Calends of March</term> <note>The first day of March. In the Roman calendar, the leap day was inserted by doubling February 24th, which was the "sixth day before the Calends."</note>: for that is its place. And one counts two days upon the same letter of the Calendar.

### ¶ On which day the feast of Saint Mathias must be celebrated in a leap year, and how to find the leap year.

The feast of Saint Mathias <note>Traditionally February 24th.</note> must not be celebrated on the leap day itself, but on the day after; for otherwise it would happen that one would celebrate it twice in the year, which is not done for a saint who does not have two distinct feasts. And if one omitted the leap year, it would happen after many years that Christmas would fall around the feast of Saint John <note>Midsummer, June 24th.</note>, and the feast of Saint John would fall around Christmas. Whenever one can divide the years of the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The years since the birth of Christ (A.D.).</note> into four equal parts, then it is a leap year. And if there remain any years over—either one, two, or three—that is how many years it has been since the last leap year. Now let us speak of the lunar year.

<meta>This page continues the medieval scientific explanation of timekeeping. Having previously discussed the solar year and the leap year (bissexte), the author now turns to the lunar calendar, explaining how the phases of the moon are aligned with the solar months using the 19-year Metonic cycle.</meta>

<header>The Heart of Secrets</header>

A **lunar year** is defined in many ways. Here, a lunar year refers to the space of one "prime" moon—that is, from one crescent to the next—and this space contains twenty-nine natural days and twelve hours (which is half a day). This is called a **lunation**. The <term>computists</term> <note>Scholars of the "computus," the medieval science of calculating calendar dates, especially for religious festivals like Easter.</note> established that the lunation of one month should be thirty days, and the lunation of the next should be twenty-nine. This was done because it would seem an inconvenient thing if one half of a day belonged to the month of January and the other half belonged to the lunation of the month of February.

It is said, therefore, that the six months which are odd-numbered have six lunations of thirty days. Those that are even-numbered have six lunations of twenty-nine days, in this manner: there are twelve months; the first, the third, the fifth, the seventh, the ninth, and the eleventh have lunations of thirty days, and the others have twenty-nine. 

And yet, when it is a <term>bissexte</term> <note>A leap year.</note>, they all consist of thirty days except for five, because the lunation of February gains a day for the leap year. But once every nineteen years—and always in the nineteenth year—there are seven lunations of twenty-nine days and five of thirty. This is because the lunation of July loses a day due to the "moon’s saltus" <note>original: "fault of the moon." This refers to the *saltus lunae* or "leap of the moon," a correction used to keep the 19-year cycle accurate.</note> which occurs in that year. Nevertheless, if a leap year falls then, the lunation of February recovers a day, and then there are six months of thirty-day lunations.

Whoever wishes to know which year of the **nineteen-year cycle** <note>Also known as the Metonic cycle, used to find the "Golden Number" to determine the date of the new moon.</note> they are in—that is to say, the number by which the moon is known to be new, from one to nineteen—should add one to the years of the **Incarnation** <note>The year AD (Anno Domini).</note>. This is because one year of this cycle had already passed when Jesus Christ took flesh. After this, let that sum be divided by nineteen as many times as possible. If it is divided equally by nineteen, the year is the nineteenth. And if any years remain—whether one, two, three, or more—the remainder will be the year of the cycle.

Next, one must know that each lunation belongs to the month in which it ends, not the one in which it begins, unless a number called an <term>embolism</term> <note>From the Greek for "intercalation." It refers to an extra month added to the lunar year to keep it in sync with the solar year.</note> prevents it.

A **lunar year** can also be called the space of twelve lunations, and such a space is called a **common year**. Two such years are always counted one after the other in the nineteen-year cycle, and the third is always an **embolism**, which sounds like and is understood as an "over-growth." This is because the third year always exceeds each of the previous two by one lunation, until nineteen years have passed.

The first and second years are "common," each having twelve lunations.
The third year is always thirteen lunations, and for this reason, it is an **embolism**: that is, "over-growing," because it exceeds the common years by one lunation.
The fourth and fifth are common.
The sixth is an embolism.
The seventh year is common.
The eighth is an embolism.
The ninth and tenth years are common.
The eleventh is an embolism.
The twelfth and thirteenth years are common.
The fourteenth is an embolism.
The fifteenth and sixteenth are common.
The seventeenth is an embolism.
The eighteenth year is common.
The nineteenth is an embolism.

Now tell me: when there is an embolism, since there are only twelve months in the year, if the embolism year has thirteen lunations, it must be that there is one lunation which does not...

...should be counted in no month. And this is what prevents, as we have said, the moon from sometimes belonging to the month in which it ends. Now we have shown that there are seven **embolisms** <term>embolism</term> <note>From the Greek "embolimos," meaning intercalary. These are the seven extra months added during a 19-year cycle to keep lunar months in sync with the solar seasons.</note> in nineteen years. The lunation that is counted in no month in the first embolism begins on the second day of December. That which belongs to the second embolism begins on the second day of September. That of the third embolism begins on the sixteenth day of March. That of the fourth embolism begins on the third of January. That of the fifth embolism begins on the second day of November. That of the sixth embolism begins on the second day of August. That of the seventh embolism begins on the fifth day of March. 

One can know in such a manner from where this increase comes, which is called an **embolism**. Look at how a solar year contains three hundred sixty-five days, or one more if it is a <term>leap year</term> <note>original: "bissexte"</note>. The lunar year, which consists of twelve lunations, has only three hundred fifty-four, which is eleven days fewer than the solar year. From these eleven days, gathered together over nineteen years, the embolisms arise. And from these eleven days, it happens that the <term>prime moon</term> <note>The "prime" or "golden number" refers to the first appearance of the new moon in the calendar cycle.</note> varies and changes each month of each year; for if the moon is "prime" this year on the <term>Kalends</term> <note>The first day of the month in the ancient Roman calendar, used here to mean the first of January.</note> of January, it will be the twelfth day in the following year, and similarly for the other months. 

And if these twelve days <note>The text likely means the eleven-day discrepancy mentioned above, though the manuscript reads "twelve."</note> did not exist, the new moon would be found equally each year in each month. But the Egyptians, who were wise in this doctrine, found two kinds of numbers to know the age of the moon on the first day of each month. One of these numbers is called the **epact**, which to us is the same as saying "an additional addition," because it is added to the "regular" to find the age of the moon, as we shall say hereafter. The other number is called the **lunar regular**; for the other regulars written before are called **solar regulars** and begin in March, but these lunar regulars begin in September in the form and order we shall describe hereafter.

# The Heart of Secrets

Look at what the year of the nineteen-year cycle is <note>Also known as the Golden Number, this indicates the year's position within the Metonic cycle used to synchronize the sun and moon.</note>; and if you do not know it, add one year to the years of the Incarnation <note>The year A.D. (Anno Domini).</note> and divide by 19 as many times as you can. For example, 1268 <note>original: "mil.cc.et.lxviii." The text suggests 1268 divides equally by 19, though 1273 is the closest multiple; this may refer to a specific base year for calculations.</note>, which is divided equally by 19. If one year remains over 19, the year of the cycle will be the first. If two remain, the year will be the second; and so on for the others up to 19. But if nothing remains beyond twenty, the year will be the nineteenth. And when you have found the year of the cycle, which extends to nineteen, in this manner: to find the number of the <term>epact</term> <note>The number of days the solar year is ahead of the lunar year, used to find the age of the moon on a specific date.</note>, place the finger which is second on the hand, which is named the <term>pointer</term> <note>original: "demonstreur." The index finger.</note>, at the tip of the thumb, and there you shall say "one." After, place it on the joint which is in the middle of the thumb and say "two"; and at the third joint [the base] say "three." And once more, at the tip of the thumb say "four." And following this same order that I have described, go on counting along the thumb until nineteen. And if the number you seek, for which you wish to know the epact, falls at the tip of the thumb, subtract one from it and the remainder will be the epact for that year. If the number falls on the middle joint, then add nine to it and you will have the epact for that year. But regarding such addition, take care that if the number exceeds thirty, subtract the thirty and keep the surplus. For the epact never exceeds thirty.

Do you want an example? "One" signifies the first year of the nineteen-year cycle. Now say "one" at the tip of the thumb, and I have told you that when the number falls there, you subtract one. Now subtract one, and from one, nothing remains. Therefore, the first year has no epact. And the number "two" signifies the second year, which falls on the middle joint. Add nine to it as I told you, which would be eleven; and that will be the epact of the second year. The number "three" signifies the third year; it falls at the base of the thumb: add nineteen <note>original: "dixneuf." The text here instructs adding 19 for the base joint calculation.</note> to it and that will make twenty-two; and that will be the epact of the third year. Once more, if the number "four," which signifies the fourth year, falls at the tip of the thumb, subtract one from four and three will remain: this will be the epact of the fourth year. And in this manner you can form all the others up to nineteen years.

One can find the epact in another way: for just as the moon is eleven days before the <term>Calends of April</term> <note>April 1st. In this system, the epact represents the age of the moon on March 22nd.</note>, such is always the epact of that year. Nevertheless, to know the epacts more easily, we write here some useful numbers which will demonstrate the years of the nineteen-year cycle, and above them other numbers which will demonstrate the epacts.

### ¶ How one knows the state of the moon at the beginning of each
### month, whether it is new, two days old, or otherwise.

If you wish to know the age of the moon on the Calends <note>The *Kalendes* (Calends) refer to the first day of the month in the Roman calendar.</note> of each month, add the <term>epact</term> <note>The "epact" is a number representing the age of the moon on January 1st, used to synchronize solar and lunar years.</note> of that year to the <term>regular</term> <note>The "regular" is a fixed numerical value assigned to each month to facilitate these calculations.</note> of the month you wish to know. The age of the moon on the Calends of that month will be the sum of the epact and the regular together. If the sum exceeds thirty, cast out thirty, and the remainder will show you the age of the moon at the start of the month. Here is an example: Let us say the epact for this year is eleven, and September has five as its regular; add eleven and five together, which makes sixteen. Therefore, the moon will be sixteen days old on the Calends of September. If the epact is twenty-eight, add it to the five regulars of September, which makes thirty-three; cast out thirty and three remain. Therefore, the moon will be three days old on the Calends of that month. You may do the same for the other months. In nineteen years, this rule fails three times: in the eighth year, the eleventh, and the nineteenth. It fails in the eighth year on the Calends of May and July, for the sum of the epact and the regular together is then one too high; if one subtracts one, it comes out correctly. It fails in the eleventh year on the Calends of March in the same manner as I have explained before, and one can correct it in the same way by subtracting one, unless it is a <term>bissextile</term> <note>A leap year.</note> year; for then it is not necessary to subtract anything, because a leap year gains one day which cancels out one from the number of the epact. It fails in the nineteenth year on the Calends of May in the manner we have told you; if one subtracts one, it comes out correctly. And it also fails on the Calends of August, for then the sum is one less than it should be; if one adds one, everything comes out correctly.

### ¶ What other things the epacts can be used for.

The solar year exceeds the lunar year by eleven days; from these eleven days all the epacts are born by adding eleven each year, provided that when the sum exceeds thirty, one casts out thirty and retains the remainder. ¶ Therefore, if you wish to know what the moon will be on this day in the coming year, add eleven to the lunar age of this day. And if you wish to know what it was last year, add nineteen to it <note>The text says "add one with nineteen," but mathematically, to find the previous year's moon, one adds 19 (which is 30 minus 11).</note>. Do you wish to know how? If the moon is new <note>original: "prime"</note> today, add eleven, making twelve; the moon will be twelve days old on this day in the coming year. Add nineteen to the one, making twenty; the moon was twenty days old on this day last year.

### lendar and what its purpose is.

### ¶ Here follows the figure to know the <term>dominical letter</term> <note>The dominical letter is a system using the letters A through G to determine which day of the week any given calendar date falls upon, essential for calculating the date of Easter.</note> of each year.

We can otherwise find the age of the moon, and what it is each day of the month; this is done by a number which is called the <term>Golden Number</term> <note>The Golden Number (Latin: *numerus aureus*) indicates the current year's position within the 19-year Metonic cycle, after which the phases of the moon return to the same calendar dates.</note> because of its great value, or because the Romans anciently used to write it in gold. Within this number are contained all the numbers from one to nineteen for each month of the Calendar.

If the year is the first, the moon will be <term>prime</term> <note>The "prime" or new moon refers to the very beginning of the lunar cycle when the moon is first visible as a crescent.</note> everywhere you find "one" in the marginal window of the calendar for each month of the year. If the year is the second, the moon will be prime wherever you find "two." If the year is the third, the moon will be prime where you find "three," and so on up to nineteen. 

And then you shall return to one; each year this number changes in January. For if "one" shows the new moon in this year, "two" will demonstrate it in the coming year, and "three" in the third year. And this change always occurs in January up to nineteen.

From this "three," all the numbers up to nineteen are formed in this manner: If the number you find written is less than twelve, add eight to it. If it exceeds twelve, or is of...

If it is twelve or if it is more than twelve, subtract twelve and write the remainder. ¶ Here is an example. I have told you that you must always write three on the <term>Kalends</term> <note>The first day of the month.</note> of January; this number is less than twelve, so add eight to it; three and eight make eleven. Therefore, you must write eleven after three. To these eleven, you must add eight; eleven and eight make nineteen. Therefore, you must write nineteen after eleven. From nineteen, eight will remain <note>This calculation refers to a specific medieval subtraction rule for the Golden Number sequence, where 11 is often subtracted from totals exceeding 19, or 12 is used as a modular base in certain tables.</note>. Therefore, you must write eight after nineteen. You must do it in this manner for all the months. In all of this, you must take care that when the number increases, you do not write one number after the other without an interval; but when it decreases, then you must write them continuously without an interval and without space between one and the other. As I have told you, one must always write three on the Kalends of January; then one must write eleven after it, but with an interval. And then nineteen with an interval likewise, as many times as the number increases; and then eight, all continuously without an interval, as many times as the number decreases. Nevertheless, this rule fails in some places, and we will say where and why. In July, and in the five months that come after, you will always find nineteen after eleven without an interval, and eight after nineteen with an interval.

Now let us see why. In the nineteenth year, it always happens because of the <term>leap of the moon</term> <note>Known in Latin as the *saltus lunae*, this is a one-day adjustment made once every 19 years to prevent the lunar calendar from drifting away from the solar calendar.</note> which occurs in that year, that one <term>lunation</term> <note>A full lunar month, from one new moon to the next.</note> is in the month of July, which is only twenty-nine days. And because of this, the number nineteen—which in that year demonstrates the <term>prime</term> <note>The new moon.</note> moon—is written one line before the place where it is in the other previous months. Otherwise, that lunation would be thirty days, when it must only be twenty-nine. ¶ Similarly, it is necessary that it be so in the five months following July; otherwise, it would happen that in these five months there would be lunations of thirty-one days because the number nineteen is written in July one line earlier than in the other preceding months; and it must never be that a lunation is thirty-one days. On the second day of February, one writes 11, then 19, and then 8 continuously. On the fourth day of April, one writes 19, then 8, then 16, and then 5 continuously. On the second day of June, one writes 19, then 8, then 16, and then 5 continuously. On the first day of August, one writes 8, then 16, and then 5 continuously. On the first day of October, one writes 16, then 5, then 4, and then 2 continuously. On the second day of December, one writes 14 and 2 side by side, all on one line. And in all other places in the Calendar, the rule of intervals is kept according to the increase and decrease of the numbers; but in these months that I have named here, it is necessary to do as I have written. For if the interval were kept between the larger number and the smaller, it would happen that each lunation would be thirty days, yet six must be of thirty days and six of <term>thirty-nine</term> <note>The original text says *trenteneuf* (thirty-nine), which is almost certainly a printer's error for *vingt-neuf* (twenty-nine), as the lunar year alternates between 30 and 29-day months.</note> days, as was said here before. In February, there must be two pairs of numbers: one of some color that shows the moon in a <term>leap year</term> <note>original: *bissexte*; referring to the extra day added to the calendar every four years.</note>, and one in ink that shows it when it is not a leap year.

### Of the Leap of the Moon.

The <term>leap of the moon</term> <note>Original: *sault de la lune*, also known by the Latin term *saltus lunae*. It is a mathematical adjustment used to synchronize the lunar cycle with the solar calendar every 19 years.</note> is nothing other than when one subtracts a day from the July <term>lunation</term> <note>The period of time between two new moons.</note> in the nineteenth year / and this is the third day before the <term>Kalends</term> <note>The first day of the month in the Roman calendar.</note> of August. It is done to the July lunation more than any other because that lunation consists of thirty days / and it is the last one in the year to have a lunation of thirty days, if you begin counting from September, which is the first month of the year for the Egyptians, where the <term>epacts</term> <note>The age of the moon in days on January 1st, used to determine the date of Easter.</note> begin. Now let us see how this can be. Astronomers have observed that the <term>solar year</term> exceeds the <term>lunar year</term> by eleven days: and beyond this by one hour / by one-quarter of an hour: and by one-nineteenth part of a quarter-hour. In nineteen years, there are therefore nineteen hours / nineteen quarters of an hour: and nineteen parts of a quarter-hour, which make one full quarter of an hour. This quarter added to the nineteen quarters makes twenty quarters: these twenty quarters divided five times by four make five hours / added to the nineteen hours, this makes twenty-four, which constitutes one natural day / which is subtracted from the course of the moon in the nineteenth year. And thus, in that year, the lunar year exceeds the solar year by twelve full days / and this day is taken away from the August lunation, which is the last in the Egyptian year, if that lunation were thirty days: but it is only twenty-nine days / if one took a day from it, it would be only twenty-eight days. And no lunation is less than twenty-nine days except for that of February. And because the increase and decrease of this matter is reached at the end of nineteen years, one must make the subtraction from the last lunation of thirty days that occurs in the year, so that this shift is only subtracted once every nineteen years. Otherwise, it would happen over two hundred and sixty years that the moon would be fifteen days old when it ought to be new.

### What the Indiction is, and its use.

<term>Indiction</term> <note>A 15-year cycle used in the Roman Empire to date documents, primarily for tax purposes, and later adopted by the Papal Chancery.</note> was anciently the name for a space of fifteen years / for when the Romans had conquered all the world, they commanded in the time of <term>Octavian</term> <note>Augustus Caesar (r. 27 BC – 14 AD).</note> that all regions should pay <term>tribute</term>; but they paid only every fifth year because of the heavy perils of travel. In the first five years, they paid copper and iron to make weapons. In the second five years, silver to provide <term>wages</term> <note>Original: *souldees*, the pay given to soldiers (the root of the word "soldier").</note> to the knights. In the last five years, gold for the common expenses of Rome. At the end of every five years, they circled the city in a procession / with wax candles / and lights / and when the fifteen years were accomplished, they began the indiction over again: and indiction means the same as "commandment" / because these taxes were thus enjoined and commanded. When I say "indiction," it can be understood as the fifteen years together / or whichever specific year of the fifteen one chooses. The indiction is useful because no privilege from the <term>Apostolic See</term> <note>Original: *lapostole*, referring to the Pope.</note> is valid if the indiction in which it was given is not written therein. If you wish to know the year of the indiction, add three to the years of the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The Year of Our Lord (AD).</note> and divide the whole sum of these years by fifteen / and whatever number remains, that is the year of the indiction. One thousand two hundred divides equally by fifteen.

### Of the five terms of the year.

There are five feast days in the year that do not have fixed places in the Calendars, and they have five "terms" <note>In this context, a "term" is a limit or a base date used to calculate when a movable feast will fall.</note> by which they are determined: for they move every year. These are <term>Septuagesima</term> <note>The third Sunday before Lent, marking the beginning of the pre-Lenten season. The text notes "when Alleluia falls," referring to the liturgical practice of ceasing the use of the word "Alleluia" in church services from this day until Easter.</note>, <term>Lent</term> <note>Original: *Karesme*. The 40-day period of fasting before Easter.</note>, <term>Easter</term>, <term>Rogations</term> <note>Original: *rouaisons*. These are days of prayer and processions for the harvest, occurring shortly before Ascension Day.</note>, and <term>Pentecost</term>. To know the dates of these feasts, certain numbers are found which are called the "keys of the terms," and they are called "keys" because they give us the entrance to finding these terms. These keys are nineteen in number, following the cycle of nineteen years. The first key serves the first year; the second key the second year; the third key the third year; the fourth key the fourth year; the fifth key serves the fifth year; and so on for the others up to nineteen. We will note below the cycle of nineteen years, with each key alongside it. Opposite the first year is the first key, and so on for the others, all in order.

These keys have five "seats" <note>A "seat" (*siege*) is a fixed base date in the calendar from which one begins counting to find the actual feast day.</note> in the Calendar according to the number of the five terms. The key for the term of Septuagesima has its seat on the seventh day of January. The keys for the term of Lent have their seats on the 28th day of January—that is, the fourth day before the end of the month. The keys for the term of Easter have their seat on the eleventh day of March. The keys for Rogations—that is, the Sunday before the Ascension—have their seat on the fifteenth of April. The keys for the term of Pentecost have their seat on the day before the last day of April <note>April 29th.</note>; and the letter that is at each seat is "g" <note>This refers to the "Dominical Letter" system used to find Sundays in the medieval calendar.</note>. 

If you wish, therefore, to know, recognize, and find any of these five terms by these keys, you shall count the number of the key for that year and begin counting from the letter that is at the seat, going downward; and where the number of the key ends, that shall be the term you seek. If the first Sunday after this term falls on a Saturday, and it is a <term>leap year</term> <note>Original: *bissexte*.</note>, you must not celebrate Septuagesima the following day, but on the next Sunday after; and if it is not a leap year, celebrate it the following day.

### Example.

If the year of the 19-year cycle is the first, you must take the first key, of which the number is 26, and it must serve for that whole year. And when you want to find the term for Septuagesima, look for the seat of the key, which is the seventh day of January, and count upon the letters...

# The Philosophy. Folio C.xvii.

A dam de ge bat ergo co fos a dii fos. <note>original: "A dam de ge bat ergo co fos a dii fos." These are mnemonic syllables used to memorize the "keys" or numerical values assigned to the movable feasts of the church year.</note>
A [is at the] pinky, [then] the index, *dan de ge bat* on the middle [finger], and
*Go ci* on the following [finger], *fos* on the others, the little finger holds the rest. <note>original: "A minimus index dan de ge bat medians et Go ci sequens fos a cetera parvus habet." This verse instructs the student on how to map the mnemonic syllables onto the specific joints and fingers of the hand to track the calendar.</note>

<meta>This page provides instructions for using a "mnemonic hand"—a common Renaissance teaching tool—to calculate the dates of movable religious feasts like Easter.</meta>

# Collection of Secrets

[Image Description: A woodcut illustration of the back of a left hand. The hand is positioned vertically within a rectangular frame with decorative corner motifs. On the four fingers (excluding the thumb), the letters A, B, and C are printed in a Gothic script across the segments of the fingers. A banner across the palm and wrist area contains the text: The left hand, seen from the outside <note>original Latin: "Manus sinistra pro parte exteriori"</note>. Below the banner, a stylized tree-like structure of veins or roots extends toward the wrist. The thumb is shown on the right side of the image.]

The rule for these **movable feasts** <note>Religious holidays, such as Easter, that change dates every year based on lunar cycles and the spring equinox.</note> is as follows. **A. B. C.** are on the outside of the hand: in such a way that **A** is situated beneath the fingernails. **B.** is at the second joints below the nails. **C.** is placed at the large knuckles <note>The text uses "racines" (roots) to refer to the base joints of the fingers.</note>: and **D** is at the inner knuckles. **E** is above the knuckles of that same finger & **ff.** is at the next following knuckle: just as it appears in the figure of the hand. Afterwards, we can find the first letter of each month by this verse. **A. dam. de. ge.** <note>This is a fragment of a common Latin mnemonic verse (often "Adam degebat...") used to assign a specific "Sunday Letter" to each month, allowing the user to calculate which day of the week any given date would fall upon.</note>

<summary>This page describes a chironomic system, using the segments and joints of the hand as a visual calculator for the liturgical calendar. It specifically explains how to locate mnemonic letters on the fingers to determine the dates of movable feasts.</summary>
<keywords>mnemonic hand, movable feasts, liturgical calendar, chironomy, computus, Sunday letters, Renaissance science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the "mnemonic hand" and the Computus—the medieval system for calculating the date of Easter. The previous page introduced the use of finger joints to track mnemonic letters; this page applies those letters to the months and the 19-year lunar cycle.</meta>

# On Philosophy. Leaf Cxviii.

...etc. In these verses there are twelve words or syllables: by the first of these we can determine the beginning of each month, for each syllable serves one month. And by the first letter of that syllable, we have the first letter of that specific month to which the syllable corresponds. For example, the first letter **A.** serves for **January**. **D**am from [the mnemonic] will serve for **February** and **March**: and **ge.** for **April**: and **bat** for **May** / and so on for the others in order. Note that **A** is the first letter of **January**, **D** of **February**, etc. This is clearly shown by the illustration of the hands appearing above.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

In **March** or in **April**, the date of Easter always falls. In these three [mnemonic] verses, there are 19 words. Those that end in **m** serve for the month of **March**, and the others serve for the month of **April**; these teach all the Easter dates <note>In the medieval calendar, the "Easter Term" (terme de pafques) refers to the date of the Paschal Full Moon, which determines when Easter Sunday will fall.</note> that occur across the 19-year cycle, for as long as the world shall last. ¶ Let us see how **To be** <note>original Latin: "Esse"</note> is the first word of the three verses and represents the first year of the 19-year cycle. If you wish to know the Easter date for the first year, look for it in **April**: for this first word serves for **April** because it does not end in **m**. Then, look at the first letter of this word, which is **E**. This letter is the fifth in the alphabet, and thus on the fifth day of **April**, near the beginning of the month, the Easter date will fall; the Sunday following will be the feast of Easter. **Heavy** <note>original Latin: "Gravem"</note> is the second word and serves for the month of **March**, because it ends in **m**; it represents the second year of the 19-year cycle. If you wish to know the Easter date for the second year of the 19-year cycle, look at the first letter of the word, which is **G**. This is the eighth <note>The text identifies G as the 8th letter, likely following a specific medieval alphabetical convention that included additional symbols or alternate counting.</note> in the alphabet. On the seventh day of **March**, counting toward the end of the month <note>The text explains that for March, one counts backward from the end of the month (March 31). Counting back seven days from the end results in March 25.</note>, the Easter date will fall, and the Sunday after this date will be the feast. **To us** <note>original Latin: "Nobis"</note> is the third word and serves for the third year of the cycle and the month of **April**, as it does not end in **m**. The first letter of this word "nobis" is **N**, which is the thirteenth <note>In the 23-letter Latin alphabet commonly used at the time, N is the 13th letter.</note> in the alphabet. On the thirteenth day of **April** the Easter date will fall in the third year of the cycle, and the Sunday after will be the feast. In this same manner, it is done for the other words of the three verses up to 19 years. After 19 years, one can return to the first year and begin again, for this rule will never fail. Note that, as I have said, when the date falls in **April**, you begin counting from the beginning of the month, one letter after another. If the date falls in **March**, you begin counting from the end of the month of **March** backwards. In 19 years, the Easter dates fall in **March** seven times: for in these three verses, there are seven words ending in **m**. And I have said that all words ending in **m** serve for **March**. For the month of **April**, the Easter dates fall twelve times in 19 years, for there are twelve words in the three verses that do not end in **m**, and all of these serve for the month of **April**. ¶ Let us review the matter again to see how the dates must be found. I say that **to be** <note>original: "esse"</note> is the first word of the three verses and serves for the first year of the 19-year cycle. One must then count and seek the Easter date in **April**, for this word does not end in **m**; therefore it belongs to **April** and you must count. You...

<meta>The catchword "Tu" (You) at the bottom indicates the next page continues the instructions for the reader to perform the calculation.</meta>

<summary>This page explains a mnemonic system using Latin verses to calculate the date of Easter over a 19-year cycle. It details how to use specific letters and word endings to determine whether Easter falls in March or April and on what specific day.</summary>

--- Page 316 ---
<meta>This page concludes the technical instructions for calculating the date of Easter (the Computus) using mnemonic systems. It connects the alphabetical letters assigned to days of the month with the 19-year Metonic cycle used to track the phases of the moon. The page ends with the printer's colophon, identifying the text as "The Heart of Philosophy," a French translation of a Latin compendium originally commissioned by King Philip the Fair.</meta>

you will say **A** on the letter that marks the first day of April / **B** on the next letter, then **C** on the third / **D** on the fourth / and on the fifth. The "Easter Term" <note>The Paschal Full Moon, which determines the date of Easter Sunday.</note> for the first year of the cycle will therefore be the fifth day of April. For "e" is the first letter of this word which is named *to be* <note>original Latin: "esse"</note> and it is the fifth letter in the alphabet (the ABCs). It shows that the term for that year is on the fifth day of April. And Easter is the Sunday following. *Heavy* <note>original Latin: "grauem"</note> is the second word of the verses and serves for the second year of the cycle / and as this word ends in **m**, it must serve the month of March: For in this month is the term of the second year. Now, you will say **a** on the last letter of the month of March. Then you will say **b** on the letter that comes before the last: and then **c** on the third, always going backwards: **d** on the fourth: **e** on the fifth / **f** on the sixth: **g** on the seventh: thus the seventh day of March, counting from the end, will be the Easter term in the second year. For **g** is the first letter of the word and is the seventh in the alphabet. Whenever the term falls in April, begin counting from the beginning of April going downwards; when it falls in March, begin counting from the end of March backwards, going upwards.

---

<margin>1534</margin>

### Here ends *The Heart of Philosophy*, translated from Latin into French at the request of Philip the Fair, King of France: newly printed in Paris for Poncet le Preux, sworn bookseller <note>A "libraire juré" was a bookseller officially recognized and sworn in by the University of Paris, granting them certain legal and commercial privileges.</note> residing on the Rue Saint Jacques at the sign of the Wolf, across from the Mathurins. And the printing was finished on the twelfth day of February, one thousand five hundred thirty-four.
